Read our Privacy notice

Russell Brand is behind bars having been found guilty of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three women at the height his showbiz career, callously treating them like “amusements” in a quest to sleep with 5,000 women.

Jurors took less than nine hours to find the comedian guilty of offences against four women between 2004 and 2009, by which time he had soared to “staggering fame”, following a dramatic four-week trial.

However, he was acquitted of orally raping one of the victims in a bar toilet in 2004, raping another woman at Labour Party conference in 1999 and one count of attempting to indecently assault an MTV worker in 2001.

The Essex-born celebrity, who appeared in Hollywood films Get Him to the Greek and Forgetting Sarah Marshall, was emotionless in the dock of Southwark Crown Court as the verdicts were returned on Thursday.

His wife, Laura Brand, was visibly upset and was led from court with his entourage after her husband was taken to the cells, having been warned he faces a “significant custodial term”.

Judge Mr Justice Bennathan refused to grant Brand bail to allow him to say goodbye to his wife and three children and remanded him in custody until Monday, when he is due to be sentenced.

“I regret any hardship caused to the children of course but the hardship has been caused by the jury finding of serious criminal offending by their father,” the judge said.

open image in gallery Brand in the dock of Southwark Crown Court ( PA )

In fraught scenes outside the courtroom, Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, launched into a verbal tirade against a Sunday Times journalist who had worked on a joint 2023 investigation with Channel 4 Dispatches and The Times accusing the comedian of sexual misconduct.

“I hope you are pleased with yourself”, he told Rosamund Urwin, the paper’s chief news correspondent. When she was heard replying: “I’m pleased justice has been done”, Mr Winter retorted: “Well, it wasn’t. You f***ed it.” He then added: “Congratulations.”

During the trial, Mr Winter had argued The Sunday Times, The Times and Dispatches reporting had “poisoned the well of justice” against his client and made an unsuccessful bid to have the trial thrown out.

As a Serco van thought to be carrying the convicted rapist left Southwark Crown Court at around 4.30pm, a man was heard shouting “hold on to Jesus, Russell”.

open image in gallery The custody van leaving Southwark Crown Court after Brand was remanded in custody ( Reuters )

Following the guilty verdicts, the Metropolitan Police confirmed the celebrity is already under investigation for two more alleged rapes, including that of a 16-year-old schoolgirl, and detectives believe further victims may come forward.

Urging any other survivors to speak out, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy said: “Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women. As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement.

“I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no-one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be.”

Speaking outside Southwark Crown Court, senior crown prosecutor David Roberts, said Brand’s “vile crimes” will have a lifelong impact on his victims.

“The evidence showed Brand to be a calculated sexual predator using his growing fame and power to create situations in which he could pursue women sexually, regardless of what they wanted,” he said.

“I’d like to thank all the women for coming forward and reporting Brand to the police. It is thanks to their courage that he will finally face the consequences of his actions.”

open image in gallery Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy outside court ( PA )

During the trial, the jury heard how Brand’s eyes changed before each attack and he “snapped from charming to frightening and nasty”.

“Many said he was nice and then it was like there was a personality change, a pivot,” prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC told the jury.

“He didn’t listen when they said no, he didn’t stop, he didn’t care, he kept pulling, pushing, tugging, thrusting.”

Jurors found the comic not guilty of pushing a woman onto a hotel bed and raping her at Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999, when he was aged 24 and not yet famous.

The woman fought back tears as she gave evidence from behind a screen to protect her anonymity, recalling how she believed Brand was gay when she invited him to her room but emerged from the toilet to find him partially undressed, prancing around doing “silly walks”.

“He changed from camp and friendly and effeminate to monster-like,” she told the jury. “I was scared in that moment.”

She claimed she was “terrified” as she complied with Brand’s request that she photograph him and baulked at the idea that she could have fled under cross examination by the celebrity’s lawyer. Pictures taken by the woman show a topless Brand, wearing white jeans, blowing a kiss towards the camera.

She added: “I had nowhere to run. I had no phone. It was a bedsit, there was no reception. Was I supposed to run into the night and have him chase after me?”

open image in gallery The jury was shown photographs of a topless Russell Brand taken by his accuser ( Metropolitan Police )

Brand was a rising comedy star and hosting shows such as Big Brother’s Big Mouth when he grabbed a woman’s breasts within moments of meeting her at a party in a Soho bar 2004. He was found guilty of sexually assaulting the woman, but acquitted of orally raping her inside the bar’s toilet.

The woman said he had a “weird maniacal grin” as he groped her and then pulled to the toilet, where she alleged he put his hand on the back of her head and made her perform a sex act.

“I remember it felt like a force and every time I tried to move away, it was strong; it was forcing me back,” she said. “I did definitely say, ‘What are you doing, I don’t want to do this.’”

At one point, Brand said “Oh, come on, don’t be a spoilsport”, the woman claimed. She recalled he was not “very well endowed; he was average sized”.

open image in gallery Brand outside court with his wife, Laura Brand ( Getty )

Brand was performing at the Hammersmith Apollo in 2009 when he selected a 21-year-old fan from the crowd to join him backstage, where they had a consensual threesome in his dressing room.

But he was found guilty of rape after she told the jury he took the condom off and penetrated her anally her during a second encounter days later at his Hampstead townhouse, leaving her hurt, bleeding and fearing she had contracted HIV.

Initially, she said she could not speak or breathe and was in pain before pleading “can you stop, can you stop, can you stop”, the court heard.

Asked by Brand’s lawyer if she knew the comedian’s sexual reputation at the time, including that he had won the Sun newspaper’s ‘shagger of the year’ three years running, she insisted: “I had not at that point heard about Mr Brand raping somebody.”

After the rape, Brand scolded the fan, telling her she was “disgusting” and “look what you have done to my f****** sheets”, the jury heard.

open image in gallery Jurors were shown pictures of Brand's Hampstead townhouse ( Metropolitan Police )

In the weeks, months and years after the incident, the woman told multiple friends, her parents and a work colleague that the star had ignored her pleas for him to stop, the jury heard, telling one that he had left her “humiliated, scared and violated, and in a lot of physical pain”.

The actor-turned-content creator was also found guilty of groping and kissing a radio station worker in 2004 or 2005 and pushing his face in a Channel 4 worker’s groin after demanding a massage in 2009.

Brand, who denied all the charges, claimed the encounters were consensual and the women had been influenced by a “devastating” 2023 Dispatches documentary which accused the star of sexual misconduct.

None of the complainants had featured in the expose but all came forward following the media reports, the court heard. Brand’s lawyer argued the reporting had “poisoned the well of justice” against his client.

During his evidence, the comedian insisted consent is “more important that the sex itself” but admitted to “misusing” his fame for sex.

Russell Brand: In Plain Sight: Dispatches will be rebroadcast on Channel 4 on Thursday at 11.40pm.

News.title: Melania Trump pushes for peace at meeting with Putin envoy and Ukraine officials at White House
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

US first lady Melania Trump brought Russian and Ukrainian representatives together at the White House on Thursday, calling on both sides to choose "humanity over war" ahead of talks next week in Abu Dhabi.

Kirill Dmitriev, a special envoy for Russian President Vladimir Putin, attended the rare face-to-face gathering with Ukrainian officials. The event marked a six-day ceasefire that Melania Trump helped negotiate in the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky, which expired on Sunday.

It came as the Trump administration is stepping up efforts to bring an end to Russia's war in Ukraine, which started when Russian troops invaded in early 2022. A trilateral meeting involving officials from the US, Ukraine, and Russia is set for November 10-11 in Abu Dhabi.

"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady stated at the event. "We must use the courage we brought to Oleshky to find common ground through a shared concern for the suffering of innocent people," she added.

open image in gallery Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, left, presents first lady Melania Trump with a state award during a meeting with Russian and Ukrainian representatives in the Grand Foyer of the White House, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, in Washington ( AP )

Melania Trump said she was "involved in every stage of the planning" for the short-term ceasefire, which included reviewing aerial photos and evaluating road and hospital access.

President Trump, who did not attend, praised his wife’s role in the Oleshky ceasefire, remarking to reporters in October that "she does better than our professionals."

RUSSIAN ENVOY SET TO MEET US OFFICIALS

Dmitriev was expected to meet US officials while in Washington, according to two people familiar with his plans.

Ukrainian lawmaker David Arakhamia and human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets also attended the gathering. They encouraged the Slovenian-born Melania Trump to maintain her peace efforts.

Both delegations presented the first lady with gifts of appreciation.

open image in gallery Russian special envoy Kirill Dmitrievon presents Melania Trump with a child's drawing ( Getty )

Russia’s Dmitriev presented her with a drawing of pink hearts by an Oleshky girl, stating the child "chose to live with her family in Russia," alluding to the dispute over displaced Ukrainian children in Russia. "I love Melania," the artwork stated.

The Ukrainian delegation presented the first lady with a state honor "for your brave heart, for saving our people, and for returning back Ukrainian children."

She provided the visiting delegates with letters addressed to Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

DEMOCRATS TAKE MAJORITY IN CONGRESS

The meeting was the first face-to-face contact between Russian and US officials following Tuesday's midterm elections, where Democrats won control of Congress from Republicans, dealing a blow to President Trump.

The incoming Democratic majority starting in January is expected to push for increased aid to Ukraine and scrutinize the Republican president's decisions to arrange a diesel deal with Russia and ease certain Moscow sanctions. Trump has heightened his criticism of Zelensky in recent weeks.

open image in gallery The art was by an Oleshky girl with ‘I love Melania’ written on it ( AFP/Getty )

The Kremlin noted it hopes Trump will persist with his peace efforts despite the Republican Party’s loss.

It also stated preparations were under way for a summit between Putin, Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting November 18 to 19 in Shenzhen, China.

Dmitriev previously met Trump's special envoy, Steve Witkoff, at the White House in 2025. Trump's predecessor, Joe Biden, did not invite Russian representatives to the White House.

Dmitriev has assisted in facilitating the release of American detainees in Russia, reuniting Ukrainian children with their families, and supporting the humanitarian effort in Oleshky.

News.title: An herbal supplement may be able to curb binge drinking
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

An herbal supplement made from an invasive species in the southern U.S. could help cut back on binge drinking, a new study has found.

Taking supplements made from kudzu root, which is a vine that originally comes from East Asia, limited the number of days people with alcohol use disorder practiced binge drinking, University of California-San Francisco researchers said.

These benefits were still seen three months after the treatment had ended.

The findings could provide a treatment path for binge drinking, the researchers say. The health condition leads to 178,000 deaths a year in the U.S.

“Binge drinking is incredibly common, but we don’t have many tools to offer people who want to cut back,” Glenn-Milo Santos, the study’s lead author and a professor at the university, explained in a statement. “Our goal is to expand that toolkit.”

open image in gallery Could taking a supplement made from an invasive vine help Americans stop binge drinking? A new study shows promising results ( Getty Images for NYCWFF )

While doctors often first recommend behavioral therapy, there is medication to treat alcohol use disorder, including one that causes unpleasant symptoms when drinking, one that blocks receptors that make people feel good when drinking alcohol and another that targets the brain to reduce cravings after stopping.

These medications are typically covered by most health insurance plans, with no or very little copay. The costs of the drugs are typically just over $30 without insurance, The Independent’s review of products sold online shows.

But just 10 percent of people with alcohol use disorder have ever received medication to treat it, the researchers note.

“What’s exciting about this approach is that people can use it when they know they may be at risk of heavy drinking, rather than taking a medication every day,” Santos said.

The study included 120 adults with alcohol use disorder who binge drank at least once a week. For women, binge drinking was defined as having four or more drinks on one occasion, while men had five or more drinks.

Half of the participants received kudzu extract and half received a placebo that they took for 12 weeks about 2.5 hours before they expected to drink heavily.

By the end of the treatment - which also included brief weekly counseling sessions - the number of binge-drinking days had fallen from 2.15 to 1.42 per week for people taking kudzu. In the placebo group, they had hardly changed, falling from 2.15 to 2.06 days.

There were similar declines in the proportion of weeks in which participants reported binge drinking, dropping by 30 percent in the kudzu group versus just 7 percent in the placebo group.

open image in gallery Kudzu supplements are made from vines that are native to East Asia and have been used in traditional medicine for thousands of years ( Getty Images/iStock )

These differences continued after the treatment stopped.

“Researchers said reducing alcohol use during treatment may have helped participants rethink their relationship with alcohol and build confidence in their ability to drink less,” according to the university.

No serious side effects were linked to taking kudzu.

Kudzu has been linked to slow blood clotting, kidney problems, liver injury and interactions with birth control, the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and natural medicine Dr. Josh Axe say. In 2020, kudzu supplements from Oregon were recalled because they had the potential to be contaminated with the sometimes fatal bacteria Salmonella.

Kudzu has been used in traditional medicine for more than 2,000 years and supplements are sold online today for just over $30.

News.title: Beloved NYC bookstore to repay nearly $1.5 million after taking COVID-era loan
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

New York’s famed Strand Bookstore will reimburse nearly $1.5 million after improperly requesting and obtaining a pandemic-era small business loan despite being legally ineligible to receive the funds, the U.S. Department of Justice has announced.

Federal prosecutors stated that the establishment was unqualified because its owner, Nancy Bass Wyden, is married to U.S. Sen. Ron Wyden, a Democrat from Oregon.

The DOJ officially announced the settlement on Tuesday.

In 2021, the Strand submitted an application for a $932,350 second draw Paycheck Protection Program loan, which required applicants to affirm that no member of Congress held a direct or indirect controlling stake in the enterprise.

While the shop previously secured a PPP loan back in 2020, those relief funds did not mandate an identical conflict-of-interest declaration.

"The Paycheck Protection Program was created to save American jobs, not to enrich those who aren’t eligible for taxpayer-funded relief, especially the wife of a U.S. Senator," said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro in a statement.

- Strand Bookstore owner Nancy Bass Wyden ( Copyright 2020 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

Bass Wyden noted in a statement that during the COVID-19 pandemic, regulations governing federal relief programs "were changing rapidly" and explained that the bookstore remained unaware of eligibility rule modifications introduced between the times it submitted its first and second loan applications.

"We stand by the facts: the circumstances arose during an unprecedented and rapidly changing public health emergency, the mistake was unintentional, and the funds were returned as soon as the issue came to our attention," Bass Wyden said.

"We regret the oversight and recognize the importance of complying with all applicable laws and regulations."

Inquiries sent to the Strand seeking comment went unanswered.

A representative for the senator's office stated that the lawmaker and his spouse refrain from discussing her business affairs, adding he played no role regarding the loan or agreement.

Famous for advertising "18 Miles of Books" across its shelving, the Strand remains an essential cornerstone of New York’s cultural scene and downtown heritage.

The location features in diverse television series and major films, such as "Sex and the City," "Julie & Julia," and "Six Degrees of Separation," among others.

Offerings span inexpensive secondhand paperbacks to valuable rare first editions, while serving as a prime setting for authors to give book talks.

Benjamin Bass, the proprietor's grandfather, established the shop in 1927. She later managed the business alongside her father, Fred Bass, until he passed away in 2018.

After coronavirus lockdowns upended retail operations, Bass Wyden issued an appeal to the public in October 2020 urging patrons to shop at the Strand in person or online. She stated in a social media post that "the loan we were given" had sustained the store for eight months, but revenues dropped 70% and the business was deemed "unsustainable."

A viral #savethestrand campaign subsequently generated over 25,000 online purchases across a single weekend, Bass Wyden told The Washington Post at that time.

Reporting by the Post showed she furloughed 188 of 217 staff members when lockdowns commenced in March 2020. She recalled 30 employees that June after securing a Paycheck Protection Program loan worth between $1 million and $2 million, before cutting 12 workers several weeks later.

Meanwhile, friction intensified between her and the workers’ union, particularly after disclosures revealed she had purchased at least $115,000 worth of Amazon stock during the global health crisis.

News.title: Tankers carrying Russian diesel change course, raising doubts about shipments to US
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump's plan to allow imports of Russian diesel appeared to falter this week after state and federal officials warned that handling any shipments could bring legal consequences and two tankers initially bound for the United States changed course.

Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 9 to make more than 300,000 metric tons of Russia's diesel available immediately to U.S. and global markets, with larger shipments to follow. The U.S. banned Russian energy imports after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and the deal angered some lawmakers and foreign allies.

The arrangement has yet to produce a confirmed U.S. delivery. Analysts have said the imports were unlikely to do much to lower U.S. diesel prices, which have reached record highs during the U.S. war with Iran.

Two sanctioned tankers that departed from the Baltic Sea port of Primorsk last month originally declared their destinations as the U.S. East Coast. As of Thursday, both had changed course, one toward Brazil and the other into the Mediterranean, according to marine data company Kpler and vessel traffic site MarineTraffic.com.

A third vessel was still in the North Atlantic headed toward the U.S. but changed its destination from New York to “for orders,” which leaves the unloading point open. Neither the White House nor the Kremlin have disclosed whether the agreement was put in writing or revealed the price, payment terms or participating companies.

Although the Treasury Department temporarily authorized Russian diesel transactions that would ordinarily be subject to U.S. sanctions, New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill advised port and terminal operators in her state to turn away ships carrying the fuel, warning in a letter dated Monday that “any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties.”

Sherrill argued that the Trump administration lacked authority to override the import ban enacted by Congress more than four years ago and said New Jersey would use its legal and regulatory powers to prevent state facilities and companies from handling Russian fuel.

A bipartisan group of senators has urged Trump to negate the deal, saying the U.S. “should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline.” Lawmakers also have warned major banks, port authorities and fuel distributors that facilitating the imports could expose companies to civil or criminal liability and future congressional investigations.

The administration maintains its authorization was lawful, and no court has ruled on the dispute.

In response to a request for comment Thursday, the Treasury Department issued a statement saying the sanctions exemption its Office of Foreign Assets Control issued for the sale, delivery, unloading and importing of Russian diesel until April 7 was consistent with previous actions and "in compliance with all applicable laws.”

A Trump administration official who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity said en route Russian diesel shipments would reduce price pressures for Americans. The official said increasing shipments was in keeping with Putin and Trump’s agreement but did not specify whether any Russian fuel would reach the U.S. directly.

Expensive diesel can have wide-ranging economic effects, including on consumer prices, since the trucking industry and many farmers use the fuel to produce and transport goods.

Trump has tried blaming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for this year's diesel spikes. He has pressed Ukraine to halt drone attacks that damaged Russian refineries and curbed production of the fuel.

The Financial Times first reported the diverted courses of the two sanctioned vessels, the Russian tanker Talisman and the Sierra Leone-flagged Leruo.

Kpler analyst Matt Smith said it was not clear if Russian diesel shipments had U.S. buyers yet and that the third tanker in the North Atlantic also might change course.

“Because of regulatory, sanctions concerns, we may not see this cargo discharge on the U.S. Atlantic coast,” Smith said. “It’s clear there’s hesitancy here in bringing these barrels onshore just because of the implications of doing so.”

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said details were not available about commercial shipments but that “all the diesel will find its buyers.”

Putin’s special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, dismissed the Financial Times report.

“Fake. Tankers destined for the US continue on course,” Dmitriev posted on X.

___

Wiseman reported from Washington.

News.title: Inside the courtroom, Russell Brand was a shadow of his flamboyant self. He knew his game was up
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Ushering his wife out of a blacked out Mercedes into a throng of photographers on the first day of hearings at London’s Southwark Crown Court last month, the dubious basis of Russell Brand’s defence should have been obvious.

Wearing a lemon-yellow suit and a large pair of tortoiseshell sunglasses, the waiting media pack were so unfamiliar with Laura Brand that, at first, no one was certain who she was. But it soon emerged that the 39-year-old, with whom he shares three young children, was the only witness prepared to stand up in court to fight back against the multiple rape and sexual assault allegations at her husband’s doorstep.

On Thursday, Ms Brand left court alone as her husband was remanded in custody after a jury panel of eight men and four women took less than nine hours to convict the 51-year-old of four counts against four women.

Before the verdicts were delivered, the comedian, 51, told his wife “I love you” from inside the glass-panelled dock, where the door – which had previously been left open – was locked behind him. He showed no emotion and kept his head held high as he was led to the cells by dock officers.

The panel of eight men and four women found him guilty of anally raping one fan and sexually assaulting three other women as he rose to fame. He was acquitted of two other counts of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.

Brand, now one of the world’s most notorious convicted rapists, is expected to be condemned to years behind bars when he is sentenced on Monday – and more allegations could follow.

open image in gallery Jurors returned their verdict at Southwark Crown Court ( AFP/Getty )

Police are already investigating the celebrity over alleged rapes on two more women and detectives believe the guilty verdicts will prompt others to come forward, as the true extent of his sexual past – which he had long insisted was “exploitative” but consensual – finally catches up with him.

One of the allegations under investigation was featured in a 2023 Dispatches documentary accusing him of sexual misconduct, court documents reveal. The woman alleges she was aged 16 when Brand sent a car to collect her from school for sexual encounters.

Detective superintendent Andy Furphy, who has led a three-year Metropolitan Police probe into allegations against Brand, has insisted “our work is not done” and there is a “very distinct possibility” that the conviction will inspire others to speak out.

A separate civil lawsuit, filed in the US in 2023, claims the former Hollywood actor sexually assaulted a woman on a movie set in 2010.

Brand argued he faced the jury as a ‘convicted-in-the-media rapist’

When Brand arrived for his trial fresh from a Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) summit in Washington, where he posed for a selfie with Donald Trump’s health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, he likely felt buoyed in the knowledge that he had found a place for himself across the pond.

His new-found religious fervour is more marketable in America where he has discovered a whole new fanbase among the evangelical right, having been baptised in the River Thames by TV adventurer Bear Grylls in 2024 a year after allegations of sexual misconduct first surfaced.

He relocated his family to Florida’s Gulf coast later that year and has spent recent months seemingly laying the groundwork for his defence in interviews and podcasts promoting his new book, How To Become a Christian in 7 Days, published by former Fox News host Tucker Carlson’s imprint.

open image in gallery Brand and Dr. Mehmet Oz joked about hugging a female member of Donald Trump’s cabinet during a panel at a summit promoting the 'Make America Healthy Again' movement ( CSPAN )

Perhaps he had reason to be hopeful. Historical sexual abuse allegations are notoriously difficult to prove and, just three years earlier, Oscar-winning Hollywood actor Kevin Spacey had walked out of the very the same court building exonerated. Not only did jurors at Spacey’s trial acquit him on all counts, many queued up to shake the former House of Cards star’s hand afterwards.

But if Brand truly believed his own delusion that he was the victim of a media conspiracy, he was soon brought back down to earth.

In a pre-trial hearing, judge Mr Justice Bennathan resolutely refused to throw out the case against him on the grounds he had received too much adverse publicity, it can now be reported.

His silver-haired lawyer, Ian Winter KC, argued Brand’s case was so unique it had “never before been seen by the courts”, insisting that the 2023 joint investigation by Dispatches and The Sunday Times alleging sexual misconduct had destroyed him as a person “in total”.

“It deprives the defendant of the presumption of innocence, but fundamentally it deprives him of a level playing field as a witness,” he said. “Because of this documentary the defendant has to give evidence as a convicted-in-the-media rapist.”

The six complainants in the trial were entirely separate from those who had spoken out in the documentary, but had all come forward after it had aired.

Mr Winter claimed it was criminal that the Dispatches episode, titled Russell Brand: In Plain Sight, was still available to download, suggesting it amounted to contempt of court or even perverting the course of justice.

However, both the judge and the prosecution countered this argument with the fact that Brand had been widely publicising his own version of events.

open image in gallery Russell Brand and his wife Laura leaving Southwark Crown Court ( PA )

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC pointed to a string of “denials, explanations” and “other material that falls in his favour”, including his own observation in his book that the media campaign against him had not worked.

Refusing to halt the trial, the judge declined to accept that a collection of “elderly, anonymous allegations” would override a jury’s commitment to fairness or their ability to follow directions.

Brand, who was spared being confined to the dock for the pre-trial arguments, sat so still he appeared to be meditating, praying or counting his breaths during the legal discussions, his rapid blink rate the only outward sign of stress.

Prayers, jokes and podcasts in their pyjamas – how the trial began

Brand’s rigid and extraordinarily upright posture made the star seem unnaturally still during four weeks of evidence as the trial attracted a global media frenzy, with at least four daily podcasts poring over every detail. As he stood for the judge during court breaks, he would clasp his hands behind his back, sometimes revealing a set of white prayer beads clutched in his right palm.

He barely looked in the direction of more than 20 journalists rammed into the press benches directly behind the dock, while up to 30 more watched on a screen in another courtroom, but repeatedly told camera operators at the court steps he felt “blessed”.

Members of the public often queued for the last remaining seats in the public gallery, but many were turned away, with one man heard shouting loudly at court staff after he was denied entry during the first week.

open image in gallery Brand sat remarkably still and upright in the dock ( Priscilla Coleman/MB Media )

Each day, the comedian-turned-Rumble-content creator was accompanied by an entourage including his close protection officer, Joe McCann, reportedly a former sparring partner of boxer Tyson Fury. One female acolyte, who travelled to court with Brand and his wife, could be seen pacing the courthouse corridor in prayer before he was due to give evidence.

For one final day of the trial, his wife was joined in the public gallery by her Ryder Cup-winning golfer father, Bernard Gallacher.

Even the Brands themselves tried to cash in on the hype, publishing their own bizarre mid-trial religious podcast episodes of Sunday Service with the Brands, filmed in their pyjamas.

After the first week of evidence, in which Brand was accused of turning into a “monster-like” rapist in an alleged attack in 1999 – a count on which he was ultimately acquitted – the comedian joked that being told to do his shirt up was “the worst of all the things I have had said to me or about me this week”.

He also extolled the virtues of right-wing activist Tommy Robinson, who was convicted of harassing journalists in a trial in the same court building, adding: “I must say I enjoy him, I enjoy his passion and I admire his bravery, his tenacity.”

open image in gallery The hour long mid-trial episode of Sunday Service with the Brands was filmed in their pyjamas at the couple's UK base ( Sunday Service with the Brands )

Brand grew ashen and social media posts stopped

But his steady stream of social media posts, frequently filled with Bible readings, prayer and anti-establishment rhetoric, stopped around two weeks in to the trial as the weight of the evidence against him mounted.

One accuser who was left bleeding and feared she had contracted HIV after he anally raped her had told up to 24 people a similar account over 20 years, the court heard. Afterwards, he even scolded her for ruining his sheets as he ordered her to clean up the mess she had made. Brand was told by the judge he will face a “significant custodial term” after he was found guilty of this offence.

A bid to throw out two of the charges, one for sexual assault and one for indecent assault, also failed mid-trial, although one count was downgraded to attempted indecent assault. He was found guilty of the sexual assault after his pushed his face in the groin of a Channel 4 worker, having demanded a massage, but acquitted of attempted indecent assault.

Brand gradually appeared more tired, ashen and gaunt as the prosecution painted a compelling picture of him as a man who treated women as a “disposable commodity” in his quest to rack up 5,000 notches on his bedpost.

open image in gallery Brand at the start versus the end of the trial at Southwark Crown Court ( AFP/Getty )

His sexual entitlement had only grown as he rose to fame, the court heard, as the six unconnected women described a similar pattern of behaviour in which his demeanour suddenly flipped.

“Many said he was nice and then it was like there was a personality change, a pivot,” prosecutor Ms Karmy-Jones said. “His eyes changed, he snapped from charming to frightening and nasty.

“He didn’t listen when they said no, he didn’t stop, he didn’t care, he kept pulling, pushing, tugging, thrusting.”

By the time Brand entered the witness box, his energy levels appeared low. Rather than the verbose and animated ramblings he was reputed for as a comic, the jury witnessed excruciating spells of silence as he struggled to answer questions in cross-examination.

Wearing a dark suit, white shirt and artfully arranged necktie, Brand told the jury that his notoriety had soared over the 10-year period of the alleged attacks between 1999 and 2009 and he had achieved “staggering fame” by the time he married Katy Perry the following year.

open image in gallery Court sketch Riel Karmy-Jones KC cross examining Russell Brand ( Elizabeth Cook/PA )

He blamed the Dispatches documentary for the accusations, insisting the “devastating” media coverage had left him unable to persuade a single person to give evidence on his behalf.

“Would they touch you with a barge pole?” Mr Winter asked, to which Brand replied: “No.”

Brand admitted to “misusing” his fame for sex but struggled to explain the inconsistencies in his recollections as Ms Karmy-Jones accused him of constructing his case around evidence disclosed by the prosecution.

The only defence witness: Laura Brand

In what was perhaps a final desperate act, the defence called Brand’s wife as the only live witness to support his case.

She told the jury she had started dating the comedian in August 2006 when she was 19 and he was 31, but they split around seven months later because he would not remain faithful.

They stayed in contact and rekindled their relationship in 2015, she told the court, describing him as a “wonderful father” and “amazingly attentive husband” following their marriage in 2017.

However, Mr Justice Bennathan was forced to interject when Mr Winter asked Ms Brand “her view as to the truth” of the allegations against her husband.

“No, no, no, she is not an expert witness,” the judge said, before he sent the jury out of court and Ms Brand was ushered from the witness box.

“Mr Winter, you really can’t ask a character witness whether they think the defendant did it or not,” the judge reprimanded him. “Obviously she doesn’t believe the allegations, she’s in love with him and they’ve got three children. That’s implicit.”

It was not the first time the judge had crossed hairs with Brand’s barrister, having told him to “shush” in a tense exchange in front the jury in the first week of the trial.

open image in gallery Laura Brand was the only defence witness who gave live evidence in support of the comedian ( Reuters )

Brand, having been utterly inscrutable during the previous weeks of evidence, suddenly became animated when his wife was giving evidence on his behalf. Smiling, laughing and mouthing prayers under his breathe, he appeared to all-but cheerlead her through her testimony as she repeatedly met his eye as he watched from the dock.

Written statements from two former girlfriends were also read to jury, with one claiming although Brand had a “bad boy reputation” he could also be “gentle, kind, warm and generous”.

In his closing speech, Mr Winter repeatedly insisted the Dispatches and The Sunday Times reporting had “poisoned the well of justice” against his client.

Despite such arguments being discredited as rape myths, he invited jurors to return not guilty verdicts because the women had not screamed, fought back or tried to get away during their attacks.

He challenged one woman’s reaction to being “raped in the mouth” in a bar toilet in 2004 and questioned why a fan in her early 20s did not “just roll over and kick out” when she was anally raped in 2009. The jury acquitted him of oral rape but found him guilty of the anal rape at his Hampstead townhouse.

“The question for you is, can you possibly be sure in this case that out of the many, many women who voluntarily had sex with Mr Brand, he raped just three of them?” Mr Winter asked.

Now the guilty verdicts have been returned, that question must be answered.

News.title: British healthcare worker with Ebola arrives back in the UK
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A British healthcare worker who contracted Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has arrived back in the UK for specialist treatment.

The patient is the first case involving a British national linked to the current outbreak in the country to test positive for the disease.

The BBC has reported that the man arrived at RAF Northolt and has been transported to a specialist infectious diseases unit at the Royal Free Hospital in north London.

A government spokesperson said that special procedures had been activated to deal with the positive case.

In a statement issued when the case was confirmed on Wednesday a spokesperson said: “A British citizen currently in the DRC has tested positive for Ebola. The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated.

“Further information will be shared in due course as appropriate. The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”

open image in gallery (FILE) The British healthcare worker is expected to go to the Royal Free Hospital in London for specialist treatment ( Reuters )

Only four confirmed cases have been recorded in Britain since 1976, according to the ⁠UK Health Security Agency. One, in 1976, resulted from a laboratory needle incident, and three involved health workers who were responding to an outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.

The new case is linked to the ongoing outbreak centred on the DRC caused by the Bundibugyo virus. So far, there have been more than 10,000 confirmed cases and more than 5,000 deaths, according to the World Health Organisation.

Ebola has a high fatality rate, with past outbreaks causing death in 25-90 per cent of infected people. People with the disease tend to fall ill two to 21 days after contact with an orthoebolavirus.

Early symptoms include fever, aches, pains, and fatigue, but they can then progress to diarrhoea, vomiting and unexplained bleeding.

open image in gallery The man is believed to be a healthcare worker who became infected while working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo ( CDC )

The man is expected to stay in a high level isolation unit run by a dedicated team of doctors, nurses, and laboratory staff. At the Royal Free Hospital, one of the two hospitals set up to deal with Ebola, access to the isolation unit is restricted. It includes a special tent with controlled ventilation that still allows care to be provided by NHS staff.

All air leaving the unit is cleaned so there is no risk to anyone inside or outside of the hospital.

Experts have said the risk to the UK public remains low. Dr Damien Tully, an expert in infectious disease from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, said: “The infection of a British healthcare worker with Ebola is deeply concerning, but it is not entirely unexpected.

“Healthcare workers are on the frontline of these outbreaks, often treating severely ill patients under extremely challenging conditions. Even with rigorous protective measures, accidental exposures can occur.

“This case is a stark reminder of the risks faced by those responding to the outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in the DRC.

“However, it does not suggest that the virus has become more transmissible or that the threat to the UK has increased.

“Unlike respiratory viruses such as Covid-19 and influenza, that can spread through the air, Ebola is transmitted primarily through direct contact with infected bodily fluids, and people are not generally infectious until they develop symptoms.

“This means that identifying and isolating cases, together with appropriate infection prevention measures, can be highly effective in preventing onward transmission. For the UK public, the risk from this planned medical evacuation is extremely low.”

News.title: Can the UK handle an Ebola infection?
News.content:
A British man who has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is being flown back to the UK for treatment.

The patient, whose identity has not been revealed, but is believed to be a healthcare worker, is said to be in a stable condition.

They will be transferred to a specialist ambulance and then on to the Royal Free hospital, a rare diseases specialist hospital in north London, which houses the UK’s primary high level isolation unit.

Yesterday, a UK government spokesperson said there were “well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this” and that the risk to the public “remains low”.

It is the first confirmed case of a UK national contracting Ebola during the most recent outbreak of the rare but deadly virus in DRC. The first cases of the Bundibugyo strain of the disease were reported in May, and there have so far been more than 10,000 cases and 5,000 deaths, making it the second largest outbreak in history.

How will the British patient be treated?

The immediate priority will be to assess their condition.

On average, symptoms appear between eight to 10 days after exposure, but they can arise as soon as two days and as many as three weeks after infection. Doctors will have to determine how far the virus has progressed and identify any complications that require treatment.

Ebola can cause severe fluid loss, through profuse vomiting and diarrhoea, electrolyte imbalances and in serious cases organ failure. Experts will closely monitor his vital signs and fluid balance, bloods and organ function, providing intravenous fluids and other supportive treatment.

News.title: Bank of England raises interest rates for first time in three years
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. The value of the pound has risen to its highest level in two months as the Bank of England prepares to raise interest rates.

Sterling climbed 0.2pc against the dollar to nearly $1.35 on Thursday, its highest level since September.

It came as traders responded to the likelihood that the Bank of England will increase rates for the first time in three years on Thursday.

This reflects the Bank’s attempt to keep inflation under control after the Iran war energy shock pushed price rises to an 11-month high.

Typically, higher borrowing costs strengthen the pound by boosting demand for UK interest-bearing assets among foreign investors.

The pound was also buoyed by a weaker dollar after the Democrats swept to victory in the US midterms on Wednesday.

Political upheaval hit the dollar as traders bet that deadlock in Washington will lead to curbs on Donald Trump’s runaway spending.

This brought down the cost of US government borrowing, which in turn brought down the dollar.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “The prospect of a divided government eased concerns about the fiscal trajectory, given it’ll now be more difficult to pass tax cuts or spending packages.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Burnham makes new North Sea drilling illegal | Energy independence bill would prevent future ministers from easily reversing exploration ban

2) Blue wave threatens to derail America’s AI boom | Democratic candidates swept to power amid voters’ growing resentment toward data centres

3) Majority of London’s bridges are falling down | Advisers warn 24 Thames crossings are in poor condition and require urgent repairs

4) Silicon Valley investor shuts London office as US dominates AI | Firm known for early backing of Apple and Google doesn’t ‘see the need’ for presence in Britain

5) Trump rages at Fox News as Republican voters switch off | Once a powerful force in US politics, the Murdoch TV channel’s influence is fading

What happened overnight

Oil, chip stocks and the dollar were under pressure in Asia ​after ‌the Democrats swept to a series of stunning midterm election wins.

Brent crude dived nearly 9pc overnight, falling below $100 a barrel, and has dropped by about 20pc so far this week.

If sustained through to Friday’s close, it would make for the largest weekly drop in oil prices since April 2020 when US crude briefly fell into negative territory.

Tumbling energy prices encouraged a rally in bonds, which lowered yields, pulled the dollar to a one-month low of $1.1273 per euro, and helped stocks. The yield on the benchmark 10-year note fell to a two-month low and was last at 4.85pc.

Broad stock indexes climbed on the clear outcome, with the S&P 500 closing 1.6pc higher and European shares notching a two-month high, although tech stocks struggled as investors fear greater scrutiny over AI infrastructure build-out.

European stocks were on track to open 0.2pc higher, while the Nasdaq in the US fell 1pc in premarket trading, indicating investor angst over chip and data centre stocks.

Democratic data-centre ⁠opponents who campaigned, in part, on moratoriums on data centre construction won stunning victories in Texas and Georgia in a sign public opinion is shifting on AI.

South Korea’s chipmaker-heavy Kospi sank nearly 6pc and remained within a whisker of a new seven-month low. Taiwan’s benchmark index fell over 3pc, poised for an 8pc weekly decline, its worst weekly performance since April 2025.

Tech equipment suppliers dragged on the Nikkei, which ​fell 2pc, although the broader Topix was 0.8pc higher, underscoring the divergent ‌market reaction to the decisive election results.

News.title: Is America on the brink of sparking a new flu pandemic?
News.content:
Of the 75 human cases in the US, at least 50 have been linked directly to cattle farming, meaning the outbreak in cows has become the main route by which the virus is reaching people.

Most human cases linked to cattle have been mild, and far less dangerous than historic cases linked to infections from wild or farmed birds. Of the roughly 1,000 human cases of H5N1 linked to birds since it first emerged in China in 1997, around half have died.

But on November 1, the first person to be infected with the cow variant of H5N1, known as genotype B.13, was confirmed to have died.

The individual, who worked on a farm in Washington where at least 40 herds have been infected with H5N1, had underlying health conditions, which may have exacerbated the disease, and died shortly after becoming sick – but the development is still of concern, say experts.

“This goes against the pattern of mild disease when infected from dairy cattle, versus severe disease when infected from birds, which is worrying given the circulation in cattle,” said Dr Sridhar.

Reassortment risks

One of the biggest fears among scientists is that bird flu could combine with ordinary seasonal influenza to create a new strain capable of spreading easily between people.

“This is a time of year when we can expect to see more circulation of [human] seasonal influenza,” said Dr Marion Koopmans, professor of public health virology at Erasmus MC Medical Centre in the Netherlands.

“A bad scenario would be that someone working with cattle brought the ‘regular’ human flu in, got [H5N1] on top of that, and that develops into a mix that can spread but to which people have less immunity.

“The chances of such an event are very low, but it is a concern shared among virologists.”

The process, known as reassortment, occurs when two flu viruses infect the same animal or person and exchange genetic material, potentially creating a new strain.

Scientists are particularly concerned as H5N1 spreads beyond cattle and into other mammals – chiefly mink.

For more than two months, an outbreak has raged on a Utah farm housing thousands of mink, according to an investigation by US news outlet ProPublica.

Mink farms have previously been described as potential pandemic “time bombs”, because their respiratory systems are similar to those of humans, meaning viruses spread easily between them and people.

Despite calls for the animals to be culled, Utah officials have so far refused to mandate action, ProPublica reported.

The investigation also suggested that state officials were prioritising the financial interests of the fur industry, which exports much of its produce to China and Russia, while federal authorities had failed to intervene.

News.title: Attacks on water infrastructure intensify in conflict zones, warns Unicef
News.content:
Water infrastructure is coming increasingly under attack in conflict zones, leading to disease outbreaks and forcing civilians to make dangerous journeys to fill buckets, according to a new report.

Water Under Fire, published by United Nations children’s agency Unicef, found that attacks have become “more frequent, varied and geographically widespread”.

It said the number of attacks that damaged or destroyed water systems tripled between 2021 and 2025.

Recorded incidents, ranging from strikes on water plants to restrictions on access to water treatment chemicals, rose from less than 45 in eight countries in 2021 to more than 135 in 15 nations by 2025, according to data from Insecurity Insight, a Geneva-based humanitarian organisation that tracks threats facing people in conflict.

Maia Giorgio, humanitarian policy specialist at Unicef, stressed that the report only covers documented attacks, warning that it may be “just the tip of the iceberg”.

“It’s a global phenomenon, and unfortunately, it’s under-documented,” she said.

“Without water, you don’t have a functioning healthcare system. Without water, you can’t prevent infectious disease, and we know that children are particularly vulnerable,” she added.

News.title: Man City have a striker who will not be stopped and a defence that cannot be trusted
News.content:
“You can look at it that it’s difficult to keep concentrated for 100 minutes or you can look at it like it’s only 100 minutes you have to stay focussed to get a chance – you can look at it in a few different ways and I look at it in the second option,” Haaland added.

This was a victory to bounce back from losing in the Premier League at the weekend, but the question will be how can City mount a title challenge with such a brittle defence. Champions League winners do not leave themselves open at the back like this, and City have now gone seven games without a clean sheet.

Maresca insisted last week that his starting line-up is Donnarumma plus 10 others, but the reality is that Haaland is the guaranteed name on the team sheet. And his goalkeeper’s errors are becoming a problem.

This one added to the goals against Aston Villa and Paris St-Germain that were also on his watch. He could have claimed the cross that led to Brighton’s winner at the weekend too.

Here he went from hero to villain in the space of a few minutes at the start of the second half. Firstly, from kick-off Christoph Baumgartner got close with his angled drive heading towards the top corner until Donnarumma’s fingertips turned the ball around the post. It was a save that had the Italian celebrating like he had scored a goal.

But he had his head in his hands after Leipzig’s next move. Nico O’Reilly could have done better after losing the ball in midfield, then failing to track the overlapping run from Baku. With Red Bull Arena waiting for a cross, Baku had spotted Donnarumma slightly out of position and beat him at the near post. It was superb improvisation, but without doubt a goalkeeping error.

News.title: Gyokeres the creator and executioner to see nervous Arsenal past Slavia Prague
News.content:
“Really good,” said Arteta of Gyokeres. “Not only the assist and the goal, but he was really connected to the team. It’s great news, because I think he needed that performance.”

Those two moments in the first half eventually ensured another European victory for Arteta’s side, but the manager was far from impressed with the second-half showing. So smooth at first, Arsenal became remarkably ragged by the end. Slavia were deserving of their goal, scored by Wiktor Nowak. It looked like complacency had infected the minds of the Arsenal players, and you could feel Arteta’s fury radiating from the touchline.

“We scored two goals and it should have been three, four or five,” said Arteta. “And at half-time the message was clear: there is still a lot to do in this game. Right from the beginning of the second half, we were extremely far from our standards in everything that we have to do, in every basic, in every concept, and in everything we discussed. So much to improve and I take full responsibility for that.”

Without Gabriel Magalhães and David Raya, who both made dramatic stops on the goal-line, this could have become an ugly night for Arsenal against one of the weaker teams in the Champions League. The Czech side have now gone 23 games without a victory in Europe’s premier competition, which equals the longest winless run in European Cup history.

It was a remarkable coincidence that this game fell on November 4, the exact date as the same fixture last season. On that occasion Arsenal were comfortable 3-0 winners, with Mikel Merino scoring twice, and they seemed to be heading towards a similar night when Madueke scored the early opener.

The goal was made by Gyokeres, who held off a defender and then hooked an excellent pass into Madueke’s path. The Arsenal winger had already established his dominance over Oskar Kubiak, his opposite number, and he reached fifth gear before the Polish defender had even reached second. Madueke then slid his finish beneath the body of Nazar Domchak, Slavia’s teenage goalkeeper.

News.title: Liverpool calamity hands Iraola his most chastening night yet
News.content:
Andoni Iraola looked up to the ceiling of Fenerbahce’s media auditorium as he tried to find the words to describe the madness he had just witnessed.

“Cheap” was his first conclusion, swiftly followed by “messy”; technically, Liverpool’s head coach was right but this was a moment when nobody would have found issue had he gone further. “Absurd” and “preposterous” would have been more accurate portrayals of this calamity.

Liverpool have won two European trophies in Istanbul, but they do not tend to enjoy visits to Turkey. Roy Hodgson, in August 2010, was the last Anfield manager to oversee a win here and there was an irony that the hero of that night in Trabzon – Dirk Kuyt – masterminded this downfall.

Kuyt, interim head coach, got a remarkable response out of a Fenerbahce team who had amassed 1,086 Premier League appearances between them and he was as giddy as the locals after Mason Greenwood, Archie Brown and substitute Vedat Muriqi scored to give the club a famous night.

News.title: Oil prices plunge after Republicans suffer midterms defeat
News.content:
Oil prices fell sharply after JD Vance blamed the Republicans’ election rout on the Iran war.

The price of a barrel of Brent, the global benchmark, fell as much as 10pc to $93 a barrel by Wednesday evening, while WTI was down more than 8pc to $88.

It marks the first time since Oct 7 that Brent has fallen below $100 a barrel.

The decline came after the vice president said that voters had abandoned the party owing to dissatisfaction with Donald Trump’s war in the Middle East.

This has boosted traders’ hopes that the US President could seek to de-escalate his conflict in the Gulf, which would increase global oil supplies.

Posting on social media, Mr Vance said: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night.”

Mr Trump later admitted Mr Vance’s comments were “largely true”.

He said he expected oil prices to “go up a lot more” than they did because of the war, reaffirming that “Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon.”

“If I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again, because long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.

“I thought the oil would go up a lot more, and I did it on that basis.

“You have no choice. You have to do it. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon, or everything that you see here someday might not exist.”

Traders also responded to the prospect that the Democrats could restrict Mr Trump’s funding for the war.

Claudio Galimberti, chief economist at Rystad Energy, said the President is now likely to come under “greater institutional pressure” to strike a peace deal with Iran.

This will ease pressure on economies around the world after oil prices have risen by roughly 70pc since the war broke out in February.

The Republican rout also prompted Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX to lose nearly $159bn (£118bn) in market value when trading opened in New York amid fears the Democrats’ success will derail the AI boom.

The carmaker and rocket company both fell 5.8pc as Wall Street opened after the Democrats swept to victory although they pared losses later.

Mr Musk, the billionaire boss of both companies, was the leading donor to the Republicans during the election campaign as he hoped for light-touch regulation of his AI ambitions.

However, analysts said the Democrat victory would slow down the pace of the rapid build-out of data centres.

Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the race for Texas Governor and is expected to oppose the rapid build-out of AI.

A sharp decline in the value of data-centre developers Tesla and SpaceX, both based in Texas, would wipe billions off Mr Musk’s nearly $900bn fortune. He spent $446m on backing failed Republican candidates.

As the Democrat victory emerged, Mr Musk wrote on X: “Data centres in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

He later wrote: “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.”

Sports.title: Man Utd ‘contact ex-France manager Didier Deschamps’ with Michael Carrick clinging on by a thread
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED are targeting Didier Deschamps if they do decide to sack Michael Carrick, according to reports in France.

Foot Mercato have reported that United are looking at the ex-France boss as Carrick’s job hangs on by a thread, though the Champions League comeback win over Roma has bought him a small slice of time.



Deschamps spent 14 years as his nation’s manager, winning the World Cup in 2018.

But, the 58-year-old had a successful management career at club level before that with Monaco, Juventus and Marseille.



He got Juventus promoted from Serie B after their match-fixing scandal, won Ligue 1 with Marseille and led Monaco to the Champions League final where he lost to Jose Mourinho‘s Porto.

He also has a small working knowledge of English football after spending a season with Chelsea at the end of his playing career in 1999-2000.



Deschamps was keen on the Real Madrid job after leaving his post with France this summer, but he lost out to Mourinho once again as the Portuguese returned to the club for a second-stint.

Although the Madrid job was his preferred choice, the reports in France say Deschamps is relaxed about getting back into a job and is in no rush to make a decision.

Would he be interested in taking over at Old Trafford? He’s open to offers, according to the report.

United have explored parting ways with Carrick in recent weeks, but decided that there was no manager ready to step into the void that they could get.
