World.title: Liberian Women Begin Three-Day Fast and Prayer for War Crimes, Anti-Corruption Courts
World.content:
Monrovia – Women from across Liberia will gather Wednesday for a three-day fast and prayer to press for the establishment of a War and Economic Crimes Court and a National Anti-Corruption Court, as efforts to create the long-promised tribunals remain stalled at the Legislature.

By Rodney D Sieh

The program runs from Wednesday, November 4 to Friday, November 6, 2026, at the Fish Market and Women Prayer Grounds, under the theme “United in Prayer for Peace, Unity, Healing, and Transformation of Liberia through the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court and the Anti-Corruption Court of Liberia.”



The site carries symbolic weight. It was at the fish market on Tubman Boulevard that the Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace staged daily sit-ins in 2003, in white T-shirts, praying and pressing for an end to the war — a campaign widely credited with helping push warring factions to the peace talks that ended the conflict. The Liberia Women Mass Action for Peace is among the organizers of this week’s gathering.

In a concept note dated October 26, 2026, organizers say they are seeking God’s intervention for the creation of the two courts and for the National Legislature to act on the proposed bills. The program also aims to promote reconciliation through truth-telling, peace and co-existence, and to encourage women to play an active role in peacebuilding.

The three days will feature fasting and prayer sessions, praise and worship, and spiritual reflections, with prayers for the President and the Legislature, for victims, for peace, and for transitional justice actors.

A war without a reckoning

Liberia’s two civil wars, from 1989 to 1996 and 1999 to 2003, killed an estimated 250,000 people and displaced hundreds of thousands more. The conflict was marked by massacres, the widespread use of child soldiers, mass rape and the plunder of the country’s natural resources.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, created under the 2003 Comprehensive Peace Agreement, concluded its work in 2009 and recommended an extraordinary criminal court to try those most responsible. For more than a decade, successive governments did not act on that recommendation.

No one has been tried in Liberia for war-era atrocities. Instead, accountability has come from abroad. Former President Charles Taylor is serving a 50-year sentence for crimes committed in neighboring Sierra

Leone, not Liberia. Other former fighters have been convicted in courts in the United States and Europe, among them Mohammed Jabateh, the first of five former warlords convicted over war related crimes in courts in the United States and Europe, whose appeals are now exhausted.

Promises and delays

Momentum built after President Joseph Boakai took office. Senator Amara Konneh has reminded colleagues of the Senate’s overwhelming vote in April 2024 to establish a War and Economic Crimes Court for Liberia, and on May 2, 2024, Boakai signed Executive Order No. 131 establishing the Office of the War and Economic Crimes Court, headed by Cllr. Jallah A. Barbu.

The office’s mandate was later expanded to include an anti-corruption court, a move some advocates opposed. Justice activists condemned the decision, saying it would distract the office from long overdue wartime justice. Under the office’s roadmap, the National Anti-Corruption Court was to begin full operations in November 2026, and the War and Economic Crimes Court in 2027.

The process has been marked by rival bills and internal friction. A coalition led by the Independent National Commission on Human Rights submitted its own war crimes bill, as advocates moved to block an earlier version co-sponsored by Senator Joseph Jallah and Senate Pro Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence. In April, Barbu’s office accused senior government officials of deliberately blocking progress, naming the justice minister, the president’s legal advisor and the national security advisor as key obstacles.

President Boakai submitted the bill for the War and Economic Crimes Court to the Legislature in May 2026, along with a separate bill for a National Anti-Corruption Court. Neither court can be established until lawmakers pass the legislation. In June, the Senate Judiciary Committee presented a seven-month legislative roadmap for passage of the bills.

But last week, Barbu said lawmakers will not take up the war crimes court bill until January 2027, and the proposed US$1.2 billion national budget sets aside no money for the court. He said his office learned through the Office of the Speaker that lawmakers were prioritizing other national matters, and warned the delay could undermine efforts to set up the court. His office’s US$2 million annual appropriation covers preparations, not the court itself.

With November now here and no law passed, the anti-corruption court’s target date has effectively slipped. Advocates have warned that further delay could see the war crimes court run into the political cloud of the next election in 2029.

Organizers

The program is being organized by a 21-member Fast and Prayer Organizing Committee, including the Office for the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court for Liberia (OWECC-L), the Liberia Women Mass Action for Peace, WIPNET, WONGOSOL, Liberia Muslim Women for Peace, the National Council of Churches, the Muslim Council of Liberia, AFELL, the Liberia Massacre Survivors Association (LIMASA), the Press Union of Liberia, the Federation of Liberian Youth and NOPSWECO, among others.

Organizers expect women from churches, mosques, communities, civil society and youth groups to take part. They hope the gathering will produce a collective commitment to the courts, greater awareness of women’s role in promoting the bills, and stronger cooperation among women in the push for justice.

“Through collective prayers and action, the women of Liberia can continue as agent of hope and justice to reduce impunity,” the concept note states.

World.title: Liberia: Local Importers Petition Legislature Over 7-Month Shipping Delays, Increased Port Fees As House Summons Major Players
World.content:
Capitol Building, Monrovia– Gathered in huge numbers early Tuesday before regular sittings of both chambers of the Liberian Legislature, a group of business owners and importers decried frustration in doing business in Liberia.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The business owners, predominately women, under the banner China Business Women United with One Voice and the Consortium of Liberia Importers, presented urgent petition to both chambers of the Legislature to demand urgent intervention over severe shipping delays and mounting port bottlenecks.



Similar petition was also presented to the National Port Authority (NPA), as the group, dressed in dominant white, proceeded to the “Gateway of the nation’s economy.”

Timeline And Unfair Fees

Reading the petition on behalf of the business community, advocate Sriya Musu Momolu warned that prolonged shipping timelines and unfair fees have pushed and continues to push local enterprises to the brink of total collapse.

In their petition, the consortium stressed that cargo shipments originating from Asia, specifically China, now take six to seven months to reach the Freeport of Monrovia.

“We, the China Business Women United With One Voice/Consortium Of Liberia Importers and commercial stakeholders of Liberia, submit this urgent petition with deep frustration over the catastrophic delays in receiving imported cargo particularly shipments originating from Asia and China-and the extreme operational bottlenecks caused by major shipping lines, most especially Mask Line,” reads the petition.

The Risk That Comes Along

With the heavy reliance of loans from commercial banks, they fear that their personal homes and properties might be lost due to the increasing interest rate caused by delays.

The pointed out that the extended transit timelines severely continue to hinder their ability to service debts or turn over capital.

Momolu emphasized that businesses are collapsing, investments are trapped, and families are suffering under the weight of the current crisis.

Arbitrary Expiration of Delivery Orders (DOS)

Due to systemic bottlenecks at port clearance and delays caused by major shipping lines like Mask Line, the petitioners alarmed that Delivery Orders (DOS) arbitrarily gets expired before cargo can be retrieved.

“Business owners are then forced to pay costly renewal fees, administrative surcharges, and penalizing demurrage and detention fees for delays completely beyond their control. Enough is enough; this must stop,” the petition furthers.

This, according to them, they (business owners) are being forced to pay costly renewal fees, administrative surcharges, and penalizing demurrage charges for delays entirely beyond their control.

Double Taxation & Financial Distress

While ther capital remains trapped at sea or stuck at the port, the cried out that loan interest continues to accumulate, while at the same time expected to meet quarterly tax obligations to the Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA), pay office rents, and settle employee salaries.

Liberians Pushed Out Of Business

The petitioners also lamented how local entrepreneurs are being pushed out of business by foreign traders who bypass regulatory frameworks to retail directly in domestic markets.

The way forward

To prevent widespread business closures and economic destabilization, the consortium outlined six-count demand for government action.

Outlined in their counts/demands, the business operators called for a formal legislative inquiry into major shipping lines regarding transit delays and surcharge structures.

They also want a government mandate that compels shipping lines and port terminal operators to waive re-issuance fees and demurrage charges on expired Delivery Orders.

The group is also seeking mandatory arrival timelines for maritime carriers, streamlined container clearance at the Freeport of Monrovia to eliminate bureaucratic red tape, strict enforcement of the Liberianization Policy to protect local small and medium-sized enterprises from unfair foreign retail competition, and the establishment of long term national logistics policies.

Among other things, the group requested an immediate formal audience with the leadership of the Liberian Senate, the House of Representatives, and the management of the National Port Authority to present their grievances and secure actionable solutions.

Commitment From Chairman On Claims And Petition, Rep. Toles

Receiving the petition on behalf of the House of Representatives, the Chairman of the House Committee on Claims and Petition, Montserrado County Electoral District #8 Representative, Prince Toles committed to bringing the women’s grievances before his legislative colleagues for prompt redress.

Rep. Toles, a lawmaker, who comes from the business sector, stated that the issues raised by the business community are deeply concerning to all stakeholders, making swift legislative and administrative intervention critical.

House Holds Emergency Session On Plight On Business Community

On the heel of the latest petition and issues already raised before the House appertaining the delays, huge taxes paid on goods and services at the National Port Authority, Plenary voted to summon key stakeholders in the country’s port management to a specialized hearing scheduled for Friday, November 6, 2026.

The hearing is intended to address growing concerns raised by the protesting businesswomen over alleged excessive port charges and prolonged shipping delays, which they say are severely affecting their businesses.

Among those summoned are the Freeport of Monrovia, the National Port Authority (NPA), the Liberia Chamber of Commerce, and the Liberia Business Association (LIBA), Medtech Scientific Limited — the company contracted by Government of Liberia (GoL) to handle Pre-shipment Inspection and Destination Inspection and Cargo Tracking Note (CTN), alongside other key stakeholders in the port sector.

During the protest, the women accused port operators, particularly APM Terminals and GTMS, of imposing unreasonable charges and contributing to lengthy delays in the clearance and delivery of goods.

They warned that the alleged practices are placing significant financial pressure on their businesses, threatening their operations and livelihoods.

The November 6 hearing is expected to provide lawmakers an opportunity to engage port authorities, operators, and business representatives on the complaints and seek possible solutions to the challenges confronting the business community.

World.title: World Bank Says Liberia’s Economy Is Growing, But Extreme Poverty Is Rising
World.content:
Monrovia – The World Bank has released a report that detailed how mining-led growth is not creating enough jobs, and that the country is wallowing into extreme poverty

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The Bank says Liberia’s economy is growing faster, but most citizens are not feeling the benefits, stating that extreme poverty has edged up even as national output expands.



At the launch of the seventh Liberia Economic Update, World Bank Country Manager Georgia Wallen described this as the “paradox at the heart of this report”: the economy is growing, yet more people are struggling to meet basic needs.

Delivering the report, she began with the good news: Real GDP growth rose to an estimated 5.1 percent in 2025, up from 4 percent the year before. Inflation was contained, and the fiscal deficit narrowed to 2.1 percent of GDP.

Madam Wallen credited the government’s and the Central Bank’s “disciplined macroeconomic management,” which she said “deserves recognition.”

The economy has also held up against external shocks. Conflict and disruptions at maritime choke points have unsettled global energy markets and pushed up fuel prices, affecting import-dependent countries like Liberia in early 2026.

Policymakers, she noted, are moving swiftly to contain the risks while maintaining prudent policies.

Even so, extreme poverty is estimated to have climbed from 34.6 percent to 36.1 percent over the past two years. Wallen said this reflects the nature of recent growth, which has come largely from mining, a capital-intensive sector that generates few jobs and offers limited opportunities for local businesses.

According to the report, agriculture, manufacturing and small-scale services, where most Liberians earn their living, have lagged. It states that about 78 percent of workers are in vulnerable informal employment, while nine in ten firms are small or micro enterprises.

“What will it take?” Wallen asked, pointing to farmers facing high transport costs, traders running generators because electricity is unreliable, and entrepreneurs struggling with taxes.

This edition focuses on state-owned enterprises (SOEs), which provide electricity, water, port and fuel services. These services shape business costs and determine whether households have light at night. They also carry significant fiscal risks for the national budget.

The report finds that policymakers cannot see the full portfolio. Many entities do not submit financial reports, while most existing audits are delayed. Wallen called the creation of the State-Owned Enterprises Authority of Liberia (SEAL) “a significant and positive step.”

SOEs alone do not explain the jobs challenge, she indicated, but better information and accountability are practical starting points. Most recommended steps can be taken under existing law.

The report also highlights two trade-offs. The government achieved fiscal consolidation partly by cutting capital spending, which fell from 8.5 percent of GDP. The World Bank Country Chief warned that this approach has limits, since roads, electricity and other infrastructure are essential to Liberia’s growth.

And with iron ore and rubber accounting for more than 90 percent of exports, public finances remain exposed whenever global prices weaken.

Macroeconomic stability is the central foundation, she furthered, and “now is the time to use that foundation to take off.”

The choices ahead, she asserted, concern the quality of public investment, services and information as much as the quantity of growth. Government cannot do it alone; the private sector, civil society and development partners all have a role.

Presenting Chapter Two, “Beyond Growth: Addressing Structural Constraints to Job-Rich Growth in Liberia,” World Bank Senior Public Sector Specialist Bonnie Ann Siroris reveals that the government lacks the reliable information needed to assess SOE performance, fiscal exposure and value for money.

“Oversight covers less than half of the operational portfolio. Over six years, financial information was submitted for only 83 of 276 potential entity-years, while 25 of the 46 entities operating through 2025 never submitted a single return. Reporting standards also vary.”

Although the PFM Act requires International Financial Reporting Standards, entities use a mix of IFRS, public sector standards and U.S. GAAP, while some have no defined accounting basis. That, Siroris told the gathering, can make aggregated figures “very misleading.”

Audits tell a similar story. Seventeen operational entities have completed at least one audit since FY19, and 29 more are underway. Only four audits across all SOEs received unqualified opinions, while all 10 available compliance audits were adverse. Where figures could be compared, 40 percent differed by more than 5 percent between audit reports and Bureau of State Enterprises or SEAL data. The General Auditing Commission has pledged to clear its backlog by June 2028.

The SEAL Act was signed in February 2026, and the former Bureau of State Enterprises is transitioning into the new body.

But oversight is only part of the solution, Siroris noted, because boards must also fulfill their responsibilities.

A 2023 sample showed uneven attendance, and there is no portfolio-wide data on directors’ qualifications, interests or compensation. She recommended a director register, conflict-of-interest declarations, board induction and basic governance records.

The 19 reporting entities show an adjusted surplus of about $28 million for FY24, but three account for roughly $47.4 million of that total. The other 16 posted a combined deficit of about $19.4 million. The largest surplus, at NASSCORP’s core, reflects pension and investment accumulation, not distributable profit.

Those results include $15.1 million in government subsidies and $16.7 million in grants from development partners. Without them, the portfolio would record a loss of about $2.7 million.

At the end of 2025, the 19 entities reported about $815.4 million in liabilities. SOE loans on-lent or guaranteed by the government stood at about $423.3 million, with the Liberia Electricity Corporation (LEC) accounting for roughly 77 percent. Even these figures are incomplete, as there is no reconciled account of arrears, unpaid government bills, supplier claims or court judgments.

LEC’s own revenue rose substantially between FY22 and FY24, but its earnings were positive only when grant income was included, much of it non-cash. It received adverse audit opinions through FY23 and is owed about $34 million, roughly $30.8 million of which is owed by government bodies.

Siroris cautioned against interpreting a subsidy as evidence of poor performance, since it may finance a legitimate public service obligation.

By the end of FY27, the report calls for classifying the portfolio, creating verified entity and director registers, introducing a common reporting template and directing audit resources to the five highest-risk entities. By June 2028, it wants the government’s full fiscal relationship with LEC, the National Port Authority and the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company reconciled.

“Stronger SOE governance will not automatically reduce electricity costs, improve services, or create jobs,” Siroris said. Instead, it creates the conditions to identify underperformance, diagnose its causes, assign corrective action and track results.

The real task, she said, is not whether every SOE turns a profit, but whether the government, the legislature and the public can determine what each entity costs, delivers and risks, and whether the portfolio offers value for money.

World.title: Liberia: From Extraction to Eco-Prosperity, What Liberia Can Learn from Anji, China’s Bamboo Revolution
World.content:
Monrovia–Liberia’s environmental future will depend on choices that go beyond one focused. The country must determine how to manage its forests, wetlands, rivers, and agricultural landscapes while expanding employment, improving public health, and creating opportunities for rural communities.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Anji County China is one area that offers evidence that ecological protection and economic development can reinforce one another when conservation is supported by investment, effective institutions, market access, and locally relevant industries.



This President Xi Xiapin’s concept in his speech at 2020 at the 75th UN General Assembly at the United Nations on Carbon Nutrality, where following that, he launch3d an initiatie of using bamboo as a substitute for plastic.

A policy was also issued on Octover 15, 2026, by the Chinese Government, which prevented the production of plastic takeaway containers for food or shopping bags in China. This is intended to address some global problems such as Climate Change, plastic polution and other environmental problems.

With approximately 10 billion tons of plastics being produced by the world and only 10 percent being used properly and efficiently and recycling plastic remains costly. China believed that using bamboo as a substitute for plastic is an answer for the world since bamboo is totally biodegradable.

What if Liberia’s forests, rivers, wetlands ,and other natural resources could become a stronger source of jobs, healthier communities, and sustainable income for the people who depend on them? That concern is gaining relevance following a visit by Liberian media representatives to Anji County in eastern China, during a two-week media seminar, where bamboo processing, ecological conservation, sustainable agriculture, and rural tourism have helped reshape the local economy.

For Liberia, a country endowed with extensive tropical forests, freshwater systems, mangroves, and other valuable ecosystems, Anji offers a development lesson, protecting nature need not come at the expense of economic growth. Under the right conditions, conservation can become a foundation for prosperity. But translating that experience into reality will require more than admiration for China’s achievements.

Financing, infrastructure, technical capacity, environmental, enforcement, and community ownership will determine whether Liberia can turn its natural resources into sustainable livelihoods.

Liberian Health and environmental science researcher and former Chairman of the Public Health Department at the University of Liberia, Forkpah Pewee and Dr. Anthony Saah Tengbh, Environmental Scientist and Academic Chairman, Department of Environmental Studies and Climate Change at the University of Liberia say elements of the Anji model could work in Liberia if they are adapted to local conditions and supported by practical investments.

However, the Environmental Protection Agency’s position remains unclear. FrontPage Africa sought comments from EPA Executive Director Dr. Emmanuel King Urey Yarkpawolo on the lessons Liberia could draw from Anji and the role environmental regulation could play in developing sustainable enterprises.

He had not responded by the time of publication. His nonresponse does not establish opposition to the approach but leaves unanswered questions about how the country’s environmental regulator would support, oversee, and measure such initiatives.

Anji’s transformation, when conservation becomes an economic strategy. Located in Zhejiang Province, Anji County covers approximately 1,886 square kilometers and has a population of roughly 470,000. It is known for its bamboo forests, white tea, and rural landscapes.

The county was not always the green destination it is today. During the 1980s and 1990s, industrial activities, including quarrying, paper production, and other pollution-intensive operations, contributed to environmental degradation. In Yucun Village, authorities subsequently moved away from environmentally damaging activities and pursued alternative livelihoods, including tourism and other businesses linked to the natural environment.

The transition required difficult economic adjustments, as closing polluting industries initially affected some incomes. Over time, Anji increasingly linked ecological conservation with bamboo processing, agriculture, and tourism.

A 2022 peer-reviewed study of the county’s ecological conservation policies found that protected areas experienced less expansion of construction and agricultural land than the study’s modeled alternative scenario.

The areas accounted for approximately 39 percent of the county’s land but more than 80 percent of its estimated ecosystem-service value in 2015. The findings support the importance of protecting ecologically valuable landscapes, although they do not establish that conservation alone caused all of Anji’s subsequent economic growth. For Liberia, the lesson is that a forest can provide more than raw materials. Properly managed, it can also protect water sources, sustain biodiversity, support livelihoods, and attract visitors. Beyond bamboo poles, Building an industry

One of Anji’s most important achievements is its ability to turn bamboo from raw material into a broad range of finished products. The resource supports manufacturing activities involving furniture, flooring, household utensils, kitchenware, packaging, building materials, and other goods.

Bamboo shoots are also used as food, while processing innovations create additional uses for plant residues. According to figures reported by China’s State Council Information Office in June 2025, Anji’s bamboo industry recorded an output value of 19.2 billion yuan in 2024, an increase of 7 percent over the previous year.

The report also said bamboo-related income benefited more than 51,000 farming households, with average additional household earnings of 6,500 yuan that year. These figures illustrate the scale of an established Chinese industry, not an earnings forecast for Liberia.

Anji’s advantage lies in the connections between growers, processors, manufacturers, traders and customers. Each stage creates opportunities for employment and income. Liberia could adapt that principle by processing suitable natural resources locally instead of relying predominantly on raw-material sales.

Liberia’s untapped bamboo wealth, an industry waiting to grow

Liberia is not starting from zero. The country possesses bamboo and rattan resources that could support furniture-making, household products, handicrafts, selected construction materials, and other manufactured goods.

Previous technical-assistance programs have also sought to develop local skills in bamboo processing. A World Bank report on Liberia’s forest sector identified bamboo and rattan as resources with considerable commercialization potential. It highlighted limited access to processing equipment and technical skills, including the ability to split, slive, and weave bamboo as an obstacle to developing the industry.

These constraints help explain why the existence of a resource does not automatically translate into jobs and business growth. With appropriate training, equipment, and market access,

Liberian entrepreneurs could explore making chairs, tables, beds, shelves, mats, window blinds, household utensils, decorative products, and selected packaging materials. Some bamboo species also produce edible shoots, while processing residues may have other uses where technical and environmental assessments establish their viability.

These are potential opportunities, not guaranteed profitable ventures. Each product would require an assessment of raw-material supply, production costs, quality standards, customer demand, and competition from imports.

Liberia has already received bamboo-related technical assistance from China. According to a Chinese government account, a bamboo and rattan weaving program began in 2007, alongside training in vegetable production and biogas technology.

AidData’s project record reports that 55 trainees had learned to make basic household products by 2008 and that approximately 900 people had received training through the program by 2022.

Those figures document training activities but do not establish how many participants subsequently operated successful businesses. In August 2025, Liberia’s Ministry of Youth and Sports also announced the groundbreaking for a China-supported technical-assistance training facility at the Samuel Kanyon Doe Sports Complex.

World.title: Liberia: EPA Puts Gender at the Center of Climate Action, Orders Every Department to Deliver
World.content:
Opening his address, Dr. Yarkpawolo argued that environmental work cannot be separated from the people it is meant to serve. The theme of the launch, he said, reflects the kind of institution and country Liberia is trying to build

MONROVIA — The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has turned the lens on itself, unveiling its first Gender Policy and a refreshed national Climate Change Gender Action Plan, and warning its own managers that the commitments must show up in everyday decisions rather than gather dust on shelves.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Executive Director Dr. Emmanuel K. Urey Yarkpawolo made the declaration on Tuesday at the Corina Hotel in Sinkor, where the two documents were launched under the theme “Advancing Gender Equality for Inclusive Climate Resilience in Liberia.”



Gender, Children and Social Protection Minister Gbeme Horace-Kollie joined government officials, development partners, and representatives of civil society, women’s and youth groups, and persons with disabilities at the event.

“A matter of people’s lives”

Opening his address, Dr. Yarkpawolo argued that environmental work cannot be separated from the people it is meant to serve. The theme of the launch, he said, reflects the kind of institution and country Liberia is trying to build.

He painted a picture of those at the heart of the agenda: a woman farming to feed her family, a young person looking for work, and a person with a disability who deserves an equal chance to contribute. Policies, he said, must recognize their circumstances and open doors for them to take part.

Findings that shaped the policy

The EPA’s first Gender Policy did not emerge in a vacuum. According to the Executive Director, it was shaped by an institutional gender assessment, consultations with staff and stakeholders, and a review of existing policies.

The assessment credited the Agency with progress but also exposed a gap: gender considerations had not yet been woven fully into the Agency’s work.

To address that, the policy sets out practical guidance on hiring and promotion, training, leadership, workplace culture and accountability. It also tackles discrimination and sexual harassment head-on. Dr. Yarkpawolo said every employee should be able to grow professionally in a workplace that protects dignity and safety.

Linking gender to national climate goals

The second document, the updated Climate Change Gender Action Plan, takes forward an earlier plan. It was developed through research, stakeholder consultations and training, with support from UN Women, and it ties gender equality to Liberia’s national climate pledges under NDC 3.0.

The EPA’s first Gender Policy did not emerge in a vacuum. According to the Executive Director, it was shaped by an institutional gender assessment, consultations with staff and stakeholders, and a review of existing policies

The plan focuses on eight sectors: agriculture and food security, coasts and fisheries, forestry, health, water and sanitation, waste, energy, and transportation.

Its core argument, the EPA chief explained, is that climate change does not hit everyone equally. Differences in access to land, finance, information and decision-making mean some people are far more exposed than others. He pointed to a woman farmer who may read shifting rainfall patterns better than most, yet lacks the means to adapt. Climate programmes, he said, should tap such knowledge while removing the obstacles she faces.

Early steps already taken

Dr. Yarkpawolo told the audience the Agency is not starting from zero. Among the steps already taken, he said, is the elevation of the gender function to senior management, ensuring it has a stronger voice where institutional decisions are made.

The Agency has also invested in women’s skills, including international training for its women environmental inspectors. Stronger skills, he said, improve the Agency’s ability to monitor environmental conditions and protect communities.

He singled out Madam Madrid Chuka Piah, head of the EPA’s radiation laboratory, as proof of what women are contributing in specialized scientific roles.

The Agency has likewise hired persons with disabilities, whom he said strengthen the institution. Even so, he acknowledged the work is unfinished, saying the EPA must keep adapting its workplace so they can participate fully.

Tough questions ahead

With the documents now launched, the Executive Director shifted from planning to performance. The Gender and Climate Change Baseline Assessment process, he said, helped pinpoint gaps; implementation must now close them, measure progress and flag where more action is needed.

He listed the questions that will guide that scrutiny. Are women benefiting from training and promotion? Can persons with disabilities participate in a meaningful way? Are climate projects reaching those facing the steepest barriers? Do budgets actually back the promises made?

No department left out

Dr. Yarkpawolo was unambiguous about who carries the load. He expects every department to take responsibility for implementation. The Gender Unit will guide and coordinate, but managers across the Agency must bring these commitments into their daily decision-making.

Beyond the EPA’s walls, he called for cooperation across government and sustained partnership with civil society, communities and development partners. Clear responsibilities, sufficient resources and regular monitoring, he said, will determine whether the policies succeed.

The Executive Director thanked Gender Coordinator Madam Grace Biah and her team, the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, technical experts, and all others who contributed. He reserved special appreciation for UN Women for backing the update of the Climate Change Gender Action Plan.

World.title: MRC Seeks strong mining Regulation as it plots2027–2031 Strategic Plan
World.content:
The Minerals Regulation Commission (MRC) has called for strengthened regulatory oversight, transparency, accountability and stakeholder collaboration to enhance the governance and management of Zambia’s mineral resources.

The Commission says its inaugural Strategic Plan for 2027–2031 will provide a clear roadmap for strengthening mineral regulation, improving service delivery and ensuring that the country’s mineral wealth contributes meaningfully to sustainable national development.

MRC Director General, Tom Hara, said this during a stakeholder engagement and consultation meeting on the draft Strategic Plan in Lusaka, which brought together representatives of Government institutions, mining companies, civil society organisations, cooperating partners, academia and other stakeholders.

Dr Hara said the development of the Strategic Plan comes at a critical time when Zambia is pursuing an ambitious target of increasing copper production to three million metric tonnes annually by 2031.

He emphasised that achieving this target requires a predictable regulatory environment, responsible investment, effective mineral rights administration, environmental protection and strict compliance with regulatory requirements.

Dr Hara said the Commission was committed to building a credible regulator that commands public confidence, earns the respect of the mining industry and provides effective oversight in the national interest.

“The success of this Strategic Plan will depend on collective responsibility and sustained collaboration,” he said.

He stressed that the consultation was not merely intended to present a document for endorsement but to solicit practical contributions that would ensure the final Strategic Plan reflects the realities and expectations of the mining sector.

Dr Hara identified transparency, responsiveness and collaboration as the guiding principles of the Commission’s strategic direction, emphasising the importance of fair, accountable and predictable regulatory processes.

He further underscored the need for stronger partnerships with Government institutions, the mining industry, communities, environmental regulators and civil society to address challenges such as illegal mining, environmental degradation, mineral security, occupational health and safety, and the formalisation of artisanal and small-scale mining.

Meanwhile, ActionAid Zambia has urged the Mineral Regulation Commission to place human rights protection, environmental accountability, gender equality and meaningful community participation at the centre of its regulatory agenda.

ActionAid Zambia Business Development Manager, Geofrey Sizala, said the country’s mineral wealth must translate into tangible improvements in the livelihoods of ordinary citizens, particularly communities directly affected by mining activities.

Mr Sizala identified five priority areas for consideration in the Strategic Plan: business and human rights, gender equality and public disclosure, formalisation of artisanal and small-scale mining, domestic revenue mobilisation, and community participation and environmental accountability.

He urged the Commission to ensure that mining companies go beyond fulfilling licensing requirements by demonstrating responsible business conduct, protecting workers’ rights, preventing environmental pollution and addressing the concerns of affected communities.

Mr Sizala also called for improved public disclosure of gender-disaggregated information in the mining sector, including employment levels, remuneration, management positions and participation in procurement opportunities.

On artisanal and small-scale mining, he advocated for accessible licensing processes, affordable financing, improved occupational health and safety, responsible sourcing and stronger market linkages to support the formalisation of miners.

He further called for strengthened oversight of mineral production, trading and exports through collaboration with institutions such as the Zambia Revenue Authority to minimise revenue leakages and ensure that the country derives fair economic benefits from its mineral resources.

Mr Sizala emphasised that mining communities must be meaningfully involved in decisions relating to mineral licensing, environmental management, regulatory monitoring and activities that affect their livelihoods.

He said the effectiveness of the Strategic Plan would ultimately depend on measurable targets, transparent reporting and accountability mechanisms that enable citizens to assess the Commission’s performance.

The MRC was established under the Minerals Regulation Commission Act No. 14 of 2024, with the mandate to regulate, monitor and safeguard the development and management of minerals in Zambia.

The stakeholder consultation is expected to validate strategic priorities, generate recommendations, identify partnership opportunities and provide a practical roadmap for finalising and implementing the 2027–2031 Strategic Plan.

The Commission remains committed to strengthening regulatory systems and ensuring that mineral resource development is undertaken responsibly, transparently and in accordance with the law, in support of Zambia’s national development aspirations.

Oxfam country focal point person, Chitimbwa Chifunda commended government for the establishment of a MRC, saying it will promote oversight in the mineral value chain.

She said the Commission is expected to streaming and enhance transparency and accountability in the mining sector.

World.title: Muchinga Province begins remembrance day preparations
World.content:
Preparations for the 2026 Remembrance Day parade are officially underway in Muchinga Province, with military personnel and cadets ramping up rehearsals ahead of the annual event scheduled for Sunday, November 8.

The parade, which honors fallen heroes who sacrificed their lives during the First and Second World Wars, is a global and national moment of solemn reflection.

A visit to the Chinsali Cenotaph this morning revealed a hive of activity, as disciplined contingents of military personnel and youth cadets perfected their drills in readiness for the commemoration.

Zambia Army Muchinga Command Staff Officer Grade One, Lieutenant Colonel Jerome Mwangala, who is also serving as the parade coordinator, confirmed the province’s full preparedness for the event.

Lt Col Mwangala highlighted the deep historical significance of the commemoration, explaining that the traditional wearing of the poppy flower serves as a poignant symbol of remembrance.

He noted that the poppy represents the resilient flowers that bloomed across the devastated battlefields and graves of fallen soldiers during the World Wars.

The commander urged the local community to bridge the gap between the barracks and civilian life by attending the ceremony in solidarity.

He said the event is not just for military personnel, but for every citizen, as we have all been affected by the sacrifices of our fallen heroes in some way,” Lt Col Mwangala said.

“Let us turn out in large numbers as citizens of this province, as Muchinga joins the rest of the world to observe this day in honor of our fallen heroes and heroines,” said Mwangala.

The Remembrance Day service in Muchinga Province is scheduled to take place this Sunday at the Chinsali Cenotaph, drawing dignitaries, veterans and residents from across the region.

World.title: Lumezi schools make progress in irrigated maize production
World.content:
Two schools selected to implement the Presidential Irrigation Initiative Programme (PIIP) in Lumezi District of Eastern Province are making steady progress in irrigated maize production.

The programme, introduced by President Hakainde Hichilema, seeks to promote year-round agricultural production, mitigate the effects of climate change and drought, and transform schools and other institutions into centres of agricultural productivity.

Lumezi Day School and Lumezi Boarding School are each cultivating one hectare of irrigated maize under the initiative, which is part of the broader Grow Zambia Agenda to increase the country’s annual maize production to 10 million metric tonnes by 2031.

Lumezi District Commissioner, Brigadier General Patrick Mtonga (Retired), has expressed satisfaction with the two schools’ commitment and dedication to the successful implementation of the programme.

Meanwhile, the Department of Agriculture in the area is providing technical support to ensure the successful implementation of the programme.

Lundazi district Senior Agricultural Officer Joris Mwale says the Schools will also receive support with the provision of inputs.

“The Department has been granted permission to provide the schools with fertiliser under the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP), while facilitating their participation in the Sustainable Agriculture Financing Facility initiative.

Learners at the two institutions have also thanked President Hakainde Hichilema for introducing the initiative, saying it will provide them with practical agricultural skills and opportunities to venture into farming.

Masida Banda, a Form One pupil at Lumezi Day Boarding School, said the initiative will help improve the school’s resource base while equipping learners with practical farming skills.

She said the programme is giving learners hands-on experience in agriculture and preparing them to consider farming as a viable business venture in the future, rather than relying solely on white-collar employment.

And Lumezi Day School Head teacher, Innocent Lungu said the sustainability of the project remains a priority for the institution.

“The school is closely working with various government departments, including Agriculture, Water Affairs and the local authority, to ensure the continued success of the initiative,” he said.

Meanwhile, the District Education Board Secretary James Chibuye has thanked President Hakainde Hichilema for extending the Presidential Irrigation Initiative to Lumezi District.

Mr Chibuye said the project is an inspiration not only to learners but also to teachers, some of whom are now considering establishing similar agricultural ventures.

He said the Grow Zambia Agenda can only be realised when everyone takes responsibility and actively participates in food production.

World.title: ZACOSO backs fish inclusion in school meals
World.content:
The Zambian Aquaculture Cooperative Society Limited (ZACOSO) has expressed optimism over the planned integration of fish into the school feeding programme, citing opportunities to create new markets for local producers while promoting entrepreneurship among learners.

The statement follows the Government’s call for the integration of nutrient-dense aquatic foods to improve learner nutrition and strengthen local food systems.

ZACOSO General Manager, Evans Chilandani said the initiative, if implemented, would increase demand for locally produced fish by encouraging schools and other production units to venture into fish farming.

Mr Chilandani emphasised that introducing fish ponds in schools would also provide learners with practical skills in fish production, including how to rear and manage fish, equipping them with entrepreneurial knowledge they could use after completing their education.

Meanwhile, Zambia Aquaculture Alliance Cooperative Society Secretary General Ferdinand Simfukwe has called on the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock to involve small aquaculture associations and cooperatives in the proposed school fish feeding programme, stating that their participation will be key to creating reliable markets for local producers.

Mr Simfukwe said the initiative will help many small-scale fish farmers who struggle with markets.

He further urged the Ministry to bring together relevant stakeholders and establish clear mechanisms for small-scale aquaculture associations to participate and benefit from the programme, saying their inclusion would strengthen its implementation and ensure that local fish farmers are not left out.

World.title: Shiwang’andu farmers urged to expand cultivation
World.content:
Farmers in Shiwang’andu District have been challenged to increase agricultural production by taking advantage of the district’s 59,200 hectares of arable land, of which only 21,000 hectares are currently under cultivation.

District Agricultural Coordinator (DACO) Chewe Mutale said the district has vast agricultural potential which, if fully utilised, could contribute to the country’s national maize production targets by 2031.

Ms Mutale told the media in an interview that about 38,200 hectares of arable land remained available for agricultural expansion.

She disclosed that the district recorded a maize output of 27,900 metric tonnes against a target of 66,000 metric tonnes during the 2025/2026 farming season.

The DACO attributed the low adoption of good agricultural practices among farmers as one of the major challenges affecting increased agricultural production.

“Low levels of mechanisation, inadequate storage facilities and poor road infrastructure were also contributing to low productivity” she said.

Meanwhile, Shiwang’andu District Commissioner Maureen Bwembya has urged farmers to embrace modern farming practices and fully utilise the available arable land to unlock the district’s agricultural potential.

Ms Bwembya has challenged farmers and agriculture officers to work towards achieving the district’s maize production target of 82,000 metric tonnes by 2031, thereby contributing to the national target of producing 10 million metric tonnes of maize within the same period.

World.title: President Hichilema calls on Leaders to prioritise service delivery
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has urged newly elected and other Members of Parliament, councillors and party officials to work for the people, saying they owe their positions to the electorate and must prioritise service delivery over political disputes.

Speaking during a community engagement in Mandevu, Lusaka, President Hichilema said the United Party for National Development (UPND) Government is in office to serve the people and deliver on its development promises.

“We are in government to serve the people and to deliver on our development promises,” President Hichilema said.

“I want you the people of Mandevu to hold your elected leaders accountable,” he added.

He said access to clean water remains a fundamental need for Mandevu constituency, hence the need for the Member of Parliament to use the component of Constituency Development Fund (CDF) for clean water provision.

“Water is a fundamental need. We must ensure that our people have access to clean water,” he said.

President Hichilema also identified security as another key priority for his administration, highlighting the need to curb junkies in the communities and take them for skills training for them to contribute to the country’s economy positively.

“Security is important. Government is committed to creating an environment in which citizens can live safely and contribute to national development,” he said.

The Head of State also stressed that every child of school-going age must be in school, adding that every citizen who is not in a position to pay school fees must utilise free education policy which is coupled with the feeding programme

“Every child of school-going age must be in school. Education is what will transform our young people into productive citizens,” he said.

He further said his administration wants to transform citizens into productive members of society through opportunities for education, skills acquisition and economic participation.

“We want to transform our citizens into productive members of society through education, skills acquisition and economic participation,” he said.

President Hichilema pointed to the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) as an important instrument for community development.

“The CDF is an important instrument for community development. We have allocated K40 million for constituency development and K40 million for skills training,” he said.

He also highlighted the importance of inclusive representation in Parliament, pointing to the participation of women, young people and persons with disabilities.

“We have provided opportunities for broader representation in Parliament, including women, young people and persons with disabilities,” he said.

The President thanked Zambians for supporting the UPND and acknowledged party structures across the country, including provincial, district and constituency officials, as well as grassroots representatives for their role in mobilising support.

President Hichilema said the government would continue working for Zambians, reiterating that service delivery remains its primary agenda.

“We will continue working for Zambians. Service delivery remains our primary agenda,” he said.

He thanked the people of Mandevu and reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to national development.

And Mandevu Member of Parliament, Adrian Banda has assured electorates of Mandevu of the much-needed development in the area with the use of the Constituency Development Fund (CDF).

“We will use the CDF to provide the much-needed development for the people of Mandevu. The people voted for development, and that is what we are going to deliver,” Mr Banda said.

He said the fund will be directed to priority areas that will improve the lives of residents, adding that his office will work closely with the community to ensure the projects reflect the needs of the people.

World.title: Nalumango calls for stronger market linkages
World.content:
Vice-President Mutale Nalumango says Zambia must go beyond increasing production to effectively connecting its products to local, regional and international markets if the country is to achieve meaningful economic transformation.

The Vice-President said Government’s ambitious production targets under the Grow Zambia Agenda will only translate into economic value if supported by strategic marketing, quality standards and competitiveness.

Mrs Nalumango said this in a speech read on her behalf by Copperbelt Province Minister Emmanuel Kasambo during the official opening of the 2026 Prestigious Copperbelt Regional Marketing Conference at Garden Court Hotel in Kitwe.

She commended the Zambia Institute of Marketing (ZIM) and its partners for convening the conference to explore how marketing can contribute to Zambia’s trade, investment and economic growth.

The Vice-President noted that increased production alone does not guarantee economic transformation.

The Vice-President said marketing Zambia and its economic opportunities is a shared responsibility.

She said the Government will continue to create an enabling environment for trade, investment and enterprise, while the private sector must invest, innovate and produce competitively.

She also urged stakeholders to embrace digital technologies, market research and intelligence to identify emerging opportunities.

Mrs Nalumango said the Copperbelt is an appropriate setting for the conference, noting that while the province has long been central to Zambia’s mining industry, its future prosperity must extend beyond mineral extraction.

World.title: Government, Partners commit to sustain school meals
World.content:
Vice President Mutale Nalumango has reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to working with partners to sustain the school meals programme.

In a speech read on her behalf by Minister of Education, Harry Kamboni at the close of the Global Child Nutrition Forum, Mrs Nalumango called for stronger partnerships and commended participating countries and stakeholders for their contributions.

Global Child Nutrition Foundation Executive Director Arlene Mitchell said participants’ actions were important in making a positive impact on children’s lives.

Ms Mitchell also thanked the Zambian Government for its commitment to co-hosting a successful forum.

Earlier, Permanent Secretary in the Office of the Vice President, Lillian Kapusana led delegates on visits to about 11 schools in Lusaka, where they observed the School Feeding Programme.

The four-day forum, held under the theme “From Vision to Action: Achieving Ambitious School Meal Programme Objectives,” brought together more than 400 participants from over 65 countries.

They collaborated to turn global knowledge and research into practical strategies.

World.title: Africa: Deadly Viruses Know No Borders, Nor Should Our Resolve to Stop Them
World.content:
Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland.

guest column

In this guest column for AllAfrica, the Dutch Trade and Development Minister and the head of the World Health Organization stress that addressing viral health crises anywhere protects everyone everywhere. The government of the Netherlands is committing funding both for the current Ebola crisis and flexible funding to quickly respond to new or emerging global threats.

COVID-19 may feel like a distant memory to many. But the virus claimed millions of lives around the world, including approximately 50,000 in the Netherlands. The lesson is clear: preparedness is not optional.

Preventing health crises abroad is in the interest of all countries, including the Netherlands.

Governments everywhere face competing priorities and constrained budgets. But infectious diseases do not respect national borders. In an interconnected world, health threats that emerge in one place can quickly become risks for all of us. No country can safeguard its health security alone.

That lesson is evident today in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where a major Ebola outbreak is unfolding in a region already affected by insecurity, displacement and limited access to health services.

Already the outbreak has crossed national boundaries, underlining how quickly a health threat in one country can become a shared international concern.

Responding effectively requires rapid action, strong local leadership and international solidarity. Under the DRC Government's leadership, the World Health Organization (WHO) is working closely with the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, local authorities, communities and partners to contain the outbreak in the DRC and save lives.

Mystic Stock Photography / Shutterstock.com The MV Hondius, a cruise ship owned by the Dutch company Oceanwide Expeditions experienced a Hantavirus outbreak last year. The Netherlands and the World Health Organized collaborated to safely evacuate passengers and crew.

To support these efforts, the Netherlands is providing €7 million to WHO for the Ebola response. But responding to outbreaks requires more than emergency funding alone. It requires flexible, predictable financing that can be directed rapidly to where needs are greatest. That is why the Netherlands is also providing a new €10 million flexible contribution to WHO for future emergencies, enabling the WHO to rapidly respond to health threats while helping countries strengthen preparedness and prevent future outbreaks whenever possible. This is additional to the existing €9.6 million yearly core funding to the WHO.

No country can safeguard its health security alone.

Some may ask why the Netherlands, or any country, should invest in health emergencies far from its own borders when domestic health systems also face challenges. The answer is simple: diseases do not stop at borders. Supporting countries to detect and contain outbreaks early is not only the right thing to do. It protects local populations while reducing the risk of wider international spread. Investing in health security abroad is also an investment in health security at home.

Outbreaks are most effectively controlled at their source. Local leadership is essential. National authorities understand their communities, their health systems and the challenges they face. WHO's role is to support those efforts, coordinate international expertise and ensure that countries have access to the tools, funding and technical assistance they need.

International cooperation remains the foundation of effective health security. This year, for example, a hantavirus outbreak on a Dutch-flagged cruise ship was swiftly contained through rapid collaboration among countries and partners coordinated through WHO. During an earlier outbreak caused by the "Sudan virus" species of Ebola in Uganda, investments that helped advance an Ebola vaccine developed by the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) and Batavia Biosciences contributed to global preparedness efforts. These examples demonstrate that cooperation works.

Dany Bitita/WHO Two new candidate vaccines to join Ebola trial as treatment research advances.

Yet this progress cannot be taken for granted. The international health system is under growing strain, even as health threats continue to increase. Climate change is altering the distribution of infectious diseases. Europe has already seen growing concern from vector-borne diseases, including West Nile virus, while other diseases such as dengue and malaria are expanding into new regions. At the same time, funding for global health, including for WHO, is declining.

Diseases spreading to new areas amid decreased global health funding is dangerous.

This is a dangerous combination. The need for cooperation, preparedness and rapid response is growing, just as the resources required to sustain them are coming under pressure.

We therefore call on European governments to strengthen their support for global health security by increasing flexible and unearmarked contributions to WHO. Such investments enable outbreaks to be detected earlier, contained more rapidly and addressed where they begin, before they become larger regional or global crises.

No one can rule out the possibility of another pandemic. . But we can ensure that we are better prepared for the next one. Strong health systems in the DRC, and in countries everywhere, are not only vital for the local communities. They are an investment in a safer, healthier and more secure future for us all.

Sjoerd Sjoerdsma is the Dutch Minister for Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation. Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus is Director-General of the World Health Organization.

World.title: South Africa: Parties Keep Close Watch As Election Results Trickle in
World.content:
The 2026 Local Government Elections results process continues to advance, with 24% of votes counted nationally. These are the results at 10am SAST on November 5, 2026.

The Electoral Commission of South Africa's (IEC) national Results Operations Centre (ROC) in Midrand is abuzz with activity, as political parties closely monitor the first results from the 2026 Local Government Elections.

Party representatives have gathered at the centre as preliminary results started trickling in this morning, following Wednesday's voting, with parties hoping for a strong showing in the contest for control of municipalities across the country.

The IEC registered approximately 29.2 million voters for the elections, with voting taking place at 23,696 voting stations. Special voting was conducted on Monday and Tuesday ahead of Election Day.

The Commission will be briefing the media at 10am.

World.title: Africa: Africa Made It Unveils Blueprint To Capture Usd 34B In Gdp And Accelerate African Industrial Sovereignty
World.content:
press release

Africa Made It, the continental movement driving Africa's industrial sovereignty, today officially launched its campaign, "Power, Protect and Purchase," at the CANEX weekend in Lagos, Nigeria. Aimed at unlocking USD 34 billion in annual GDP contribution through a structural transition from unprocessed raw cotton exports to end-to-end local garment processing, the initiative seeks to turn Africa's vast natural wealth into sovereign, self-sustaining economic power.

Africa Made It is driven by a consortium of leading pan-African organisations, advocacy groups, and media organisations who are positioning Africa as a global investment hub. Its flagship campaign, spotlighting the fibre-to-fashion value chain, presents a clear roadmap for continental industrialisation: securing competitive energy power for local industrial mills, enacting policy measures to protect emerging domestic manufacturers from unfair foreign imports, and rallying African consumers to purchase locally manufactured apparel. Together, these three pillars ensure that value created from African resources remains on African soil.

Africa Practice research shows that Africa exports up to 98% of its raw cotton overseas and captures only 2% of its total value while incurring a USD 35 billion annual trade deficit. Building the continent's domestic processing capacity in spinning, weaving, and sewing locally produced cotton will sustain nearly two million permanent industrial jobs and inject approximately USD 33 billion directly into domestic household incomes every year, in addition to a recurring contribution of USD 34 billion to the continent's GDP.

While these figures reveal the immense macro-economic potential of the value chain, the true heart of this transformation lies in its human impact. Industrial wages and local lint purchases leading to increased capital circulation in rural communities can drive community micro-economic vitality and contribute to rural poverty reduction. Additionally, formal employment opportunities can expand drastically for women, as they currently make up between 70-90% of garment factory workers on the continent.

Realising this vision and changing the lives of millions of people requires a deliberate combination of targeted investments, supportive trade policies, and consumer mobilisation. A USD 1.8 billion capital allocation toward critical structural enablers for garment transformation is the foundation for bridging Africa's missing middle in the fibre-to-fashion value chain.

Marie Wilke, editor-in-chief of the Africa Made It magazine, said, "African culture, design, and storytelling influence global fashion, music, and media like never before. Yet, without domestic manufacturing infrastructure, Africa's creative authority yields very little economic return. Linking raw cotton harvest directly to local processing ensures that the intellectual property, commercial margins, and industrial jobs remain on the continent. It is time to wear our power."

To learn more about the potential of Africa's fibre to fashion value chain, watch the campaign video or read the Africa Made it magazine . Access the campaign website and resources in English and French .

About Africa Made It

Africa Made It was established as a continental advocacy platform to accelerate Africa's transition from a primary exporter of raw materials to a global powerhouse that controls, processes and monetises its own resources. The fashion industry is only the first example. It is coordinated by a network of partners including AllAfrica Media, Africa24, Africa No Filter, Africa Practice, Afreximbank, AKAS Consulting, Bird Story Agency, IC Publications, and Research Alpha.

For regular updates on the campaign and its progress, follow Africa Made It on Instagram ( @africa_madeit ) and LinkedIn ( Africa Made It )

World.title: Nigeria: Court Nullifies Atiku's Candidacy, Sacks All ADC Candidates, Party Leadership
World.content:
The judgement, if upheld by the higher courts, means the ADC, a major challenger to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), is barred from fielding candidates in the upcoming general elections.

The Federal High Court in Abuja on Thursday sacked the leadership of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) under former Senate President David Mark and voided the party's presidential ticket held by former Vice President Atiku Abubakar.

Judge Peter Lifu said the "Mark-led Caretaker Committee, which conducted the party's presidential primary that produced Atiku Abubakar as its flag bearer," is illegal.

The judge sacked the entire national officers of the party, including Rauf Aregbesola as the National Secretary, alongside all the candidates the party presented to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) for the 2027 elections.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The judgement, if upheld by the higher courts, means the ADC, a major challenger to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), is barred from fielding candidates in the upcoming general elections.

The former ADC Deputy National Chairman, North-East, Nafiu Bala Gombe instituted the suit challenging the process through which Mr Mark and other members assumed the party's leadership.

Mr Gombe sued the ADC, INEC, Messrs Mark, Aregbesola and Ralph Nwosu.

On Thursday, the judge directed INEC not to recognise the decisions taken at the party's 99th National Executive Committee meeting of 27 July 2025.

The decision will be most likely challenged up to the level of the Supreme Court, which will give its final verdict before the general elections start in January.

An appeal against the verdict will set off a return journey to the appellate courts, which initiallly gave an interim resolution with the Supreme Court restoring the Mr Mark leadership of the party in April.

The Supreme Court's decision at the time was not the final one on the matter a five-member panel of the court ordered that the Federal High Court in Abuja, where the suit originated, should see the stalled proceedings to the end.

World.title: Tanzania/Uganda: Billions Pour Into Stadia - How EAC Nations are Investing for AFCON
World.content:
DAR ES SALAAM — TANZANIA, Kenya and Uganda are investing heavily in modern sports infrastructure ahead of the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON), combining new stadium construction with the modernisation of existing facilities to meet international football standards.

The investments, which involve hundreds of millions of dollars, are expected to strengthen East Africa's capacity to host major sporting events while creating lasting infrastructure for football development, sports tourism and commercial activities.

The projects include new stadiums in Arusha, Zanzibar, Nairobi, Hoima and Lira, alongside major upgrades to established national facilities in Dar es Salaam, Nairobi and Kampala.

Beyond providing venues for the continental tournament, the investments reflect the three East African region's ambition to develop modern, multifunctional sports facilities capable of hosting international competitions, entertainment events and other major gatherings.



Tanzania's AFCON 2027 infrastructure programme is anchored by three principal match venues: Samia Suluhu Hassan Stadium in Arusha, Benjamin Mkapa National Stadium in Dar es Salaam and Fumba Stadium in Zanzibar.

The projects combine the construction of new stadiums with the modernisation of existing facilities, expanding the country's capacity to host international football competitions.

The new Samia Suluhu Hassan Stadium in Olmoti, Arusha, represents one of the country's largest investments in sports infrastructure, with a cost of 338.54bn/, equivalent to approximately 128.2 million US dollars.

The project includes a planned seating capacity of approximately 32,500 spectators and is being developed as a modern sports complex with facilities designed to meet international competition requirements.

According to the Tanzanian government, the contract value increased from an original estimate of 187bn/- to 338.54bn, representing an 81 per cent increase.

Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Information, Culture, Arts and Sports, and Chief Government Spokesperson Gerson Msigwa, attributed the increase in the construction cost of the stadium to changes in the project's scope and technical requirements following Tanzania's selection to co-host AFCON 2027.

Msigwa explained that the initial budget was prepared in 2021, before Tanzania secured the rights to co-host the continental tournament alongside Kenya and Uganda.

He said the original design was based on general stadium requirements, but the country's selection as an AFCON host necessitated substantial improvements to meet CAF Category Four standards, which are required for hosting toplevel international matches.

The stadium's engineering design incorporates a reinforced-concrete structural frame, complemented by a sophisticated steel roof and facade system featuring trusses and a singlelayer spatial grid.

The roof structure uses approximately 7,762 tonnes of steel to provide extensive coverage over spectator areas.

The facility also incorporates modern spectator seating, VIP and hospitality facilities, players' and officials' facilities and technical installations.

Its development is intended to meet the enhanced requirements for CAF Category Four stadiums, including improved playing surfaces, floodlighting, safety systems, media facilities and emergency power.

In Dar es Salaam, the 60,000-capacity Benjamin Mkapa National Stadium is undergoing extensive rehabilitation to meet the technical and operational requirements of AFCON 2027.

The government initially disclosed a rehabilitation programme valued at approximately 39bn/-, equivalent to US$14.7 million. A major component involved replacing all 60,000 spectator seats, which is estimated at 39bn/-.

Other improvements have covered the playing surface, drainage, floodlighting, VVIP facilities, players' dressing rooms, media areas, sound systems and supporting technical infrastructure.

The latest rehabilitation phase has placed particular emphasis on reconstructing the playing surface to improve drainage and meet international football standards, alongside improvements to hospitality, spectator movement, security and backup power.
