World.title: Did Republican efforts to redistrict the House turn into a dummymander?
World.content:
Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' Congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on Tuesday night as the GOP was on track to lose all of the districts it tried to gerrymander.

There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP.

But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday, with CBS News estimating Democrats could end up with 251 to 268 House seats.

With the House decisively swinging toward Democrats and Democrats undertaking measures in a few states to counter the GOP's efforts, Republicans are faced with the possibility of having created a so-called "dummymander," a situation in which a party tries to gerrymander, but ends up benefiting the other party.

Here's a state-by-state breakdown of how the redistricting efforts panned out:

Texas

Texas Republicans went into Election Day controlling 24 seats, while Democrats controlled 13 seats and there was one seat in a GOP-leaning district that was vacant. In redrawing the map, Republicans sought to emphasize Mr. Trump's gains in South Texas to win five more seats.

As of Wednesday, Republicans had won 24 seats and Democrats had won 14 seats, making Texas a dummymander.

Ohio

A commission comprising mainly Republicans hand-picked by GOP lawmakers redrew Ohio's map to net two more seats for their party. Republicans heavily targeted longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur's district in the northern part of the state and Rep. Greg Landsman's Cincinnati-area district.

Heading into Tuesday night, Ohio Republicans controlled 10 seats and Democrats controlled five. Seven Democrats, including Kaptur and Landsman, won Tuesday night, and CBS News estimates another district is likely Democratic. Republicans have only won seven districts, making Ohio a dummymander.

North Carolina

Although North Carolina has a Democratic governor, Republican lawmakers have a veto-proof majority in the statehouse and pushed through a new map that attempted to oust Democratic Rep. Don Davis.

North Carolina Republicans controlled 10 House seats going into Election Day, while Democrats controlled four, including Davis' district. As of Wednesday, four Democrats had won and CBS News estimated that another five were likely Democratic. Republicans had not yet won any races, with CBS News estimating one race was likely Republican and another four were toss-ups.

If Democrats ultimately win any of the undecided races, North Carolina will be a dummymander.

Louisiana

Louisiana lawmakers redrew their districts after the Supreme Court ruled in June that compliance with Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act could not justify the state's use of race in redrawing its House district lines.

Louisiana went into Election Day with four House seats controlled by Republicans and two controlled by Democrats. The new map aimed to eliminate one of the majority Black districts that currently have Democratic representatives.

As of Wednesday, Republicans had won three districts, while Democrats had won one. CBS News estimates Louisiana's 6th District is a toss-up and the 5th District race will go to a runoff. If Democrats win either of those districts, Louisiana will be a dummymander.

Alabama

After the same Supreme Court decision, Alabama Republicans sought to eliminate the state's two majority Black districts, both of which are represented by Democrats. Both incumbents won reelection on Tuesday, so Republicans did not net any more than the five they already controlled, making Alabama a dummymander.

Tennessee

Tennessee lawmakers also redrew their map after that Supreme Court decision to target the lone Democratic district in Memphis.

Going into Election Day, Republicans had eight seats and Democrats had one. As of Wednesday, Republicans had won six seats and CBS News estimates two races are set to go to a runoff, including the newly drawn 9th District in Memphis. If Democrats win one or both districts, Tennessee will be a dummymander.

Florida

Led by Florida's Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, GOP lawmakers redrew their map to net up to four more seats for their party.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled 20 seats and Democrats controlled eight. As of Wednesday, Republicans had won 16 seats, Democrats had won seven and there were five districts that CBS News estimated were toss-ups. If Democrats win any of the toss-up races, Florida will be a dummymander.

Missouri

Missouri's GOP-led legislature last year redrew their map to make one of the state's two Democratic-held districts more friendly to Republicans. But the map's legality was challenged, and a state court ruled the map could not be used unless it was approved by voters. The Supreme Court three times blocked Missouri from using the new map, leaving the 2022 congressional districts in place for Tuesday's election.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled six districts while Democrats held two. Democrats flipped another district, giving them three seats to the Republicans' five.

Indiana

Mr. Trump had also pushed lawmakers in Indiana to pass a map that would edge out the state's two Democratic lawmakers and make it a 9-0 Republican delegation. Despite pressure from Mr. Trump, the GOP-led state Senate rejected the new map.

Using the same boundaries as the last two cycles, Democrats held onto their two seats and flipped a third, making the state's representation 6-3.

South Carolina

South Carolina Republicans also sought to redraw their map after the Supreme Court decision in an effort to edge out powerful Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn and make the state's representation 7-0 for Republicans. But the measure failed in the state Senate, and Clyburn won reelection on Tuesday. Two other races are considered toss-ups.

California

In response to Texas' redistricting efforts, California's Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom put forth a ballot measure to redraw the map to gain five seats for Democrats, which was decisively approved by voters.

Heading into Election Day, Democrats held 43 districts and Republicans held nine. As of Wednesday, Democrats won in 42 districts, while CBS News estimates another six are likely Democratic. Republicans have won two districts and another two are likely Republican.

Since Democrats picked up seats in California, it is a successful gerrymander for Democrats.

Utah

A judge in 2025 rejected Utah's congressional map that favored Republicans in all four districts, and then a district court rejected the redistricting map selected by the GOP-controlled legislature and instead selected a map that would create a Democratic-leaning congressional district in Salt Lake City.

Under the new map, Democrat Ben McAdams won the 1st District in Salt Lake City by 47 points.

Virginia

Virginia voters decisively approved a ballot measure in April to redraw the congressional map to favor Democrats in 10 districts and Republicans in one. But the map was thrown out by the Virginia Supreme Court, putting back in place the map drawn in 2021.

Heading into Tuesday, Democrats held six seats while Republicans held five. Using the same boundaries as the past two cycles, Democrats won seven seats, Republicans won two and two are considered toss-ups.

Maryland

Maryland's state constitution requires that congressional districts be compact and connected, and Democratic Gov. Wes Moore and other Democratic lawmakers championed a ballot initiative to remove those restraints on redistricting.

The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, passed by 20 points on Tuesday, so Democrats are likely to redraw their map now to edge out their sole GOP representative.

World.title: Black candidates for governor make history with midterm victories
World.content:
Americans elected their first Black woman into a gubernatorial role during the 2026 midterms, alongside four other Black candidates who won races for governor around the United States on Tuesday.

The races culminated, respectively, in victories for Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, in Georgia; Byron Donalds, a Republican, in Florida; David Crowley, a Democrat, in Wisconsin; Aaron Ford, a Democrat, in Nevada; and Wes Moore, also a Democrat, who was reelected to serve a second term as governor of Maryland. He became the state's first Black governor when he was elected in 2022.

Including Moore, only three Black Americans have previously been elected to serve as U.S. governors. Former New York Gov. David Paterson, who is also Black, became governor when Eliot Spitzer resigned in 2008.

Once Bottoms and Crowley were projected the winners in their races, Moore reflected on their wins to CBS News on Tuesday, calling the victories "incredibly important."

"This is exciting, because up until this moment, I was the only Black governor in America. And I was very clear that that's a title that I did not want to hold onto for very long," said Moore. "I'm only the third African American ever elected governor in the 250-year history of this country, and, now, in one cycle, we have at least doubled that number. I just think it's incredibly important. It's a historic moment."

Bottoms has been hailed as a trailblazer for more reasons than one, as she will become the first Black woman elected to a gubernatorial position in U.S. history. She will also be the first woman to serve as governor of Georgia when she joins the ranks of a record-high number of women — 17 — in governor's offices nationwide.

She told "CBS Mornings" co-host Gayle King on Wednesday that she had been trying to tune out the results when she learned that she won.

"I had put in my AirPods to work on my speech, and my husband was on the sofa near me, laying near me, and he kicked me," said Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor. "I went like, 'What?' He said, 'They called it.' And I said, 'Called what?' And so that's how I knew."

Donalds, who served as U.S. representative for Florida's 19th District after his election to that spot in 2020, is now also slated to become Florida's first Black governor. He is also the first Black Republican elected governor in the nation.

In Wisconsin, Crowley, a moderate Democrat, defeated Republican challenger Tom Tiffany in the culmination of a governor's race that played out in one of the country's most purple states. Tiffany, a U.S. representative, is also one of President Trump's top allies.

Ford, who was elected as Nevada's attorney general in 2018, won his state's gubernatorial race against Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, CBS News projected on Thursday. He will become Nevada's first Black governor and the first Black governor ever elected west of the Mississippi.

World.title: Democrat Aaron Ford beats GOP incumbent in Nevada governor's race
World.content:
Democrat Aaron Ford won the Nevada governor's race, CBS News projects, defeating incumbent Gov. Joe Lombardo as the state struggled because of tariffs and a decline in tourism.

Ford, who has been elected statewide twice as attorney general, will be Nevada's first Black governor and the first Black governor elected in a state west of the Mississippi.

Nevada Democratic gubernatorial candidate and current Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford at a get-out-the-vote event with U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-GA) to encourage early voting on Oct. 07, 2026 in Las Vegas. Ethan Miller / Getty Images

Lombardo, a moderate Republican who was first elected in 2022, had a massive war chest, but was unable to overcome the challenges stemming from the state's economic woes. Nevada's largest city, Las Vegas, is driven by tourism and has seen a dropoff in international tourists under President Trump, particularly from Canada. Nevada has also been hit hard by tariffs.

Mr. Trump won Nevada by three points in 2024, the first Republican presidential candidate to win the state since 2004.

Although Lombardo touted his successes with the Democratic-led state legislature, Ford successfully tied him to national Republicans and Mr. Trump. According to an October poll by Noble Predictive Insights, 58% of Nevada residents disapprove of Mr. Trump's performance.

Democrats racked up stunning wins across the country on Tuesday, including Nevada, where Democrats flipped the 2nd District that encompasses the northern part of the state.

World.title: Harmeet Dhillon, DOJ's controversial civil rights chief, resigns
World.content:
Washington — Harmeet Dhillon, the assistant attorney general in charge of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, resigned on Thursday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said.

"Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division with conviction the past 18 months," Blanche wrote in a post on X. "She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor. The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."

Dhillon oversaw a mass exodus from the Civil Rights Division last year, with more than 75% of its staff departing. She upended many of the division's traditional priorities that focused on combating discrimination against some of the nation's most vulnerable and historically marginalized groups.

Since taking over the division, often lauded as being the "crown jewel" of the DOJ, she has reoriented it to focus instead on other priorities that have included protecting gun owners' rights, curbing the use of equity, diversity and inclusion policies at universities, and adopting legal positions that oppose civil rights protections for transgender people.

Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon speaks to reporters on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on May 29, 2026. Anna Moneymaker / Getty Images

During her tenure, the Justice Department closed many of its cases involving discrimination targeting Black Americans and announced it had dismissed more than 50 decades-old consent decrees with public schools, many in the Deep South, that were in place to protect Black students from unlawful discrimination.

Dhillon nixed two pending consent decrees last year with the Minneapolis and Louisville Police Departments over systemic abuses that were investigated in the wake of the killings of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor, and rescinded the investigative findings of misconduct into six other police departments.

Earlier this year, after immigration agents shot and killed American citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis as they were protesting the administration's immigration crackdown, the Civil Rights Division did not move to open any criminal civil rights investigations, in violation of longstanding practice for such high-profile officer-involved shootings.

The division ultimately got involved in the Pretti case after the Justice Department faced staunch criticism and questions about why Homeland Security Investigations — and not the FBI — was leading the probe into its own agency.

To date, no charges have been filed in the Pretti case, which is also separately under investigation by state officials.

Stacey Young, a former Civil Rights Division attorney who founded the nonprofit advocacy group Justice Connection, called Dhillon "the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history" in a statement on Thursday.

"Americans' civil rights don't enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded. Dhillon decimated it."

Dhillon, a staunch ally of President Trump who for years ran her own law firm in San Francisco, is a frequent guest on conservative podcasts and a very active poster on social media.

Unlike her predecessors, she frequently took to X to post her own videos about the work that her division was undertaking. She acknowledged in media interviews that she often generated ideas for civil rights investigations based on various posts she encountered on social media.

She has sometimes announced the opening of civil rights investigations online, a stark departure from historical practice. She also handed out challenge coins to fellow DOJ attorneys with the term "FAFO" ("f*** around and find out") printed on it.

One of the areas where she has been the most vocal has been voting rights.

Under her leadership, the Civil Rights Division filed 31 lawsuits against primarily blue states and the District of Columbia in an effort to gain access to unredacted voter rolls.

Lawyers from the division repeatedly argued that they needed the information to ensure states were complying with two federal voting laws that require them to maintain clean voter lists. However, they later admitted in court that the Justice Department intended to share the information with the Department of Homeland Security so they could use it for criminal and immigration enforcement purposes.

So far, the Justice Department has lost 27 of those cases.

During the midterm elections on Tuesday, the Civil Rights Division sent out more than 1,000 monitors to polling sites across the country, a record number that required the Justice Department to solicit volunteers from unusual parts of the DOJ, including the Bureau of Prisons and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.

However, in more recent weeks, Dhillon has been noticeably less involved in the effort.

She did not appear at an election integrity briefing at DOJ for journalists, and the Office of Deputy Attorney General, who does not have oversight authority on civil rights, solicited election monitor volunteers, according to a Sept. 10 memo seen by CBS News. Historically, that program is run directly by the Civil Rights Division.

A senior Justice Department official denied that the election integrity work had been taken away from Dhillon when asked at the briefing, saying the department was spreading around resources due to the increase in the workload.

"I don't agree that anything has shifted away from Harmeet. I think she's as busy as the rest of us. We're spreading the wealth," the official said.

World.title: Dow posts biggest gain of the year after Democrats sweep Congress
World.content:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared nearly 1,600 points, or 3%, on Wednesday, its biggest gain of the year, as investors digested the impact of the Democrats' sweeping victories in the midterm congressional elections.

Other indexes also jumped, with the broader S&P 500 climbing 120 points, or 1.6%, to close at 7,689 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index gaining 1.4%.

"Investors are happy to have the midterms out of the way," market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, told investors in a report. "This was a major source of uncertainty, and putting it in the rear-view mirror removes a key obstacle heading into a very favorable time of year seasonally."

The shifting political winds could affect a range of issues that influence investment returns, from the pace of the data center buildout and cryptocurrency industry regulation to proposals to cap credit card interest rates.

At the same time, Wall Street analysts do not expect the outcome to derail a stock market being driven more by robust corporate profits and solid economic growth than by politics.

"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown of Capital Economics said in a note to investors.

Stocks of solar power companies, dollar stores and hospital owners helped lead the way as Wall Street tried to sort the winners from losers following the widespread losses for Republicans.

Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Mr. Trump's social media company, the artificial intelligence sector and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans. Trump Media & Technology's stock price fell nearly 25% on Wednesday, while shares of Musk-owned SpaceX and Tesla sank 3.8% and 3.3%, respectively.

Gridlock good for stocks?

Investors also expect the election results to heighten gridlock in Congress, with Democratic lawmakers now in control of both the House and Senate, and Mr. Trump threatening to wield his veto power to block any legislation he opposes.

Political gridlock has historically been good for markets because it limits Congress' ability to pass sweeping tax and spending legislation, reducing the risk of volatility, according to Wall Street analysts.

Meanwhile, stocks have generally performed well following midterm elections. The S&P 500 stock index rose an average of 15.5% in the six months after the last 14 midterm races, dating back to 1970, according to figures from investment firm Edward Jones.

"Economic growth, inflation, interest rates and corporate earnings have historically mattered more to broad investment performance than the party composition of Congress, especially if the president and congressional leadership come from different parties," analysts with the Wells Fargo Investment Institute said in a report.

"We do not expect sweeping policy changes," they added. "More likely, in our view, is a split-government alignment on affordability, energy policy and opportunities from artificial intelligence."

Beyond the Beltway, the midterm electoral results could affect key issues for investors, such as the pace of data center construction, with enormous spending on artificial intelligence helping drive stocks to record highs this year while also raising concerns about a bubble in tech stocks.

"In divided government, the policy implications at the federal level may be limited, but data center policy decisions sit at the state and utility-commission level, making gubernatorial and utility races important alongside Congress, particularly Governor Abbott's loss in Texas," Jeff Buchbinder of LPL Research told investors.

"LPL Research continues to expect the buildout to occur, but strong performances by Democrats in key data center states (and pushback from the 'not in my backyard' folks) may slow it down some, potentially increasing regulatory pressure on AI infrastructure stocks including semiconductors, machinery and power generation," he added.

World.title: Nithya Raman ousts incumbent Karen Bass in LA mayor's race, CBS News projects
World.content:
Councilmember Nithya Raman will be Los Angeles' next mayor after defeating incumbent Karen Bass in the November general election, CBS News projects.

Raman's win comes after resounding victories for Democrats across the country on Election Day.

Raman, a Democratic socialist, has been riding her momentum after pushing past Spencer Pratt in the June primary, but suffered a setback with voters a week before the election, according to the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times.

Nithya Raman defeats incumbent Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayoral election, CBS News projects. CBS News

A survey released by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the LA Times shortly before the election showed Bass and Raman tied, with 40% support among likely voters.

Bass and Raman became frontrunners after the primary election when they rallied ahead of third-place candidate Spencer Pratt. A week before the election, 41% of Pratt's primary voters shifted their support to Bass, up from her previous 22%.

"A lot of the voters who were previously supporting Spencer Pratt in the primary have now weighed in, and they have moved to Bass," said Mark DiCamillo, director of the Berkeley IGS poll.

Raman had a slight drop among Pratt supporters, falling from 16% in September to 14% in October. However, the new poll showed that a large contingent of Pratt voters, 45%, remained undecided on the candidates.

Councilmember Nithya Raman

Raman announced her surprise bid for mayor in February after previously endorsing Bass' reelection bid.

During the primary, Raman called her campaign a "long shot" before ultimately overtaking Spencer Pratt to face Bass in the general election.

Before being elected to Los Angeles City Council in 2020, Raman served as the co-chair of the Silver Lake Neighborhood Council Homelessness Committee and co-founded a homeless advocacy nonprofit.

One of her most notable acts in office came in 2025, when she introduced a motion capping maximum annual rent increases for tenants in rent-stabilized apartments built before 1978. It eventually passed 13-2. She said she hopes to undertake similar work to help small businesses.

Mayor Karen Bass

After serving more than two decades in public office as a congresswoman and as LA's 43rd Mayor, Bass said this race will be her last campaign for office.

Bass was raised in LA with her three brothers. She began her professional career as a nurse and physician assistant, where she later founded the Community Coalition to help underserved residents of South LA battle substance abuse, poverty and crime.

She kickstarted her career in politics in 2004 as a member of the California Assembly, where she became the first Black woman to serve as Speaker of a state legislative body. She left the Assembly in 2010 to run for Congress, where she served in the House for 12 years.

Leading up to the primary election, Bass received endorsements from notable politicians including California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris. Nearly a week before the November election, billionaire Rick Caruso threw his support behind his former rival in the 2022 mayoral race and vowed to vote for her in November.

"For the love of LA, I must put the past behind me because this election must be about our future," Caruso said in a post to X. "I will be casting my ballot for Mayor Karen Bass."

He also said in the video that he had concerns about Raman that were not "much about ideology, but about competence."

World.title: Stocks crater as investors recoil from tech companies
World.content:
The stock market tanked on Thursday amid concerns that a shift in congressional political control following the U.S. midterm elections could slow the construction of data centers that power artificial intelligence services.

Stocks sank across the board, but technology companies with a hand in the AI sector were hit especially hard. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index tumbled 1,285 points, or 5%, in early-afternoon trading, a sign investors are reacting to the growing "headline" risks around AI, according to Wall Street analyst Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge.

The broader S&P 500 dropped 300 points, or 3.9%, while the blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged 1,586 points, or nearly 3%. U.S. equities are now on track for their worst day since the "Liberation Day" shock in April 2025, when President Trump announced tariffs on countries around the world, noted Joe Maher, a markets economist at investment research firm Capital Economics.

The rout marks a sharp reversal from Wednesday, when the Dow posted its biggest gain of the year. Other indexes also surged after the election results eased uncertainty about who will control Washington.

"Even though the market rallied Wednesday after the midterm elections, there were visible cracks in the AI ecosystem, and they widened on Thursday amid investor concerns about a potentially slower data center buildout with Democrats in charge of Congress," Chris Larkin, a managing director of trading and investing for E*TRADE from Morgan Stanley, said in an email.

Market watchers think the Democrats' sweeping electoral victories this week could bolster opponents of data centers and slow the rollout of the facilities, which have spurred widespread public opposition.

A slowdown in erecting data centers could deal a major blow to AI companies, which are pouring billions into the buildout and banking on widespread adoption of the technology.

Pricking the bubble?

Investors worry that the enormous investment in AI is creating a stock market bubble, which happens when sky-high valuations become detached from companies' underlying fundamentals.

"Whether the midterms shock turns out to be the catalyst that derails the AI equity boom remains to be seen, but it strengthens our sense that the boom is in its final innings," Maher said.

Chip and other AI-exposed stocks are taking a particular beating. Nvidia shares fell 7.5% and were the heaviest weight on the S&P 500, a day after dropping 3.2%. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 14.6%. CoreWeave, a company that rents access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 12.1%.

In other financial markets, the initial reaction to the election results faded a bit. The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.6% to $97.11 and recovered much of its nearly 9% drop from the day before. Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal.

World.title: McDonald's plans to cook up new affordable menu bundles
World.content:
McDonald's is testing new affordable menu bundles as it works to attract inflation-weary customers struggling with the cost of living.

McDonald's CEO Christopher Kempczinski said Wednesday during a call with Wall Street analysts that the fast-food chain recently launched an eight-week pilot program to test value-offerings at 1,900 U.S. locations. The company is testing different "mix and match bundles" and "fixed bundles" to see which will drive sales, he said.

McDonald's plans to launch the bundles most popular with customers nationwide in 2027, Kempczinski said.

The news came after McDonald's earnings report, released Wednesday, showed comparable sales growth fell 0.2% at U.S. locations from July to September, after growing 2.4% during the same period last year. Overall foot traffic at the chain's U.S. stores was down 4.6% from a year ago, according to data from analytics platform Placer.ai.

Kempczinski acknowledged that the company has not done enough to meet the expectations of low-income diners, who are looking for "great entry-level value."

"We talked quite extensively about how [in] Q2 we didn't land that like we needed to," he told investors. "And so that's what we're in the midst of getting resolved right now and through testing."

His comments come the day after the U.S. midterms, where affordability concerns took center stage. Many candidates campaigned on addressing cost-of-living issues and bringing down gasoline prices, which have risen 38% since the start of the war in Iran, according to AAA data.

U.S. consumer spending has remained resilient even in the face of stubborn inflation, which remains stuck above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. However, economists note that lower-income consumers are feeling particularly strapped, as a larger share of their income goes toward expenses like gas.

Low-income consumers "are disproportionately feeling the effect of higher food and gasoline prices," Ryan Sweet, chief global economist at Oxford Economics, said on Wednesday during an event in New York City.

World.title: Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
World.content:
Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse

toggle caption i Jorge Saenz/AP

ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguay's lower house voted unanimously Thursday to impeach President Santiago Peña just minutes after he announced his resignation, as the collapse of a major digital bank tied to his government froze millions of people's savings, sent protesters surging into the streets and turned his own party against him.

The 78-0 vote marked a stunning repudiation of Peña by lawmakers from his long-ruling Colorado Party, who joined the opposition in backing his impeachment after three days of demonstrations rocked the capital, Asunción. The vote sends the charges to the Senate, where a two-thirds majority is required to convict the president and formally remove him from office.

Sponsor Message

The impeachment came as thousands protested for a third day, as they attempt to recoup lost savings, wages and pensions from Ueno Bank, a major digital lender.

Peña, a close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, announced his decision in a video posted to X as lawmakers debated his impeachment, saying he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."

toggle caption i Ted Shaffrey/AP

The president, who until last year held a stake in a company related to Ueno Bank, expressed contrition but stopped short of accepting responsibility for the banking crisis that has plunged a South American nation long prized by foreign investors for its stability into financial and political turmoil.

"I also want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me."

The extraordinary turn of events set the stage for a transfer of power later Thursday. Congress was expected to formally accept Peña's resignation at 5 p.m., clearing the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to be sworn in as president an hour later. Alliana would serve out Peña's term through August 2028, with lawmakers expected to choose a new vice president.

Sponsor Message

From star lender to seized bank

Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. They are now left scrambling to recoup their savings, government pensions, and, for 7,000 employees impacted by the bank's closure, unpaid wages.

Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president, who until last year had a stake in Ueno's holding company, could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its dubious lending practices.

The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña's long-ruling Colorado Party to the country's regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth made Paraguay a darling of international investors in recent years.

"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder."

Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.

Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.

As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.

Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. On a single day in September 2025, nearly $39 million had gone to three such companies.

Sponsor Message

Peña repeatedly brushed off the warnings. As recently as last month, he defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.

Long lines outside branches but customers are locked out

But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets.

Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank seized the lender Tuesday and announced plans to move customers' accounts, along with whatever assets still hold value, to other banks before liquidating what's left.

Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside with no way to cash out their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fueling public panic.

Officials appealed for calm and said they had begun repaying depositors, opening new accounts elsewhere for about 280,000 who had banked only with Ueno.

"The banking system is sound," insisted Pedro Acosta Bernal, appointed interim central bank president Wednesday after Carvallo resigned at Peña's request.

Authorities have detained eight senior Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale. Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud. Lawyers for several of the detained said they needed time to review the allegations before they could comment.

Protesters in the streets

Hundreds of employees of Ueno Bank and other companies belonging to Grupo Vázquez, the bank's parent conglomerate, protested outside the Labor Ministry on Thursday, demanding severance and unpaid wages with their jobs in limbo and their salaries trapped at the failed bank. A day earlier, hundreds of retirees, depositors, university students and workers flooded the streets of Asunción, the capital.

Sponsor Message

"We want your head, Peña!" they shouted. Their signs demanded Peña's impeachment, called him "the enemy of savers" and pleaded "Give us back our money." Riot police fired pepper spray and rubber pellets to push back the crowds.

Many demonstrators saw Ueno's collapse not just as the result of risky banking but as a case study in official corruption. Only Venezuela ranks worse in South America on the latest index of perceived corruption from Transparency International, a global watchdog.

"This is yet another assault on honest, hard-working citizens, people whose small savings are the fruit of years of labor," said protester Belarmino Balbuena.

At the national stadium that once bore Ueno's name, the bank's logo had already been scrubbed away. But across the capital, fresh graffiti denounced politicians as thieves.

World.title: Head of Justice Department office on Civil Rights resigns
World.content:
Head of Justice Department office on Civil Rights resigns

toggle caption i Andrew Harnik/Getty Images North America

The head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, Harmeet Dhillon, is out after 18 tumultuous months in charge.

Dhillon is the first senior department official to depart the Trump administration since Democrats retook control of the House and Senate in midterm elections.

Attorney General Todd Blanche announce Dhillon's departure on X.

"Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who led the Civil Rights Division with conviction the past 18 months. She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor. The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors," he wrote.

Sponsor Message

During her tenure Dhillion radically reshaped the Civil Rights Division, pushing out roughly 300 attorneys, hiring inexperienced ideological allies to replace them and using the division's enforcement powers to advance President Trump's MAGA agenda.

The changes marked a dramatic shift for the Civil Rights Division, which was created some 70 years ago during the movement to end racial segregation in the U.S. For decades, it fought to protect the constitutional rights of all Americans across all aspects of life, from housing and employment to education and policing.

Dhillon, a conservative attorney and Trump loyalist, came into office with a different view. In her eyes, the division had only been protecting the rights of people of color, and she promptly shifted to aggressively pursuing conservative priorities.

"We don't just slow down the woke," she said at a Federalist Society event in 2025. "We take up the cause to achieve the executive branch's goals."

Under her leadership, the division redirected its energies to enforce Trump's executive orders, including ending the alleged radical indoctrination in schools, defending women from "gender ideology extremism," and combatting antisemitism and purported anti-Christian bias.

In the run-up to the midterm elections, the Civil Rights Division sued dozens of states demanding they turn over voter information—in furtherance of Trump's allegations of voter fraud.

Election officials pushed back, and courts tossed the department's lawsuits.

The division also accused numerous universities and law schools of discriminating against white and Asian students, and sued UCLA and Harvard for allegedly allowing antisemitism to flourish on campus.

Sponsor Message

Many Civil Rights Division veterans say Dhillon's view of the unit and its mission is a perversion of

"Harmeet Dhillon has been the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history," said Stacey Young, a former division attorney. "Dhillon wielded the enormous power of the Justice Department to threaten universities, state and local officials, and election workers in spurious cases that rarely won in court."

"Americans' civil rights don't enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded. Dhillon decimated it," said Young, who now heads who Justice Connection, a group of department alumni that provides support to DOJ employees.

World.title: Discursive Verses: Is 'Spend Dat' the best financial indicator of America's grift economy?
World.content:
Discursive Verses: Is 'Spend Dat' the best financial indicator of America's grift economy?

toggle caption i Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images for BET

After spending three hours counting the pores on Elizabeth Holmes' and Nathan Fielder's faces, I couldn't help but think how perfect Yung Miami's "Spend Dat" would've played over the closing credits. Whatever you feel about the veracity of the protagonist in the blockbuster doc You Can See Everything, there is no doubt about her innate ability to cop and blow money fast. She's probably about as familiar with Diddy's favorite City Girl as she is with Abbott & Costello. But a scammer of such ill repute deserves an apropos theme song. Hell, maybe we all do.

Sponsor Message

When people complain about hip-hop no longer being political, what they're really talking about is commercial rap's long-fizzled countercultural agenda. The politics of consumption and corruption however have never enjoyed a louder ringing endorsement. Like a billionaire hogging the bully pulpit. To that end, no song in 2026 comes closer to mimicking the feeling of being the violated and the violator. On its face, "Spend Dat" is a get-money flex dedicated to all the "scammers" and "booster b*****s." But behind that seductive veneer is the sadomasochistic loop of late-stage capitalism's long, punishing con. An inflation indicator like no other, it's easily our most American anthem of the year. And we're all transfixed, nodding along in unblinking commitment to the charade.

The video for "Spend Dat" feels like a throwback to the early 2000s, when making it rain in strip clubs was still obligatory signposting for selling the dream. It almost feels trite now that prediction markets allow us to place digital bets on democracy and buy-now, pay-later loans keep expanding on our freedom to fall deeper in debt. At least a good lap dance came with a tangible return on investment. Now we're all just being teased to death.

YouTube

When India.Arie echoed the public denouncement of "Spend Dat" — which included a call for Black folk to boycott the Billboard-charting song of the summer — another film, I Love Boosters, had just hit streaming. Unlike the aforementioned documentary on the blonde-haired, blue-eyed, white-collar scammer Holmes, rapper-turned-director Boots Riley's fictional narrative centered on the supposed scourge of the hood. In it, Keke Palmer plays an illegit booster, selling high-end fenced clothing out of the abandoned fast-food chicken joint she's squatting in while harboring her own fashionable aspirations. It takes an international worker-led intervention — and a sci-fi bopgun full of Marxist intentions — for her to realize the minor disruption she and her shoplifting girlfriends are causing is but a necessary cog in the ever-churning, exploitative wheel of global capitalism.

Sponsor Message

What Riley wants us all to understand, as an avowed communist who switched his weapon of choice from fronting Bay Area rap group The Coup to writing screenplays, is that we the people are hardly the problem. Even when sufferers turn into self-styled hustlers out of desperation instead of pooling their collective power. Like WEB DuBois before him, Riley calls his art propaganda. And he's equally adamant about calling art on the other end of the spectrum of propaganda, too. "When The Coup first came out they would call us a political rap group. And we'd be like, 'No,' " he said on a recent episode of Novara Media's podcast Downstream. "Don't call us that unless you're calling everybody that. Because what it then made it seem like was as if everything else was just what it is." Rather, art magnifying the status quo is not some benign representation of a fixed reality but an uncritical regurgitation of everything indoctrinated by the moneyed elite.

When the controversy surrounding "Spend Dat" reached a fever pitch earlier this summer, it came with the usual diatribe. The song was criticized for being culturally degrading. Even India.Arie caught a bunch of flak for stating the obvious when she said, "Everything you listen to see or eat is going to influence you." I don't blame anybody Black for getting in their feelings over the seemingly negative portrayals or stereotypical depiction centered in rap. But the buck doesn't stop there. It never has. "We are bound by all sorts of customs that have come down as second-hand soul clothes of white patrons," as DuBois so eloquently stated 100 years ago this month in his essay Criteria of Negro Art. "We are ashamed of sex and we lower our eyes when people will talk of it," he says, concluding with this thought: "Our worst side has been so shamelessly emphasized that we are denying we have or ever had a worst side."

Sponsor Message

YouTube

The same week "Spend Dat" went platinum, Yung Miami appeared on "The Breakfast Club" to promote the release of her solo debut, Watch Dis. When asked about the criticism the song received, she defended it as inspirational music "that builds you up to want to be somebody." Rap may have started at the bottom. But at some point the script flipped. The systems hip-hop was oriented to rebel against became the metric for its success. The victors, in this case, were found striving for the same spoils. Having finally achieved the market share and visibility we'd been denied for decades, we became centrists: a marginalized culture subsumed by the mainstream. Commercial rap made itself a useful tool of the establishment, and the perfect racially coded scapegoat.

If the American Dream really is a pyramid scheme, as commonly critiqued, all hail the original scammers who bricked up the foundation. Even with their fuzzy slave-owner math (discounting Blacks as three-fifths human) and gender restrictions on equal rights (ratified while rocking powdered wigs), the nation's so-called founders created a system even the lowest caste could be constrained and cajoled into aspiring to.

It reminds me of the funniest meme I encountered online last week: a comic strip calling cap on the promise of Black capitalism. It pictures two brothers chopping it up, with one plainly stating, "You can't buy your way out of a system that was built on selling you." Totally undeterred, the other replies back, "Well, I'm gonna try!" before invoking the Black power era's "by any means necessary" rhetoric. In the next panel, Malcolm X expresses frustration over his words being misused to validate participation in the futile American experiment.

We've been hoodwinked, indeed. Bamboozled. Led astray. Run amok and flat-out deceived like a mug.

The grift is so complete that it's almost impossible to distinguish the mark from the actual con artist. Whether it's a convicted felon hiding fraudulence behind white tears, or a ride-or-die who bossed up with the boosters and got it off the muscle. In a year when prediction markets and predatory installment loans sucked us all dry, inflation skyrocketed and tech billionaires quickened the apocalypse, an ode to America's undying hustle and flow might be the closing credits theme we all deserve.

World.title: Russell Brand is convicted of rape, and judge says he'll get a prison term
World.content:
Russell Brand is convicted of rape, and judge says he'll get a prison term

toggle caption i Alberto Pezzali/AP

London — Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of rape and sexual assault charges involving four women on allegations dating back more than 20 years.

Judge Joel Bennathan said the British actor-comedian faces a "significant" prison term when he is sentenced Monday. Brand had been free, but the judge rejected a bail request because of the possibility he might flee and he was taken into custody.

"I regret the hardship caused to the children, of course," the judge said. "But the hardship has been caused by serious criminal offending by their father."

Brand was a ruthless, calculating, manipulative "sexual predator," prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said at trial.

Sponsor Message

Brand, 51, denied the charges and testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man and once led a promiscuous life but had never forced anyone to do something against their will.

He was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Brand closed his eyes as the guilty verdict on the rape count was read but showed no emotion otherwise. When bail was denied, he gestured to his lawyers that he was OK and repeatedly said, "I'm good, I'm good, I'm good," before being taken away.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of London's Metropolitan Police said the conviction was "a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them."

"Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women," he said. "As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement."

The jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court deliberated more than eight hours over two days.

Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him to the Greek and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.

Sponsor Message

In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.

Brand was convicted of sexually assaulting a woman during a birthday party at a London bar in 2004, but cleared of orally raping her in a restroom.

He was also found guilty of kissing and groping another woman at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005 and of anally raping a fan he met backstage at one of his comedy shows in 2009.

The final conviction was for sexually assaulting a different woman who says the comedian demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an  in 2009.

Brand was acquitted of raping another woman in a hotel room during the Labour Party's annual conference in the seaside town of Bournemouth in 1999, and of attempting to indecently assault a woman by dragging her into the men's bathroom at the London office of music channel MTV.

The Associated Press doesn't name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.

Brand said in the witness box that the criminal case had a devastating impact on his life and family.

"My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations," he said.

Brand's lawyers argued that the alleged victims were undermined by the fact that they only went to police years after the alleged assaults and following the broadcast of a 2023 documentary that contained anonymous allegations against Brand.

Brand testified that friends and colleagues had abandoned him.

His wife, Laura, who accompanied him to court, testified as a character witness in his defense, but no one with relevant evidence was willing to give evidence on his behalf, Brand said.

World.title: First-time homebuyers remain scarce, but a record share of them pay all cash
World.content:
First-time homebuyers remain scarce, but a record share of them pay all cash

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

The share of first-time homebuyers remains at a near-record low of 22% as a housing shortage and high prices sideline many, according to a new report by the National Association of Realtors. But those who are managing to buy are older and wealthier than in the past, and 1 in 10 paid all cash, a record high since such data was collected starting in 2003.

"Inheritances are really driving this," said Jessica Lautz, deputy chief economist at the NAR.

First-time buyers who paid all-cash were more likely than those who financed a house to use an inheritance (28%) or proceeds from the sale of an inherited property (21%). They were also older.

Sponsor Message

NAR finds the median age of all first-time buyers remains at 40, a record high. For first-time buyers who financed a purchase it was 38, while for those who paid all-cash it was 54. "They waited a significant period of time for that generational transfer of wealth to come through," Lautz said.

For first-time buyers overall, personal savings was the biggest source of funding for a down payment. But in another shift, more people used assets – like a 401(k), stocks, or cryptocurrency – than financial help from family or friends. Older buyers have had more time to save up, Lautz said, but she thinks there's another factor: "I think it's uncomfortable to ask mom and dad for a gift or loan when you're hitting 40 versus your young 30s."

The share of first time buyers using an inheritance is likely to grow in coming years as boomers reach their 80's and beyond. As the report noted, "there is a growing divide among those who are saving independently and priced out of homeownership, versus those who are waiting on the sidelines but then given a generational transfer of wealth."

Real estate agents around the country are seeing the change.

"I would say in the first 15 years of my career, I saw virtually zero first-time home buyers paying all cash," said Jason Miller, a broker with Trust Real Estate Company in St. Cloud, Minn.

But he's had a number of them since the COVID-19 pandemic, when homebuying surged. "They knew they had to absolutely have the most sterling offer possible to compete in the competitive marketplace," he said.

High mortgage rates are also driving all-cash bids, Miller said, since they make it far more expensive to finance a home for 30 years. And not all families wait until death to pass on wealth. Miller sees more clients getting help from family members who may have paid off their own home, or have equity in a second property they can sell and "are gifting some or all of that money." They're viewing it as a kind of "future inheritance," he said.

Sponsor Message

For some younger first-time buyers, relatives may only be "lending them the cash" to make a bid more attractive, said Nate Johnson, a broker associate with RedKey Realty Leaders in St. Louis. Even with much of the national housing market in a major slump, he said his local market is still intensely competitive for buyers.

"They just know that if we're looking at five or six offers on the table, let's call it 10 offers on the table, which is not uncommon…maybe three of those offers will be all cash," he said.

After closing on a property, Johnson has seen some buyers refinance into a mortgage and pay back their family member.

The rise of all-cash offers makes the market even tougher for those who struggle to save up for a down payment with today's sky-high home prices.

"For a long time I thought I wanted to buy a house," said Seth Daphne Esmeson, who lives in Seattle and will soon turn 33. They and their spouse have good jobs, but also debt, including a car payment and student loans. Not only does Esmeson think they may never be in a position to buy, they've also decided it does not make sense at today's prices.

toggle caption i Jane Corbit

"Being that debt burdened, and also having to fix things on your home, like, it sounds really terrible," they said.

Esmeson is also not convinced that home equity would outpace other investments. They like their current rental and landlord so are sticking with it for now.

Still, it's frustrating that the housing market worked better for previous generations. "We have the short end of the deal," they said, and "the gap is expanding."

There's probably only one way they might ever be able to buy. "If I received an inheritance," they said. But "I love my mom dearly and I don't want to look forward to that, or really want to strategize around that."

World.title: Teens worldwide aren't getting enough exercise -- especially girls
World.content:
Teens worldwide aren't getting enough exercise — especially girls

toggle caption i Mohamed Abdiwahab/AFP/via Getty Images

The World Health Organization recommends adolescents spend at least one hour a day exercising enough to basically break a sweat — a brisk walk or a more intense pick-up soccer game. Lot's of research suggests this level of activity is crucial for supporting growing bodies and minds.

But new global data suggests only a small minority of kids and teens get that much. In fact, one in four report not hitting 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous exercise any day of the week, according to a new study in The Lancet Global Health. Girls, as well as adolescents from middle- and lower-income countries reported even lower levels of exercise.

Sponsor Message

"The findings are disappointing, because one of the major results is that the trend over the last 15 years is flat," says Fiona Bull, head of the physical activity unit at the World Health Organization, who co-authored the study. "These data are a call for us to relook at what we're doing. Business as usual will not change these trends."

Changing habits in those teen years could have a lifelong impact, says Solveig Cunningham , a global health researcher at Emory University. "As an adolescent, if your baseline is zero days of physical activity, that's going to be your baseline as you go into adulthood."

What 3 million teens revealed

So how do researchers know whether adolescents are — or aren't — working up a sweat? It's tricky. Researchers would love to be able to strap smartwatches to kids to get detailed data, but that would be costly. The next best strategy is to ask a basic question — how many days during the past week were you active for at least 60 minutes?

The report draws on data from surveys posting some version of this question to over 3 million adolescents from 140 countries over the past 15 years. Only about 14% of kids worldwide reported getting an hour a day of exercise. Globally, the average adolescent reported less than 3 such days a week, the study found.

Sponsor Message

Kids from low- and middle-income countries tended to be less active than their counterparts from wealthier Western countries, the study found. There's no one explanation for this pattern, but a few likely causes stand out.

"Physical activity is an issue of opportunity," says Andrea Ramirez Varela , an epidemiologist at the University of Texas Health Science Center in Houston. In many lower income countries, she says that the environment — where they live, go to school and play — often restricts opportunities to be active. The study didn't break down the urban and rural divide, but some research suggests rural adolescents in lower-income countries move more, she says, often out of necessity. In increasingly populated urban areas, activity is lower.

Many cities aren't designed to be walkable, says Varela. In Latin America, where she does most of her research, "many parents think it's unsafe to just let your kids walk alone to and from places," she says — much less go out and play independently. In some urban centers, air pollution can make being active outdoors unhealthy too.

Screens may play a role as well. After school, "kids and adolescents, when they arrive home, they start watching TV, they are in front of a screen," says Valrela. "Because this digital world is so attractive, they are going to be sedentary the rest of the day."

Cultural barriers

The report also revealed a stubborn gender gap.

Girls were less active than boys in virtually all countries. Nearly 30% don't exercise at all during the week compared to 22% of boys. Only 11% of girls were active daily compared to 17% of boys. And girls' weekly average of active days was lower (2.4 vs 3).

"It's very worrying to see this gender difference so early," says Bull, noting that the difference often persists into adulthood.

Different norms around what's appropriate for girls often drive that divergence.

Sponsor Message

"In many places, when girls reach puberty, there are taboos to engaging in physical activity," says Cunningham. Take India, for example, where Cunningham has focused much of her research. "Mothers or grandmothers will say, 'Well, you know, we don't want girls spending a lot of time outside. Their skin might get darker. That might have negative implications for whether they can get married."

Cunningham notes that girls are active in other, often less intense ways. "In South Asia, as well the United States, a substantial proportion of girls' active time is doing chores," she says "If the guys are outside playing and the girls are inside sweeping, they're both active, but it's kind of not the same thing."

What would get them moving?

Improving these trends won't be easy, experts told NPR. Redesigning cities to be more walkable, for instance, takes many years and substantial investment. Many experts point to schools as a practical place to start. "To move the needle, we need to focus on the settings where kids and adolescents spend most of their time," says Varela.

In fact, data suggests that countries with higher levels of adolescent exercise tend to have more structured time for sport during or after the school day. Building up such programs in other countries might help close the gap, says Varela, especially if done in ways that make sport accessible and affordable.

Such efforts will require sustained attention from policymakers, Varela says, who face pressures from all sorts of competing interests. But she says it's worth it.

"Not solving the problem in this stage of life will perpetuate the problem in adulthood," she says, where the costs to society, in terms of poor physical and mental health, only become greater.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: What's next for Democrats after the midterms. And, a look at the outstanding races
World.content:
What's next for Democrats after the midterms. And, a look at the outstanding races

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Democrats won this week in districts and states that President Trump carried by double digits just two years ago. The party now has its largest Senate majority since the passing of the Affordable Care Act during Obama's early presidency. Senate results from Alaska and Mississippi are still pending. If those races favor Democrats, their majority could grow to 54, plus the two independents who caucus with them.

toggle caption i Allison Robbert/AP

🎧 A few tight House races remain uncalled , but the swing toward Democrats already rivals the post-Nixon Watergate backlash, NPR's Tamara Keith tells Up First. She highlights two notable race surprises that happened this week. One was in Nevada's 2nd District, which has been Republican since the 1980s. Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson claimed victory overnight. The other was in Alabama's 2nd District, where Shomari Figures overcame redistricting that favored Trump by 14 points. Figures won by more than seven points.

Here's a summary of the results.

Sponsor Message

For more than a year, Democrats urged voters to elect them to lower costs and eliminate corruption. Now, the party must act to fulfill its campaign promise. The new Congress is unlikely to see much major legislation signed into law, but Democrats plan to launch ambitious investigations in the House and Senate. Democratic Party leaders and political analysts shared their insights with Morning Edition on the midterm election results, discussed the impacts of mid-decade redistricting efforts and outlined the party's next steps.



🎧 Most legislation still requires 60 votes to pass the Senate, and Trump has fluctuated between saying he will be Mr. Veto and expressing willingness to work with Democrats, NPR's Sam Gringlas says. Democrats are interested in restoring enhanced ACA health subsidies, reversing Medicaid cuts, asserting control over tariffs and pushing to end the war with Iran. Gringlas says this election has intensified pressure on Democrats. He points to a voter he met this summer, who said that if Democrats gained control, they would have to enact real changes, otherwise it wouldn't matter who they nominated for president in 2028.

Trump focused on his East Wing ballroom construction project during his first public appearance after the Republicans lost the House and Senate. When asked about the election, he said he wasn't to blame for his party's losses.



Sponsor Message

🎧 Trump quickly pointed out that he wasn't actually on the ballot , NPR's Emily Feng says. But he did urge voters to imagine he was. Voters associated his signature policies, like tariffs and the war in Iran, with rising inflation and gas prices. After Vice President JD Vance posted on social media yesterday suggesting that the war in Iran contributed to GOP losses, Trump somewhat agreed. The president cited its impact on pump prices, but doubled down on the war, saying he would act the same way again if he had to. With a Democratic Congress, Trump will encounter greater legislative gridlock, and Democrats could wield stricter funding controls on issues like immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict in Iran, Feng says.
