But directly influencing fuel prices, which are tied to the complex international oil market, will be challenging.

Life advice

Jan Hakan Dahlstrom/Getty Images/Stone RF

Have you ever found yourself drowning in a sea of your own mail or other documents? Well, it is time to tackle that paper chaos. Don't panic. Kacy Paide, a professional organizer with more than 20 years of experience, has shared tips with Life Kit to make the task less overwhelming.

✉️ Focus on your closest pile and separate it into active and inactive ones. Active items require follow-up, like calls or bill payments, while inactive items do not.

✉️ Clearly mark the due date on active documents with a bold, permanent marker on a sticky note.

✉️ Save important documents like birth certificates, passports, product manuals, tax papers and medical records. Choose a method that suits your habits: alphabetize, color-code or simply label. For easy access, place vital documents in a brightly colored folder.

✉️ You don't need to shred everything that has your name and address on it. The Federal Trade Commission advises destroying documents containing sensitive information, such as account numbers, birth dates, passwords, signatures and Social Security numbers, to protect against identity theft.

✉️ Start small by dedicating just 25 minutes to decluttering. Remember, organizing is an ongoing process that needs regular maintenance and adjustments.

Sponsor Message

Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Picture show

toggle caption i Svet Jacqueline for NPR

In Ukraine's Kherson region, a brief ceasefire brought a momentary return to normalcy. Brokered by first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo last week, the truce allowed hundreds of residents to evacuate from a Russian-occupied town and provided a rare few days of peace in a frontline city. Russia and Ukraine agreed to the deal to help Oleshky, a town near Kherson that was occupied by Russian troops in 2022. The troops had mined the land around it, and food and medicine were rarely able to reach the people. This short pause in hostilities was a welcome relief, allowing families to fill the sidewalks, shoppers to hurry to stock up and cafe-goers to enjoy art-filled spaces. These photos capture a brief glimpse of everyday life for these people.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Barbara Glassman Dell

At Connecticut's Old State House, the annual Election Cake Bake-Off has been celebrating the sweet civic tradition of election cake for more than 250 years. This dessert has evolved from what it once was: a tough fruitcake, often soaked in alcohol. Chemical manufacturer 3M has reached a $7.35 billion settlement to resolve thousands of personal injury claims related to toxic chemicals found in firefighting foam. (via PRE News & Ideas) A new study shows that loon populations are declining across the birds' southern breeding range, but Maine stands out with a slight increase in loon productivity, according to Birds Canada. (via Maine Public)

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Sen. Gillibrand says Democrats must end Iran war, hold Trump accountable. But how?
World.content:
Sen. Gillibrand says Democrats must end Iran war, hold Trump accountable. But how?

toggle caption i Graeme Sloan/Getty Images

Democrats have won back Congress. Now comes the harder question: How much can they actually change with President Trump still in the White House?

"I dare him to veto that," Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York told Morning Edition, challenging Trump to reject bipartisan legislation restoring Medicaid coverage.

Gillibrand said Democrats would focus on lowering costs, restoring health care access and ending the war in Iran.

Democrats also face pressure to hold the Trump administration accountable, with new investigative powers and the possibility of a third impeachment.

Asked about impeachment, Gillibrand did not commit to pursuing it.

"We can do both," she said, proposing a ban on stock trading by members of Congress and senior administration officials.

Sponsor Message

Like other Democrats, Gillibrand cited the war in Iran as a factor in the party's election victories, saying Trump had broken his promise to avoid prolonged wars as the conflict drove up costs.

"We have to end this war in Iran," she said.

Trump acknowledged Wednesday that the war had contributed to Republicans' election losses. But the conflict continues, with Iranian officials warning against renewed U.S. attacks. How Democrats intend to bring the war to an end remains unclear.

In her interview with NPR's A Martínez, Gillibrand also discussed Democrats' gains in Republican states, Trump's ballroom and cuts to food assistance and medical research.

Listen to the full conversation by clicking the blue button above.

The digital version was edited by Treye Green.

World.title: Family of injured Wainwright soldier holds bedside vigil in burn unit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The family of a Canadian soldier severely burned during the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta tells CBC News they're just as worried about his mental health as they are about his physical trauma. With catastrophic burns over much of his body, Pte. Liam Ramage can barely move or speak.

The mother of a soldier fighting to recover from severe burns he sustained in last month's CFB Wainwright fire says she worries not only about his physical injuries, but also his mental health.

Pte. Liam Ramage, 27, of Red Deer, Alta., was one of dozens of service members hurt in an out-of-control grass fire on the central Alberta military base on Oct. 17. Four died.

Roughly 40 per cent of Liam’s body was affected, mostly third- and fourth-degree burns, mainly to his face, neck and throat, according to his mother Cheryl Ramage.

“Some to his arms, really bad to his hands, the upper and the palms," she told CBC News in an interview this week. "Some of his legs, … some to his back and some to the top of his feet.

"They’re doing skin grafts to the majority. His eyelids even have skin grafts on them, so he can’t open his eyes.”

Marisa Ramage, left, the wife of Pte. Liam Ramage, and Cheryl Ramage, right, Liam's mother say they are taking it day by day, knowing his recovery could take years. (Kory Siegers/CBC)

Cheryl, and Liam’s wife Marisa, have been constants at his bedside at the University of Alberta Hospital in Edmonton. He can barely move, speak or see.

“Being locked in your own mind is a form of torture right?” said Cheryl, who’s a nurse. “His mental health is going to have to be addressed right away.”

She describes the days since the fire as devastating.

Being a nurse can sometimes help her compartmentalize her feelings, but it doesn’t shield her from them, Cheryl said.

“I can kind of turn clinical. When I go into his room, especially if I’m with somebody else, I can be like, ‘This is what this line’s doing and that’s what this dressing is for.’ I can kind of remove myself from it, if that makes sense — I can just talk about the injuries, not looking at it like it’s my son. But if I’m there by myself or go home by myself, I’m a disaster."

‘Identified him by his toes’

Marisa said she first learned something might be wrong in a text from her father alerting her to the situation in Wainwright on the day of the fire. The last time she had heard from Liam was a text earlier in the day.

Cheryl’s other son Rowan, who was also training at CFB Wainwright, texted his mother to let her know he was OK. But she did not hear back from Liam. She went to Liam and Marisa’s house in Edmonton to wait for word.

Hours later, at around 3 a.m. local time the next day, warrant officers knocked on the door and gave them the terrible news — “a mother’s worst nightmare,” Cheryl said.

A photo of Marisa (left) and Liam (right) on March 31, 2024. Liam joined the military in March 2024 and went to basic training the following month. (Supplied by Marisa Ramage)

“I don’t think I stopped shaking for the entire amount of time that they were there,” Marisa said.

The pair rushed to the hospital.

“We couldn’t recognize his face,” Cheryl said. “He was completely covered in dressings and so swollen. He was not recognizable. We identified him by his toes.”

‘It’s so unpredictable’

Liam is fighting pneumonia. He has had three surgeries and three strokes, which paralyzed the left side of his body, though he’s showing some toe, hip and leg movement. He has necrosis — the death of body tissue — on several fingers, his ears and nose.

He can now breathe on his own, though he is placed on a ventilator at night to give his lungs a break. Thanks to a special device, he has been able to speak a few words in recent days.

“He mouthed my name when I was in there with my dad and that was shocking for me,” Marisa said. “I did have a really good cry after.”

Marisa and Liam started dating in 2020 and married in 2023. (Supplied by Marisa Ramage)

Both women say it’s hard to imagine what life will look like for Liam, an outgoing, active man who loves music, cooking and playing hockey.

“It is so unpredictable,” Cheryl said. “He’s got a stroke — is he going to be able to walk again? He’s got skin grafts — does he have to learn how to walk again? Is he going to lose his fingers?

“We really try to take it day to day. … We do know it’s going to be months and months and months — if not years — of recovery. But what that recovery looks like? We just can’t tell at this point.”

She worries about Liam's mental health; the deadly fire still haunts him.

“He does say he remembers it," Cheryl said. "He does say that he thinks about it.

"I can’t imagine the torture of going through that, not being able to open your eyes or move or talk.”

A radio has been placed by Liam’s bedside to distract him, playing classic rock and NHL games with his favourite team, the Montreal Canadiens.

“A lot of us talking to him is reminding him that he’s safe and he’s at the hospital ... and that he is OK,” Marisa said.

Military career

The military was always a passion for her son, Cheryl said.

“Liam tried a few other things first, but the military was always what he wanted to do.”

A sign for Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright, on Oct. 18, 2026, the day after a serious incident that resulted in a fire caused deaths and injuries. (Jennifer Gauthier/Reuters)

He enlisted in March 2024 and completed a tour in Latvia. He was training in Wainwright to prepare for a second Latvia tour.

As a military mother, Cheryl said she knows the risks that soldiers face but never expected something like this.

“I never dreamt something would be two hours from home.”

Military, community support

Both women said the support from family, friends and the wider community has given them strength.

Their priority now is Liam and his recovery, not the fire or the military’s response. Three investigations are underway.

“That was a freak accident,” Marisa said. “They couldn’t have predicted that that would happen. And the military has been supportive of everything.

"We’ll have questions later but we are definitely focused on Liam.”

“Nothing [about] what started the fire will change where we’re at,” Cheryl said. “I have no interest in that at this moment. … They don’t stop war because it’s windy or anything like that. They have to prepare in all conditions.

“Do I place blame? Am I angry right now? No. I wish it wouldn’t have happened.”

Marisa and Cheryl say this Remembrance Day has new meaning for them.

“Hold your family a little closer,” said Marisa. “You never know what could happen. Honestly. Hold them close.”

“I didn’t hope that this would happen to my son,” said Cheryl. “I wish it hadn’t. But I’m proud for him.”

World.title: Mexican judge arrested over alleged $2M bribe to release Ryan Wedding's second-in-command
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Mexican judge has been arrested on allegations that he accepted a $2-million US bribe in exchange for granting bail to a man accused of acting as second-in-command to Ryan Wedding, the former Canadian Olympic snowboarder turned alleged drug kingpin, American officials said on Thursday.

The U.S. Department of Justice said Luis Benitez Alcantara is accused of using his official position to secure the release of Andrew Clark, a 36-year-old Canadian man alleged to play a key role in a violent international drug trafficking ring, thus allowing Clark to evade detention.

Benitez Alcantara, 49, was arrested on Sunday in Colombia and a request will be made for his extradition, U.S. officials said. He was arrested on a nine-count federal indictment and, if convicted, could face a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison for each count, they said.

"Crooked public officials, no matter where they are, who assist drug traffickers operating here at home will face justice in the United States," U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a news release.

Clark was first arrested in Mexico in October 2024, on U.S. charges of drug trafficking, murder and attempted murder, the release said. Wedding was also named on the charges.

The following month, American officials formally requested that Clark be extradited to face prosecution in the U.S., it said. From then through February 2025, it's alleged that Clark transferred about $2.75 million in small increments and through intermediaries in a bid to be freed from Mexican custody.

Officials allege Clark also struck a deal to pay Benitez Alcantara, the district judge overseeing his extradition proceedings, about $2 million in exchange for ordering his release. It's alleged Benitez Alcantara granted him bond and ordered his release in February of last year, on the same day he allegedly received the bribe.

Clark was arrested again days later and taken to the United States, where his criminal case is pending.

Wedding, meanwhile, was arrested in Mexico in January of this year and taken to the United States to face drug trafficking, murder and attempted murder charges. He remains in federal custody awaiting two trials in March and October of next year.

World.title: What to watch for as Carney introduces his 2nd federal budget
World.content:

Prime Minister Mark Carney will deliver his second federal budget on Thursday as the Liberal government reveals next steps in its plan to support the country through an affordability crunch and the trade war.

Carney has spent much of the first 20 months of his prime ministership retooling the Canadian economy with an eye toward growth. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne is promising more details on what's to come next to further boost economic expansion.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday while helping make his own shoes — continuing the budget tradition of finance ministers getting a new pair before delivering an economic update — Champagne said this document will reveal how Canada will become "masters of our destiny."

"You need to invest in growth, you need to invest alongside businesses. You also need to invest in sovereignty," he said.

Champagne holds up a boot during a tour of the Pajar shoe factory in Montreal on the eve of the budget. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)

Some indicators suggest those investments are paying off: the Bank of Canada and the International Monetary Fund are projecting roughly two per cent GDP growth next year. The OECD expects growth to be lower than that, but still higher than all other G7 countries except the U.S.

The unemployment rate, which has seen some relatively wild swings amid the trade uncertainty, is lower than it was a year ago.

Foreign direct investment into Canada is high and the government's recently announced "productivity mega-deduction," a big ticket item that lets companies write off investments in a tax-advantaged way, is designed to spur things along even more.

Canadians will also get a chance to take some ownership in the projected growth: the budget may include details on how individual investors could eventually buy into the Canada Strong Fund, a new Crown-controlled sovereign wealth fund that will take ownership stakes in some major projects and businesses.

Affordability measures

Still, Champagne suggested more work is needed on the issue many voters tell pollsters they care about most: the rising cost of living, which worsened late last month when the Bank of Canada raised interest rates to tame inflation.

"Mark Carney remains one of the most popular prime ministers we've ever had. And all of that is happening in the context of people still saying that affordability is the top issue," Abacus Data pollster David Coletto said in an interview.

"But it doesn't mean that that immunity lasts forever. People still need to feel that this government cares about those day-to-day issues."

The most recent Statistics Canada jobs data also shows that while average hourly wages rose about 2.3 per cent year-over-year as of September, that fell short of the three per cent climb in consumer prices reported over the same period.

Canadian food bank usage hit record highs this year as some people struggle to buy the groceries they need.

Food bank usage continues to grow in Canada. (Alex Lupul/CBC)

The government has kept a lid on immigration since coming into office, dramatically dialling back the number of temporary migrants to tamp down housing prices.

That may have worked to some extent: national average home sale prices are 22 per cent lower than they were at the March 2022 peak while rent has dropped about nine per cent from its all-time high in May 2024, according to the latest industry figures.

The budget will reveal immigration targets for the coming two years.

The Conservatives have hammered the government for rising prices, demanding Carney do more to help consumers shoulder energy price increases largely driven by the U.S. and Israel-Iran war.

They also want Ottawa to cut immigration levels further, framing it as part of the affordability agenda.

"Save you money — that's our mission as Conservatives, and it's our demand for the budget," Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre told reporters on Wednesday, reiterating his call for further tax relief on energy products.

"After a year and a half of Mark Carney, everything's worse."

WATCH | Poilievre on U.S. trade talks: After Democrats retake Congress, Poilievre says Canada must pressure for tariff-free trade | Duration closed caption 1:12 Asked about the U.S. midterm election results, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said 'Americans hate tariffs.' Suggesting Canada is the most popular country with the American people, Poilievre offered to work with Prime Minister Mark Carney to 'leverage' that goodwill to get a trade deal.

NDP Leader Avi Lewis, meanwhile, wants Ottawa to create a wealth tax, build 50 government-run grocery stores and make "a nation-building investment in health care."

The government is sensitive to the charge that it hasn't done enough to address affordability concerns, routinely pointing to last year's income tax cut, the move to scrap the consumer carbon tax and temporarily lifting federal levies on gas as ways it has helped.

WATCH | NDP proposes wealth tax: NDP's Lewis proposes tax on wealth over $10M before Carney tables federal budget | Duration closed caption 0:52 NDP Leader Avi Lewis proposed on Wednesday a 'wealth tax' starting at one per cent on those with assets worth $10 million or more in a plan he suggests could generate $40 billion in annual government revenue. 'It is time to tax wealth in Canada, not merely income,' Lewis said.

But after U.S. voters handed Trump's Republican Party a shellacking in this week's midterms, partly due to higher prices, politicians in this country are clearly attuned to demands that more needs to be done to avoid a voter backlash.

"We need to take care of Canadians, make life more affordable," Champagne said.

"We've already taken a number of measures to support Canadians, but at the same time we understand we need to support them now."

Deficit management

While Ottawa rolls out new initiatives it's also mindful of the deficit, which could be smaller than expected thanks to higher oil prices that have been a huge boon to government coffers.

Even if smaller than planned, the figure is still expected to be higher than the historical norm before the 2020s — and the parliamentary budget officer expects those figures to remain elevated for years.

The spring economic update pegged the deficit at $75 billion for the 2026-27 fiscal year.

This number will almost certainly change after accounting for energy-related revenue spikes and increased spending on initiatives like propping up tariff-hit industries like autos and steel.

The PBO projects the deficit will be about $63 billion this year before rising to $70 billion in the next, further adding to the federal debt, which is increasingly costly as interest rates rise.

Carney has rejigged how the government reports its spending, dividing federal outlays into two buckets: day-to-day operational spending and capital infrastructure. The government is expected to lay out its plan to balance the operational budget by 2027-28.

Canadians will also learn more details in this budget about the government's plan to privatize some of Canada's major airport operations. Those sales would result in a cash windfall, which could then be used to spend more on other planned capital-intensive infrastructure projects or pay down debt.

Whatever comes about, Poilievre isn't buying it: "Mark Carney is out of touch. His spending is out of control. Canadians are out of money."

Defence spending

Canadians will likely get a better sense in the budget of how much the Carney government's defence buildup is costing, where the money is going and where it will be coming from.

Tens of billions of dollars have been poured into national defence over the last year and a half to meet the old NATO benchmark of two per cent of the gross domestic product.

The Western military alliance is now asking members to increase spending further to five per cent of GDP (3.5 per cent direct military expenditures and 1.5 per cent on defence infrastructure) by 2035.

At the conclusion of the recent NATO summit in Turkey, Carney pledged his government would offer a full accounting for taxpayers.

"We will lay out in the budget an update with the decisions we're taking, where the fiscal track is, where the defence spending is, how we're spending the one-and-a-half per cent on defence-related expenditures, resilience expenditures, and that's the right time to do it," Carney said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the budget would provide an update on how it's meeting NATO defence spending targets. (Nicole Osborne/The Canadian Press)

Defence analyst Dave Perry of the Canadian Global Affairs Institute said details on how Canada met the two per cent target and what the pathway is to five per cent are long overdue.

He said there were 215 words devoted to defence spending in last year's budget, which was a disappointment in terms of explanation and justification.

The government, he said, needs to be more specific about what equipment it intends to buy and how it will pay for it.

World.title: Google offers schools AI-boosted search or none at all
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Google weaves artificial intelligence more deeply throughout its applications, the tech giant says school board leaders can choose to flip AI tools on — or off — for elementary and secondary students using their classroom apps.

But to keep using Google's ubiquitous search engine within that school-tech ecosystem, an AI-boosted version will soon be the only option.

For kids today, the company name itself is synonymous for researching online, so coupled with how deeply its products are embedded in education systems, this week's announcement quickly set off alarm bells — especially among those questioning putting AI tools at students' fingertips.

Yet others see the move as an impetus for schools to prioritize AI literacy and teaching responsible usage now, from the earliest grades onward.

WATCH | Google offers schools AI-boosted search engine, or none at all: Google tells schools to accept using its AI tools or lose full web search access | Duration closed caption 1:54 Concerned Canadian educators are speaking out after Google announced that students will not be allowed to access its main search engine unless their school systems also opt in to its AI features.

Entrenched in education systems

Google and Microsoft are the dominant tech players in Canadian schools, says education technology researcher Beyhan Farhadi, with their apps entrenched into the student experience.

In the case of the former, for example, teachers might post and mark schoolwork in Google Classroom. That, in turn, connects with their students' Gmail accounts, apps like Google Docs or Slides where kids create assignments and a version of Google's web browser for searching information, said Farhadi, an assistant professor of educational policy and equity at the University of Toronto.

Many students also work within this ecosystem on school-issued Chromebooks, the pared-down laptops running Google's operating system and apps .

Given that integration, Farhadi is concerned about Google making "pedagogical decisions that often school boards are beholden to, because they have already invested so much money into the technology."

Considering how central online research is for student learning today and Google having the most popular search engine, "I don't think you can understate how big of a thing it would be to suddenly have Google search just not be available," said Adam Dubé, an associate professor of learning sciences at McGill University in Montreal.

Google revealed updates to its offering to schools on Tuesday, including a new chatbot feature that coaches students to learn through back-and-forth exchanges that was made available immediately inside Google Classroom

That "guided learning" capability will also be blended into Google Search for students "in the coming months," Chris Phillips, Google's vice-president and general manager for education, wrote in a blog post, following a pilot in some U.S. schools this month.

The company offered more details in a social media post later Tuesday in response to ripples of negative reaction, saying the changes stem from educator feedback in recent months.

"If a school is not comfortable with that and simply wants AI off, then they have the choice to not have search on at all," Phillips told education outlet Chalkbeat.

A Google statement on X this week offered more details about the changes, saying they were informed by recent feedback from educators. (News from Google/X)

Alternatives and workarounds

Non-profit group Common Sense Media deemed Google Search's AI Overview and AI Mode as an "unacceptable risk" for kids and teens this summer, and some may be considering AI-blocking browser extensions or rival search engines to keep a more traditional web search for students, says education policy consultant Tom D'Amico.

But going that route doesn't solve ongoing issues such as youngsters accepting AI-fuelled search summaries without checking sources or using chatbots for schoolwork instead of doing it themselves, he added.

"As soon as that student leaves school and they go home ... they have access" to AI, perhaps through a Google or ChatGPT search on a non-school device, said D'Amico, a former director of education at the Ottawa Catholic School Board who now consults school leaders on AI policy.

LISTEN | Google search revamp leans into AI: Cost of Living 11:17 So long, Google search bar Google is changing how we Google. It's revamping its iconic search function and handing the reins over to AI. So, is this the end of the search engine as we know it? Paul Haavardsrud searches for answers with Siva Vaidhyanathan, the authour of The Googlization of Everything [https://www.ucpress.edu/books/the-googlization-of-everything-2/paper].

Instead, D'Amico believes now is the time for schools to prioritize teaching students AI literacy and responsible use of the technology across subjects and from the earliest grades.

"Students are going to go for the easy route," he said from Ottawa. "We need our teachers to teach them why that's not the right path."

Pushback on inevitability

That Google is positioning its search engine "as synonymous with artificial intelligence ... saying if you use Google, you're using AI" comes at a time of major debate about and emerging evidence suggesting AI usage leaves students worse off, said Dubé.

Art teacher Joyce Hatzidakis uses the AI tool Google Gemini in her high school classroom on Jan. 22 in Riverside, Calif. (Damian Dovarganes/Associated Press)

Polls have also indicated Canadians have "a negative or cautious stance towards AI and yet we're seeing it pushed ... and we're being told that it's inevitable," he added.

Farhadi feels schools are right to consider gradually exposing kids to AI tools, but she also thinks students don't have to be using them to learn about them.

"Just because students are using something outside of the classroom all the time doesn't mean that the classroom [can't] be a space of exception," where young people can practise thinking and communicating without being constantly shaped or influenced by technology, she said.

World.title: Maple Leaf Foods plans to raise prices again early next year, CEO says in earnings call
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There's more bad news coming your way in the grocery store.

The head of Maple Leaf Foods, one of Canada's leading prepared meats and poultry producers, says the company plans to hike its prices — again.

In a third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday, CEO Curtis Frank told analysts the company is dealing with higher fuel and poultry prices, on top of general inflation.

Maple Leaf raised prices earlier this year to help offset higher costs — the second such price increase in a year — but it hasn't been enough to mitigate rising expenses.

"We've seen more inflation enter the business than we have expected. That's accelerating," Frank said.

"We do have plans to adjust our prices in Q1," he added, noting that the company hasn't yet announced the price changes to customers, so it would be premature to comment on them further.

WATCH | Why is food so expensive? Marketplace: Why is food so expensive? | Duration 1:51 Canadians continue to suffer from sticker shock at the grocery store, but what are the real reasons food prices are taking a huge bite out of our budgets?

Shoppers have been dealing with persistent high food prices thanks to a combination of factors including climate change, fuel costs, tariffs and retailer pricing. Overall, grocery prices have increased 33 per cent since September 2020, according to Statistics Canada's most recent inflation numbers.

Meat has been behind much of the push. Beef prices have skyrocketed, for instance — ground beef cost on average $9.18/kg in September 2020, according to Statistics Canada monthly retail data, and by September 2026, it cost $16.92. And a striploin that cost $20.73/kg in September 2020 now costs about $35.74/kg.

Chicken, often considered a cheaper protein alternative, has also faced higher prices thanks in part to increasing demand and limited supply, although not to the same extent as beef. Chicken breasts cost on average $14.48/kg in September, compared to $12.03 in September 2020. Thighs increased to $13.36/kg from $9.60 during that same time period.

Poultry farmers have raised prices for live birds by about three per cent in the fourth quarter, "with very short advance notice," explained Frank.

"[That] is eight per cent year-over-year, which is a pretty material move in the poultry business," the Maple Leaf Foods CEO added.

CEO cites rising costs of feed and fuel

In addition, fuel surcharges have gone up 17 per cent since the second quarter, which Frank also called a "pretty material change."

"Those are really the two components — feed and fuel," he said. "Inflation and agricultural commodities that are a direct implication of what we've seen from a conflict situation in the world."

The continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz stemming from the war in the Middle East has disrupted oil shipments from the Gulf region, driving prices for fuel and other critical inputs, such as fertilizer and animal feed, higher.

That's on top of general inflation "in damn near everything else: labour, packaging and ingredients," Frank said.

Maple Leaf Foods is far from the first company to recently announce price increases or changes to its products to offset rising costs. The world's top consumer goods and food companies, from Coca-Cola and Procter & Gamble, to Nestle and Reckitt, have all warned of further price hikes next year.

In September, soup-maker Campbell's also announced it would be implementing more price increases. And just this last week, cereal producer Kellogg's revealed it had changed its recipe in the U.K., swapping out whole rice grains for rice flour due to "changing weather conditions" affecting the quality and availability of rice.

Meanwhile, Canadian food bank usage hit record highs this year. And a new report from the Salvation Army says nearly one in three Canadians is skipping or reducing meals because they can't afford groceries.

World.title: I thought extra academics made me a good mom. Now I wonder what my daughters lost
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This First Person column is the experience of Gurpreet Virdi-Bains, who lives in Caledon, Ont. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ .

One night, I looked up from wiping down the kitchen counter and noticed how dark it was outside. My daughters' backpacks were still by the door where they always dropped them. The dishwasher hummed in the background, the familiar signal that we were moving toward bedtime. I realized how much of the evening had already slipped by, and we hadn't really been together in it.

It was like this almost every evening.

A few months earlier, I had enrolled my daughters in a math enrichment program. They weren't struggling with math. I enrolled them because I didn't want them to fall behind — because I didn't want to be the parent who left an advantage on the table.

But standing there in the kitchen, I felt what that decision had quietly cost us. Our evenings had become a series of tasks. There was less lingering. Less room to simply exist.

My kids were already spending seven hours in a structured academic environment. Home was supposed to be the break. A craft might get started on a whim, or someone might pick up a book because there was nothing else to do.

When I think back to my childhood growing up in the 1990s, what stands out most is how little was expected of us after school.

I'm the youngest of three and the daughter of immigrants adjusting to life in a new country. When my two older brothers and I came home from school, we did our homework and then we scattered. Some of us were on the couch, some at the table, the TV humming in the background.

Virdi-Bains, pictured as a two-year-old, grew up in the 1990s. Her parents moved from India to Canada in the 1980s. (Submitted by Gurpreet Virdi-Bains)

We didn't sit down for formal family dinners. Sometimes we ate at different times, half on the sofa, half at the table. No one organized the evening. It simply unfolded.

There were no tutoring or academic enrichment programs waiting for us. We watched Family Matters and Full House. We played outside until it got dark. We read, got bored and figured out what to do next. School stayed at school.

At the time, it felt ordinary. Now I understand how much freedom lived in those evenings.

It wasn't that our parents were absent. They were navigating language and work in a place that still felt new, trying to create something steady for us. We felt safe and cherished in quieter ways — in the routines, in the meals waiting for us, in the expectation that we'd be home before dark.

That didn't mean education was unimportant. It simply looked different. Learning wasn't confined to worksheets or programs. It was woven into everyday life: helping in the kitchen, measuring rice into a pot, shaping roti balls between our palms, counting change at the store, noticing the trees on our walk home and asking questions about them. Nobody called it preparation but it was. We were learning how to look after ourselves.

My parents' version of involvement was sacrifice. It meant long work hours, putting our needs ahead of their own, and doing what they could to keep our lives stable, even if it meant not being present for every moment. They trusted that school would teach us what it needed to, and that we would figure out the rest. Looking back, I see how much faith was embedded in that approach. That kind of separation feels harder to hold onto now.

I care deeply about education. Before my children started school, I made sure they felt prepared and confident. I practised letters with them at the kitchen table, not as part of a structured plan but in small, unremarkable moments that felt more like play than preparation. We counted steps on the way to the park. I assumed that once school began, learning would mostly stay there, the way it had for me.

Instead, I found myself second-guessing every decision.

Was I doing enough? Should I be doing more?

The pressure crept in through small conversations with other parents. A casual mention at pickup. A program name said in passing. Just enough to linger.

Slowly, I began to believe that being a good parent meant adding more: more structure, more measurable academic progress. Letting evenings unfold started to feel irresponsible, even if my husband didn't fully see it the same way.

Writing this column has forced me to admit that some of the pressure wasn't coming from school or other parents. It was coming from me, the daughter of immigrants who doesn't want to squander opportunity. I had internalized the idea that if there was a way to get ahead, you took it, that leaving something on the table — whether it was extra practice, extra support or an added advantage — meant risking falling behind.

After about five months, I withdrew my kids from the program. It was thoughtful and well-run. I understood why families valued it. But I had lost sight of what I wanted our home to feel like.

Virdi-Bains has come to appreciate the value of unstructured time with her daughters. (Submitted by Gurpreet Virdi-Bains)

I still believe deeply in education. What has changed is what I feel compelled to protect: the ordinary moments that make up a childhood. I want my daughters to remember laughter in the kitchen more than the rush from one commitment to the next.

I notice it in small ways. My kids play longer without checking in with me. They ask more questions, even the ones that seem to come out of nowhere at bedtime. When something doesn’t work the first time, they’re more likely to try again on their own before coming to find me. I’d forgotten how much happens in the time I used to think was wasted. That’s often where they figure out what they actually like.

Some evenings, when I notice the light fading earlier than I expected, I remind myself that a free evening doesn’t mean my kids are falling behind. They can play or talk or be bored for a while, and that matters, too.

It's a choice I find myself coming back to again and again.

World.title: Ramayana: Part 1 has the muscle, but lacks a certain epic soul
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Growing up in Toronto, my family got our Indian cinema fix in the late ‘90s by renting bootleg VHS tapes from the basement of a shop on Lawrence Avenue. Usually, that meant fanciful Bollywood romances, but occasionally we'd pick up an episode of an 1987 TV series depicting the ancient Hindu epic poem, the Ramayana.

It was full of telenovela-esque facial reactions, tinfoil jewelry and my favourite: arrows that transformed into other things through the awesome magic of jump cuts. It was appointment viewing for millions of people in India, where it originally aired, and for the diaspora for years to come.

Now, nearly 40 years later, there's the first of two mega-budget adaptations in theatres, Ramayana: Part 1. And despite how visually impressive and modern it is, it's missing the soul found in that melodramatic low-budget TV series.

Believed to have been written several thousand years ago, the Ramayana is a story rooted in Hinduism. But it extends beyond one religion, culture or country. Generally, it's the journey of Prince Rama, a god in human form, as he is drawn into a war with the villainous King Ravana, who abducts the noble princess Sita. The film was directed by Nitesh Tiwari with actors from across Indian cinema — the Hindi-language A-lister Ranbir Kapoor, the Kannada-language star Yash and the Tamil- and Telugu-language actor Sai Pallavi, respectively.

The story's details change across South and Southeast Asia so much that, to quote the scholar A.K. Ramanujan , "one conception [of the story] is quite abhorrent to those who hold another."

And yet the characters are part of everyday life for millions of people, says Aparita Bhandari, an arts and culture reporter in Toronto who grew up in New Delhi.

"You go to the temple, the idea of Ram/Sita, this whole thing is just there in your kind of collective consciousness," she said.

Ranbir Kapoor stars as Prince Rama, a god in human form who is drawn into a war with the villainous Ravana. (Sony Pictures)

Beyond entertainment, the story is full of parables, dealing with struggles and ethics. For example, Prince Rama sacrifices his birthright to be king to his brother, Bharat, and accepts an unfair exile to satisfy his stepmother.

But even with a runtime of over three hours for the Hindi version — and much less for the English dub — some major characters had to be erased or sidelined.

"They had to really cut a whole bunch out of it. You know, like Kaushalya and Sumitra just never spoke," Bhandari said, referring to Rama's birth mother and another stepmother.

Shiv Reddy, a film reviewer who watched both the Hindi and English versions, says the latter even removes a scene with Bharat begging his brother to come back.

A shadow puppet theatre group performs the Ramayana in Jakarta, Indonesia, on Feb. 9, 2025. Southeast Asian cultures have many versions of the myth, which are told in various ways. (Yayuyoshi Chiba/Getty Images/AFP)

"It immensely changed my perception of Ranbir Kapoor's performance as Rama, and also his duty as a king," Reddy told CBC News from Orange, Calif. "And to remove it entirely feels like that conflict that [Rama] faces is removed also."

The end result feels like it's hurrying audiences along, with characters rarely dissecting their motivations, instead telling you something to get you to the next part.

Some glory

And in between that stiff dialogue were often-bombastic action sequences.

From the opening moments, we're greeted with a fantastical battle of angels and demons on an icy battlefield, with war rhinos and a flying elephant battling like Lord of the Rings met God of War and 300.

A flying war elephant arrives on a frigid battlefield in a scene from Ramayana: Part 1. (Sony Pictures)

Loud and crunchy sound design, punctuated by a score from Hans Zimmer, who co-composed it with the equally legendary A.R. Rahman, helped drive these scenes.

For a kid who grew up on that ‘80s series and comic book adaptations, the graphics were impressive (save for a few facial expressions of some demons).

Meeting the moment

The film is timely not just because it's out in theatres for the Diwali weekend — a holiday that celebrates Rama's victory.

It also meets a need for international audiences expecting grand action from the Indian film industry ever since S.S. Rajamouli's RRR in 2022 — and in the process brought together talent from across India and the world to work on both films, which together reportedly cost $500 million US.

Part 1 is playing in more than 50 theatres across this country. Part 2, which has a lot more of the story to cover, has now been delayed to 2028.

"The ambition helped…to tell this grand story," Bhandari said, adding that the money went to a whole wall of artists featured in the end credits. "There's a lot of people that have put a lot of effort into making this work. And I guess to a certain extent, it shows."

WATCH | The English-language trailer for Ramayana:

But one aspect of the film that some critics feel missed the mark was the use of AI, in post-production, to try to give this story more universal appeal.

In the English dub, which used human voice actors, AI changed the mouths of the actors on-screen to appear as if they were speaking English.

Tiwari, the director, said during the L.A. premiere that this was to "present the film to the world in their language."

For Reddy, it didn't work.

"It's uncanny, for sure," Reddy said. "Because the face is also changing, it feels like it's just not their performance."

Ultimately, AI is an apt analog for this adaptation. Ramayana: Part 1 feels like an AI-generated summary of the ancient epic. You get the gist, you get the polish, but none of the depth until you choose to seek it.

World.title: LIV Golf shutting down operations, lawyer says in bankruptcy hearing
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LIV Golf is winding down operations instead of launching a new version because of a lack of financial support.

A lawyer representing the organization announced the decision in a bankruptcy court hearing Thursday in New Jersey.

“The debtors are not currently proceeding with the LIV 2.0 plan,” Matthew Williams of Gibson Dunn said. “Instead, the debtors are toggling to a value-maximizing wind-down in their business."

LIV Golf lost Saudi Arabia funding in April after having spent more than $5 billion since 2022. LIV filed for bankruptcy in September. Since announcing plans for a new version, top players like Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton have bailed.

The league was originally run by Greg Norman. A few months after the start of the Iran war, PIF changed its investment strategy in April and said it would no longer pay for LIV Golf after the 2026 season.

The Asian Tour, which received a financial boost from LIV for an International Series, decided in July to renew an alliance with the PGA Tour and European tour.

And as LIV was trying to emerge from bankruptcy, filed on Sept. 8, the European tour laid down a crushing ultimatum by saying anyone who signed with LIV 2.0 need not apply for membership in the commercially known DP World Tour.

That would make European players ineligible for the Ryder Cup.

Guy Kinnings, the European tour CEO, called out LIV in an interview with The Scotsman when he said, “But we also have to protect the tour against an entity who spent, so we are told, over $7 billion, with one of their aims being to ‘destroy the DP World Tour.’”

Rahm, Sergio Garcia, Louis Oosthuizen and Tyrrell Hatton also said they would no longer stay with LIV, and the rival league also lost young players like David Puig of Spain and Tom McKibbin of Northern Ireland.

The year began with Brooks Koepka getting out of his LIV deal with one year remaining, and the PGA Tour created a path - with financial penalties - to return. Patrick Reed chose not to extend his deal and now is poised to return to the PGA Tour next year through his performance in Europe.

Rahm had said on Tuesday he would be willing to pay the same price as Koepka, though it was unlikely that same deal would be offered.

LIV 2.0 was pushing player equity and prize money that was more than half the $20 million purses for individuals when it began in 2022. LIV’s final event was in August in Indianapolis, won by Michael La Sasso. He failed to get through the second stage of European tour Q-school last week.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: Ibero-American foreign ministers unanimously back Argentina’s Falklands claim
World.content:
Ibero-American foreign ministers unanimously back Argentina’s Falklands claim

5th Thursday, November 2026 - 07:21 UTC Full article

“The Ibero-American community reaffirms, once again, its support for the Argentine Republic,” said Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno

Ibero-American foreign ministers meeting in Madrid unanimously approved a special communiqué backing Argentina’s sovereignty claim over the Falklands and calling on Argentina and the United Kingdom to resume negotiations, on the eve of the Hamburg hearing on the Sea Lion oil project.

The document, approved at the foreign ministers’ meeting held during the 30th Ibero-American Summit of Heads of State and Government, urges both governments to resume talks on the dispute “as soon as possible” and acknowledges Argentina’s “constructive attitude”. The Ibero-American Conference, which brings together the countries of Latin America with Spain, Portugal and Andorra, routinely adopts such a statement at its summits.

“The Ibero-American community reaffirms, once again, its support for the Argentine Republic,” said Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno, who called the issue “a sacred cause for Argentines” and defended the diplomatic route to end what he considers an anachronistic colonial situation.

The backing comes five days before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea holds hearings in Hamburg on November 10 and 11 on the four provisional measures Argentina requested on October 13 to halt Sea Lion, which is being developed by Israel’s Navitas Petroleum and Britain’s Rockhopper Exploration. According to the tribunal’s schedule, Argentina will present on the first day from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. and the United Kingdom from 3 p.m. to 6 p.m.; on the second day, Argentina will speak from 10.30 a.m. to noon and the UK will close from 5.30 p.m. to 7 p.m. Argentina’s agent is Ambassador Mario Oyarzábal. The tribunal’s 21 permanent judges include Argentina’s Frida María Armas Pfirter, its vice-president, while the United Kingdom, which has no judge of its nationality, has chosen British professor Vaughan Lowe as judge ad hoc.

Argentina is not asking the tribunal to rule on sovereignty, but on rights to maritime resources and the environmental obligations set out in the Law of the Sea Convention. Sea Lion is expected to begin development drilling in 2027 and commercial production in 2028.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has called Argentine attempts to interfere with commercial activity in the area “unacceptable”. According to Infobae, the British government will activate legislation before the end of the year to protect Navitas and Rockhopper from possible Argentine sanctions. London maintains that it will not negotiate sovereignty unless the islanders wish it.

World.title: One dead and more than 2,000 affected by El Niño flooding in the Galápagos
World.content:
One dead and more than 2,000 affected by El Niño flooding in the Galápagos

5th Thursday, November 2026 - 07:14 UTC Full article

Authorities announced repairs to the road linking the airport with the island and the removal of debris

Heavy rains linked to the El Niño phenomenon triggered a flash flood on Santa Cruz island in Ecuador’s Galápagos archipelago overnight from Friday to Saturday, leaving one person dead and more than 2,000 affected, according to local mayor Fanny Uribe. Water reached up to three metres deep in some neighbourhoods of Puerto Ayora, the island’s main town.

After some ten hours of heavy rain in the highlands of Santa Cruz, water rushed down a ravine towards the inhabited coastal areas. “Rescues were carried out using kayaks and Zodiacs, and most people were brought to safety,” said fire chief Freddy López, who estimated the water reached three metres in the La Cascada and La Unión neighbourhoods. There were no alarms: firefighters, Red Cross volunteers and young residents went door to door to wake people, some of whom had to swim out of their homes. Most took refuge in the Puerto Ayora Coliseum. A local foundation says it has identified at least 500 more people affected who are not on the official register because they are staying with relatives.

Authorities announced repairs to the road linking the airport with the island and the removal of debris. Uribe said she was negotiating housing vouchers with the government for families who lost their homes, was preparing to distribute 1,000 food kits and that the relocation of the La Cascada neighbourhood was being studied. Residents have organised community kitchens and aid networks; a fishermen’s foundation is serving three meals a day to some 1,200 people. According to El País, President Daniel Noboa had not commented publicly on the emergency.

The Environment Ministry said no deaths of giant tortoises or wild birds have been reported as a result of the rains. Farmers in the island’s highlands, whose produce largely feeds the local population, fear for their crops.

Santa Cruz, with about 15,000 inhabitants, is the most populated island in the Galápagos, some 1,000 kilometres from the mainland. Ecuador’s National Risk Management Secretariat declared a nationwide red alert for El Niño on September 29, and its effects are expected to peak in December.

World.title: Paraguay seeks to return part of the savings frozen at Ueno Bank within 24 hours
World.content:
Paraguay seeks to return part of the savings frozen at Ueno Bank within 24 hours

5th Thursday, November 2026 - 07:08 UTC Full article

Paraguay’s Senate on Wednesday approved a reform of the deposit guarantee law that would allow customers of Ueno Bank, taken over by the Central Bank on Tuesday, to receive an advance of up to 40 minimum wages, about 121 million guaraníes, within 24 hours of the bank’s resolution. The bill now goes to the Chamber of Deputies, which was due to consider it on Thursday.

The current law set a deadline of 15 days, extendable by a further 15, for the Deposit Guarantee Fund to pay savers at a failed bank. The approved text specifies that customers with loans from the bank will have only overdue instalments deducted, not their entire debt, and that the advance is a payment on account that does not change the total coverage of up to 75 minimum wages, about 228 million guaraníes per depositor. According to the Central Bank, that limit covers 97% of customers. Above that figure, the Social Security Institute, the pension fund, will be paid before large savers. The Senate rejected a proposal to extend the guarantee to all public funds deposited in the bank.

The Central Bank’s interim president, Liana Caballero, who took over after Carlos Carvallo’s resignation, said a first payment would be up to 10 million guaraníes and that depositors would be divided into three tranches, although there are still no dates, locations or requirements. “The operational side is the problem in paying out,” she acknowledged. The Association of Banks of Paraguay backed the advance but urged caution over using the fund to return money from pension funds.

“The priority of the government of Paraguay is and will be to protect with all our strength the fruit of that effort and to provide concrete, rapid and responsible answers,” President Santiago Peña said in a televised address. Peña cancelled his attendance at the Ibero-American Summit in Madrid. The opposition has said it will push for impeachment proceedings against him and Vice President Pedro Alliana.

The Central Bank took over Ueno after its solvency ratio fell to 5.56%, against a minimum of 12%, and it detected irregular loans to companies owned by the bank’s owners, the Vázquez Group. Eight executives were detained, according to the press. The crisis also affects South American football’s governing body, Conmebol, which has US$14 million deposited in the bank, although it says payment of prize money for the Copa Libertadores and Copa Sudamericana finals is not at risk. The Vázquez Group’s media outlets closed, leaving about 300 employees without pay. Groups of savers gathered outside the Central Bank on Wednesday night to demand their deposits.

World.title: Republicans look for culprits after defeat: Speaker of Congress steps aside and Vance points to Iran
World.content:
Republicans look for culprits after defeat: Speaker of Congress steps aside and Vance points to Iran

5th Thursday, November 2026 - 07:05 UTC Full article

Johnson, 54, a congressman from Louisiana, has been Speaker since October 2023, when his colleagues chose him as a consensus candidate after the ousting of his predecessor

Speaker of the US House of Representatives Mike Johnson, a Republican, said he will not seek to continue leading his party in the new Congress, while Vice President JD Vance blamed the Iran war for the Republican defeat in Tuesday’s midterm elections, an explanation President Donald Trump called “largely true” even as he defended the conflict.

Johnson, 54, a congressman from Louisiana, has been Speaker since October 2023, when his colleagues chose him as a consensus candidate after the ousting of his predecessor, Kevin McCarthy. The Speaker is third in the presidential line of succession, after the vice president, and has been one of Trump’s most loyal allies in Congress. With the Democratic victory, he will lose the post when the new House convenes on January 3, and Republicans will become the minority.

Johnson told his staff on Wednesday that he will not run to lead Republicans in that new phase. In a letter to colleagues he cited the toll three years in the job have taken on his family. “While the outcome of this midterm is not what we’d hoped and fought for, a new battle is just beginning,” he wrote. Congressmen Jim Jordan, chairman of the Judiciary Committee, and Steve Scalise, the majority leader, have already announced bids to succeed him, in a vote expected next week. Trump called Johnson “fantastic” and said he had not asked him to step aside.

Vance, seen as a contender for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, blamed the defeat on the Iran war and rising gasoline prices. “If you want to argue it was worth it — that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it — go ahead. But everyone knows why we lost,” he wrote on X. Asked about the post, Trump replied: “I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit, short term.” But he defended the war, now more than eight months old: “The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”

Republicans have lost at least seven Senate seats and could lose nine if results in Mississippi and Alaska, still being counted, are confirmed, according to El País. In the House, dozens of seats remain to be called, although Democrats have already passed the majority. The result also opens the race within the Republican Party to succeed Trump, who cannot run again in 2028.

World.title: Peru declares an El Niño emergency in nearly three-quarters of the country ahead of the Pope’s visit
World.content:
Peru declares an El Niño emergency in nearly three-quarters of the country ahead of the Pope’s visit

5th Thursday, November 2026 - 07:00 UTC Full article

Peru’s scientific commission on the phenomenon expects the episode to last until June 2027

Peru’s government has declared a two-month state of emergency over the risk of heavy rains linked to the El Niño phenomenon in 1,380 of the country’s 1,891 districts, about 73%, including all the places Pope Leo XIV will visit in northern Peru from November 13. The measure covers districts in all 24 departments and the province of Callao.

Rains in recent days flooded homes and streets, leaving 324 people affected in Tumbes, on the border with Ecuador, and caused flooding in Chulucanas, in the Piura region, where the pontiff lived in 1985 during his first years as a missionary. President Keiko Fujimori cancelled her trip to the Ibero-American Summit in Madrid on Sunday to oversee the response and warned of further rain in Tumbes and Piura on November 7 and 8. In October she had already acknowledged that prevention works might prove insufficient for “an El Niño we have not seen in recent decades”. The declaration allows regional and municipal governments to carry out prevention, response and rehabilitation measures with the National Civil Defence Institute.

The emergency includes all 38 districts of Lambayeque, on the northern coast. The Pope, who holds Peruvian nationality and was bishop of Chiclayo, the regional capital, from 2015 to 2023, will celebrate Mass on Friday 13 at the Pampas de Pimentel, by the Pacific, which organisers expect nearly a million faithful to attend. On Saturday 14 he will celebrate another Mass in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, in the Andean region of Cajamarca, and visit Zaña to close the jubilee year marking 300 years since the canonisation of Saint Toribio de Mogrovejo. The security operation will involve some 2,500 police, 1,000 soldiers and 6,500 volunteers.

“We expect the Pope’s visit to Chiclayo may coincide with episodes of rain. They will not be heavy rains,” said Grinia Ávalos, director of meteorology at the National Meteorology and Hydrology Service, who forecast temperatures of up to 32 degrees Celsius in Chiclayo, four to five degrees above normal. The regional coordinator for the visit, Jorge Chávez Cresta, said that according to the forecast scenarios, heavy rains would reach Lambayeque after the Pope has left the country, although he said contingency plans were in place. The region suffered severe flooding during the El Niño episodes of 1982-1983 and 1997-1998, and Chiclayo lacks a comprehensive drainage system.

Peru’s scientific commission on the phenomenon expects the episode to last until June 2027. In Ecuador, El Niño rains left one dead and more than 2,000 affected on Santa Cruz island in the Galápagos last week. Leo XIV will visit Uruguay and Argentina before arriving in Peru.

World.title: Milei skips the opening of the Ibero-American Summit and meets Abascal in Madrid
World.content:
