Milei skips the opening of the Ibero-American Summit and meets Abascal in Madrid

5th Thursday, November 2026 - 06:49 UTC Full article

It is Milei’s second visit to Madrid in two weeks. On October 21, at a breakfast event, he called Sánchez an “unpresentable dictator” and “corrupt”, and did not meet Abascal on that occasion

Argentine President Javier Milei did not attend the opening of the 30th Ibero-American Summit in Madrid on Wednesday or the dinner hosted by the King and Queen of Spain for the delegations, and that evening met Santiago Abascal, leader of the Vox party, in the middle of the campaign for Spain’s November 29 general election.

Milei arrived in the Spanish capital from Buenos Aires on Wednesday afternoon but did not attend the opening ceremony at the Teatro Real or the gala dinner at the Royal Palace for the heads of the 22 delegations. According to diplomatic sources quoted by El País, the Argentine president had requested, through Spain’s Foreign Ministry, a private audience with King Felipe VI, as other leaders had, but the ministry did not process the request, considering it inappropriate for him to meet the monarch before meeting Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. The Argentine government has not explained his absence.

“President Javier Milei met in Madrid with the deputy and presidential candidate Santiago Abascal,” the Argentine Presidential Office said, sharing a photograph of the meeting. Abascal wrote: “Tonight I met my friend and ally Javier Milei, President of the Argentine Republic, whom I thanked for attending the Ibero-American Summit.”

It is Milei’s second visit to Madrid in two weeks. On October 21, at a breakfast event, he called Sánchez an “unpresentable dictator” and “corrupt”, and did not meet Abascal on that occasion. At the time, the Royal Household said a meeting with Felipe VI must necessarily be accompanied by one with the prime minister. Chilean President José Antonio Kast, also attending the summit, met Abascal this week and received an award from Madrid regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso.

Milei is expected to coincide with Felipe VI and Sánchez on Thursday at the summit’s plenary session, which brings together the countries of Latin America with Spain, Portugal and Andorra.

World.title: Democrats retake control of the US Congress in a heavy blow to Trump
World.content:
Democrats retake control of the US Congress in a heavy blow to Trump

4th Wednesday, November 2026 - 09:09 UTC Full article

CBS News projected a Democratic majority in the House shortly after 10 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday; with dozens of seats still to be decided, Democrats had passed the 218 needed

The Democratic Party on Tuesday regained control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate in the midterm elections, winning in Republican strongholds such as Texas, Ohio and Kansas in a heavy blow to President Donald Trump, who will govern for the remaining two years of his term with Congress in opposition hands.

CBS News projected a Democratic majority in the House shortly after 10 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday; with dozens of seats still to be decided, Democrats had passed the 218 needed. In the Senate, they secured a majority with victory in Iowa and hold at least 53 of the 100 seats, with results in Alaska and Mississippi still pending. According to El País, it is only the seventh time the party in power has lost both chambers in a midterm election.

Democrats won Senate seats in states where they had not done so for decades. In Texas, James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton; in Ohio, Sherrod Brown regained the seat from Jon Husted; in Kansas, Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton became the state’s first Democratic senator in almost a century. They also won in Iowa, with Josh Turek; in Maine, where Troy Jackson defeated Republican Susan Collins, a senator since 1997; in North Carolina, with Roy Cooper; and in South Carolina, with Annie Andrews. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, will be the first Muslim senator in US history. Republicans held seats in Florida, Idaho and Montana.

In governor’s races, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Greg Abbott in Texas and will be the first Hispanic woman to lead the state; Xavier Becerra will be California’s first Hispanic governor since 1875; and Deb Haaland, in New Mexico, the first Native American woman to govern a state. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds will be the state’s first Black governor.

Trump told Fox News he was “a little surprised” and that the Democrats “did a good job”, attributing part of the defeat to the Iran war and higher fuel prices. He told The New York Times he would accept the results and hoped to reach agreements with the opposition. On his social network, however, he wrote: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”, and posted an image of his cap bearing the word “VETO”, a reference to his threat to veto the new Congress’s laws.

With majorities in both chambers, Democrats will be able to block the White House’s legislative agenda and open investigations into the first half of the term. Former president Barack Obama said voters had sent “a clear message” in favour of “a politics that brings people together rather than divides them”. China said it was ready to “keep working” with Washington, and the Kremlin said it expected Trump to maintain his foreign policy. Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said “Americans have said no to war”.

Polls had identified the cost of living, corruption and the Iran war as voters’ main concerns, and turnout was at record levels for a midterm election.

World.title: Paraguay takes over Ueno Bank, with 3 million customers, and freezes its deposits
World.content:
Paraguay takes over Ueno Bank, with 3 million customers, and freezes its deposits

4th Wednesday, November 2026 - 08:27 UTC Full article

“We proceeded to close the entity; therefore, neither the app, nor the cards, nor any service of the entity is active,” said a member of the Central Bank’s board. Photo: EFE/ Juan Pablo Pino

Paraguay’s Central Bank on Tuesday took over Ueno Bank, one of the country’s largest banks, after its solvency ratio fell below 50% of the legal minimum, and froze all its assets and liabilities, including the savings of some 3 million customers and more than US$800 million in public funds. The bank immediately suspended all its services.

“We proceeded to close the entity; therefore, neither the app, nor the cards, nor any service of the entity is active from today,” said Liana Caballero, a member of the Central Bank’s board, which took the decision unanimously. According to its own figures, Ueno’s customers are equivalent to 60% of the country’s adult population, and it manages public funds including about US$380 million from the Social Security Institute, which runs pensions and public healthcare.

The Deposit Guarantee Fund covers savings of up to 75 minimum wages, about 228 million guaraníes or roughly US$38,200 per person. Those with larger balances will have to wait for the Superintendency of Banks’ final accounting. “The priority will always be small savers,” said Central Bank President Carlos Carvallo, who described the situation as “an isolated, one-off event” and said the financial system “remains sound and healthy”.

According to Carvallo, the takeover followed months of investigation that revealed loans to companies linked to the bank’s owners. On October 18, the Association of Banks of Paraguay had asked the Central Bank to report on the solvency of institutions that benefited from facilities in merger processes and warned about a bank’s credit exposure, which it did not identify, to companies in its own group. Days earlier, senators from the ruling party and the opposition had called on President Santiago Peña to dismiss the Central Bank’s leadership, which Peña backed.

Carvallo, who ran Ueno Bank before Peña appointed him to head the Central Bank in 2023, said he had signed his resignation, although he will remain in office until the bank’s resolution is complete. According to the Paraguayan press, several of the bank’s executives were detained, including its president, Miguel Vázquez.

The crisis had immediate political fallout. Vice President Pedro Alliana “paused” his bid for the ruling Colorado Party’s presidential nomination in order to “put the house in order”. The opposition Authentic Radical Liberal Party said it would push for impeachment proceedings against Peña and Alliana. “They plundered the pensioners’ money and this cannot be left like this,” said its presidential hopeful Ricardo Estigarribia, according to the newspaper ABC Color. In 2024, the Social Security Institute’s purchase of about US$32 million in Ueno bonds caused controversy; Peña, who called the reports a “media campaign”, was a shareholder in Ueno Holding, not the bank, and sold those shares in April 2025.

World.title: Sheinbaum says immigration raids ‘very likely’ cost Republicans Latino votes: Thursday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🗳️ Sheinbaum says U.S. immigration raids “very likely” influenced midterm results: The president said analyses have found that many Latino Americans, including people of Mexican descent, who voted for Trump and the Republican Party in 2024, voted for Democrats on Tuesday. She said “it’s logical to think” that racism and immigration raids were related to Latinos’ decision to vote in large numbers for the Democratic Party.

📊 69% of Hispanic voters backed Democrats, per NYT estimate: Republicans received 29%, and the Democrats’ margin among Latino voters widened to 40 percentage points, up from 11 points in 2024.

🇨🇳 Sheinbaum confirms bilateral meeting with Xi Jinping at APEC: She said she will meet with the Chinese president and government ministers at the leaders’ summit in Shenzhen on Nov. 18 and 19. Sheinbaum said she will announce several other bilateral meetings soon.

🇺🇸 Meeting with Trump depends on whether he attends APEC: Sheinbaum said there is no confirmation yet that the U.S. president will travel to China. If he does, “of course we’re interested in meeting with him,” she said.

Why today’s mañanera matters

Two days after the U.S. midterm elections, President Sheinbaum expressed her view that opposition to the Trump administration’s immigration raids was a factor in the Democratic Party’s victories in the House and Senate elections.

Since returning to office in January 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump has pursued an aggressive deportation agenda supported by immigration raids carried out by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

During Trump’s second term, 18 Mexicans have died in ICE custody or during ICE raids, leading the Mexican government to file complaints with U.S. prosecutors’ offices.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was Sheinbaum’s revelation that she will hold a bilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ summit, which will be held in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18 and 19.

Trade and Chinese investment in Mexico could be among the issues the Mexican and Chinese presidents discuss. Mexico imposed new and higher tariffs on a broad range of Chinese goods at the start of 2026, angering the Chinese government.

On Thursday morning, Sheinbaum said she also hoped to hold a bilateral meeting with Trump in China. Trade would likely be a central part of their discussions as Mexico and the U.S. are seeking to reach a deal that resolves a range of bilateral trade differences.

Such an agreement could improve the likelihood of the Trump administration agreeing to a 16-year renewal of the USMCA — an extension it declined to endorse in July — although Washington and Ottawa would also need to resolve their trade differences.

‘Very likely’ that immigration raids influenced US midterm results, says Sheinbaum

A reporter asked the president whether she believed that immigration raids in the United States influenced the results of the U.S. midterm elections.

“Yes, it’s very likely,” Sheinbaum responded.

She said that analyses have found that many Latino Americans, including people of Mexican descent, who voted for Trump and the Republican Party in 2024, voted for the Democratic Party in Tuesday’s midterms.

Sheinbaum said “it’s logical to think” that factors such as racism and immigration raids were related to Latinos’ decision to vote in large numbers for the Democratic Party.

According to an estimate by The New York Times, 69% of Hispanic voters supported the Democratic Party on Tuesday, compared to 29% who voted for the Republican Party. Democrats’ margin over Republicans among Latino voters widened to 40 percentage points, up from 11 points in 2024.

Checking in on realignment (via NYT Voter Data):

Accounting for national swing, younger voters have more than reversed their 2024 shift right, nonwhite noncollege and Hispanic voters back to 2020 position. Some changes with *college* nonwhite, Black, and Asian voters persist. https://t.co/e6ielALiCO — Will Jordan (@williamjordann) November 4, 2026

Record numbers of Latinos voted on Tuesday, reaching as many as 14.5 million, according to Janet Murguía, CEO of UnidosUS, the largest U.S. ​Latino civil rights organization.

In a report headlined “Latinos, motivated by immigration and economic woes, drive Democratic gains in Republican strongholds,” Reuters reported that recent immigration raids in Kansas helped drive voter registrations in “three solidly red counties” that “turned blue in the U.S. Senate race” in that state, won by Democrat Adam Hamilton.

Sheinbaum ‘interested’ in bilateral meeting with Trump in China

Sheinbaum said she will depart Mexico for China on Sunday Nov. 15 and return on Nov. 20.

“We’re going for practically the whole week because it’s practically two days of flights,” she said, referring to her outbound and return flights.

Sheinbaum said she will hold “several bilateral meetings” in Shenzhen, adding that she will announce them soon.

She confirmed that she will attend a bilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi.

“There will be a bilateral meeting with the government of China, with the president of China, with ministers of the government of China,” Sheinbaum said.

Asked whether she would hold a bilateral meeting with Trump at the APEC leaders’ summit, she responded:

“We still don’t know for sure whether President Trump will go. If he goes of course we’re interested in meeting with him. It will depend on how long he is there for. There is not yet confirmation that he will go to this meeting.”

Various media reports say that Trump is expected to travel to China for the APEC summit, where a trilateral meeting between the U.S. president, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin could take place.

World.title: Mexico and My Money: The fintech revolution in Mexico is just getting started
World.content:
As I wrote about previously, Mexican citizens have a longstanding distrust of traditional banks, stemming from trauma caused by the 1994 Tequila Crisis.

If you ask a random person on the street about Mexican banks, they might also tell you they are painful to do business with. The rigid operating hours, long lines, mountains of paperwork, strict requirements and hidden fees one encounters at traditional banks here can feel like something from a bygone era.

On top of a poor customer experience, the lack of traditional banks in rural areas, combined with their longstanding risk aversion, means that many Mexicans (especially moderate- to low-income workers and those with informal employment) have historically been shut out of the formal banking sector.

So, Mexico’s financial sector was ripe for a revolution.

What is fintech, and why is it such a big deal?

Fintech companies are fundamentally different from traditional banks in that they have no physical presence. They conduct business entirely through digital channels, with most users connecting to them via mobile applications.

According to a recent report from FinTech México, there were 795 fintechs operating in Mexico as of 2025, with more than half focused on digital payments and credit.

The COVID-19 pandemic was a key catalyst for the sector, and its arrival triggered a massive shakeup in Mexico’s financial markets. Forced to stay at home, many people found themselves shopping online for the first time. And with so many physical banks closed, digital payments became a practical way to pay for life’s necessities.

This prompted more Mexicans to apply for debit and credit cards, with many embracing digital payments over cash. It was possible thanks to a parallel trend — the widespread adoption of smartphones across Mexican society.

Who is the typical Mexican fintech customer?

Fintech customers in Mexico do not look like traditional banking clients. For one, they are notably younger.

According to BBVA Research, roughly 60% of fintech customers are between the ages of 18 and 39, with a nearly equal balance between men and women. Unlike their elders, fintech customers in Mexico strongly prefer mobile payments over physical cash.

Similar to traditional banking clients, fintech predominantly attracts middle- and upper-class people living in urban areas like Mexico City, Monterrey and Guadalajara. So, while these new businesses have had a dramatic impact on financial behavior in big cities, they have altered financial behavior much less in poorer, rural communities long deprived of banking services.

But we are starting to see some green shoots.

Fintech is starting to reduce Mexico’s unbanked population

With their accessible and low-cost services such as no-fee digital banking and electronic payments, credit cards, digital money transfers (peer-to-peer), high-yield savings accounts, stock trading platforms and more, fintech products have wide appeal across Mexico.

INEGI’s most recent survey of financial inclusion released in 2024 found that fintech is helping to improve access to financial services in Mexico, after a long standstill.

Overall inclusion, i.e., the percentage of adults with at least one financial product, rose to 76.5% in 2024, up nine percentage points from the previous survey. Individuals with a formal savings account increased to 63%, while access to credit inched up to 37%.

And most relevant to fintechs, digital financial account usage increased fivefold from 2021 to 2024 and now stands at 10%.

Who are the most important fintechs in Mexico?

While there are hundreds of fintech startups in Mexico, only a portion target retail customers (many others offer business solutions). Below are a handful worth knowing.

Brazilian giant Nubank (operating here as Nu México) entered Mexico as a fintech back in 2022 with a fiercely customer-centric value proposition.

Nu targeted consumers neglected by traditional banks with a user-friendly mobile app, cheeky advertising and credit card offers. For anyone with a smartphone, opening an account was easy (even for expats), with zero paperwork and no annual fees. Most appealing, Nu’s basic debit account came with a high-yield savings cajita attached to it, which in the early days yielded more than 12% interest, annualized (it is now 6.5%).

Their offer was so compelling that Nu rapidly became one of the largest financial institutions in Mexico, serving 12 million customers by 2025. Earlier this year, Nu obtained a Mexican banking license and transitioned to operations as a commercial bank (but will remain 100% digital).

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Nu México (@nu.mx)

Fintech startups

Plenty more startups have followed Nu’s lead. Klar and Stori offer fee-free deposit accounts and extend credit to individuals who lack formal credit scores. Hey Banco (a fintech launched by Banregio), Plata (started by a Russian expat) and 100% homegrown Finsus are other examples.

Kueski is a startup that pioneered buy now, pay later (BNPL) microlending in Mexico. It allows users to make online purchases and pay in cash at physical OXXO locations.

Traditional Mexican retailers are also capitalizing on this massive opportunity in the fintech space. E-commerce giant Mercado Libre launched Mercado Pago to process payments for its gigantic online business.

While different from the rest, Clip was Mexico’s first homegrown fintech unicorn (a startup valued at US $1 billion or more). It revolutionized business practices at mom-and-pop retail shops when it started selling affordable, pocket-sized card readers at stores like OXXO with zero monthly fees, instant activation and no need for a traditional bank account.

Through this innovation, Clip single-handedly doubled the number of retail outlets in Mexico that could accept digital payments.

Protections for investors in Mexican fintech companies

For digital investors who seldom worry about risk, last week’s unprecedented crypto heist at Binance and a smaller, unrelated theft at Polymarket are wake-up calls.

Protections for fintech depositors range from thin to nonexistent. Though the landmark Ley Fintech (Fintech Law) passed by Mexico’s Congress in March 2018 put some guardrails in place, it does not mean that fintech investors are insulated from risk.

Notably, deposits at fintech companies are not protected by IPAB insurance because they are not fully regulated banks.

Instead, funds deposited at fintechs regulated as SOFIPOs (Sociedad Financiera Popular) are covered up to 25,000 UDIs (221,000 Mexican pesos or US $11,764), while deposits in digital wallets at fintechs regulated as IFPEs (Institución de Fondos de Pago Electrónico) have zero protection.

In plain English, if a major fraud occurs inside a Mexican fintech, depositors face a greater risk of losing their money than they would at a traditional bank.

That is why it is a good idea to perform due diligence before choosing a fintech and maintain a balance below the covered threshold. Due to their popularity with scammers and total lack of deposit protection, IFPEs are best avoided.

From tipping and working with local contractors to moving money into Mexico from abroad, check out more from MND’s “Mexico and My Money” archive.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: US $40M Pilgrim’s Pride plant will open Thursday in Gómez Palacio, Durango
World.content:
Pilgrim’s Pride Corporation, the multinational chicken producer, will launch on Thursday its US $40 million El Porvenir plant in Gómez Palacio, Durango, which is expected to create over 300 jobs.

The project is part of Pilgrim’s broader plans to invest $1.3 billion in Mexico between 2026 and 2030 under the Sheinbaum government’s Plan México economic strategy, which is expected to increase production by more than 373,000 metric tonnes and generate over 4,000 direct and 16,000 indirect jobs.

The investment will be divided among several states, with $200 million allocated to Durango and Coahuila in the northern border zone, $150 million to Querétaro, San Luis Potosí and Hidalgo in El Bajío and the center, and $950 million to the southeastern states of Veracruz, Campeche and Yucatán.

Durango’s Foreign Investment Attraction Unit head, Arturo Ortiz Galán, said that the new production line will support local suppliers and the region’s poultry businesses, helping to reinforce Durango’s position as an industrial and agri-food hub. The plant will also expand Pilgrim’s value-added product range by producing cooked chicken.

Ortiz Galán said the expansion was made possible through collaboration with the federal government, which has provided investment incentives.

“Thanks to the good relationship that [Durango] Governor [Esteban] Villegas has with President Sheinbaum, I have been able to easily initiate discussions and secure support from all the relevant ministries,” Galán said. “It’s very positive that there’s a plan to digitalize all processes and create a one-stop shop for investments.”

It delivers food to approximately 30 million Mexicans, employs around 12,600 people across Mexico, and provides 50,000 indirect jobs through its partner farmers, logistics providers and supply chain.

In January, President Sheinbaum praised the Mexican business environment for attracting high investment from Pilgrim’s.

“This investment they are making… is because they have been successful and because they know that investing in Mexico is safe and allows them to continue growing,” Sheinbaum said during a morning press conference.

With reports from Milenio and Mexico Industry

World.title: As Ibero-American Summit gets underway in Madrid, foreign ministers cite ‘excellent’ Spain-Mexico relations
World.content:
Mexico-Spain relations are in “excellent” shape, Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco said Wednesday after a meeting with his Spanish counterpart in Madrid.

In a social media post, Velasco said that he and Spanish Foreign Affairs Minister José Manuel Albares spoke with “our usual closeness and trust” about the “excellent” state of relations between Mexico and Spain, a leading source of foreign investment in Mexico.

“We highlighted the good rapport between President [Claudia] Sheinbaum and Prime Minister [Pedro] Sánchez, which drives a constructive, results-oriented agenda,” he wrote.

“Mexico and Spain will continue to strengthen this fraternal friendship and the dialogue that unites us,” Velasco said.

His meeting with Albares took place on the first day of the Ibero-American Summit, a gathering of leaders and officials from Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries. Velasco is representing Sheinbaum at the event.

After meeting with the Mexican foreign minister, Albares also described Mexico-Spain relations in positive terms.

“Spain and Mexico have strengthened our political, economic and cultural relations over the past year for the benefit of our sister nations,” he wrote on social media.

There is no doubt that Mexico-Spain relations have improved during Sheinbaum’s presidency after they deteriorated considerably during Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s six-year term in office.

In 2019, López Obrador requested an apology from Spain for human rights violations during the Conquest of Mexico, while in 2022 he advocated a “pause” in bilateral relations while asserting that Mexico had been “looted” for years due to “economic-political promiscuity in the leadership of the governments of Mexico and Spain.”

AMLO’s 2019 request for an apology was “vigorously” rejected by the Spanish government, but in March of this year, King Felipe VI of Spain acknowledged that during the Spanish conquest and colonization of the Americas, “there were significant abuses” and “moral and ethical controversies.” As Mexico News Daily reported at the time, his remarks constituted an unprecedented statement on the matter for a king of Spain.

In April, Sheinbaum met with Prime Minister Sánchez at the “In Defense of Democracy” summit in Barcelona.

Sheinbaum had also called for an apology for abuses committed by Spain during the Conquest and the fall of Tenochtitlán, but in Barcelona, she acknowledged that there had been “a rapprochement from both the Spanish … [prime minister] and the king himself.”

The Ibero-American Summit

In a statement released on Tuesday, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (SRE) noted that Sheinbaum had designated Velasco to lead the Mexican delegation at the 30th Ibero-American Summit in Madrid on Nov. 4 and 5.

“The Mexican delegation’s presence will be key to continuing to advance cooperation in areas of interest to Mexico, such as the environment and climate change, human mobility, disaster risk reduction, education, gender equality, and science and technology,” the SRE said.

“At the meeting, the host country will report on its results over the past two years in charge of the Pro Tempore Secretariat of the Summit and will hand the presidency over to Honduras for the 2026-2028 period,” the ministry said.

“The first Summit was held in Mexico, in Guadalajara, in 1991. Since then, it has been an important forum for dialogue and cooperation between the two regions,” the SRE said, referring to Latin America and Europe.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Mexican-Americans among historic winners in Tuesday’s US elections
World.content:
Mexican American candidates captured the governorships of Texas and California, and at least three Latino Democrats flipped Republican congressional seats in Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections.

Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who defeated Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, will become the state’s first Latina governor ever, and Texas’ first Democratic governor since Ann Richards from 1991 to 1995.

Her victory helped end a Democratic drought in Texas statewide elections dating to 1994.

In the California governor’s race, Democrat Xavier Becerra — whose mother was born in Jalisco and whose father was born in Sacramento but raised in Mexico — had a 64% to 36% lead over Republican Steve Hilton, a former Fox News host, in preliminary returns.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum welcomed their victories Wednesday morning.

“We are very pleased that Mexican Americans have this recognition,” she said in her daily press conference.

Becerra, who previously served as California attorney general and U.S. Health and Human Services secretary under President Joe Biden, became the first Latino elected governor of California.

A previous Latino governor of California, Romualdo Pacheco, was not elected to the post but served nine months in 1875 after the seated governor left to join the Senate. Pacheco was the lieutenant governor at the time.

Hinojosa grew up in the border city of Brownsville, Texas, where her parents began their careers as legal aid lawyers representing farmworkers. Her mother, Crisanta Guerra Lozano, was born in the city of San Luis Potosí, and her father, Gilberto Hinojosa, chaired the Texas Democratic Party from 2012 to 2025.

She recalled crossing into Mexico regularly with her family for breakfast and shopping as a girl.

In South Texas, Tejano singer Bobby Pulido — winner of Latin Grammys for best Tejano album in 2022 and 2025 — defeated incumbent Republican Rep. Mónica De La Cruz in the 15th Congressional District, flipping a seat in a district President Donald Trump carried by 18 percentage points in 2024.

Pulido said last month he lacked U.S. health insurance and had traveled to Mexico for medical care.

The conservative Democrat campaigned on border security and support for government-funded healthcare and safety net programs, according to the New York Times. His outreach included free performances at quinceañeras and other local celebrations.

His victory marked a reversal in a district viewed as a test of Latino voters’ political loyalties after Trump’s gains two years earlier.

“Hispanics, they’re not so partisan,” Pulido said by way of an explanation. “It’s very much, ‘Are you gonna go fight for me?’ That’s what matters.”

Added Javier Palomarez, president and CEO of the United States Hispanic Business Council: “We are a community that doesn’t vote party. It votes person.”

Democrat Katy Padilla Stout was projected to win Texas’ 23rd Congressional District against Brandon Herrera, a gun-focused YouTube personality, according to CBS News, flipping another Republican seat.

The sprawling border district stretches from San Antonio to El Paso. Its previous Republican representative, Tony Gonzales, resigned in April. Trump carried the current district by 14 points.

In Nebraska, Democrat Denise Powell defeated Republican Brinker Harding to become the state’s first Latina elected to federal office and the first woman to represent its 2nd Congressional District.

Powell, who co-founded a group helping local women run for office, also became the district’s first Democratic winner in a decade. She flipped the seat held by retiring Republican Rep. Don Bacon.

In another notable Texas victory, Democrat and longtime sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia defeated Trump-backed Republican Carlos de La Cruz in a San Antonio-area district redrawn by Republicans to favor their party. As redrawn, the majority-Hispanic district would have backed Trump by more than 10 percentage points in 2024.

With reports from El Financiero, Quadratín San Luis Potosí, CBC, Hindustan Times, Fast Company and Nebraska Examiner

World.title: El Jalapeño: Chipotle mystified after Mexican diners treat fast-casual burrito bowl as lunch instead of cultural offense
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

SAN PEDRO GARZA GARCÍA, Nuevo León — Executive leadership at Chipotle Mexican Grill confirmed Tuesday that they are currently re-evaluating their entire global strategy after local diners surprisingly failed to fiercely oppose their version of Mexican-inspired cuisine.

After the U.S. fast-casual chain opened its first Mexican location in the affluent municipality of San Pedro Garza García earlier this year, corporate analysts fully expected a wave of diplomatic friction, or at least a sternly worded statement from local culinary boards. Instead, customer volume has remained consistently high, forcing corporate strategists to confront the unsettling possibility that people simply enjoy a large, convenient bowl of rice, beans and meat without converting their meal break into a cultural referendum.

“We prepared extensive crisis-management protocols for the inevitable national backlash against charging 180 pesos for a scoop of guacamole,” said Chipotle Director of Global Brand Strategy Mark Henderson, speaking via video conference from the packed dining area of the company’s Nuevo León restaurant. “Our market research explicitly warned us that bringing an Americanized version of Mexican food into actual Mexico was the culinary equivalent of selling canned air to a mountain town. We were braced for total outrage, but people keep coming back and asking for extra salsa.”

According to company officials, early performance metrics far exceeded initial corporate expectations, which had originally budgeted for three weeks of novelty-driven foot traffic followed by a swift, dignified retreat from the market. Company leadership now plans to open four additional locations in Nuevo León before expanding into Mexico City, where executives are reportedly preparing an entirely new set of contingency plans in case diners there also treat lunch as just lunch.

Internal memos revealed that brand researchers initially attributed the sustained high sales to a clerical error, suspecting that local patrons were under the mistaken impression that Chipotle was an upscale American salad bar.

At press time, Chipotle board members were reportedly holding an emergency summit to discuss whether the chain could safely introduce hard-shell tacos without triggering a public outcry.

World.title: Mexico’s economy nearing ‘strong’ according to the latest MND Economy Index™
World.content:
Listen to this article

THE MND ECONOMY INDEX™

Providing broad insight into the Mexican economy

MND Intelligence · Sixth edition

Welcome to the sixth edition of the MND Economy Index™, part of the MND Intelligence™ suite of data products from Mexico News Daily.

The MND Economy Index™ is a 10-pillar, 19-indicator composite index that compiles a broad range of economic data into a single score between 0 and 100, giving Mexico News Daily readers a clear, accessible picture of how the Mexican economy is performing across multiple dimensions.

In the inaugural MND Economy Index™ article, published in late May, we not only analyzed the index score — 63.4 out of 100 — but also explained what the index is, why we developed it and how it works. Click here to read (or re-read) those explanations.

In this edition of the MND Economy Index™ — which uses economic data primarily from the month of August — the index score is 74.5, an increase of 1.4 points compared to the previous score.

The score for August is the highest since we began publishing the MND Economy Index™, reflecting improvements in various parts of Mexico’s economy.

Before we look more closely at the latest index result, here is a short guide to what the overall index score means.

85–100: Exceptional — the economy performing at a high level across nearly all indicators.

— the economy performing at a high level across nearly all indicators. 75–84: Strong — strong broad-based performance with only minor areas of concern.

— strong broad-based performance with only minor areas of concern. 60–74: Above neutral — meaningful strengths, but with notable room for improvement.

— meaningful strengths, but with notable room for improvement. 50–59: Mixed — passing marks overall, more indicators above benchmark than below.

— passing marks overall, more indicators above benchmark than below. Below 50: Broad underperformance — more indicators below benchmark than above.

Mexico’s economy on the verge of a ‘strong’ assessment

As noted above, the latest MND Economy Index™ score is 74.5, an increase of 1.4 percentage points compared to the previous score. The latest score is just 0.5 percentage points below the score required for a “strong” assessment for Mexico’s economy.

Below you will see the score for each of the ten pillars that make up the index, expressed out of 10 to reflect each pillar’s exact contribution to the final composite score.

Pillars are color-coded using a traffic light system: green (a score above 7.5) indicates strong performance; yellow (5.0–7.5) signals decent performance but with room for improvement; and red (below 5.0) flags a pillar that is falling short of its benchmark. Where a pillar score has improved compared to the previous month, an upward arrow appears alongside its corresponding traffic light; a downward arrow indicates a deterioration; and a pause symbol denotes no change.

As you’ll see below, scores for four of the ten MND Economy Index™ pillars increased in August compared to the previous month. Scores for five pillars declined, while the score for one was unchanged.

Collectively, the increases were more significant than the decreases, allowing the index score to rise.

🟢 ⬇️ INFLATION (9.54)

The score for this pillar fell to 9.54 in August from 9.68 in July. Despite the decline, the inflation pillar retained its position as the top contributor to the overall MND Economy Index™ score.

Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate increased to 3.26% in August, ending a four-month streak of declines. The increase caused a slight decrease in the score for the current inflation component of the pillar as the headline rate moved away from the Bank of Mexico’s 3% target.

The score for the pillar component that considers the 12-month forward inflation forecast was unchanged as the Bank of Mexico’s outlook for the third quarter of 2027 is applicable to both July and August. The central bank is predicting a headline inflation rate of 3.2% in the third quarter of next year.

🟢 ⬆️ MONETARY POLICY (9.46)

The score for this pillar increased to 9.46 from 9.32 in July.

The Bank of Mexico’s benchmark interest rate remained at 6.50% in August after the central bank’s board voted to keep it at that level at a monetary policy meeting on Aug. 6. Therefore, there was no change in the interest rate component of the pillar score.

The increase in the pillar score was due to a decline in Mexico’s real interest rate in August — i.e., the Bank of Mexico’s benchmark interest rate minus the annual headline inflation rate.

The real interest rate in August was 3.24%, a reading 0.54 points above the 2.7% neutral midpoint.

The real interest rate in July, at 3.38%, was further away from the neutral midpoint than the reading in August.

🟢 ⬆️ MANUFACTURING SECTOR HEALTH (8.53)

The score for this pillar increased in August, rising to 8.53 from 7.9 in July.

The exports component of the pillar remained at the maximum score due to a 40.4% annual increase in export revenue in August, well above the 16.7% threshold needed for a perfect ten. Official data shows that over 94% of Mexico’s export revenue in August came from the shipment abroad of manufactured goods.

The increase in the overall pillar score was due to 4.1% year-over-year growth in manufacturing output in August. The year-over-year gain represented a significant improvement from the 1.6% increase in July.

🟢 ⬆️ ECONOMIC GROWTH (8)

The score for this pillar increased to 8 in August from 7.6 in July.

The increase was due to a higher annual economic growth rate in August. The annual growth rate in August was 3.5%, according to final data published by INEGI on Oct. 23. Year-over-year growth in July was slightly lower at 3.3%.

At her morning press conference on Oct. 26, President Sheinbaum said that growth of 3.5% in August was “very good news.”

She noted that construction, including housing and public infrastructure projects, was helping to drive growth. Sheinbaum also noted that the production of electronics in Mexico was providing momentum to the economy.

🟢 ⬆️ SOVEREIGN RISK (7.72)

The score for this pillar increased to 7.72 in August from 7.41 in July.

The score for the sovereign credit ratings component of the pillar remained unchanged in August, as there were no month-over-month changes to the Mexico ratings of Moody’s (Baa3/stable); S&P (BBB/negative); and Fitch (BBB-/stable).

The increase in the overall pillar score was due to a narrowing in Mexico’s 5-year credit default swap spread. The credit default swap spread was 77.89 basis points at the end of August, down from 87.19 basis points at the end of July. The narrower spread reflected a decrease in the market-implied cost of insuring against a Mexican sovereign default.

🟡 ⬇️ CURRENCY STABILITY (6.73)

The score for this pillar declined slightly to 6.73 in August from 6.79 in July.

The standard deviation of daily exchange rate movements decreased to 0.25% in August from 0.40% in July, leading to an increase in the score for that component of the pillar.

The decrease in the pillar score in July was due to a lower spot rate score. The score for that component declined because the peso strengthened against the US dollar in August to trade at 16.99 to the greenback at the end of the month, an appreciation of 1.9% compared to the end of July.

The exchange rate was thus more distant from the index’s 19.00 USD:MXN baseline, which is based on the 2025 average rate. This pillar penalizes significant deviation from the 19.00 USD:MXN baseline in either direction, recognizing that a peso that has strengthened too far from this benchmark can erode export competitiveness and reduce the purchasing power of remittances, just as a weakening peso raises import costs.

The spot rate component of the currency stability score will increase in the next MND Economy Index™ as the peso depreciated 6% in September to trade at 18.08 to the dollar at the end of that month.

🟡 ⬇️ INVESTMENT CLIMATE (6.46)

The score for this pillar decreased to 6.46 in August from 6.58 in July.

The decrease was due to lower annual growth on the S&P/BMV FIBRAS Total Return Index, which tracks the performance of Mexico’s listed real estate investment trusts. The index grew 24.9% annually to the end of August, down from a 27.4% year-over-year increase at the end of July.

The score for the foreign direct investment component of the pillar remained steady as the latest available data is still that published by the Economy Ministry in late August. That data shows that foreign direct investment in Mexico increased 2.1% annually in the first six months of 2026 to reach a record-high $34.96 billion. Annual FDI growth of 25% is required for a perfect score in that component of the investment climate pillar.

🟡 ⏸️ PRODUCTIVITY (6.4)

The score for this pillar remained steady at 6.4 in August after increasing to that level in July from 3.8 in June.

Data published by the national statistics agency INEGI on Sept. 10 showed that the IGPLE — INEGI’s quarterly productivity measure — increased 1.7% annually in the second quarter of 2026. That level of productivity growth was significantly stronger than the +0.1% reading in the first quarter of 2026.

INEGI will publish productivity data for the third quarter of 2026 in early December.

🟡 ⬇️ LABOR AND EMPLOYMENT (6.11)

The score for this pillar decreased to 6.11 in August from 6.18 in July. Scores for two of the pillar’s three components stayed the same while one declined.

The number of people in formal sector jobs rose 1.5% in the 12 months to the end of August, on par with the annual growth rate at the end of July.

Nominal wages were up 6.7% year-on-year at the end of August, the same increase recorded at the end of July.

Year-over-year growth in Mexico’s informality rate was 0.2 points at the end of August, up from an annual increase of 0.1 points at the end of July. In August, 55% of all Mexican workers worked in the informal economy. Lowering the informality rate is a major challenge for the Mexican government.

🟡 ⬇️ EXTERNAL INCOME (5.51)

The score for this pillar increased in August, rising to 5.51 from 5.26 in July. A year-over-year reduction in remittances in August — just the second decline this year — was a drag on the pillar score, but a strong increase in international tourism revenue more than offset it.

Incoming remittances declined 3.6% year-on-year to US $5.45 billion in August, the first decline of any month since January.

Thus, the score for the remittances component of the pillar fell sharply, although not so far as to warrant a score of zero, as that would require a year-over-year decline of 16.67%.

The pillar score increased in August as international tourism revenue grew compared to the same month of last year, whereas it declined in July. International tourist spending increased 7% year over year in August to reach $2.4 billion.

The MND Economy Index™ trend

In the graph below you can see how the MND Economy Index™ score has changed over time.

We have now calculated a total of ten index scores in the period between March 2025 and August 2026. The difference between the lowest score (56.9 in March 2025 — predating the publication of the first MND Economy Index™ article) and the highest (74.5 in August 2026) is 17.6 points.

The much higher score in this edition of the MND Economy Index™ indicates that Mexico’s economy is performing much better now than it was early in President Sheinbaum’s six-year term.

The improvement in the index score this year has been significant, increasing more than 10 points between March and August.

World.title: Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice is ‘67% complete,’ Sheinbaum reports: Wednesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🕊️ Government presents progress under Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice: The mañanera focused on advances made over the past year under the plan, which the government devised after the assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo on Nov. 1, 2025. President Sheinbaum said the presentation would cover areas other than security.

The mañanera focused on advances made over the past year under the plan, which the government devised after the assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo on Nov. 1, 2025. President Sheinbaum said the presentation would cover areas other than security. 📊 Sheinbaum says Plan Michoacán is 67% complete: The president said 1,680 of more than 2,500 “actions” under the plan have been completed.

The president said 1,680 of more than 2,500 “actions” under the plan have been completed. 💰 Planned investment more than doubles to 118 billion pesos: Sheinbaum said 118 billion pesos (US $6.3 billion) is slated for Plan Michoacán between 2025 and 2030, up from the 57 billion pesos originally announced. She said 72.43 billion pesos, or 61% of the total, has already been spent.

Sheinbaum said 118 billion pesos (US $6.3 billion) is slated for Plan Michoacán between 2025 and 2030, up from the 57 billion pesos originally announced. She said 72.43 billion pesos, or 61% of the total, has already been spent. 🎪 115 “Well-being Fairs” held across all 113 Michoacán municipalities: Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez said residents completed more than 1.1 million administrative procedures at the fairs over the past year, including ones that facilitated access to welfare programs.

Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez said residents completed more than 1.1 million administrative procedures at the fairs over the past year, including ones that facilitated access to welfare programs. 🛣️ 41 billion pesos invested in Michoacán highways: Infrastructure Minister Jesús Esteva said the government is upgrading 411 kilometers of highway, with the government and private sector investing more than 41 billion pesos (US $2.2 billion) in six projects.

Infrastructure Minister Jesús Esteva said the government is upgrading 411 kilometers of highway, with the government and private sector investing more than 41 billion pesos (US $2.2 billion) in six projects. 🏭 Work on Bajío Industrial Park to start this month: Deputy Economy Minister Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez said 9.3 billion pesos (US $498.5 million) will be invested in the park in Zinapécuaro, which will primarily cater to the agroindustrial and automotive sectors.

Deputy Economy Minister Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez said 9.3 billion pesos (US $498.5 million) will be invested in the park in Zinapécuaro, which will primarily cater to the agroindustrial and automotive sectors. 🎓 795,000 Michoacán students receive government scholarships: Education Minister Mario Delgado said primary, middle school, high school and university students all receive monetary assistance, funded with an investment of 5.7 billion pesos (around US $306 million).

Why today’s mañanera matters

A presentation on the progress made under “Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice” over the past year was the central focus of President Sheinbaum’s Wednesday morning press conference.

The government devised the plan in response to the assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo on Nov. 1, 2025, and general insecurity in Michoacán.

At the start of her Wednesday mañanera, the president noted that today’s presentation would focus on progress in areas other than security. She said that an update on the security situation in Michoacán would be presented at her press conference next Tuesday.

Data presented at Sheinbaum’s Oct. 13 mañanera showed that homicides in Michoacán declined 40.3% in the first nine months of 2026 compared to the same period of last year.

The president was accompanied on Wednesday by various high-ranking officials, each of whom spoke briefly about Plan Michoacán initiatives.

Today’s mañanera allowed the government to both highlight progress on the plan and explain how funds have been spent. Sheinbaum characterizes her weekday press conferences as exercises in transparency, a principle she says is central to her administration.

115 ‘Well-being Fairs’ held in Michoacán

Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez reported that 115 “Ferías del Bienestar,” or “Well-being Fairs,” were held across all 113 municipalities of Michoacán over the past year.

She said that officials helped Michoacán residents complete more than 1.1 million trámites (administrative procedures) at the fairs, including ones that facilitated their access to government welfare programs.

Rodríguez also noted that Michoacán residents exchanged 673 firearms for cash over the past year under the Sí al Desarme, Sí a la Paz (Yes to Disarmament, Yes to Peace) program. Those exchanges, she said, will save lives.

Key advances under Plan Michoacán

Officials presented key advances under Plan Michoacán across a range of areas. Not all of the investment they outlined is directly linked to Plan Michoacán funding. Summarized below are the presentations made by 10 officials.

Deputy Economy Minister Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez reported that work will start this month on the Bajío Industrial Park in the municipality of Zinapécuaro. He said 9.3 billion pesos (US $498.5 million) will be invested in the project. The industrial park will primarily cater to the agroindustrial and automotive sectors.

Agriculture Minister Columba López reported that more than 177,000 residents of Michoacán are working in the government’s reforestation/employment program called Sembrando Vida (Sowing Life). She said the government is investing almost 2.2 billion pesos (US $117.9 million) in the program in Michoacán this year.

María Luisa Albores, director of the Mexican Food Security agency (Segalmex), reported that the government has purchased more than 63,000 tonnes of corn directly from some 2,400 small-scale farmers in Michoacán.

Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena reported that the government is investing 168.2 million pesos (US $9 million) in “sustainable forestry” projects in Michoacán.

Energy Minister Luz Elena González reported that more than 1,200 electricity projects have been completed in Michoacán, increasing electricity coverage to 99.99% of homes in the state. She said that 508 million pesos (US $27.2 million) were invested in the projects.

Tourism Minister Josefina Rodríguez reported that more than 2.46 million tourists visited Michoacán between January and August. She said tourist numbers increased 10.1% compared to the same period of last year. She said that tourism-related spending injected more than US $186 million into the Michoacán economy between January and August.

Infrastructure, Communications and Transport Minister Jesús Esteva reported that the government is upgrading 411 kilometers of highway in Michoacán. He said that the government and the private sector are investing more than 41 billion pesos (US $2.2 billion) in six highway projects in the state.

Welfare Minister Leticia Ramírez reported that the government is spending more than 30.4 billion pesos (US $1.6 billion) on welfare and social programs in Michoacán in 2026. She said that more than 1 million Michoacán residents benefit from the programs, which include pension schemes, educational scholarships and the distribution of fertilizer to farmers.

Education Minister Mario Delgado reported that over 795,000 students in Michoacán receive government scholarships. He said that primary school, middle school, high school and university students all receive monetary assistance. He said that the scholarships are funded with an investment of 5.7 billion pesos (around US $306 million).

IMSS Bienestar director Alejandro Svarch reported that a new hospital focused on the treatment of addictions had opened in Apatzingán. He also reported that a mental health center had opened in Huetamo. The combined investment in the two projects was 76.1 million pesos (US $3.6 million).

118 billion pesos in investment planned for Plan Michoacán by 2030

Presenting Plan Michoacán on Nov. 9, 2025, Sheinbaum described it as a “comprehensive strategy” and told reporters that it was based on 12 central tenets and included “more than 100 actions.”

Her presentation on Wednesday showed that there are, in fact, more than 2,500 Plan Michoacán “actions,” 1,680 of which have been “completed.” Sheinbaum said that represented progress of 67%.

She also said that 118 billion pesos (US $6.3 billion) is slated to be invested in Plan Michoacán between 2025 and 2030, the final year of her six-year term. That amount is more than double the 57-billion-peso investment that was originally announced.

Sheinbaum said that 72.43 billion pesos has already been spent on the plan. That amount represents 61% of the projected total.

Sheinbaum said that Plan Michoacán involves “very intense work” that is coordinated by the Interior Ministry. She also said that all of the federal government ministries have a “permanent presence” in Michoacán, one of 23 Mexican states governed by the Morena party.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Paraguay’s President Peña Resigns Over Bank
World.content:
Politics: Paraguay

Key Facts Who. Paraguay’s president, Santiago Peña, announced his resignation on 5 November over the failure of Ueno Bank, a major lender.

Why. Lawmakers had opened impeachment proceedings; Congress has received his letter but not formally accepted it.

Next. Vice President Pedro Alliana is expected to finish the term to August 2028; not yet confirmed.

Time. As of 5 November 2026, 17:30 GMT

Paraguay’s president looked into a camera on Thursday and told his country he was stepping down. Santiago Peña, a conservative who took office on 15 August 2023, announced his resignation in a video on 5 November as the failure of Ueno Bank turned into an impeachment fight.

Ueno Bank, a Paraguayan lender with almost three million customers, was put into closure by the central bank on Tuesday 3 November. Savers are now waiting for payouts from the state deposit guarantee fund.

For US readers, Paraguay is a major exporter of soy and beef and a South American partner of Washington, so a sudden change at the top is worth watching. We have no information yet on any reaction from the US government or from markets.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 with 35.0 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (55); weakest: future resources (13). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

In plain English The president says he is quitting before lawmakers could vote to remove him over a bank that failed. Congress still has to accept the resignation, and the vice president is expected to take over.

What We Know

Peña posted the video on his own and the presidency’s official X accounts. “I have decided to submit my resignation as President of the Republic,” he said.

He said he was acting for social peace and to preserve democratic institutions. He called it one of the hardest moments of his life.

He apologised to the people in the same video. “No office should stand above the wellbeing of Paraguay,” he added.

He then turned to the savers hurt by the crisis. “My greatest wish is that the return of those funds is guaranteed,” he said.

Peña wants depositors repaid through the Deposit Guarantee Fund (FGD), the state scheme meant to protect bank savings. Deputies took up an advance payout from the fund in an extraordinary session on Wednesday.

The Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of Congress, had opened an impeachment debate, known in Spanish as a juicio político, over Ueno Bank. The charge sheet lists five grounds.

The opposition alleged a conflict of interest tied to a stake Peña held in Ueno’s parent company until 2025. The charge sheet also raises the use of money from the IPS, the state pension institute.

The Colorado Party, the ruling conservative party, had said it would back impeachment, and former president Horacio Cartes, the party’s leader, backed it too. The Chamber’s president, Raúl Latorre, had said Peña would submit to the process.

After the resignation, the Chamber put the session in recess.

Paraguay’s National Congress in Asunción, where lawmakers must act on the resignation. File photo.

We send a confirmation link first, and the same address then receives The Rio Times Brief, our daily briefing. Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

Inside the Ueno Bank Crisis

The central bank ordered Ueno’s resolution, a legal closure process, on Tuesday 3 November, and the central bank’s president, Carlos Carvallo, resigned, as we covered in our earlier report.The bank’s solvency, a measure of whether it can cover its debts, fell below 50% of the required minimum.

Ueno had also drawn large public deposits, including money from the IPS.On Thursday a judge ordered prison for six former Ueno directors, including Miguel Vázquez, and house arrest for two others.

The wider case has 27 defendants. The central bank has opened a web platform where savers can check their payout from the guarantee fund.

Peña also cancelled his trip to the Ibero-American Summit in Madrid, a gathering of leaders from Latin America, Spain and Portugal. The resignation document reached Congress on Thursday afternoon, and Congress has confirmed receipt.

Formal acceptance has not yet been confirmed. Local reports say the Senate president would call a joint session of Congress to take up the resignation, and a new president could be sworn in within a day.

The timing is unconfirmed, and some senators have said they might reject the resignation. Vice President Pedro Alliana is expected to take over and finish the term, which runs to August 2028.

That is expected rather than confirmed.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether Congress will accept the resignation, or who will be sworn in and when. It is also unclear whether the impeachment will be dropped or only paused.

Nobody has said how large the FGD payout will be or how fast it will arrive. It is also unknown whether prosecutors will pursue Peña once he leaves office.

What It Means for Travelers and US Readers

Paraguay is a major soy and beef exporter, so US companies and investors with business there will want to see an orderly handover. We have no information on any US government reaction or any market reaction so far.

Anyone holding an account at Ueno should use the central bank’s web platform to check their payout. Visitors should follow official announcements from Congress, and our background piece on who holds power in Paraguay in 2026 explains the political landscape.

Our earlier report on the impeachment push shows how the case reached this point. More coverage is in the Paraguay section.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Peña resign?

He said he acted for social peace and to protect democratic institutions, as lawmakers weighed impeachment over the Ueno Bank crisis. He also apologised to the public.

Who becomes president of Paraguay?

Vice President Pedro Alliana is expected to take over until August 2028, but that is not confirmed. Congress has confirmed receiving the resignation, but formal acceptance is not yet confirmed.

What happens to Ueno Bank depositors?

Peña said he wants savers repaid through the Deposit Guarantee Fund (FGD). The central bank has opened a web platform for payout queries, but we have not confirmed amounts or dates.

Does this affect US travellers or investors?

We have no information on any US government or market reaction. Paraguay is a major soy and beef exporter, so investors may watch whether the handover stays orderly.

Sources Presidency of Paraguay (video on X, 5 November 2026) · Paraguayan Congress · Court order in the Ueno Bank case · Central Bank of Paraguay

World.title: Macron Trust Falls to Record Low in Poll
World.content:
The Élysée Palace, the French president’s official residence in Paris. File photo. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

France in Turmoil

Published Thursday, Nov. 5, 11:59 a.m. ET (5:59 p.m. Paris) · Source: Elabe, Odoxa, Polymarket

On the day France’s unions filled the streets, its president hit a new low in the polls. Only about one French person in eight now trusts Emmanuel Macron to solve the country’s main problems.

Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Just 13% of French respondents trust President Emmanuel Macron, according to the November barometer from Elabe, a French polling firm, published on Thursday, Nov. 5. Elabe calls it the lowest confidence rating the survey has ever measured, below even the record low of François Hollande, the former Socialist president.

The result lands on a day of national strikes, part of our France protests coverage. Our guide to whether France’s government could collapse explains what is at stake.

Key Facts The number. 13% trust Macron, down 4 points in a month and 11 points since August.

The record. It is below Hollande’s 14% in November 2016 and Macron’s own 14% low in October 2025.

The prime minister. Sébastien Lecornu, who runs the government, is at 17%, his lowest rating.

Prediction markets. Polymarket, a prediction market, gives Marine Le Pen, the National Rally’s leader, about 42% to win the next presidency (11:55 a.m. ET, Nov. 5).

This story is part of our coverage of the why France is in crisis. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: France Calls Pay Talks After Strike Day

In plain English Elabe asks people each month how much they trust the president to deal with the country’s main problems. This month, 13% said yes and 82% said no, the worst result since the series began.

Even His Own Voters Are Leaving

The slide is steady: 24% in August, 17% in October and 13% now. It has come as unions and students protest over prices and the government fights over its budget.

Distrust stands at 82%, including 60% who say they have no trust at all. A year ago, in October 2025, the figures were 82% and 59%.

Among people who backed Macron in the first round of the 2022 election, trust fell 7 points to 36%. Among his second-round voters, it fell 6 points to 23%.

Among retirees the rating is 12%, down 6 points. Among 18-to-24-year-olds the rating is 18%, down 14 points in two months.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Prime Minister Is Slipping Too

Lecornu is trusted by 17% of respondents, down 2 points in a month and 9 points since August. Among Macron’s prime ministers, only former prime minister François Bayrou has scored lower, at 12% in September 2025.

His rating has fallen as the autumn protests have grown. Marine Le Pen, who leads the National Rally, France’s main conservative-nationalist party, scores 35% in Elabe’s ranking of political figures, and Jordan Bardella, the party’s president, is at 33%, his lowest since April 2024.

A Second Poll Points the Same Way

A separate poll by Odoxa, another French firm, found that 83% of French people call Macron a bad president and 16% a good one. Odoxa questioned 1,005 adults online on Oct. 21 and 22.

The two surveys ask different questions, so their numbers cannot be compared directly. Both, however, show the lowest marks of his presidency.

The next test is Monday, Nov. 9, when Lecornu hosts unions and employers at Matignon. If the talks fail, more strikes would likely deepen the slide.

What Prediction Markets Say Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, priced Marine Le Pen at about 42% to win France’s next presidential election on Nov. 5 at 11:55 a.m. ET, with about US$166 million traded. Édouard Philippe, a former prime minister, was at 11.5%. The next vote is due in 2027, so these prices move with the news. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

A weak president means a weak government, and a weak government finds it harder to pass a budget. That is the main thing French bond and share investors in the United States will watch in the coming weeks.

The poll does not change travel plans, but the strikes may. Check rail and airline notices before visiting.

What Is Not Known

Elabe’s page does not state the fieldwork dates or sample size. We have found no reaction yet from the Élysée, the president’s office, or from Matignon, the prime minister’s office.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many French people trust Macron, according to Elabe?

Elabe’s barometer published on Nov. 5 puts trust in Macron at 13%. That is the lowest the barometer has recorded, below Hollande’s 14% in November 2016.

How does the Elabe result compare with the Odoxa poll?

Odoxa found 83% call Macron a bad president, its highest for him and just below Hollande’s 84% record. The two polls ask different questions, so the numbers are not comparable.

When is France’s next presidential election?

The next presidential election is due in 2027. Macron cannot run again after two terms.

Sources: Elabe political observatory, November 2026, Odoxa barometer, Polymarket. Related: France 2027 election odds, France 2027 poll tracker.

World.title: France Calls Pay Talks After Strike Day
World.content:
French riot police line a Paris street near Boulevard Voltaire during a student march on 6 October 2026. File photo. (Photo: Jules*, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

France in Turmoil

Published Thursday, Nov. 5, 11:59 a.m. ET (5:59 p.m. Paris) · Source: Prime Minister’s office, French Interior Ministry, CGT, Polymarket

France got its biggest street day of the autumn, and by evening the prime minister had a new plan: sit everyone down on Monday. The unions want pay rises, and the government has called talks.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every France in Turmoil story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will hold a “conférence sociale”, a formal round of talks with unions and employers, at Matignon, his Paris office, on Monday, Nov. 9. His office announced it on Thursday, Nov. 5, to give “answers” on purchasing power and wages.

The announcement came as the Interior Ministry, which runs France’s police, gave a provisional count of nearly 600,000 marchers nationwide at about 11:00 a.m. ET (5:00 p.m. Paris). It is the latest chapter in our France protests coverage, and why France is protesting explains the anger over prices.

Key Facts The talks. Lecornu invites unions and employers to Matignon on Monday, Nov. 9, to discuss wages and purchasing power.

Turnout. The Interior Ministry’s provisional count is nearly 600,000; the CGT union claims nearly 1.6 million.

Order. The Rhône prefecture reported 24 arrests in Lyon; the Interior Ministry noted incidents in Nantes.

Prediction markets. Polymarket puts a French state of emergency by Dec. 31 at 6.5% (11:55 a.m. ET, Nov. 5).

This story is part of our coverage of the why France is in crisis. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: French Strike Fills Lyon With Up to 55,000

In plain English France’s big unions called a one-day national strike over pay and prices. The government counts fewer marchers than the unions do, but even its figure is the highest of the movement so far.

Two Counts, One Big Day

At 1:00 p.m. Paris time (7:00 a.m. ET), the ministry had counted 270,000 people in 180 marches outside Paris. The CGT, the General Confederation of Labour and one of France’s biggest union federations, counted more than 250,000 in 73 cities at the same hour.

Later the CGT claimed nearly 1.6 million people, almost three times the ministry’s provisional number. The ministry’s own tally is also above the 550,000 it counted on Oct. 17, the last big day, which turned violent.

Strike rates at midday, published by the Ministry of Action and Public Accounts, the finance ministry, were 9.89% in the state civil service, 4.60% in local government and 3.93% in hospital staff. The CGT’s map listed more than 250 actions across France.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Arrests in Lyon, Clashing Counts in Bordeaux

In Paris, the unions’ march ran from Place de la République along Boulevard Voltaire to Place de la Nation, two squares in eastern Paris. Police said hooded individuals caused damage, and that they tried to isolate troublemakers at the front.

The head of the march reached Nation while many marchers were still waiting at République, more than 3 km (about 1.9 miles) behind. We found no Paris turnout figure or arrest count.

In Lyon, the Rhône prefecture, the state authority for the area, reported five shops damaged and 24 arrests for mortar fire, projectile throwing and “outrage”.

Counts clashed in Bordeaux too. The prefecture counted 21,000 marchers and the CGT 120,000, a gap of nearly six times.

Will the Talks Change Anything?

The unions are pressing for higher pay and more public funding. Lecornu has also asked Labour Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou to finish consultations by Sunday, and the government says it is still talking to civil-service representatives.

The talks would mean more if unions attend and the budget moves. A boycott, or no wage offer on Monday, would likely bring more strikes.

What Prediction Markets Say Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, priced a French state of emergency by Dec. 31 at 6.5% on Nov. 5 at 11:55 a.m. ET, with about US$2.7 million traded. On a thinner market of about US$26,000 traded, it put the chance that France passes a national budget by Dec. 31 at 54%. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

A government that has to bargain over wages while it writes a budget is a risk signal for holders of French bonds and shares. Visitors should expect crowds near march routes and possible rail and school disruption, so check operators’ notices first.

What Is Not Known

The ministry’s final count, the Paris figure and national arrest totals are not out. Which unions and employer groups will attend on Monday, and any union reply to the invitation, are also unconfirmed.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Prime Minister Lecornu announce?

He will hold a “conférence sociale” with unions and employers at Matignon on Monday, Nov. 9. His office says the aim is answers on purchasing power and wages.

How many people marched in France on Nov. 5?

The Interior Ministry gave a provisional count of nearly 600,000, while the CGT claimed nearly 1.6 million. Final figures have not been published.

Were there arrests?

The Rhône prefecture reported 24 arrests in Lyon, and police noted incidents in Nantes. No Paris arrest count was available.

Why are French workers striking?

Unions are pressing for higher pay and more public funding, after weeks of protests over prices and wages.

Sources: French government, Interior Ministry and prefecture statements, CGT statements, Polymarket. Related: will France’s government collapse, France 2027 election odds.

World.title: Jailed Maduro Hits 92% in Venezuela Market
World.content:
Central Caracas, Venezuela. (File photo)

Prediction Markets: Venezuela

Key Facts Prediction markets. Polymarket, a crypto-based exchange, prices Maduro at about 92% to lead Venezuela on 31 December, up 17 points in 7 days (11:25 Eastern Time, 5 November 2026).

Reality check. Maduro has been held in a New York jail since January. Delcy Rodríguez, his former vice president, is acting president.

Why. No single trigger was reported for the jump.

Volume. The Venezuela leader event has traded about US$99.5 million in total, but only about US$30,000 on Maduro in 24 hours.

Traders on Polymarket now put the chance that Nicolás Maduro, the jailed former president, is Venezuela’s head of state on 31 December at about 92%, up about 17 points in a week.

That price sits awkwardly with the facts. Maduro was captured by US forces on 3 January 2026 and has been in custody in New York ever since, while Delcy Rodríguez, his former vice president, runs Venezuela as acting president.

For a US reader the gap matters, because Venezuelan oil, sanctions, bonds and migration all depend on who governs Caracas. A market that looks wrong is also a warning about how much weight one thinly traded price can carry.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket lets people trade contracts that pay out if an event happens. The price, in cents on the dollar, is read as the crowd’s probability.

This contract, “Venezuela leader end of 2026?”, pays on whoever officially holds the post of head of state on 31 December 2026 at 12:00 Eastern Time. Our read at 11:25 Eastern Time on 5 November 2026:

Nicolás Maduro: about 92% (bid 91.3%, ask 92%), up about 17 points in 7 days and about 2 points in 24 hours.

about 92% (bid 91.3%, ask 92%), up about 17 points in 7 days and about 2 points in 24 hours. Delcy Rodríguez: 7.5%, down about 6.5 points in 7 days.

Volume: about US$99.5 million for the whole event, about US$126,000 in the last 24 hours, and about US$30,000 on the Maduro contract. The Maduro contract is thinly traded, so a few orders can move it. We found no matching Kalshi market, the exchange regulated in the US by the CFTC (Commodity Futures Trading Commission).

Our own daily snapshots show the climb. The Maduro price was 80.8% on 29 October, 85.5% on 4 November and about 91.5% on 5 November.

Why the Odds Moved

No single trigger was reported. We checked official statements and regional coverage from the last 48 hours and found no event that would make Maduro’s return to office more likely.

The recent news points the other way. The case against Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, passed to a new judge, Analisa Torres, in late October after the death of the previous judge, Alvin Hellerstein, at 92.

Maduro has pleaded not guilty to the charges, including a torture conspiracy count added in October. His trial was set for June 2027, so he is due to remain in custody well past 31 December.

Our earlier report on the judge’s death is here. That story does not explain a price jump on 5 November, and we do not link the two.

The wording of the contract is the other thing to watch. It resolves on who “officially holds” the post, and we have not tested how every edge case would be settled.
