Who Runs Venezuela Today

Rodríguez took office as acting president after the January capture, and she is still described that way in current reports.

Other Polymarket markets treat the question very differently. One on the next presidential election winner puts Machado near 70% and Rodríguez near 10.5%, though that contract has only about US$65,000 in total volume.

A market on when an election is called gives 31% for a date by 31 March 2027, 8.5% by 31 December 2026 and 4.2% by 30 November 2026. These contracts ask different questions, so they cannot be set side by side with the leader market.

What It Means for US Readers

Investors in Venezuelan debt and in Citgo, the US refiner long tied to Venezuela’s state oil company, watch the question of who has authority in Caracas. Our report on the US delay to bondholder action over Citgo is here.

For readers following US sanctions, oil supply and migration from Venezuela, the practical message is simple. Official sources, not one market price, tell you who holds power, and today those sources point to Rodríguez.

Treat the 92% as a data point about the market, not as a signal that Maduro is about to return. A price this far from the known facts may reflect thin trading or contract wording rather than new information.

What Is Not Known

We do not know why the Maduro contract rose. We do not know who is buying, and we found no report of any legal or political change that would explain it.

We also do not know how the market operator would settle the contract if the situation on 31 December is unclear. Readers can follow developments on our Venezuela page, on the Latin America odds page and on our prediction markets hub.

The next court date in New York is the signal that matters most for his legal position. Reports differ on whether Maduro’s next hearing falls on 17 November or 17 December, so we do not give a date.

Frequently Asked Questions

What do the prediction markets say about Venezuela’s leader?

On 5 November 2026, Polymarket priced Nicolás Maduro at about 92% to be head of state on 31 December, Delcy Rodríguez at 7.5%. These are bets, not forecasts by The Rio Times.

Why did the Maduro odds jump?

No single trigger was reported. Maduro remains in custody in New York with a trial set for June 2027, so the move is unexplained.

Who is Venezuela’s leader now?

Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro’s former vice president, is acting president after the January 2026 US capture of Maduro.

Is a prediction market the same as a poll?

No. A poll asks people what they think; a market shows what traders will pay to bet on an outcome. Polymarket is a crypto-based platform, and its prices are not official forecasts.

Should US investors rely on this price?

No. The Maduro contract traded only about US$30,000 in 24 hours, so a few orders can move it. Official sources decide who holds power.

World.content:
Independence Square in Kyiv, Ukraine. (File photo)

Prediction Markets: Russia and Ukraine

Key Facts Prediction markets. Polymarket prices a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire by 31 December 2027 at about 44%, down roughly 9 points in 24 hours (read 10:28 Eastern Time, 5 November 2026).

Why. No single trigger was reported. The fall came days before US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi.

Next. Ukraine, Russia and the US are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November.

Volume. The ceasefire event has traded about US$3.4 million in total and about US$66,000 in 24 hours.

Traders on Polymarket now put the chance of a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire by the end of 2027 at about 44%, down from roughly 53% a day earlier, even as new peace talks get ready to open.

Why the Odds Moved

No single trigger was reported. We looked at the last 48 hours of official statements and regional coverage and found no event that explains a drop of this size.

What did happen is a build-up to talks. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, said this week that negotiations must move “at full throttle” to end the war as quickly as possible.

He had held a detailed call of about 90 minutes with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s special envoys. Negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States are due to meet in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday, 10 November, and Wednesday, 11 November.

They would be the first talks between all three sides since February. That makes the move puzzling at first glance, since talks usually lift ceasefire odds.

One reading is that traders see little chance that a first round produces a deal, but we cannot confirm that.

What It Means for US Readers

The US is now a direct party. Two White House envoys are preparing the talks, so a result would be read as a verdict on Washington’s diplomacy as well as Kyiv’s and Moscow’s.

Markets that react to the war are oil, natural gas, European defence stocks and wheat. A lower ceasefire price is not a signal to trade; it shows only that bettors see the end as further away than they did yesterday.

Our earlier piece on talks odds is here.

What It Means for Latin America and Africa

Both regions feel the war through food and fuel. Brazil is a heavy buyer of Russian fertiliser, and many African importers rely on wheat from the Black Sea region.

A longer war keeps those costs exposed; a ceasefire would ease them, though we have no market prices to show for that. See also our Africa odds and Latin America odds pages, and the prediction markets hub.

What Is Not Known

We do not know who will sit at the table in Abu Dhabi, what Russia will bring, or why traders cut the odds now. The talks are planned, not held, so their outcome is open.

The markets also say nothing about the terms of a ceasefire, such as lines on the map or security guarantees. Zelensky said Ukraine has presented its proposals to the US side.

The odds will probably move again after 11 November.

Frequently Asked Questions

What do the prediction markets expect on a Ukraine ceasefire?

On 5 November 2026, Polymarket priced a ceasefire by 31 December 2027 at about 44%, by 31 March 2027 at 17.5% and by 31 December 2026 at 9.5%. These are bets, not forecasts by The Rio Times.

Why did the ceasefire odds fall?

No single trigger was reported. The fall came while Ukraine, Russia and the US were preparing talks in Abu Dhabi for 10 and 11 November.

What are the Abu Dhabi talks?

Negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November. They would be the first talks between all three sides since February.

Is a prediction market the same as a poll?

No. A poll asks people what they think; a market shows what traders will pay to bet on an outcome. Polymarket is a crypto-based platform, and the contract here does not count as an official forecast.

What does this mean for readers in Latin America and Africa?

A ceasefire would matter for grain, fertiliser and fuel prices, and for citizens recruited into the war. We report only what is documented, and the markets do not say how any of this would play out.

World.title: Traders Put Spain’s Opposition at 89%
World.content:
Spanish People's Party candidate Alberto Nunez Feijoo and Spain's Prime Minister and Socialist candidate Pedro Sanchez talk before a televised debate ahead of snap election in Madrid, Spain, July 10, 2023. REUTERS/Juan Medina

Published Thursday, Nov. 5, about 10:40 a.m. ET (4:40 p.m. Madrid) · Source: Polymarket, INE, Spain’s electoral decree, polling firms

Traders now put Alberto Núñez Feijóo, Spain’s conservative opposition leader, at about 89% to become prime minister after the Nov. 29 election. That is up from 84% in our Spain Election 2026 coverage earlier this week.

The jump comes after a deadly train collision and a minister’s resignation. Polls, meanwhile, show a much closer race, so the gap between bettors and voters is the story to watch.

Key Facts What. Spain votes on Sunday, Nov. 29, 2026, to elect the 350-seat Congress of Deputies and the Senate.

Prediction markets. Polymarket: Feijóo 88.5%, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez 9.3% to lead the next government (Nov. 5, 10:28 a.m. ET).

Polls. Sondaxe, a Spanish polling firm, on Nov. 1: conservative People’s Party 29.2%, Socialists 26.9%, Vox 19.2%.

Debates. Sánchez and Feijóo are set for a one-on-one debate on Monday, Nov. 16.

Next step. The new Congress meets on Dec. 23, and only then can a new prime minister take office.

This story is part of our coverage of the Spain Election 2026. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Spain's Economy Minister Covers Transport

In plain English Spaniards vote for parties, and parliament then picks the prime minister. Bettors are guessing who can build a majority, which is why a party at about 30% in polls can be a strong favourite.

Why Traders Favour Feijóo

Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, showed Feijóo, leader of the conservative People’s Party (PP), at about 89% to become prime minister on a page updated at 9 a.m. ET on Nov. 5. Sánchez, the Socialist (PSOE) leader, stood at about 9%.

Traders had US$886,600 on Sánchez’s contract and US$594,108 on Feijóo’s, and total volume on the market was US$2,771,225. The prices were not time-stamped separately and may lag.

File photo: Óscar Puente at La Moncloa, the prime minister’s office in Madrid. He resigned as Transport Minister on Nov. 3.

Polls Point in Different Directions

Sondaxe, a polling firm working for the newspaper La Voz de Galicia, published a poll on Sunday, Nov. 1, with fieldwork on Oct. 26 to 28. It put the PP at 29.2%, the PSOE at 26.9% and Vox, a conservative party, at 19.2%.

Its fieldwork ended on Wednesday, Oct. 28, the day a high-speed train collision near Urda, a town in Toledo province, killed 69 people. A Hamalgama Métrica poll published on Nov. 2 gave the PP 135 seats and the PSOE 106, but its interviews ran from Oct. 22 to 28.

No poll we found was conducted after the collision. The PP and Vox together are reported at or above the 176 seats needed for a majority in the 350-seat Congress.

The CIS, Spain’s state-run polling institute, published an October survey on Oct. 14 with the PSOE at 34% and the PP at 22.2%. That contradicts the commercial polls, and its fieldwork (Oct. 1 to 6) also predates the collision.

Dates That Matter

Sánchez called the election for Sunday, Nov. 29, after parliament rejected his government’s housing measures in early October. The INE, Spain’s national statistics institute, counts 38,728,356 registered voters, including about 2.77 million living abroad.

Sánchez and Feijóo are set for a one-on-one debate on Monday, Nov. 16. A four-way debate is planned for Thursday, Nov. 26, though the PSOE and the PP disagree on which broadcaster should host it.

After the vote, a successor can take office only once the new Congress meets on Wednesday, Dec. 23. Until then Sánchez stays prime minister with full powers, even though parliament is dissolved, and he becomes a caretaker leader only after the vote.

The Train Crash Backdrop

Transport Minister Óscar Puente resigned on Tuesday, Nov. 3, after the Urda collision. He also gave up heading the PSOE list for Valladolid.

What It Means for US Readers

Prediction markets such as Polymarket are increasingly followed in the United States alongside polls, and the Spanish contract is a live read on trader expectations. A conservative-led government would matter to US investors in Spanish banks, energy and infrastructure firms.

Spain’s next prime minister is not decided by the popular vote alone, since a candidate must win a parliamentary investiture vote. That is why a party polling near 30% can be priced near 89% to lead the government.

What Is Not Known

We found no poll taken after the collision, so its effect on voting intention is unclear. The broadcaster of the Nov. 26 debate, broadcast times and the exact campaign dates are unconfirmed, and we found no Senate projections.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Spanish general election?

Spain votes on Sunday, Nov. 29, 2026, for the Congress of Deputies and the Senate. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called the early vote after parliament rejected his government’s housing measures in early October.

What are the odds that Feijóo becomes prime minister?

Polymarket showed Alberto Núñez Feijóo at about 89% on a page updated at 9 a.m. ET on Nov. 5. These are traders’ bets rather than polls and can change quickly.

When are the televised debates?

Sánchez and Feijóo are set for a one-on-one debate on Monday, Nov. 16. A four-way debate is planned for Thursday, Nov. 26, but the broadcaster is disputed.

Why can a party near 30% be priced near 89%?

Spain’s prime minister is chosen by a vote in Congress, not by the popular vote. The market bets on who can win that vote, which depends on coalition arithmetic.





Sources: Polymarket prediction markets (Nov. 5); INE election figures (Oct. 9); royal decree calling the election (BOE, Oct. 6); Sondaxe, Hamalgama Métrica and CIS polls; Rio Times Spain Election 2026 hub and our earlier poll and markets report.

World.title: Mexico Expects US$12.6B From Buen Fin Sale
World.content:
Perisur shopping centre in Mexico City at dusk, in a file photo from 2025. Liverpool opened a new zone there on 10 September. Photo: Ehécatl Cabrera / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

Published Thursday, Nov. 5, about 10:30 a.m. ET (9:30 a.m. Mexico City) · Source: Concanaco Servytur, SAT, Profeco, Secretaría de Economía

Mexico’s biggest shopping weekend is eight days away, and its business chambers expect 235 billion pesos (about US$12.6 billion) in sales. Our El Buen Fin 2026 hub tracks the sale, now in its 16th edition, which runs from Friday, Nov. 13, to Tuesday, Nov. 17.

El Buen Fin is Mexico’s answer to Black Friday, a government-backed discount campaign. Since our earlier reports, a business forecast, a consumer price-checking site and a tax-agency prize draw have all been announced.

Key Facts What. Mexico’s 16th El Buen Fin, an annual discount sale, runs Friday, Nov. 13, to Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026.

Forecast. Concanaco Servytur, Mexico’s business chambers confederation, expects about 235 billion pesos (US$12.6 billion) in sales, up 7.3%.

Prize draw. The SAT, Mexico’s tax agency, draws prizes on Friday, Dec. 4, at 1 p.m. ET (noon Mexico City).

Prices. Profeco, the federal consumer watchdog, lets shoppers compare prices on more than 490 products online.

This story is part of our coverage of the El Buen Fin 2026. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Mexico's Buen Fin Sale Starts Nov. 13

In plain English El Buen Fin (“the good weekend”) is a yearly sale that Mexico’s government, retailers and banks run together. Shoppers get discounts and a chance to win prizes in a draw run by the tax agency.

The Spending Forecast

Concanaco Servytur forecast on Oct. 28 that national spending will reach about 235 billion pesos (US$12.6 billion), up 7.3% on 2025. That is a slowdown from the 26.1% rise between 2024 and 2025.

Octavio de la Torre, the confederation’s president, said the forecast assumes more than 200,000 participating businesses. About 49 billion pesos (US$2.6 billion), or 21%, is expected to come from online sales.

Physical stores should keep 186 billion pesos (US$10.0 billion), or 79%. Fashion, electronics, personal care, appliances and mobile phones are the categories shoppers say they most want to buy.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 70.8 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

All peso figures here use about 18.6 pesos to the dollar, the market rate on Nov. 5.

File photo: a public market in Coyoacán, Mexico City.

How to Check Prices and Win Prizes

Profeco has launched a price-comparison site at elbuenfin.profeco.gob.mx. It covers more than 490 products, mostly appliances, electronics and large household goods, and shows prices by city and store along with price history.

Profeco says the data is for reference only, because stores can change prices during the sale. Its head, Iván Escalante Ruiz, presented the tool at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s daily morning press conference.

The SAT prize draw is open to purchases of at least 250 pesos (about US$13) paid by credit or debit card from participating banks at registered businesses between Nov. 13 and 17. Cash purchases do not count.

The prize pool is 500 million pesos (about US$27 million), of which 100 million pesos (about US$5.4 million) is reserved for businesses. The top consumer prize is 250,000 pesos (about US$13,400), and the top business prize is 260,000 pesos (about US$13,900).

Dates to Mark

Business registration, run by the Secretaría de Economía (Mexico’s economy ministry), closes at the end of Nov. 12. The sale starts on Friday, Nov. 13, and ends on Tuesday, Nov. 17.

The SAT draw takes place on Friday, Dec. 4, at its Mexico City headquarters. The winners list is due from Monday, Dec. 7, and prizes are to be paid before Jan. 5, 2027.

What It Means for US Readers

Black Friday in the United States falls on Nov. 27, ten days after El Buen Fin ends. Mexico’s sale therefore comes first in the calendar for shoppers comparing offers, including Americans living in or visiting Mexico.

Last year’s edition ran Thursday to Monday, so this year’s Friday-to-Tuesday dates are a change. Our El Buen Fin dates guide and our earlier report on the Nov. 13 start have the background.

What Is Not Known

No official start hour for Nov. 13 has been confirmed. The final count of registered businesses and any revision to the 235 billion peso forecast are also unknown.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is El Buen Fin 2026?

It runs Friday, Nov. 13, to Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026, five days. An official start hour has not been confirmed.

How do shoppers qualify for the SAT prize draw?

They must spend at least 250 pesos (about US$13) by credit or debit card at a registered business between Nov. 13 and 17. Cash purchases do not count.

When is the SAT prize draw?

It takes place on Friday, Dec. 4, at 1 p.m. ET (noon in Mexico City). The SAT, Mexico’s tax agency, holds it at its Mexico City headquarters.





Sources: Concanaco Servytur forecast (Oct. 28); SAT prize-draw rules; Profeco price site elbuenfin.profeco.gob.mx; Secretaría de Economía registration terms; Rio Times El Buen Fin hub.

World.title: Puerto Rico Officer Faces Teen Death Charges
World.content:
Puerto Rico’s Department of Justice said on Thursday 5 November 2026 that it will file criminal charges against a police agent over the death of Dianelys P. Ortiz López, 19, in Bayamón. Puerto Rico is a US territory and its residents are US citizens, so the case concerns an American police force and an American family.

Key Facts Who. Police agent Nivea I. Arce Rivera; victim Dianelys P. Ortiz López, 19.

What. Puerto Rico’s Justice Department says charges will be filed; counts not yet announced.

Where. Bayamón, a city just southwest of San Juan, near a public housing complex.

When. Announced Thursday 5 November 2026; Ortiz López died on 31 March 2026.

Status. As of 5 November 2026, 14:30 GMT

What We Know

Puerto Rico’s Department of Justice announced on Thursday 5 November 2026 that charges will be filed against Nivea I. Arce Rivera, an agent of the Puerto Rico Police Bureau (Negociado de la Policía), the island’s police force. The charges relate to the death of Dianelys P. Ortiz López, who was 19.

Ortiz López was struck by a vehicle in March 2026 near the Virgilio Dávila public housing complex in Bayamón, a city just southwest of San Juan. She died on 31 March 2026.

Reports say the officer did not stop at the scene, which is an allegation and has not been proved. The victim’s father, Efraín Ortiz, told a television news programme (in Spanish, “no se detuvo en la escena”) that the officer did not stop at the scene.

According to one report, the officer did report the crash at a police station. The officer has not been convicted of any offence and is presumed innocent.

Prosecutors must still show a court that the evidence supports the charges. The charges will be filed through the Bayamón Prosecutor’s Office, the local office that brings criminal cases in the city.

The officer was cited to a Rule 6 hearing, the first court step, in which a judge decides whether there is probable cause for an arrest. It takes place in the investigation room of the Bayamón court, and no date has been reported.

The Capitol of Puerto Rico in San Juan. (Archive photo)

What Is Not Known

The specific charges have not been announced, and they are expected to be stated when the charges are filed. Reports say the officer was cited to a hearing, not arrested.

Reports differ on the exact date of the crash, with 15 March and 29 March both cited, and on the type of vehicle involved. They also differ on whether the officer was on duty at the time.

We do not know the outcome of the hearing, because no result had been reported when this article was written.A public account from the officer was not available at the time of writing.

Until a court rules, the officer has not been convicted and every claim above remains an allegation. We report only what officials and relatives have said, out of respect for the victim and her family.

We will update this article when the charges are set.

What It Means for US Readers

Puerto Rico is a US territory, and its residents are US citizens who can live and travel freely across the 50 states. A case like this therefore concerns Americans and an American police force.

The Puerto Rico Police Bureau (Negociado de la Policía) is the island’s own police force. Officer-involved cases are handled by Puerto Rico’s own Department of Justice, the island government’s legal office.

Its prosecutors bring criminal cases in the island’s courts, including the Bayamón court named in this case. The process is run locally, not by a federal agency in Washington.

Charges are an accusation, and a court must still weigh the evidence. Under US legal principles, a defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

For readers on the mainland, the next public step is the Rule 6 hearing in Bayamón. The specific charges are expected to become public when they are filed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is being charged?

Prosecutors say charges will be filed against Nivea I. Arce Rivera, a Puerto Rico Police agent. She has not been convicted, and the specific charges have not been announced.

What is a Rule 6 hearing?

It is a hearing in Puerto Rico’s courts where a judge decides whether there is probable cause for an arrest. In this case it is scheduled in the Bayamón court’s investigation room.

Who was Dianelys P. Ortiz López?

She was a 19-year-old struck by a vehicle near a public housing complex in Bayamón in March 2026. She died on 31 March 2026.

Why does this matter to US readers?

Puerto Rico is a US territory and its residents are US citizens. The case is handled by the island’s own Department of Justice and courts.

Sources Puerto Rico Department of Justice (announcement of 5 November 2026)

World.title: National Geographic Names Costa Rica Central America’s Ultimate Nature Escape
World.content:
National Geographic has published a new essential travel guide that shows Costa Rica as Central America’s ultimate nature escape, a country where rainforest meets reef and volcanoes rise above cloud forest. The guide, written by New York and Lima-based journalist Nicholas Gill and published Oct. 22, credits decades of environmental stewardship for protecting that natural wealth.

It holds Costa Rica up as a model for sustainable tourism and maps six regions for visitors, from Arenal to the Caribbean coast. It is the latest in a string of international nods from the publisher this year. National Geographic named Costa Rica a forest bathing paradise in August, and the country took two top honors at the National Geographic UK Travel Awards in October.

Gill describes Costa Rica roughly the size of West Virginia that packs misty cloud forest, surf beaches, active volcanoes and jungle into a short drive. He points to scarlet macaws, three-toed sloths hanging from cecropia trees and howler monkeys calling at dawn as the everyday backdrop.

The guide splits the year into two seasons. The dry months from December to April bring the best beach weather on the Pacific coast, along with higher prices and bigger crowds. The rainy months from May to November bring greener landscapes, fuller rivers and waterfalls, and thinner crowds, with September and October singled out as especially good on the Caribbean side.

Hans Pfister, co-founder of the Cayuga Collection hotel group, told the magazine that the stretch from mid-April to mid-December is what he calls “wildlife season.” He said the rainforest is at its most active then, with migrations and nesting cycles at their peak. Arenal and the northern highlands lead the regional tour.

The guide highlights trails across old lava fields in Arenal Volcano National Park, canopy ziplines, rappelling down waterfalls, rafting on the Balsa and Sarapiquí rivers, and the hot springs around La Fortuna. In the Tilarán Mountains, Monteverde’s cloud forest gets attention for its hanging bridges, moss-draped trees, glasswing butterflies and the resplendent quetzal.

The guide also recommends night walks for kinkajous, tarantulas and glowing fungi, and notes the area’s Quaker dairy-farming roots. Quetzals have been turning up beyond the classic hotspots too, including a first recorded sighting at a little-known Cartago refuge last month.

Guanacaste is shown as the home of Tico cowboy culture, with the surf of Tamarindo, the turtle nesting beach at Ostional, the resorts of the Papagayo Peninsula and the bubbling mud pots of Rincón de la Vieja National Park. Next door, the Nicoya Peninsula draws praise for Santa Teresa, Nosara, the year-round surf at Playa Guiones, Cabo Blanco Absolute Natural Reserve and its status as one of the world’s Blue Zones.

On the Central Pacific, Manuel Antonio National Park anchors what the guide calls the most cinematic mix of rainforest and beach. On the Caribbean coast, it points readers to Puerto Viejo de Talamanca, the reefs off Cahuita National Park, cacao farms and Afro-Caribbean cooking built on coconut milk and seafood.

Food gets its own section. Gilberto Briceño, chef and owner of Road Less Traveled Cuisine in Playa Potrero, told the magazine that the roadside sodas keep Costa Rica fed day to day, and he named Soda y Mirador Cinchona in Alajuela as home to the best tortilla aliñada he has tasted. Chifrijo, casado, Caribbean rondón and ceviche round out the list.

Three hotels are named. El Remanso is an eco-lodge above the canopy on the Osa Peninsula, Hotel Belmar is a family-run Monteverde retreat with its own microbrewery and regenerative farm and The Springs Resort & Spa sits on 67 hectares (165 acres) of hot springs facing Arenal Volcano.

The practical advice is standard but useful. The guide recommends a 4×4 for rural roads in the rainy season, learning some Spanish before arriving, and the 16-day Camino de Costa Rica trail for hikers who want to cross the country from the Caribbean to the Pacific. It also notes that Costa Rica abolished its army in 1948.

On safety, Gill calls Costa Rica one of the safest places in the Americas but warns of organized and petty crime in parts of San José and in port areas, and advises against flashing phones or jewelry or walking empty streets at night. The Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) recorded 873 homicides in 2025 and has projected fewer than 800 for 2026, with most killings tied to the local drug trade and score-settling between gangs.

The sustainability section asks travelers to book lodges certified under the Costa Rican Tourism Board’s Certification for Sustainable Tourism, hire official guides in fragile areas, stay on marked trails, use reef-safe sunscreen and never feed wildlife. It notes that nearly a third of the country’s land is protected.

The spotlight lands as the tourism industry heads into high season on uneven footing. Figures from the Costa Rican Tourism Board (ICT) show 2.31 million international arrivals through September, up 4.8% from a year earlier, but September arrivals fell 2.4%, the second monthly decline in a row, after air arrivals from the United States dropped 13.9% in August.

The promotion group Proimagen Costa Rica has pointed to the country’s high prices compared with its neighbors and the strength of the colón against the dollar as pressures on demand. Rivals to the north are also competing harder for nature travelers.

For a destination that sells itself on forests, wildlife and protected land, a high-profile guide from one of the world’s best-known nature brands is the kind of attention money struggles to buy. Whether it translates into arrivals will show up in the ICT’s numbers over the coming dry season.

World.title: Pacific Low Has a 60% Chance of Turning Tropical as Costa Rica Braces for Rain
World.content:
A broad low-pressure area off Central America’s Pacific coast now has a 60% chance of becoming a tropical depression within the next week. Whether it develops or not, it could bring heavy rain to parts of the region through the weekend. The odds climbed in less than a day. Yesterday morning, the U.S. National Hurricane Center gave the system a 30% chance of forming within 48 hours and 50% within a week. By its late Wednesday outlook, those numbers had risen to 40% and 60%.

The low is producing a wide, disorganized area of showers and thunderstorms. Forecasters expect it to develop gradually while drifting slowly north, and a depression could form by this weekend. A tropical depression is the first stage of a tropical cyclone, with an organized circulation and sustained winds below 63 km/h (39 mph). For Costa Rica, the bigger concern is water, not wind.

Costa Rica’s National Meteorological Institute (IMN) flagged the system’s cyclonic potential last evening. The low sits next to an already very active band of tropical moisture, the Intertropical Convergence Zone, which has kept afternoons and nights stormy across much of the country this week.

Under that setup, IMN forecast 20 to 50 millimeters (0.8 to 2 inches) of rain in six hours, with peaks of 60 to 80 mm (2.4 to 3.1 inches) in the Caribbean mountains and near the Pacific coast. Storms can bring gusts of up to 80 km/h (50 mph), strong enough to bring down branches and power lines.

As we have mentioned in multiple previous articles, the ground is why this rain matters more than usual. Soils are already 70% to 90% saturated in the South Pacific, on the Nicoya Peninsula and in the mountains of the Northern Zone, and they have had little time to dry since October’s nationwide rain alert. When the ground can’t absorb more water, rain runs straight into streams and drains. Creeks rise fast, culverts back up and slopes along roads can give way.

That is what happened in mid-October, when soil saturation reached 85% to 100% and flash floods trapped people in Heredia and Escazú. The National Emergency Commission (CNE) put the whole country on green alert on Tuesday, which keeps emergency committees active in all 84 cantons.

IMN expects cloudier conditions from Friday through Sunday, with fog on the Pacific slope early in the morning and cooler starts to the day. The hurricane center says heavy rain could reach parts of Central America through the weekend even if the low never becomes a depression.

If you plan to drive or hike, build your day around the morning. Storms this week have been strongest in the afternoon and at night. Don’t cross a swollen river or a flooded road, on foot or by car. You can’t tell how deep or fast the water is until you are in it. Keep away from riverbanks and steep slopes during and after heavy rain.

On the Pacific coast, expect rough seas on top of the rain. Small boats, fishing trips and water tours face the most risk, so check with your operator before you head out. Forecasts for developing systems can change quickly. The hurricane center updates its outlook every six hours, and the CNE can raise its alert level if conditions get worse.

World.title: Kilos of Marijuana Seized Off Costa Rica’s Border With Panama
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Coast Guard intercepted a speedboat carrying 2,648 packages of marijuana in the South Pacific this week in an operation coordinated with the US Drug Enforcement Administration, according to the Ministry of Public Security. Two Ecuadorian crew members were detained.

Public Security Minister Gerald Campos Valverde said the vessel was stopped about 52 nautical miles (96 kilometers, or 60 miles) southeast of Punta Burica, the peninsula that straddles the border with Panama. According to the minister, the operation began Tuesday and concluded Wednesday, Nov. 4.

The ministry said each package weighed roughly one kilogram (2.2 pounds), putting the load at more than 2.6 metric tons (about 5,800 pounds). Agents also seized 11 drums of fuel and other items that authorities consider relevant to the case.

The interception was carried out by the Coast Guard’s special operations group, known as GOPES, which stopped a 38-foot (11.6-meter) go-fast boat. The ministry said the DEA coordinated the operation, while the US Joint Interagency Task Force South and Panama’s National Aeronaval Service (SENAN) provided air and intelligence support.

Costa Rica’s Drug Control Police (PCD), the Special Support Unit (UEA) and the Directorate of Intelligence and Criminal Analysis (DIAC) also took part, according to the ministry.

The suspects were identified by their surnames as Trejos Domínguez, 25, who allegedly captained the vessel, and Flores Bawi, 49. Both were placed at the disposal of the Public Prosecutor’s Office, which will determine their legal situation. As of Thursday morning, authorities had not said whether prosecutors would request pretrial detention.

The boat was towed to the port of Golfito in Puntarenas province, where Drug Control Police agents inspected the cargo alongside prosecutors. The investigation continues into where the drugs came from and where they were headed, the ministry said. Authorities have not said whether the shipment is linked to other international cases or to any criminal group operating in Costa Rica.

The seizure adds to a run of maritime interceptions along Costa Rica’s southern Pacific coast, a stretch of water that has emerged as a prime drug route for shipments moving north from South America. Last month, a US surveillance plane helped authorities seize 1.5 tons of cocaine off Osa, a short distance up the same coastline.

Joint operations with US agencies have become a fixture of Costa Rica’s anti-drug strategy. Under a joint maritime patrol agreement in place since 1999, US aircraft and vessels regularly support Costa Rican interceptions at sea. The country authorized US Coast Guard vessels to take part in 2026 anti-drug operations, and in September a US military plane flew 45 tons of seized drugs out of Costa Rica. Seizures have climbed this year, with cocaine seizures up nearly 50% in 2026.

For a country that sits between South American producers and North American markets, the steady pace of seizures at sea reflects both the volume of drugs moving past its coastline and the growing reach of the international cooperation built to stop them before they land.

World.title: Cristiano Ronaldo Announces Portugal Retirement at 41
World.content:
Portuguese football legend Cristiano Ronaldo announced on Thursday he was retiring from international football at the age of 41. Ronaldo made his debut for Portugal in 2003 and went on to play a world record 234 times for his country, scoring 146 goals. But the forward’s powers have been waning in recent years and he fell out with national coach Jorge Jesus last month after refusing to play him in a Nations League match.

Ronaldo immediately left the team camp and was handed a 30-day suspension. He apologized and it was rumored he intended to return to the international fold, but on Thursday the five-time winner of the Ballon d’Or released a video on his Instagram account in which he said he had played his last match for Portugal.

“To the Portuguese people, the day has come for me to hand back the number seven shirt of our national team,” Ronaldo said, as images of his career were played. “I never felt it belonged to me alone, but for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world.

“Today the time has come to pass it on to the future. It was not an easy decision, because some decisions are not made with the mind alone — they are also made with the heart. “A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever has come to an end,” he added.

Will stay with me forever

The Portuguese Football Federation said it would organise a “fitting tribute” to Ronaldo’s “immense career”. Ronaldo will continue to play for his current club in Saudi Arabia, Al-Nassr, where he is under contract until June 2027. In the highlight of his international career, Ronaldo won the European Championship with Portugal in 2016 in France, although he had to leave the field during the final with an injury.

“I won Euro 2016 and, for me, that’s just as important as the World Cup. It will stay with me forever,” he recalled. At this year’s World Cup in the United States, Canada and Mexico, he scored three goals but Portugal were knocked out in the last 16 by eventual winners Spain.

In a notorious moment at a previous World Cup, a 21-year-old Ronaldo was caught by TV cameras winking at his bench after appearing to exhort the referee to send off his then Manchester United teammate Wayne Rooney as Portugal faced England in the 2006 quarter-finals in Germany.

Rooney was red-carded and Ronaldo scored the winning spot kick in the penalty shootout to send Portugal into the semi-finals where they lost to Zinedine Zidane’s France. His departure from the international stage follows that of his long-term rival, Lionel Messi, who played his final match for Argentina last month.

World.title: Call Center Cuts Costa Rica Job Pledge Over Asian Competition
World.content:
A US-owned customer service company operating under Costa Rica’s free trade zone program has cut its minimum employment commitment by more than half. It told the government it can no longer compete on cost with call centers in India and the Philippines. TTEC Customer Management Costa Rica, which began operating here in 2007 as Teletech Customer Care Management, received approval from the Ministry of Foreign Trade (Comex) to lower its required workforce from 111 employees to 45.The original commitment dates from executive agreement 067-2007.

In its request, the company said it faces growing competitive pressure in international markets, chiefly from firms in India and the Philippines. It said operating costs and salary structures there are far lower than in Costa Rica. The company described that gap as a significant structural disadvantage. It said the disadvantage had weakened its ability to keep international contracts and attract new clients.

TTEC carried out a partial reduction of its staff before seeking the change. It has not disclosed how many people it currently employs in the country. Companies in the free trade zone regime receive tax and customs incentives in exchange for minimum investment and employment commitments. Those commitments are written into executive agreements and can be modified at the company’s request.

TTEC is far from the only company to ask for that change. Executive agreements published in La Gaceta show that at least 38 free zone companies have lowered their employment targets since 2023. Their combined commitments fell from about 38,450 jobs to about 19,864. The largest adjustment came from Amazon, which halved its commitment from 16,450 positions to 8,225 in January. Align Technology lowered its minimum from 4,992 to 2,500 under an agreement published in May. Align said artificial intelligence and automation had raised output per worker.

Service firms make up most of the companies that have reduced their targets. They include IT consultancies, technical support providers, back-office centers, call centers and data processors. The reasons the companies gave vary. Several, like TTEC, pointed to lower labor costs in Asia. Others cited automation and artificial intelligence, or a shortage of specialized talent.

A smaller group blamed the strong colón, which raises costs for companies that earn in dollars but pay salaries and local bills in colones. One of them, Sistemas Globales, estimated that its operating costs had risen by 23.6%. TTEC did not cite the exchange rate in its request. The pullback is now showing up in the overall numbers. Direct employment in free zone companies fell from 197,101 to 195,410 jobs through August, a 0.9% drop, according to Central Bank data published in its monetary policy report.

Central Bank president Róger Madrigal attributed the decline mainly to fewer jobs in administrative support, professional and technical services, and information and communications. A lower commitment does not always translate into an equal number of layoffs. Some companies are revising targets set at peak hiring rather than cutting existing staff, as Align said in its request.

Even so, the trend points to mounting pressure on service jobs in a regime that directly employs nearly 200,000 people. Those jobs have been among the steadiest sources of formal private-sector employment.

World.title: El Niño Leaves Gulf of Nicoya Fishermen With Catches Too Small to Pay for Fuel
World.content:
Fishermen in the Gulf of Nicoya say the unusually warm water El Niño has pushed against Costa Rica’s Pacific coast has left their nets close to empty, with many boats now returning from a day at sea with less fish than it takes to pay for the fuel. Giselle Campos, who fishes and gathers shellfish in Costa de Pájaros, Puntarenas, said her family now spends five hours on the water and may come back with two fish and 300 grams (about 10 ounces) of shrimp.

The same trips used to bring in 10 to 40 kilograms (22 to 88 pounds) of shrimp and 70 to 100 kilograms (155 to 220 pounds) of fish, she said. Accounts from Costa de Pájaros, Isla Venado and neighboring communities describe sharp drops in shrimp, snapper, snook and corvina, the catches that have long sustained small-scale fishing in the gulf.

They come less than two weeks after the National Emergency Commission (CNE) placed the waters off the entire Pacific coast under a red alert for El Niño, the first time the agency has extended an emergency alert to the sea. CNE President Alejandro Picado said at the time that the maritime alert was a response to the damage warming seas were doing to fishing and to the families who depend on it.

The alert zone covers 12 nautical miles, about 22 kilometers (14 miles), from the shoreline of Guanacaste and Puntarenas, including the gulfs of Nicoya and Papagayo. Picado said no end date had been set. According to the CNE, sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific have run above normal for the past five months, reaching the highest values recorded since 1950. Along Costa Rica’s Pacific coast, readings are 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal, the commission said.

Andrés Beita Jiménez, a marine biologist and science coordinator at the MarViva Foundation in Costa Rica, explained that in a normal year, winds crossing from the Caribbean through low-lying areas such as Guanacaste push the Pacific’s surface water offshore. That movement draws cold, nutrient-rich water up from the depths toward the coast, where sunlight turns those nutrients into plankton that feed the rest of the food chain.

El Niño weakens those winds, Beita said. Warm surface water stays put, more warm water flows in from across the Pacific, oxygen levels drop and the nutrient-rich upwelling stalls. He described the current event as one of the strongest on record, with warming reaching deeper layers of the ocean as well as the surface.

Beita stressed that the fish have not died off. Species that can move are heading to deeper or cooler water where they are not normally found, he said, which forces fishermen to travel farther and fish deeper to reach them. Less mobile life such as mollusks and corals cannot escape the heat and may suffer stress or bleaching.

That extra distance is where the numbers stop working. Ezequiel Álvarez, a 64-year-old fisherman in Costa de Pájaros who was born on Isla Caballo, said a catch of around seven kilograms (15 pounds) now barely covers the gasoline for boats that burn 15 to 19 liters (four to five gallons) per trip in two-stroke engines. He described the last 10 months as very hard.

Álvarez still goes out, but only on the most favorable tides, and he can afford to because he also uses his boat for tours of the gulf. Many of his neighbors have no such cushion, he said.

On Isla Venado, Yolanda Bolívar, 54, estimated that fewer than 30% of the island’s fishermen are still working. Catches have been falling for three years, she said, but the gulf used to recover somewhat after each seasonal fishing ban, which this year ran from May 1 to July 31. This time it did not.

Fishermen now risk spending fuel for two or three days, or even a week, and coming home with nothing, Bolívar said, so many have stopped going out. Sardines are what keep some families going, sold as bait to boats chasing mahi-mahi farther offshore. Others on the island have moved into tourism and transport, ferrying visitors between islands, building cabins or, as her own family has done, selling meals and produce from a home garden to neighbors and visiting tourists.

Campos said younger people from Costa de Pájaros, Manzanillo, Chomes and Punta Morales have found work on the Barranca–Limonal highway widening, but she worries about what they will do once the project ends in an area with few jobs. Older fishermen have little choice but to keep going out with hand lines and nets.

She said the monthly assistance payment from the social welfare agency IMAS, 145,000 colones (about $320), does not stretch far for households of seven or eight people. El Niño has struck a fishery that was already under heavy strain. Campos also blamed overfishing and illegal fishing for the losses.

A 2022 marine and coastal atlas of the Gulf of Nicoya produced by MarViva found that fishermen were already reporting declines from overfishing and from some species moving to cooler water. It also documented illegal gear such as explosives, shrimp drags, purse seines and undersized mesh, along with pollution carried into the gulf by the Tárcoles and Tempisque rivers.

How deep this year’s drop runs is still unmeasured. The Costa Rican Institute of Fisheries and Aquaculture (Incopesca) has published national catch statistics only through 2024 and has said its 2025 and 2026 figures are still being processed. The institute has not yet detailed any assistance plan for fishermen affected by El Niño.

Relief is unlikely to come quickly. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) has said conditions typical of a very strong El Niño could continue through the November-to-January period, part of an event forecasters have long expected to stretch into early 2027.

World.title: Corcovado’s Sirena Station Is Back to 366 Visitors a Day. Who Decided?
World.content:
Corcovado National Park has spent the past five months caught in a tug of war that has left many in the Osa Peninsula’s conservation community asking the same question: who is actually deciding how many people the park can handle?

The dispute centers on the Sirena Biological Station, the heart of Corcovado and its most visited sector. Technical reports compiled in June concluded that the station’s wastewater treatment plant had been discharging sewage since at least 2024 into the Camaronal creek, a tributary of the Sirena River, inside a protected area created in 1975.

The problem was not new to authorities. The Health Ministry had ordered a remedial plan as early as 2024, with a deadline of Dec. 31, 2025. A ministry inspection in October 2025 found wastewater discharges into the creek and no operating records or quality controls at the plant, and a follow-up inspection in March 2026 found the orders still unmet.

In late June, the acting director of the Osa Conservation Area, Juan José Jiménez Espinoza, cut Sirena’s daily limit to 150 visitors through September, 100 on day visits and 50 staying overnight. His resolution kept the same cap for November and December but limited it to day visits until overnight stays could be cleared.

Jiménez cited not only the sewage problem but an August 2025 Constitutional Chamber ruling that struck down a 2023 increase in park visitation because it had no technical or scientific justification. The court had given the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC) one month to issue new rules that clearly set out how visitor limits are calculated.

That deadline had long passed. The reaction in the southern zone was swift. Tourism groups, guides and transport operators protested the cut, arguing it lacked a technical basis and was hurting families who depend on the park.

On July 1, the same day residents and tourism business owners blocked roads in Uvita demanding more capacity and Jiménez’s removal, Environment Minister Mónica Navarro transferred him to head a department at SINAC’s national headquarters. Navarro acknowledged the move came after the capacity cut but said his services were more useful in another area of the ministry and that the decision responded to institutional needs.

On July 8, his replacement, Ólger Méndez Fallas, raised the limit to 225 visitors a day, even though the new resolution itself acknowledged that the treatment plant was still out of service. That decision rested on a report from the national water utility, AyA, stating that separate sanitary systems at the station continued to function for certain uses, and on a block of restrooms at the station entrance that operates independently of the plant.

Then, in a resolution that took effect Sept. 17, SINAC raised the limit again, to 366 people a day. The total breaks down into 230 day visitors, 105 overnight guests, 16 places for the Carate-Corcovado community development association that holds the use permit at the station and 15 for park administration.

That is 63 percent above the July figure and more than three times the 100 visitors a day long considered Sirena’s technical limit. SINAC describes the figure as a restoration of the station’s capacity rather than an increase. The Environment Ministry says the change followed compliance with the Health Ministry’s orders and the rehabilitation of the treatment plant, carried out with local communities and volunteer groups who contributed labor, logistics and money.

Yet the September resolution did not make clear whether the plant was operating. Instead, it framed the decision as a way to guarantee the continuity of socioeconomic activities that depend directly on the park. The same document disclosed that the Osa Conservation Area had asked the Constitutional Chamber for an extension to comply with the August 2025 ruling, more than a year after the court issued it.

That sequence is what conservationists find hard to square. The official who acted on a court order and a documented pollution problem was moved out. Capacity was then raised twice, to more than triple the station’s historical limit, while the agency asked the court for more time on the very ruling that requires a scientific basis for those numbers.

Some in the conservation community believe the real beneficiaries are small cruise ships. Their concern is how the tickets get used. Park entry must be reserved in advance, and critics on the peninsula say cruise operators can buy large blocks of the expanded capacity for passengers who arrive by tender, spend a few hours in the park and return to the ship for the night.

When those blocks are gone, they argue, independent travelers who book a lodge in Drake Bay or Puerto Jiménez, hire a local guide and boat captain and eat in local restaurants find fewer places left. In that view, a higher limit does not necessarily bring more money to Osa communities, and could bring less.

There is a precedent behind the suspicion. The legal challenge that led to the 2025 ruling, filed by then-lawmaker Ariel Robles, argued that the 2023 increase included 100 daily places at the San Pedrillo station for the exclusive use of cruise ships. Guides and residents have also complained that boat access has turned many Corcovado visits into same-day trips, which they say leaves less money in towns such as Puerto Jiménez.

Day visitors now take 230 of Sirena’s 366 places, and the increase arrives just before high season, when small expedition ships call along the Osa coast. SINAC has not said cruise traffic played any role in the September decision, and the published breakdown for Sirena includes no separate cruise allotment.

Supporters of higher limits make an argument that carries real weight on the peninsula. Corcovado anchors the economies of Puerto Jiménez, Drake Bay, Sierpe and surrounding communities, and a sudden cut during the busy months hits guides, boat operators and small lodges that have few alternatives.

Critics counter that visitor numbers at Sirena have been building for years while other stations such as Los Patos, La Leona and El Tigre went without investment, and that the infrastructure never kept pace. In June, SINAC asked the Rural Development Institute (Inder) for about 2.63 billion colones (roughly $5.8 million) to overhaul the station and set aside 50 million colones (about $110,000) for immediate work.

Sirena, El Tigre and Los Patos closed to tourists during October for regular maintenance and the heaviest rains. When it cut capacity in June, the Environment Ministry set Dec. 1 as its target for Sirena to run normally with a working treatment plant. With high season about to begin, the central question remains open: whether 366 visitors a day is a figure backed by science or by pressure. For now, the answer rests with the Constitutional Chamber.

World.title: El Refugio Costa Ballena: Making a Difference for Animals and the Community
World.content:
From rescuing animals in need to providing affordable spay/neuter surgeries and supporting community members’ loving pets, one local nonprofit is changing the lives of thousands of animals across the region.

In communities throughout the southern Pacific coast region, countless dogs and cats need help. Some have been abandoned and left to survive on their own. Others have loving families who simply cannot afford the food or veterinary care their pets need. Since 2017, El Refugio Costa Ballena has been working to change that reality, each and every day.

Located in Uvita, El Refugio Costa Ballena was founded with a straightforward but important mission: to help the dogs and cats in the community. Today, it is the only physical animal shelter in the area, providing a place of safety for animals in need.

Rescue, Rehabilitation, and Second Chances

At the heart of El Refugio’s mission is the rescue and rehabilitation of dogs and cats in need. To date, the shelter has rescued more than 1,200 animals, giving them an opportunity for care, recovery, and a better future.

Take Furia, a recent rescue. She was found on the streets in terrible condition – she has ehrlichia, chronic bacterial and fungal dermatitis, and her eyes are infected. She weighs only 12kg but should be double that. Now, she is receiving daily medical care and proper nutrition. In time, she’ll be ready for a home of her own.

Rescue is only the beginning. Once animals are ready for their next chapter, the rescue works to find them loving homes where they can become cherished members of a family. So far this year over 110 dogs and cats have been adopted through the organization, representing countless opportunities for new beginnings for both animals and the people who welcome them home.

Helping animals means addressing more than immediate emergencies.

Prevention and Community Assistance

El Refugio Costa Ballena provides free and low-cost castracion services to help control the population of unwanted dogs and cats. To date, the organization has provided more than 7,700 spay/neuter surgeries. These procedures are an important part of addressing animal overpopulation for the long term. By making sterilization more accessible, El Refugio helps reduce the number of unwanted animals and the suffering that often results when communities lack the resources to care for them.

The commitment also extends to pets who already have loving homes. Through its community assistance program, El Refugio Costa Ballena has provided food and medical care for thousands of dogs and cats whose families cannot afford these necessities. For families facing financial hardship, help with pet food or veterinary expenses can make an enormous difference. This combination of rescue, adoption, prevention, and community assistance reflects an important understanding: improving animal welfare requires not only caring for animals in crisis, but also helping prevent the crisis from happening in the first place.

A Community Effort That Needs Everyone

While El Refugio has made a substantial difference since its founding, the need for animal welfare services continues. The work of caring for vulnerable animals also requires the involvement of the wider community. There are many ways residents and visitors can help. Donate to provide essential support for the rescue’s work, including animal care, food, medical treatment, and spay/neuter programs.

Volunteer your time and energy to the organization’s mission. People who want to make a hands-on difference can reach out to learn what assistance is needed.

Foster an animal to provide a temporary home and create space and opportunities for other animals who need care.

Adoption offers one of the most direct ways to change an animal’s life. By welcoming a rescue dog or cat into the family, adopters provide a home and make it possible for the shelter to continue helping others.

Learn more about how to adopt, foster, volunteer, and donate, by visiting the website www.elrefugiocostaballena.com

Every Animal Deserves a Chance

The challenge of animal welfare is too great for any one organization to address alone. Every donation, every volunteer hour, every foster home, and every adoption can contribute to a better future for the dogs and cats of Costa Rica.

Helping animals starts with a community that cares. Together, we can give more animals the chance to live healthier, safer, and happier lives.

World.title: Belize advances development of National Employment Policy for 2027–2031
World.content:
Belize advances development of National Employment Policy for 2027–2031

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Immigration, Governance and Labour, through its Labour Department, is advancing the development of Belize’s National Employment Policy 2027–2031 through a three-day stakeholder consultation workshop held from November 3 to 5, 2026.

The workshop was organized in collaboration with the International Labour Organization (ILO), with funding from the European Union, and brought together national stakeholders to help shape the country’s employment priorities for the next five years.

The opening ceremony featured remarks from Chief Executive Officer Tanya Santos and CEO Valentino Shal of the Ministry of Rural Transformation, Community Development and Local Government.

Minister of Immigration, Governance and Labour Kareem Musa delivered the keynote address and officially opened the workshop. Abdelmalik Muhummed, Employment and Labour Market Policies Specialist with the ILO Decent Work Team and Office for the Caribbean, also introduced the objectives and consultation process.

Throughout the 3 days, participants examined eight key policy areas, including youth employment and the transition from school to work, women’s participation in the workforce, skills development, productivity, job quality, formalization and foreign labour. Discussions also addressed the inclusion of underrepresented groups, workforce development and labour market governance.

The final day focused on identifying policy priorities, institutional responsibilities, implementation gaps and the resources needed to put the proposed policy into action. The consultations provided an opportunity for stakeholders to share experiences, identify challenges and make recommendations toward developing a comprehensive employment framework that responds to Belize’s changing labour market.

The Ministry acknowledged the leadership of Labour Commissioner Rissela Dominguez Patt and the Labour Department, as well as the technical assistance provided by the ILO and financial support from the European Union.

Special recognition was also given to CEO Valentino Shal for his early vision and support in initiating the policy’s development.

World.title: Escape the winter cold with an Ambergris Caye vacation at Las Terrazas Resort and Residences
World.content:
Escape the winter cold with an Ambergris Caye vacation at Las Terrazas Resort and Residences

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): As winter approaches in North America, travellers looking to exchange freezing temperatures for sunshine, turquoise waters and Caribbean relaxation can find an inviting escape at Las Terrazas Resort and Residences on Ambergris Caye, Belize.

Located on one of Belize’s most popular island destinations, Las Terrazas offers a tropical retreat for couples, families and travellers seeking a memorable winter getaway.

Ambergris Caye is known for its beautiful Caribbean waters, access to the Belize Barrier Reef, snorkeling, diving, fishing and laid-back island atmosphere. Visitors can spend their days exploring the sea, enjoying local cuisine or simply relaxing beneath swaying palm trees.

This winter, Las Terrazas is making the experience even more attractive with three special vacation offers.

Stay four nights, get the fifth night free. Travellers booking a five-night getaway can enjoy the fifth night complimentary. The offer is advertised as valid through December 15, 2026.

Stay four nights and receive US$100 resort credit. Guests booking four consecutive nights or more can receive a US$100 resort credit per room, per stay, adding extra value to their island vacation.

Complimentary couples massage. Couples booking three consecutive nights or more can enjoy a complimentary 60-minute couples massage, making the resort an appealing option for romantic escapes.

Beyond the special offers, Ambergris Caye provides an excellent base for exploring Belize’s marine attractions, including snorkeling excursions and visits to the surrounding reef.

For travellers planning a December holiday or an early winter escape, the resort’s promotions offer several ways to enjoy more of Belize while adding value to their stay.

Visitors can explore the available packages and booking conditions at Las Terrazas Resort website: https://lasterrazasresort.com/offers.

World.title: Belmopan Aggregates and Hardware offers Troy-Bilt riding and zero-turn mowers for Belizean homeowners
World.content:
Belmopan Aggregates and Hardware offers Troy-Bilt riding and zero-turn mowers for Belizean homeowners

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belizean homeowners, landscapers and property managers looking to make lawn maintenance easier can explore a selection of Troy-Bilt riding and zero-turn mowers available at Belmopan Aggregates and Hardware (BAH).

Located at 5 Forest Drive in Belmopan, the company is promoting lawn care equipment designed to help customers maintain their properties with less physical effort.

BAH offers Troy-Bilt riding mowers, which combine operator comfort with reliable mowing power, as well as zero-turn mowers designed for efficient manoeuvring around corners and obstacles.

The equipment is suitable for customers maintaining residential lawns, commercial properties and larger landscaped areas.

With Belize’s tropical climate encouraging rapid grass growth, having the right equipment can make routine property maintenance more manageable.

BAH encourages customers to visit its Belmopan location to explore the available models and determine which mower best suits their needs.

For additional information, customers can contact the company via WhatsApp at 610-0715, telephone 822-3715, or email [email protected].

World.title: Redistricting won’t be done before 2027, says Elections Commission
World.content:
Redistricting won’t be done before 2027, says Elections Commission

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize’s long awaited redistricting exercise will stretch into 2027, according to the Elections and Boundaries Commission.

In a statement, the Commission said it cannot set a timeline for completing the process until a review of proposed constitutional amendments is finished.

The Commission noted that its last redivision exercise was completed in 2023. A report recommending changes to electoral boundaries went to the National Assembly in July of that year, but those changes were never passed into law.

That exercise flagged constitutional issues with Sections 89 and 90, which deal with the number of electoral divisions and how voters are distributed among them. The Commission then asked the Attorney General’s Ministry to examine whether amendments are needed to clarify population distribution and the allowable variation between divisions.

That review has not yet been completed.

According to the Elections and Boundaries Department, Belize had 212,000 registered voters across its 31 electoral divisions as of September 2026.

The Commission says it is continuing to work on the legal and technical framework for a new exercise.

World.title: Minister of Tourism participates in World Travel Market Ministers’ Summit in London
World.content:
Minister of Tourism participates in World Travel Market Ministers’ Summit in London

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Tourism, Youth, Sports and Diaspora Relations, Anthony Mahler, participated in the Ministers’ Summit at the World Travel Market in London, held in collaboration with UN Tourism and the World Travel & Tourism Council (WTTC).

The summit brought together more than 50 tourism ministers from around the world to discuss how tourism can drive positive change, address industry challenges and attract investment to support a more sustainable and prosperous future for the global tourism sector.

The summit forms part of the activities of the World Travel Market London, which is taking place from November 3 to 5, 2026.

World.title: Ministry of Education commences National Student Assessment field trials across Belize
World.content:
Ministry of Education commences National Student Assessment field trials across Belize

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology (MoECST) has begun secondary field trials of the National Student Assessment System (NSAS), an initiative aimed at strengthening student assessment and improving education planning across Belize.

The project is being supported by the Millennium Challenge Account–Belize (MCA-Belize) through the Belize Compact’s Education Project.

The field trials are scheduled to run from November 2 to December 4, 2026, across all six districts.

The initiative is intended to establish a modern, competency-based assessment system that will provide valuable information on student learning and help improve teaching methods, classroom instruction and education planning.

The Ministry explained that the NSAS is designed to support improvements in the education system rather than rank students or schools. It also assured that information collected during the assessments will remain confidential and will be used for education planning and research.

The trials will allow officials to test and refine the system to ensure it aligns with Belize’s curriculum before wider implementation.

Through the initiative, MoECST and MCA-Belize are working to establish a stronger and more responsive education system that better addresses the needs of students and educators.

World.title: Opposition Leader says a UDP government will put people first
World.content:
Opposition Leader says a UDP government will put people first

By Zoila Palma: Today, Leader of the Opposition Tracy Panton said that a UDP Government under her leadership would put people first.

“We cannot treat our young men as less than human and expect them to become productive citizens. Accountability and human dignity must go hand in hand.

No SOE can, on its own, solve the serious challenges facing our society. We need effective policing that earns public trust, alongside education, skills training, employment opportunities and support for families. Our young people need real pathways to a better life,” Panton said.

Panton says that life is hard and cost of living as stretching families beyond limits.

“Life is hard. The rising cost of living is stretching families beyond their limits. Belizeans are waiting for the Government to present a clear, practical plan to ease their burdens, protect their communities and restore hope.

A UDP Government will put PEOPLE FIRST,” she expressed.

World.title: Eden High School breaks ground for new 5-a-side synthetic field
World.content:
Eden High School breaks ground for new 5-a-side synthetic field

By Zoila Palma: On November 2, 2026, Mayor of San Ignacio and Santa Elena Earl Trapp addressed students of Eden High School in Santa Elena for the ground-breaking ceremonies for the development of a synthetic five-a-side football field on the compound in Santa Elena.

Mayor Trapp, on behalf of the council, committed to assisting with technical support for both the construction of the perimeter, the compaction and installation of the turf and also provide equipment for this worthwhile project which will serve to instill discipline and sportsmanship among students.

The new facility is expected to provide students with a dedicated space to develop their football skills, encourage teamwork and promote a healthy, active lifestyle.

World.title: Bahia Principe Explore Jamaica to reopen in Runaway Bay on December 1
World.content:
Bahia Principe Explore Jamaica

Bahia Principe Explore Jamaica, formerly Bahia Principe Grand Jamaica, will reopen in Runaway Bay on December 1 following a comprehensive renovation carried out over approximately one year, the hotel chain announced in a press release Thursday.

The reopening brings 647 rooms back into operation and approximately 1,000 jobs on Jamaica’s north coast ahead of the winter tourism season, the release stated.

According to Bahia Principe, as part of the Explore sub-brand, the renovated property is designed for families and groups who travel together and want to enjoy their vacation at their own pace.

It said the renovations covered rooms, common areas, dining, leisure and entertainment spaces, “with a stronger connection to Jamaican culture and local identity.”

The hotel chain said the reopening of Bahia Principe Explore Jamaica reinforces a new chapter for Bahia Principe, marked by the evolution of its brand architecture, clearer positioning and a more premium hotel offering, segmented and connected to culture and destination. In this context, the release stated, the Explore and Escape sub-brands help organise Bahia Principe’s offering and make it easier for each guest to identify which hotel best fits their needs, motivations and travel style.

Explore is aimed at families, groups and travelers who want to combine relaxation, leisure,

entertainment and a connection with local culture, while Escape is geared toward an adult audience

seeking a more relaxed, sophisticated stay focused on disconnecting.

“This differentiation strengthens the identity of each property and builds a more coherent experience from the moment of choice, in line with a more current, experiential way of traveling that is tied to the surroundings,” the release stated, adding that the initiative is part of the 50 per cent joint venture between Hyatt and Piñero, which manages the Bahia Principe resorts and owns the brand.

Bahia Principe maintains its brand identity and hotel essence, and Hyatt integrates its resorts into the inclusive collection, strengthening its international reach and connecting them with the company’s global platform, the release stated.

Julio Pérez, CEO of Bahia Principe Hotels & Resorts, highlights that the reopening as a significant step in strengthening the company’s presence in Jamaica.

To mark the reopening of Bahia Principe Explore Jamaica, the brand has launched a promotional

campaign for the hotel, with exclusive discounts of up to 50 per cent.

World.title: Haunted House?
World.content:
GREEN... I think what we have happening too much is that where a decision is made and it does not find favour with the Opposition, they resort to some form of protest.

WHAT should be a place for elected representatives to challenge one another through debate has been interrupted, on several occasions over the past year, by protests, walkouts and heated exchanges, with Tuesday’s confrontation over the Cuba censure motion being the latest flashpoint.

However, Leader of Government Business Floyd Green and Leader of Opposition Business Phillip Paulwell have expressed contrasting views over what is driving the repeated breakdowns in order.

In separate interviews on Wednesday with the Jamaica Observer following Tuesday’s sitting, Green blamed what he described as a lack of discipline and leadership among Opposition members, while Paulwell argued that the management of Parliament, particularly the Speaker’s handling of proceedings, was increasingly putting the Opposition at a disadvantage.

Their contrasting accounts have brought into focus the growing strain between the two sides of the House and raised questions about whether the country’s Parliament can return to more orderly proceedings.

Green said members of Parliament were responsible for maintaining proper conduct, even when disagreeing with decisions made by the Speaker or other parliamentary authorities.

“I think what we have happening too much is that, where a decision is made and it does not find favour with the Opposition, they resort to some form of protest, and that is more than unfortunate, that is unparliamentary, quite frankly, and should not be the approach,” he told the Observer after speaking at a post-Cabinet press briefing on Wednesday.

Green said he could not recall a previous period in Jamaica’s parliamentary history when an Opposition had responded to unfavourable decisions by attempting to halt proceedings.

He pointed to past Opposition responses, including walking out of the chamber or holding press conferences, as ways of expressing disagreement without stopping the business of Parliament.

He also rejected the suggestion that the problem was with the House itself, instead placing responsibility on the Opposition’s leadership to ensure its members followed parliamentary rules.

“It’s a challenge with the Opposition not appreciating that they too are bound by the principles of the House, and it’s unfortunate because every opposition wants to be Government, and when you set a precedent like this it just creates a very difficult situation,” he said.

Green said the way forward was for Opposition leader Mark Golding to exercise greater control over his members and encourage them to use other avenues when they felt aggrieved by a parliamentary decision.

He also suggested that Golding was sometimes contributing to the conduct he was criticising, making it difficult for him to correct the behaviour of his members and also blamed him for not allowing Paulwell to do his job as leader of opposition business effectively.

However, Paulwell rejected Green’s assessment, arguing that the repeated confrontations were rooted in how Parliament was being managed and the treatment of the Opposition.

He said the minority had been increasingly disadvantaged over the past year, particularly in its efforts to question decisions and hold the Government accountable.

“Well, I believe that the Parliament has declined into a state of disrepute, and it has to do with largely the management of the Parliament, all the affairs of the Parliament. I believe from our standpoint that we are seeing greater oppression of the minority in Parliament over the last year or so, when in fact there has always been a presumption that to enable greater accountability, and transparency, great leeway ought to be given to the minority in Parliament,” he said.

Paulwell said the interpretation of the standing orders, which govern how the House conducts its business could place Opposition members at a disadvantage depending on how the Speaker applies them.

He argued that the Speaker, who has the final authority to interpret the rules in the chamber, should remain above the political rivalry between Government and Opposition members.

“What I think has happened, and it might be due to the inexperience of the leader of government business, is that the Speaker is now embroiled in the cut and thrust of the democratic process that results from the two-party rivalry and competition,” he said.

“Now, the practice of the past, the leaders of Government business and Opposition business, they work things out, and it is true that he and I have a cordial relationship, and I believe that if he and I are allowed to manage the affairs of the Parliament, things wouldn’t go much further. But it cannot be that the Speaker, who is to be the final arbiter, the umpire, that person ought not to be engaged in the rivalry,” Paulwell added.

He said he had previously called for regular meetings involving himself, Green and Speaker Juliet Holness to settle disagreements away from the public proceedings of the House.

He also rejected Green’s suggestion that he was unable to maintain discipline among Opposition members, pointing to his own experience serving as both leader of Government business and leader of Opposition business.

“That is absolute nonsense, there are only a few persons on their side with the level of experience that I have, having served as leader of Government business for years, and also leader of Opposition business, and what has happened in the past is for the leader of opposition business and government business to work out the accommodation and the facilitation, and to make sure that there is greater harmony in the running of the Parliament,” he expressed.

Paulwell is therefore calling for a cooling-off period and renewed discussions involving the parliamentary business leaders, with the possibility of Prime Minister Andrew Holness and Golding also participating.

He said the matter could be addressed through renewed engagement between the country’s political leaders, including as part of the Vale Royal talks on constitutional reform.

World.title: Lower the temperature!
World.content:
HENRY-WILSON...I’m not sure if we are at a stage where, because of a person’s political persuasion, they can’t be civil towards other people
