TWO former prominent Members of Parliament (MP) — Maxine Henry-Wilson of the People’s National Party (PNP) and Othneil Lawrence of the Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) — are appealing to politicians currently serving in the nation’s Parliament to “lower the temperature”, and bring civility back to the legislature.

The two have called for a reset in the Parliament, while highlighting the approaches taken by former prime ministers PJ Patterson and Bruce Golding who were able to maintain order during some of the most robust debates in the country’s recent history when they served in the Parliament.

Their appeal follows Tuesday night’s dust-up in the House of Representatives that saw two senior MPs having to be separated by their colleagues after they appeared to come close to exchanging blows. The two are Mikael Phillips, PNP MP for Manchester North Western, and JLP’s Desmond McKenzie, MP for Kingston Western, who’s also minister of local government and community development.

The incident followed the adjournment of the parliamentary sitting after a tense and disruptive debate on a motion centred on the Government’s decision to abstain from a recent United Nations vote on the punishing United States economic embargo on Cuba. The MP for St Andrew Western Anthony Hylton who moved the motion, even called for the Government to be censured.

Both Henry-Wilson and Lawrence credited the prime ministers under who they served for keeping things in line when they threatened to go off the rails. Henry-Wilson served two terms as MP for St Andrew South Eastern during the Patterson era, while Lawrence served one-term under Golding from 2007-2011.

“One of the things that Patterson did was to try and bring down the tempo and the animosity between the two sides because there was a period when the animosity was really high, Henry-Wilson recalled.

“One of the things he did was to have social events where they [PNP and JLP members] interacted with each other. And, also downstairs, in the dining room, we actually ran jokes and we knew who and who were friends and so on,” she shared. The former minister of education and information minister, who was also the first female general secretary of a major political party in Jamaica, said the level of hostility and polarisation was abated by the deliberate social interactions.

“I’m not clear how that goes now, I’m not sure if we are at a stage where, because of a person’s political persuasion, they can’t be civil towards other people,” she said, while pointing out that, “We have to work in the best interest of the nation”.

“It’s a question of respect also, and a question of understanding that politics is about bargaining and compromise and negotiation and nobody ever gets everything they want,“ Henry-Wilson added. “It seems like some of that has gone and issues have become intensely personal. Why would you in Parliament talk about anybody’s mother? They’re not a part of the debate, the discussion or the cut-and-thrust. We can’t stoop to that level,” she remarked.

“We must understand what the parliamentary debate is about; it’s not about personal attacks. As Norman Manley said, “elevate the thing, take it up off the ground,” she added.

Henry-Wilson said it appeared MPs are not taking the time to learn about parliamentary rules.

“Some of the things that I hear people talking about, they contravene the parliamentary standing orders but whether you like the standing orders or not the fact of the matter is that it is there and you have to observe it”.

She opined that the breakdown in the Parliament also has to do with the exercise of leadership of the House of Representatives. She recommended that the Leader of Government Business in the House, Floyd Green, sit with the Leader of Opposition Business Phillip Paulwell and “come up with some kind of ground rules about how you interact with each other. I think it is important”.

For his part, Lawrence said he is “very disappointed seeing what has been taking place — not only yesterday [Tuesday] but previously”.

Although two senior multiple-term MPs were at the heart of Tuesday’s altercation, Lawrence seemed to point the finger of blame for disruptions in recent parliaments squarely at the feet of younger, inexperienced politicians. “I don’t know if proper training needs to apply,” he said.

A former minister of state, Lawrence said when he was elected, training sessions were organised for the incoming class of parliamentarians. “It guided us as to how we should conduct ourselves,” he said. “I served on about eight different committees including the Ethics Committee and that has guided me well,” he added.

“I’m wondering if we [serving politicians] are not cognisant of the fact that from the moment you walk through those doors [of the Parliament] each day, we must remember that the country is looking at us.“

He recalled experiencing robust debates involving members of both sides “and at the end of the day persons who just had a heated debate were seen sitting together having lunch”.

He told of a particularly heated exchange between the late Roger Clarke of the PNP and Robert Montague who serves in the current JLP cabinet. “It was really heated but I can tell you that at the end of the day, five minutes after that, Roger was downstairs giving joke”.

Like Henry-Wilson, Lawrence believes the leadership of the Parliament needs to take charge.

“I don’t know if they need to be a bit more firm but at the end of the day, they must understand that while we want to rule, we still must respect each other regardless of which side we sit on”.

He went further to suggest that politicians may be influenced by the crassness that is played out daily on social media. And going back to the younger parliamentarians, Lawrence opined that youthful exuberance was taking over.

“Because if you go back to the persons who are behaving a certain way, the younger ones are showing disrespect to the seniors and it’s a concern that’s creeping into the Parliament.“

He worried that with increasing conflicts in schools, with some turning physical with deadly consequences, it is becoming increasingly difficult to tell young people how to conduct themselves properly “when we’re not setting any example”.

“After [Tuesday’s] behaviour, how do we speak to students about proper behaviour? It cannot continue, we have to set a better example”.

Having sat through some of the most contentious debates, including during the global recession of 2008-2009 and the Christopher ‘Dudus’ Coke extradition saga which ultimately ended Prime Minister Golding’s political career, Lawrence said he never saw the disrespect like what is being played out today.

“We debated robustly, we didn’t always see eye to eye but there was mutual respect. When I watched yesterday I cannot understand how they almost got physical. I’m saying, lower the temperature because the world is watching us”.

World.title: Shauna Chin: An actress with a diplomatic vision
World.content:
Jamaica’s honorary consul to Los Angeles Shauna Chin.

For Shauna Chin, becoming Jamaica’s honorary consul to Los Angeles was never a far-fetched ambition. It was a matter of time.

In March 2008 the actress sat down with Headline Entertainment’s Jerome Hamilton to discuss the future of her career. During that conversation, she voiced an aspiration she had previously shared only with her family — becoming a diplomat.

Nearly two decades later, that long-held vision has become reality, placing Chin in a position to represent Jamaica and its nationals in Los Angeles and Southern California, while opening doors for greater collaboration between the island and one of the world’s most influential centres of entertainment, business, and culture.

“Most people can’t see the vision of how an actress can also be a diplomat, but, to me, it’s so clear. I’m actually late on this goal, but I always knew it was coming,” she told the Jamaica Observer. “I guess my first reaction, then, is gratitude that this current Jamaican Administration also sees the vision clearly and supports that.”

For Chin, the appointment represents more than the fulfilment of a personal ambition. It is an opportunity to bring together the different parts of her professional life in service of Jamaica, while challenging conventional ideas about who can occupy a diplomatic space.

“I’m actually pretty excited to be the first and set the benchmark on what is possible,” she said.

It is a considerable undertaking, but one she does not regard as an abrupt departure from her previous work. Since 2010, Chin has served the Jamaican Diaspora in several capacities, including three years as an ambassador for the National Association of Jamaican and Supportive Organisations (NAJASO), five years volunteering with the Los Angeles Consulate, and six years as a representative of the Global Jamaica Diaspora Council (GJDC).

Her experience as a diaspora leader, including her tenure as vice-chair of the GJDC, has given her insight into the needs of Jamaicans overseas and the possibilities for stronger partnerships with their homeland.

“A nuh today me a work,” she said with a laugh.

Chin’s responsibilities include representing the interests of Jamaican nationals in Los Angeles and Southern California through passport and citizenship services, emergency assistance, and other official government services. She is also responsible for fostering trade relations between Los Angeles and Jamaica at the Government level.

Having previously pursued such connections as a cultural ambassador, she views the appointment as a natural progression.

“It’s been 16 years in the making. Today is just me continuing walking in my purpose,” she said.

That accumulated experience is now informing nine strategic priorities she has identified for her tenure. Developed from gaps and opportunities she observed during her years of service, the priorities have also been shaped through discussions with government officials, including the prime minister, the minister of foreign affairs and foreign trade, and other senior personnel.

Chin has already begun engaging several government ministries and agencies on initiatives spanning trade, agriculture, labour, policing, and film production.

Among the possibilities are collaboration between the Jamaica Constabulary Force and the Los Angeles Police Department, opportunities within California’s agricultural sector for Jamaica’s farm work programme, and stronger export links for Jamaican produce.

The film industry, however, offers a particularly natural meeting point between her official responsibilities and artistic experience.

Jamaica has long attracted international productions, but Chin wants the relationship with Hollywood to evolve beyond the island serving primarily as a location for overseas productions.

“One major goal with a partnership is to see our creatives, from crew to talent, as primary production players and not just background support,” she explained.

She is also measuring the success of her tenure by the tangible benefits it delivers to both countries.

“I’m starting from scratch with these priorities, so at the end of my third year each of the priorities should show initiation established with key partners, and tangible financial progress and intellectual gain to both Los Angeles and Jamaica’s benefit. My priorities focus on equal benefit to both countries,” she said.

For Chin, that means creating opportunities for Jamaican actors, writers, directors, and technical professionals to participate more meaningfully in international productions, while helping local films secure financing and distribution. She is equally interested in broadening the stories that reach international audiences

Jamaican cinema has no shortage of narratives shaped by crime and violence, she acknowledged, but she believes the country’s storytelling possibilities extend far beyond them.

“We have love stories, comedies, and stories about redemption that are also very colourful for mainstream audiences,” she said.

Her familiarity with both the creative industry and government processes, she believes, could give her an advantage in bridging the gap between the two.

“Los Angeles is renowned for Hollywood being a blueprint for the creative industries. This is why it’s exciting for Jamaica that the representative is an actress,” she said.

“For example, where Hollywood might pass on filming in Jamaica, I can speak clearly to the Ministry of Industry and Commerce and explain why carving out a tax incentive would be beneficial, and help them shape what that can look like. Same for musicians seeking to get Grammy nominations and wins, my office is positioned to facilitate more collaboration to get our musicians in the rooms with voters,” Chin continued.

It is an approach that reflects the breadth of a career that has moved through entertainment, military service, and health care. Still, representing a country while remaining an artist requires careful negotiation. Chin acknowledges that her new position has made her more restrained, particularly when it comes to the projects she accepts and the opinions she expresses publicly.

“It’s a hard daily balance that I evaluate on a case-by-case basis,” she said.“My ambitions are already overzealous, so I have to pace myself. I’ll get it done, but I have to pace myself,” she said.

Among the most significant opportunities on the horizon is the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles. With Jamaica’s celebrated track-and-field tradition likely to draw considerable attention, Chin wants the country’s engagement with the Games to extend beyond its athletes and sporting achievements.

She is already holding preliminary discussions with government representatives, sports business leaders, and community stakeholders, while preparing to engage Los Angeles partners on how Jamaica’s vision can align with the city’s plans.

Her broader ambition is to use the international spotlight to promote Jamaica as a destination for tourism, investment, and business partnerships, while creating opportunities for its creative industries.

World.title: No big bill
World.content:
Minister of Mining and Geology Floyd Green speaks at a post-Cabinet press briefing on Wednesday as Information Minister Dr Dana Morris Dixon looks on. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

AS the Government tightens its belt and orders a review of public spending, it has created a new Ministry of Mining and Geology. But Minister Floyd Green insists taxpayers will hardly feel the cost, arguing that the ministry is being built largely from resources and positions that were already in place.

Green, who also has responsibility for agriculture and fisheries, said the new ministry would not require the Government to recruit additional staff, establish new agencies or provide separate office accommodation.

He made the comments at Wednesday’s post-Cabinet press briefing, where he outlined the ministry’s plans and defended its creation against the backdrop of the Government’s drive to reduce expenditure and redirect resources towards national recovery.

Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness recently announced a series of spending restrictions, including a moratorium on non-essential overseas travel and a pause on official vehicle purchases until March 31, 2027.

The Government has also ordered a review of public-sector property leases, discouraged hotel retreats and reinstated restrictions on official Christmas parties.

The measures are part of a wider effort to control spending as Jamaica continues to recover from last year’s Hurricane Melissa.

The creation of another ministry therefore raised questions by many about the cost of expanding the Government’s administrative structure at a time when it is urging public bodies to spend less.

However, Green, said mining already had much of the technical structure needed to operate as a ministry because it had previously been a ministry before being reduced to a division.

“So mining used to be a ministry years ago, and then it moved and became a division. But it never changed its structure in relation to the various technical officers that you have. So we have a director of mining who happens to be here with us, we have a commissioner of mining who is here with us, we have two deputy commissioners of mining, [and] all of those positions were already there,” Green said.

He also noted that the Jamaica Bauxite Institute and Jamaica Bauxite Mining Limited are also existing agencies, while the new ministry will share human resources and accommodation with the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries.

“So no new entities have been established or are being established. Additionally, we are practising a shared service model. Again, this is something that the Ministry of Finance has been pushing forward. So we are not developing new human resources and new accommodations. All of that will be shared with the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries. So when you look at the cost for the new ministry, it is genuinely minimal,” he said.

He said the new structure was intended to speed up work in a sector that the Government believes can play a greater role in economic growth, particularly as Jamaica rebuilds following Hurricane Melissa.

He revealed that the ministry’s main task will be to expand the country’s mining industry beyond its traditional focus on bauxite and alumina, while improving the benefits Jamaica receives from its mineral resources.

Green said the bauxite and alumina sectors had been affected by two major hurricanes, setting back production and making a fresh approach necessary.

One of the areas being targeted is the system used to collect revenue from bauxite production. Green said the Government was reviewing the levy formula, which dates back to the 1980s, with work already involving the Jamaica Bauxite Institute, the mining division and the Ministry of Finance.

He said the proposed changes were expected to be brought to Parliament in the coming weeks.

But the Government also wants to make greater use of Jamaica’s limestone resources by encouraging companies to process the material locally instead of exporting it for further manufacturing overseas.

Green said Jamaica had chemical-grade limestone, which is used in products such as antacids and toothpaste, and that the ministry would develop incentives to attract investors to process it here.

Green said the intention was to encourage companies to invest in Jamaica and create more value from the resource before it is sold.

“How do we get companies to invest in Jamaica to do the value-adding here? In order to do that, we need to craft an incentive regime that will say to investors, this is what we have to offer, this is what we think can work, and we want you to come here,” he said.

The ministry is also expected to play a role in preparing the country for possible gold and copper production. Green said international companies were working with Jamaican firms to explore the potential, but stressed that it was too early to say whether commercially viable deposits existed.

World.title: EARN YOUR WAY BACK!
World.content:
West Indies’ Nicholas Pooran reacts after being run out during the ICC men’s Twenty20 World Cup 2024 group C cricket match against Afghanistan at Daren Sammy Cricket Ground in Gros Islet, St Lucia on Monday, June 17, 2024. (Photo: AFP)

FORMER West Indies and Jamaica bowlers Daren Powell and Nehemiah Perry say Cricket West Indies (CWI) must reach a suitable agreement with Trinidadian batter Nicholas Pooran should he decide to return to international cricket.

Pooran has seemingly softened his stance to play for the West Indies again after his decision to retire last year at age 29.

The power-hitting left-hander, who made over 160 appearances for the Windies between 2016 and 2024, didn’t give reasons when he announced his decision in June 2025 but opted to focus on global franchise cricket, including the Indian Premier League and the Caribbean Premier League.

However, on the opening day of his “Nicky P” Batting Academy in Trinidad last Saturday, Pooran, a former T20 captain said, “I’ve never shut that door completely. Time changes fast. I don’t know what the future holds.”

Powell, who picked up 156 wickets in 92 caps for the Windies, says Pooran needed time off to realise his worth to the Caribbean team.

“He probably heard the cry of the people on wanting to see more of him in West Indies colours and he had thought about it, probably fleshed out what the problem was and came to this consensus that he potentially wants to represent West Indies again,” Powell told the Jamaica Observer. “When you look at what has happened in the last few weeks, there is a pay cut which is going around for the players and if he is making his intention clear to come back as a West Indies player, it has nothing to do with salary. It has something to do more with the love of cricket and him wanting to represent the West Indies.

“I don’t think that Pooran has any stripes to earn. When you look around the region, we don’t have that X-factor like Pooran. He’s competing against nobody to get into our city’s team. We have good talent, yes, but good talent alone can’t bring success in sport. Pooran has proven himself in the region that he is not any ordinary cricketer, he is somebody who is way above the rest.”

Recently, CWI President Kishore Shallow told the Super Over podcast that he had conversations with Pooran before he announced his retirement and said, “You just have to accept the direction people want to take.”

With the ICC T20 World Cup two years away, Perry, who played 25 times for the Windies, says CWI needs to have a serious meeting with Pooran before potentially bringing him back into the fold.

“At the end of the day you don’t want a man to have West Indies cricket as a patty shop where you hop in and out and can do anything you want. You need to make a commitment and if the commitment is to represent your region at the highest order and perform, then we don’t have a problem with that,” Perry told the Observer.

“At the end of the day, if a man wants to apologise to the public, then he just apologises and says he made a mistake and he misses the game, he misses the camaraderie with his teammates, and he misses the competitiveness of the cricket and wants to see if he can win a World Cup for us, then fine, I don’t have a problem with that. We have to develop that sort of culture that you have to be committed to our cause — and when I say ‘our,’ I mean West Indies.”

Powell shared similar sentiments, that Pooran could help generate more revenue for CWI, which is facing financial challenges. However, he says a proper agreement must be reached to avoid future complications.

“I am not saying that they should accept him with open arms,” Powell said. “They have to have a good agreement. Not just take him and just say come play because you’re going to the World Cup and we’re going to need you. Don’t come and play because we need sponsorship and the sponsors need you. If that is the situation and that’s the agreement, he’s going to go back to square one, he’s going to pack up and leave when he wants to leave.

“He is a star player; West Indies need him, we need him, but it should not be a case you just walk in. There has to be some rules of engagement and some way in which no parties will be uncomfortable when he returns or is at a disadvantage to the other. It should be a mutual agreement with every other player, if anything should happen, it’s the same rules and regulations for the rest of the players.”

Perry says Pooran, the West Indies’ second-highest run-scorer in T20 internationals with 2,275 runs, must be fully committed if he decides to return to the team.

“He has to have that discussion with whoever — whether it’s the coach, the president, vice president or whoever the hierarchy of CWI designates to have that discussion with him and set some parameters and some conditions. And they need to say if you are not on the same page then we’ll do without you because cricket will always be here,” he said.

“We are not bigger than the game, we have to show that respect for the game itself because persons were before you and persons will be after you. So, it is imperative that we have that sit down and then we can shake hands and then we chart our way forward as a body.”

World.title: Flavours Of Japan
World.content:
Saki Salmon roll (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Foodies, take note. Koi Sushi has arrived at the Super Valu Towne Centre on 144 Constant Spring Road. Marrying traditional Japanese finesse with bold Jamaican flair, the new outpost promises maximum flavour in every bite.

Eager for our own Japanese fix, Thursday Food visited the stylish new spot last week Thursday.

The offerings cater to every palate, bridging raw indulgence — consider Sashimi Sampler with tuna, yellowtail, and salmon — and cooked specialities like Teriyaki Chicken roll or the island-accented Scotchie Shrimp roll, boasting a spicy Scotch bonnet punch. For substantial mains, look no further than the miso-glazed salmon or the beef yaki noodles.

Behind the bar, the Japanese influence remains unmistakable with sake-infused mixology. Cocktails like the Lychee Sake Spritz and the Tokyo Mule offer a crisp, inventive alternative to conventional drink menus, delivering a refreshing balance of traditional finesse and modern flair.

What began in 2021 as a pandemic-era takeout concept on Hillcrest Avenue took full flight in 2022 as a complete dining destination. Through co-principals Lisa-Gaye and Kirk Chin and Chef Shuzo Hanasaki, the brand swiftly cemented its presence, captivating local palates whose appetite for premium sushi remained steadfast — even amidst limited opening hours and without a dedicated dining space.

“Our patrons didn’t mind eating [sushi] from boxes because of how great the sushi was. And the partnership that we shared with Chef Hanasaki was because of the love that he puts in his food as well,” Lisa-Gaye told Thursday Food. “So, we said, you know what? People love this so much, let’s turn this into a sushi restaurant.”

That success is evident in the brand’s steady evolution for the past four years, which culminated in a move to the more spacious Super Valu Towne Centre. The relocation answers a clear surge in consumer demand while bringing a refreshed ethnic dining experience to the neighbourhood.

“In the stretch between Constant Spring and Manor Park, we were really lacking options because Kingston 6 is usually where all the different ethnic restaurants are based,” Lisa-Gaye noted. “We just thought, ‘You know what? This is exactly where we need to be.’”

A departure from her signature Fromage brand, the venture is a passion project for Lisa-Gaye, driven by her deep love for Japanese cuisine.

“Usually, you’d have to travel for such great cuisine, especially Japanese, because it’s so hard to get the right ingredients here in Jamaica. We were up to the challenge, however, and decided to go all-in,” she said.

Indeed, Chef Hanasaki’s unwavering insistence on authentic, high-grade ingredients and meticulous attention to detail elevates every plate. Yet, the true secret to the brand’s success lies deeper: in the absolute trust Lisa-Gaye places in Hanasaki’s expertise, and the genuine passion he pours into every dish.

“He just formed this love for what we do. I was always pushing him to do it [open a restaurant] for himself and he said, ‘I won’t do it unless I do it with you’. And he believed in me, I believed in him. So here we are… a great partnership.”

Thursday Food raises a Lychee Sake Spritz toast to the continued success of this latest venture. Kanpai!

World.title: WATCH: US midterm results unlikely to shift Holness’ diplomatic approach – Chang
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica – Political commentator Kevin O’Brien Chang does not expect the results of the United States midterm elections, which saw the Democrats take control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, to influence the Jamaican government’s approach to diplomacy.

Chang, in an interview with Observer Online reporter Carlysia Ramdeen, suggested that Jamaica’s foreign policy direction is unlikely to be altered by the shifting political balance in Washington, noting the Holness administration’s approach to “get along” with the superpowers of the world.

“Mr Holness himself and Ms Kamina Johnson Smith, they’ve been very good diplomats in my view. They’ve made no enemies, they get along with the three great powers of the world,” Chang said. “They get along with America, they get along with China, and they get along with the EU [European Union].

“We’re a little small country. Why do we want to have any quarrel with any bigger country than us?”

The Holness administration has been widely criticised for its recent abstention at the United Nations on the resolution calling for an end to the United States embargo against Cuba, raising questions about the shift in policy as the island has long voted for the resolution.

World.title: EU targets large firms to unlock budget deal
World.content:
Lourtie overhauled an unpopular corporate tax known as CORE — which charges a lump sum on companies’ revenues exceeding €100 million — that the European Commission proposed last year.

According to his proposal, the EU would charge a 0.05% levy, as opposed to a lump sum. It would also only apply to firms with an annual turnover of more than €750 million.

These changes are expected to soften opposition among a group of countries led by Germany that challenged CORE on the grounds that it undermines competitiveness and takes a toll on medium-sized enterprises.

Going further

But two diplomats fear these concessions will not be enough to muster support for the new levy. “I don’t think this is going to solve the problem on CORE,” one told POLITICO. They, like others in this story, were granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive negotiations.

France is pushing to introduce new taxes to reduce contributions to the EU budget.

In a concession to Paris, Costa’s team indicated that they won’t cut down on the total revenue projections from the Commission’s tax proposal from last year, which was expected to generate €65 billion annually.

World.title: Farage criticizes Trump’s ‘broken promise’ on foreign wars after midterms kicking
World.content:
The Reform leader has been more critical against a backdrop of global economic woes triggered by the war waged against Tehran by America and Israel.

Farage, leader of the insurgent right-wing Reform UK party, told reporters after a defense speech in London that he wouldn’t have supported a drawn-out conflict with Iran. He said it was “bizarre” that Trump, of all people, took such action, considering he took power on a pledge to avoid endless foreign wars.

Asked about the biggest lesson he took from the midterms carnage for the Republicans, Farage said: “Keep your promises.”

He praised Trump’s “very good” track record of staying faithful to the electorate during his first term, but said, “He broke a promise — that was no more foreign wars.”

“We’re eight months in, and the resultant rise in gas and diesel prices, more than anything else, is what did them in,” Farage said.

He later told broadcasters that he worries the U.S. president will “continue aggressively attacking Iran” now that he has lost Congress.

World.title: CBD edibles can’t be labeled organic, says EU court
World.content:
CBD, or cannabidiol, is a non-psychoactive chemical component found in marijuana that’s gained a reputation as a way to take a chill pill without getting high. In some European countries, wellness shops are using a legal grey zone to sell CBD products that aren’t explicitly marketed for human consumption — often with a wink.

In France, some hemp sellers wanted to sell them with an organic label. But the the judges shut that down.

The European Commission classifies natural CBD as a so-called novel food, and it has yet to receive authorization to be sold on the EU market.

The hemp sellers had challenged the refusal by France’s National Institute for Origin and Quality to grant organic certification to CBD edibles.

The high court said that CBD can be certified as organic only after it is authorized for sale on the EU market.

The certification is more than a decorative badge, the court reasoned, saying it “conveys a more general promise of quality and acceptance of a given product in the eyes of consumers, with this positive image being an intended commercial effect.” Putting it on a product that has not been approved for sale could be misleading. The Court’s ruling is also consistent with earlier national-level measures.

The organic label setback looks to be the least of hemp sellers’ problems in France: Paris ordered edible CBD products to be pulled from the shelves completely this past May.

World.title: Farage says he’ll meet Le Pen ‘at some point in time’
World.content:
The Reform leader’s comments came after POLITICO reported that the French far-right leader was keeping Farage hanging on a desired Paris rendezvous.

LONDON — Nigel Farage insisted on Thursday he will meet Marine Le Pen “at some point in time” as the French presidential hopeful keeps the Reform UK leader waiting for a Paris visit.

The leader of the British right-wing insurgency had been hoping for a jaunt to France before the end of October — but has been kept waiting for now.

Reform had insisted he would meet the president of the far-right National Party before the end of the year — but four of her officials told POLITICO this is not on Le Pen’s schedule.

World.title: France, US clash over G7 effort on AI safety
World.content:
“They are not prepared, at this stage, to issue a joint statement with the other six G7 nations, and have asked us to wait for the findings of their own assessment,” said Le Hénanff. “Naturally, we regret this, but we are continuing to move forward as Europeans on this issue.”

A White House official, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said that the French government proposed a “poorly defined body” to cooperate on AI that the administration feared would “create unnecessary bureaucracy.”

The official pointed to U.S. President Donald Trump’s Super Intelligence Force, saying it brings government and industry together to accelerate innovation and ensure the safe deployment of models.

Digital Minister Anne Le Hénanff speaks in the French parliament in Paris on Oct. 28, 2026. | Magali Cohen/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

France, which holds the rotating presidency of the G7 for 2026, issued a chair’s summary statement after the Oct. 20 virtual G7 tech ministerial, which noted that ministers considered closer coordination on identifying risks and sharing incident information, as well as a dedicated high-level group. It was not a joint statement endorsed by all G7 members.

Le Hénanff has proposed resuming talks in December.

SI acceleration

Trump began promoting “super intelligence” as a replacement for “artificial intelligence” at the U.N. General Assembly in late September. A week later, he ordered federal agencies to use the new term.

World.title: Meloni urges ‘disorganized’ EU to speak with one voice on Ukraine
World.content:
While the EU has repeatedly insisted it gets a “seat at the table” at Ukraine peace talks, to safeguard the region’s interests and bolster Kyiv’s ability to resist a lopsided deal, the bloc has yet to agree on a single leader or institution to spearhead negotiations.

“I’m convinced that we all realize how, by projecting the image of a Europe that’s all over the place, we’re doing nothing but serving the interests of those who want this war to continue,” the Italian prime minister wrote. “And I think this is unacceptable, given that human lives and the future of our security are at stake.”

“Proceeding in a disorganized manner, with initiatives that chase one another and overlap, will not help us — neither with our partners nor with those we must convince to

stop this senseless aggression,” she added.

“I am not asking for a seat for Italy in this or that format,” she said.

EU leaders meet in Dublin for an informal European Council on Nov. 13. A meeting of the European Political Community, which involves all EU states plus Ukraine and other allies, takes place the day before.

As the format for talks increasingly coalesces around the E3 — the U.K., France and Germany — alongside the EU, NATO and Ukraine, Italy has found itself sidelined.

World.title: Mélenchon’s mission for his young fans: Debate boomers on Facebook
World.content:
More than 40% of voters younger than 35 plan to vote for Mélenchon, according to a recent Cluster17 poll commissioned by POLITICO. That figure drops to 14% or less across the age brackets over 50 — groups that, if they use social media at all, tend to favor Facebook over its newer rivals.

According to Médiamétrie, France’s leading audience measurement company, platforms like Instagram and Snapchat have 35% more daily users than Facebook among 15-to-24-year-olds.

On TikTok, which skews younger, Mélenchon has about twice the following of any other presidential candidate.

“Their digital campaign is paying off very quickly,” said a strategist from a competing campaign, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. The strategist also underlined that the share of comments on social media posts describing Mélenchon in a positive light was rapidly rising despite how he’s been vilified by his opponents.

But on Facebook, Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally reigns.

Since June, National Rally posts have drawn more than 2 million reactions, more than those of any other French political party, according to data from social monitoring platform Visibrain shared with POLITICO. The page of the National Rally’s local branch in the small region of Vienne alone generated more reactions than the pages of Macron’s Renaissance party.

World.title: How NATO can turn data into defense advantage
World.content:
It also speaks directly to the permission bottleneck Ellermann-Kingombe describes. Because data stays under the control of the nation or system that owns it, access can be governed by policy at the source, with classification boundaries and national rules enforced where the data lives rather than negotiated away in a central repository.

Rather than consolidating everything into a traditional data lake, a data mesh approach manages data where it originates and lives, without moving or duplicating it.

A data mesh approach is sustainable because of its reliance on open standards. They enable defense organizations to connect systems that were never designed to work together, from legacy platforms to dispersed infrastructure, so data stays findable and can be effectively analyzed across the environment. Interoperability stops being a barrier as new partners and data sources join, and new tools can be integrated without rebuilding systems or making major investments. The architecture scales alongside the Alliance’s growth.

Without a unified view, the risk of losing operational advantage to adversaries extends from the battlefield into cyberspace. Zero Trust depends on connecting authentication logs, network traffic and application telemetry where they already sit, so that traditionally separate domains can be visualized and analyzed together. When a user accesses sensitive data, the system must verify not only who they are but also their device status, network path, and the time and location of access. If those checks are slow or impossible, threats can remain undetected and escalate through systems. A data mesh built on open standards connects the pillars of a Zero Trust architecture, allowing organizations to accelerate implementation without replacing the tools they already have.

When the manual efforts of military data analysts struggle to keep pace with the scale and speed of events on the ground, AI can work faster and more accurately.

The same logic is already visible in large government organizations: CISA’s new SIEM-as-a-Service platform uses open standards to give US federal civilian agencies a consistent approach to threat detection and response.

As AI’s value in supporting human decision-making becomes increasingly clear, a data mesh architecture provides the foundation to apply agentic AI capabilities holistically. It enables complex organizations to analyze the vast amounts of data their systems generate, find actionable correlations and separate signals from noise. When the manual efforts of military data analysts struggle to keep pace with the scale and speed of events on the ground, AI can work faster and more accurately. It also lets analysts ask questions across structured and unstructured data and rapidly receive answers grounded in reliable sources.

The numerous tech challenges facing the modern military calls for closer NATO-industry cooperation, and that’s why NATO Edge 26 is such an important event. All 32 sovereign member states that make up the Alliance use different systems, yet they rely on secure, trusted data-sharing with each other as the foundation for cooperating on military operations and sharing intelligence. It’s vital that they can turn to industry innovators to support their operational needs.

World.title: Paraguayan president resigns amid bank collapse leaving 3M people without access to bank accounts
World.content:
Paraguayan President Santiago Peña has resigned on Thursday amid a banking crisis just before the Chamber of Deputies voted unanimously to impeach him.

 

Ueno Bank, the bank that was placed under intervention earlier this week, had close to three million customers, who have suddenly found themselves without access to their accounts.

Protests have roiled the South American nation after its central bank took control of Ueno Bank on Tuesday, citing a severe capital shortfall.

Peña, a close ally of US President Donald Trump, announced his decision in a video posted to X as lawmakers debated his impeachment, saying he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."

"I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed. It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," the right-wing president said in the video.

The Paraguayan president, who until last year held a stake in a company related to Ueno Bank, expressed contrition but stopped short of accepting responsibility for the banking crisis that has plunged a South American nation long prized by foreign investors for its stability into financial and political turmoil.

People protest against the government and Ueno bank, which Paraguay's central bank has seized amid a solvency crisis in Asuncion, Paraguay, Wednesday, 4 November, 2026. AP Photo/Jorge Saenz

Some three million people lost access to bank accounts

Long lines of people trying to withdraw their money from Ueno branches snaked down Asuncion's streets on Tuesday and Wednesday, while angry protests swarmed the capital on both evenings.

Regulators investigating the bank found poorly documented lending and expenses wrongly accounted for as assets. But once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital fell half below the legal minimum, which led to the central bank seizing the lender.

Ueno’s app, cards and transfers went dark, and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside with no way to cash out their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks’ mobile apps, fueling public panic.

"In the face of these accusations, I can't pretend to be oblivious," said ruling party deputy Alejandro Aquilera during the debate. "We have more than three million Paraguayans who have been harmed, who feel betrayed, swindled, deceived," she said.

A demonstrator holds a mock U.S. dollar bill depicting Paraguayan President Santiago Peña during a protest against the government and Ueno Bank in Asuncion on 4 November 2026. AP Photo/Jorge Saenz

Ueno claimed 60% Paraguay's adults as customers

Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay’s adults as customers. They are now left scrambling to recoup their savings, government pensions, and, for 7,000 employees impacted by the bank's closure, unpaid wages.

Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president, who until last year had a stake in Ueno’s holding company, could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its dubious lending practices.

The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña’s long-ruling Colorado Party to the country’s regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth made Paraguay a darling of international investors in recent years.

“Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings,” said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. “We are fed up with 70 years of plunder.”

Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.

Ueno highly financed by Peña's government

Government money poured into Ueno’s coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.

As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million (€712 million) in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay’s giant hydroelectric dams.

Even as retirees’ savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper.

Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. On a single day in September 2025, nearly $39 million (€35 million) had gone to three such companies.

Peña repeatedly brushed off the warnings. As recently as last month, he defended Ueno and the central bank’s oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.

World.title: British comedian Russell Brand found guilty of rape and three sexual assaults by London jury
World.content:
British comedian Russell Brand has been found guilty of rape and three sexual assaults by a London jury on Thursday, the offences involving four women in total.

 

Eyes closed when the verdict was delivered, Brand showed no emotion as he was also cleared of two rapes and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The 51-year-old actor who turned into a conservative, religious online guru faces "significant custodial term," as said by Judge Joel Bennathan.

Brand's wife Laura watched from the public gallery as the jury at London's Southwark Crown Court delivered their four unanimous guilty verdicts. He was remanded in custody and will be sentenced on Monday. The maximum sentence in the UK for rape is life imprisonment.

Russell Brand and his mother, Barbara, arrive before the 83rd Academy Awards, in the Hollywood section of Los Angeles, 27 February 2011. AP Photo/Matt Sayles

Briefly married to US pop star Katy Perry, Brand reportedly also faces accusations of raping two other women, including a 16-year-old schoolgirl. These allegations were revealed during previous hearings of his four-week trial, thus not included in the trial.

'Courage' of victimes

After the verdicts, the Metropolitan Police paid tribute to the "extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them."

"Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women," the Met's Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy said in a statement.

"As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement. I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be," Furphy added.

Brand's bail refused

Senior prosecutor David Roberts said outside the court Thursday that Brand's behaviour was "predatory" and that he "used his celebrity status to commit sexual crimes."

"He was a manipulator with an insatiable desire to get what he wanted regardless of whether consent was given or not," Roberts added.

Russell Brand attends Cosmopolitan Magazine's 'Fun Fearless Males of 2011' event in New York, 7 March 2011. AP Photo/Evan Agostini

His offences involved four women between 2005 and 2009 in different locations, a radio station, the set of a DVD recording and Brand's home. He had pleaded not guilty to all the charges saying that although he used to be promiscuous he had always had consensual sex.

The prosecution had earlier described him as a "ruthless, calculated and manipulative" sexual predator. Following the guilty verdicts, Brand's lawyer Ian Winter urged the judge to renew his bail over the weekend as "an act of humanity" and to "put his affairs in order and in particular to say goodbye to his three young children."

But Judge Bennathan refused to grant bail, saying Brand had "considerable resources" and whatever his good intentions might be, there was "fear he might in the end not feel able to come along and face his sentence."

From the dock, Brand signalled to his defence team that he was okay, adding: "I'm good, I'm good, I'm good" before being led out of the dock.

World.title: Greece: Students march in Athens demanding more education funding
World.content:
The rally began at 11am outside the University of Athens, then wound to Syntagma Square, where crowds gathered in front of parliament behind police lines. Protesters carried banners declaring "From Greece to France, we fight for free public education" and placards bearing the French slogan "Étudier ou survivre?" ("Study or survive?"), borrowed from France's school student protest movement. Outside parliament, some dumped sacks of rubble from deteriorating schools to highlight the conditions pupils face, from leaking roofs and crumbling plaster to broken radiators.

 

Police put turnout at about 4,000 across Athens and Thessaloniki combined, well below the 20,000 who marched in 50 Greek cities on 21 October; organisers disputed the figure.

The demands are concrete: more state funding, urgent inspections and repairs of school buildings, permanent posts to fill thousands of vacancies, smaller classes, and withdrawal of new national exams and of a proposal to remove Article 16 of the constitution, which protects public higher education. The secondary teachers' union, OLME, staged a four-hour walkout from 10am so staff could join.

Behind it lies the cost of living. Students describe rents of 800 euros a month and say many can no longer afford to study at all, with unions demanding a monthly housing allowance and rent caps.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 5th, 2026 – Evening
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: World Investment Forum in Doha examines what attracts investment and what holds it back
World.content:
The World Investment Forum brought governments, investors and business leaders together in Doha to discuss how countries can attract investment and create jobs. Organised by UN Trade and Development, the event examined why investment reaches some countries more than others and what governments can do to improve their chances.

 

Discussions covered practical needs, from ports and reliable infrastructure to skilled workers and clear rules. Speakers also addressed the difficulties businesses face when expanding, including rising costs and disrupted supply chains. For smaller countries, working with their neighbours could offer investors access to a larger market.

The forum also examined how public institutions could encourage investment in countries considered riskier. Options included guarantees to cover some potential losses and funding projects alongside other partners. Beyond attracting money, speakers highlighted the importance of creating jobs, supporting local businesses and measuring whether investments improve people’s lives.

World.title: Putin seizes Russian operations of cigarette giant Japan Tobacco International
World.content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin placed Japan Tobacco International's (JTI) operations under state control on Thursday, ordering their transfer by decree to a state-linked holding company AO Promyshlennye aktivy.

 

The order covers JTI's factories in St Petersburg, Rostov-on-Don, the Lipetsk region and the Leningrad region.

The company employs around 4,000 people in Russia and holds roughly 40% of the Russian cigarette market, making it the country's largest manufacturer.

Its Russian product range includes the international brands Winston, Glamour, Camel, LD and Sobranie, and the domestic labels Pyotr I, Russky Stil and Donskoi Tabak.

JTI, whose headquarters are in Geneva, entered the Russian market in 1999 and acquired local producer Donskoi Tabak in 2018.

Dmitry Medvedev, president of the Russian Federation in 2011, with JTI president and CEO Pierre de Labouchere at the Gorki presidential residence: Labouchere was awarded the Order of Friendship. Mikhail Klimentyev/AP2011

JT Group has invested $4.6bn in its Russian operations over more than 20 years, according to a company profile updated in November 2025.

After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the company did not leave the country but suspended new investment in Russian production and marketing.

The seizure follows Russia's arrest last month of Yuki Imai, a journalist with the Japanese newspaper Hokkaido Shimbun, on espionage charges.

The Russian Foreign Ministry has accused Tokyo of systematically using journalists to gather intelligence inside the country. Japan has rejected the accusation.

Japan, which has a long-standing dispute with Russia over the Chishima Islands in the Pacific Ocean, has also joined some Western sanctions over the ongoing all-out war in Ukraine.

JTI joins a list of European companies whose Russian assets have been transferred to state management under the same mechanism, including Swiss food group Nestlé, French retailers Auchan and Leroy Merlin, and German retailer Metro.

Moscow has presented the external management process as a response to sanctions imposed after the 2022 invasion.

Restrictions introduced for companies from states deemed "unfriendly" include caps on dividend payments, which trap profits inside Russia, and substantial fees on sales of Russian business assets.

Putin said on 1 October the mechanism also gave Russia the ability to prepare retaliatory measures against any possible future nationalisation of Russian assets abroad, while leaving open the possibility of returning control to former owners if "conditions improved".

External management involves appointing state-linked administrators to run a company’s Russian assets without the foreign owner’s consent or compensation, transferring effective control to the Russian state regardless of who retains nominal ownership.

World.title: Everyday people: Jeans, plastic and paper among Met Gala's surprising new fashion themes
World.content:
Jeans, T-shirts, puffer jackets and even plastic and paper will take centre stage at the 2027 Met Gala, as New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art turns its attention to the endless possibilities of everyday fashion.

 

The museum announced on Thursday that its next Costume Institute exhibition will be called 'extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday'.

The exhibition next spring will explore how fashion designers transform familiar clothes, objects and ordinary materials into unexpected creations through craftsmanship, construction and experimentation. From denim and metal to paper and plastic, the show will invite visitors to look at everyday objects differently, revealing how designers can give them new forms and meanings while retaining their original associations.

The exhibition will bring together pieces from the museum's Costume Institute collection, alongside loans and new acquisitions.

A new direction after the Galliano controversy

The move marks a dramatic change of direction for the museum after it cancelled a planned exhibition dedicated to British designer John Galliano.

The original retrospective was dropped following fierce criticism from donors and Jewish community leaders over Galliano's involvement given his past anti-Semitic and racist remarks, for which he's repeatedly apologised for.

Andrew Bolton, head curator of the Costume Institute, said the replacement exhibition had to be developed from scratch.

What is the Met Gala?

The Met Gala is one of the fashion world's biggest annual events. Held at New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art, it raises funds for the museum's Costume Institute.

Taking place traditionally on the first Monday in May, the event brings together leading designers, celebrities, actors and musicians, who attend in elaborate outfits inspired by the exhibition's theme.

The red carpet attracts worldwide attention, with fashion often becoming as much a talking point as the exhibition itself.

World.title: EU plans to deliver 'AI literacy' certificates to students
World.content:
The European Union plans to launch an "AI literacy" certificate for schoolchildren in the hope of addressing the impact of fast-developing technology on education.

 

"It will help young pupils understand how AI works, check what it tells them, spot manipulation, and know when to switch off," said European Commission vice president Roxana Minzatu.

Brussels said it would look to launch this new certificate for 15-year-old students for the next 2027-2028 school year. This project comes at a time when teachers and learners around the world are struggling with the impact of AI in schools.

As a persistent decline in basic skills has been observed in the latest PISA 2025 statistics, with around one in three 15-year-olds in the EU underachieving in literacy and mathematics, Brussels aims to use AI to help teachers and students learn better.

Although the EU does not control the educational policies of its member states, it is already backing efforts to study how to safely implement AI in children's teaching.

Brussels says that improving AI literacy for the youth and teachers, understanding how it works and what its risks are, will empower their ability to learn.

At the same time, Brussels is pushing legislation to curb access to social media for young teenagers. Minzatu insisted the two initiatives were not contradictory.

"AI has the potential of really amplifying certain educational processes: tutoring, personalised learning," she said.

"Those are ways to use technology and AI that have nothing to do with the addictive algorithms of platforms."

World.title: Does the Oleshky ceasefire signal progress to come in Ukraine?
World.content:
Hundreds of civilians were evacuated from the city of Oleshky after Russia and Ukraine agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire. Some observers have expressed optimism that more such humanitarian missions might follow.

Nearly 800 residents have been evacuated from the Russia-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine. This was announced by US first lady Melania Trump, who was credited with helping to mediate the ceasefire. The mission was coordinated by Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova.

Most evacuees chose to be sent to Ukrainian-controlled territory, although some opted for transfer to Russia. Currently, more than 1,000 people remain in Oleshky, according to Kherson's regional administration. They were supplied with food, water and medicine.

Melania Trump hailed the mission as a success, taking to social media to thank Kyiv and Moscow for their "leadership and cooperation." She said the Oleshky ceasefire could go on to inspire a "lasting peace between the two peoples."

Dmytro Lubinez similarly wrote on the Telegram messaging platform that it is "important to maintain this cooperation mechanism," adding that "we are currently exploring options with Yana Lantratova to continue similar humanitarian efforts."

Ukraine's Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets (center) poses for a photo with residents evacuated from the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky Image: Genya Savilov/AFP

The Kremlin, however, was quick to dampen any such expectations, making clear that no further plans for humanitarian missions exist at this stage.

Did Russia exploit the ceasefire to strengthen military hold?

One day after the ceasefire ended, Ukraine's general staff stated that Russia had "used the humanitarian pause to fortify its positions." It also said Russia had carried out troop rotations, expanded its anti-drone defenses, and brought in ammunition.

British broadcaster Sky News aired drone footage, produced with the support of the Ukrainian army, showing the Russian army transporting heavy equipment, weapons, personnel and food to Oleshky and neighboring villages.

"It was clear to the Ukrainian government and international mediators that Russia could exploit the pause in this way. But it was the right thing to do to allow people to leave the country," Volodymyr Vyatrovych of the Ukrainian European Solidarity opposition party wrote on Facebook.

Oleshky evacuees recount survival under occupation To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He believes Russia would do the exact same thing if Kyiv were to withdraw its troops from the Donetsk region, as Russian President Vladimir Putin is demanding.

"Russia would use this to prepare for its next offensive, to further destroy Ukraine," Vyatrovych wrote. That said, humanitarian missions have their place, says Ihor Chalenko of the Ukrainian Center for Analysis and Strategies. "We shouldn't speak ill of the Oleshky mission, even though it's clear that the Russians have used the ceasefire in the occupied territories to their advantage," Chalenko told DW. That's why he says Kyiv should insist on banning such behavior in future ceasefires.

What did Washington and Moscow gain from the pause in fighting?

The Oleshky mission took place just shortly before US voters headed to the polls in the midterm elections. Dmytro Levus of the United Ukraine research center believes the timing was no coincidence. "The Russian side played right into the hands of US President Donald Trump, whose Republican Party was expected to face a crushing electoral defeat," Levus said.

Involving Melania in the mediation was a "subtle public relations move" for Trump, through which he hoped to score points ahead of the election, Levus explained. First Lady Melania Trump has long been an advocate for humanitarian causes.

First Lady Melania Trump played a leading role in the ceasfire deal Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Chalenko says the Oleshky ceasefire was in Washington's interest because it allowed Donald Trump to cast himself as a "peacemaker."

Moscow also hoped it could improve its image through the humanitarian mission, especially as it caused Oleshky's humanitarian catastrophe in the first place, Chalenko said. Rescuing civilians is intended to serve as proof that "not everything is bad in Russia."

What can the Ukrainian and Russian human rights commissioners accomplish?

Cooperation between the two human rights ombudspersons had reached "a new level," Chalenko said, adding that the Oleshky case was just one of several noteworthy examples that also included prisoner swaps and foreign representatives gaining access to Ukrainian political prisoners held in Russia.

He does not, however, believe that Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova makes her own decisions. "We are seeing a certain top-down realignment of Russian policy," Chalenko told DW. He also said it was important to further develop this communication channel. The lessons learned from the evacuation of Oleshky could be applied to other towns along the front, Chalenko believes.

Dmytro Levus says the Oleshky mission has proven that, if Moscow were so inclined, a ceasefire could be established along the entire front line. Yet Russia has so far shown no willingness in doing so, partly because Ukraine has not agreed to Putin's terms, Levus explains.

Will the ceasefire inject momentum into the upcoming talks?

Preparations are underway for a new round of negotiations between Ukraine, the US and Russia on November 10 and 11 in Abu Dhabi. Dmytro Levus believes the Oleshky ceasefire could provide substance to talks on humanitarian issues. He does not, however, think there will be much progress on a political level, even though he does see scope for a ceasefire at sea, for example.

Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpark Dmytro Lubinets speak to the press ahead of the evacuation Image: Office of the Ombudsman of Ukraine/AP Photo/picture alliance

Levus says that the US will be particularly keen to present further humanitarian successes. Ukraine may use the talks to negotiate a new prisoner exchange, though Levus says Russia will likely only budge under pressure.

Ihor Chalenko says one should not expect too much of the upcoming talks. He believes that Russia is looking for a pretext to withdraw from the negotiations, preferring instead to expand its cooperation with the US, without wanting to make any concessions to end the Ukraine war.

Samuel Greene of King's College London is similarly skeptical. "I assume that at some point, the Kremlin will come to realize that there is nothing left to gain on the battlefield and that they will have to reach an agreement."

"That moment hasn't yet come though," Greene told DW, adding that Russia was still trying to buy time by feigning a willingness to engage in dialogue with the US.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: France: More than 600,000 protest as anger grows over cost of living
World.content:
Demonstrators took to the streets in several French cities to call for government action on the high cost of living. Protests were largely peaceful, but there were some reports of escalation, including in Paris.

Hundreds of thousands of people descended on the streets of French cities on Thursday for a new round of protests over rising cost of living.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the total number of protesters ballooned over the course of the afternoon, from 270,000 to 600,000 by the evening.

The five unions that organized the protests represent public and private sectors, and are calling on the government to address deteriorating public services and high prices of goods.

Public and private sector workers were joined by students, who have organized their numerous protests of their own over the course of the past month.

Protesters gather in Place de la Republique in Paris Image: Geoffroy Van Der Hasselt/AFP

One of the biggest student protests in October turned violent, with rioters having vandalized stores. Flames went up from the roof of the town hall of Limoges in central France.

French President Emmanuel Macron blamed ultra-left groups for the violence and vowed more security personnel at protests.

Cost of living protests in major French cities

Like what was seen in October, major rallies took place in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and elsewhere, with about 70,000 police officers and security forces deployed throughout the country.

Protests were largely peaceful, though there were reports about riot police having clashed with protesters in Lyon.

There were reports about incidents of escalation in Paris, where the Eiffel Tower remained closed for the day. Police at one point used tear gas against protesters in the French capital.

A protester throws a tear gas canister back at police in the city of Lyon Image: Denis Balibouse/REUTERS

Some reports of violence earlier in the day in Brittany, Rennes, Toulouse

Demonstrations kicked off in the southern cities of Marseille and Lyon, and Nantes in the west, on Thursday morning.

Authorities in the western region of Brittany said "masked individuals" had tried to block roads in the city of Rennes.

Broadcaster BFM TV reported that a high school near the southwestern city of Toulouse was set on fire.

The main protest in Paris began at 2 p.m. local time (1300 GMT). Daily newspaper Le Monde reported that the demonstrators in Paris began to clear by the evening.

Reuters reported that high school students and other protesters had already faced off against riot police in the French capital on Thursday morning after they blocked a street with rubbish bins.

France has seen frequent nationwide protests over the cost of living in recent weeks Image: Christophe Archambault/AFP

Public services go on strike

Public and private education unions called for staff to walk off the job, as well as unions representing rail workers, public hospitals and postal services.

They are demanding an increase in the minimum wage, across-the-board wage raises, tax reforms and better learning conditions for young people.

The Education Ministry said just over 15% of French teaching staff went on strike. French power unions also joined the action, state-owned utility EDF said.

About a third of France's high schools were closed, either because of student blockades or striking teachers.

Media reports said state railway operator SNCF expected only minor disruptions to long-distance services.

World.title: Arrests and investigations as Serbia begins post-election clean-up
World.content:
The landslide victory of the Students' List in Serbia's general election seems to have removed a blockage in the justice system: Cases that were long stalled are now suddenly moving forward.

Air Serbia flight JU134 from Belgrade to Moscow on November 3 was already deep in Lithuanian airspace when the crew received instructions to return to the Serbian capital.

Among the passengers were three senior figures from the regime of former President Aleksandar Vucic: Aleksandar Vulin, former defense and interior minister and former head of Serbia's Security Intelligence Agency (BIA), Dusan Bajatovic, long-serving director of state-owned gas company Srbijagas, and Nenad Popovic, a minister without portfolio.

All three are well known in Serbia for their close ties to Moscow and for controversies, including allegations of corruption and abuse of public office.

According to unofficial reports published by several media outlets, the plane was ordered back because of a security breach: Vulin had allegedly boarded without undergoing the mandatory security screening.

Since 2023, Vulin has been under US sanctions over what Washington described as "engaging in corrupt and destabilizing activities that undermine the rule of law in the Western Balkans."

Unusual episode

Vulin told the media that he was travelling to Moscow to discuss extending a gas agreement with Russia.

Former Serbian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandar Vulin (left, pictured here in 2024 with Russian President Vladimir Putin) has been under US sanctions since 2023 Image: Kristina Kormilitsyna/Sputnik/AP/picture alliance

Bajatovic, however, said he did not know why Vulin and Popovic were travelling to Moscow and denied that the two would attend the scheduled meetings on gas supplies.

The incident might have remained nothing more than an unusual news item had it not occurred at a time when Serbia is undergoing a major political transformation.

Judicial developments unfold at remarkable speed

Just nine days earlier, on October 25, the student-backed list won a landslide victory over the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the parliamentary election, ending 14 years of political dominance by Aleksandar Vucic and the SNS, who maintained close relations with Moscow.

Although the new majority has yet to take control of any levers of power, the days after the election brought a series of developments that would have seemed unimaginable just a few weeks ago.

Arrests, new criminal proceedings and the reopening of previously unresolved cases began to unfold at remarkable speed. Some of these cases strike at the very foundations of the system built during the SNS years in power.

"This paints a sad picture of the Serbian prosecution service," prosecutor Bojana Savovic told DW.

Public prosecutor Bojana Savovic told DW that the burst of activity from prosecutors shows 'what they could have done but were unwilling to do until just ten days ago' Image: Maxim Konankov/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Savovic sees the sudden action on the part of prosecutors as an attempt to ingratiate themselves with the new authorities.

"With these actions, they are showing what they could have done but were unwilling to do until just ten days ago," she told DW. "I hope this speed of action will not come at the expense of the quality of indictments and that these are not personal vendettas within the old regime."

Allegations of vote-buying and high-level corruption

Prosecutors have also launched a series of investigations into suspected electoral manipulation, corruption and abuse of public office.

Four people were arrested on suspicion of vote-buying in Novi Sad. Six others were detained in Mali Zvornik on suspicion of helping citizens from Bosnia and Herzegovina register their residence in Serbia so they could vote.

One of the most high-profile cases is the arrest of Davor Macura, the owner of Alta Bank, who is suspected of illegally accessing the bank's vault and removing the equivalent of about €383 million ($430 million).

His arrest came just days after the National Bank of Serbia revoked Alta Bank's license and initiated bankruptcy proceedings. Macura has been publicly associated with the SNS, while his bank had significant business dealings with the state and a large number of Russian clients.

Senior police officials, the head of the Republic Hydrometeorological Institute and several managers of public companies have also been arrested over suspected abuses of office and rigged public procurement procedures.

Alleged destruction of documents

Students and representatives of the new political majority are demanding investigations into corruption cases that have remained unresolved for years.

Their message is that no one should be above the law and that prosecutors and courts must do their jobs — or be held accountable for failing to act.

'It would be tragic if the biggest players […] were prosecuted without sufficient evidence. Or if they were charged with something far less serious than what they actually did,' lawyer Tanja Arsic told DW Image: Maxim Konankov/NurPhoto/picture alliance

"When you want the rule of law and when you want something to be done, it is possible. Our regulations allow for it. But it was obvious that there were people obstructing the entire system, putting cases in drawers and leaving them unresolved," Tanja Arsic, an incoming MP from the Students' List, told DW.

In the days after the election, however, reports and video footage emerged that suggested official documents may have been removed or destroyed in state institutions and public companies.

On October 29, Prosecutor General Zagorka Dolovac responded by issuing a binding instruction to all chief public prosecutors to prevent the destruction of official and other records.

The Students' List also called on employees in state institutions and the media to report any destruction of documents to prevent what they called abuse by the outgoing authorities during the transition of power.

Savovic points out that even an attempt to destroy official records is punishable by law.

How high up will investigations reach?

But will the institutions really investigate those who were once at the very top of Serbia's political power structures?

Former President Aleksandar Vucic said he is not afraid of being arrested and that no evidence of financial wrongdoing will be found against him.

"I don't sign or do anything when it comes to money, and nothing can be found in that regard," he said.

But accountability is not just about who signed a document. It is also about establishing who made the decisions, who gave the orders and who wielded the real power to influence the deals now under investigation.

After years of stalled and unresolved cases, police and prosecutors in Serbia have begun making arrests and launching investigations Image: Sanja Kljajic/DW

"It would be tragic if the biggest players, whose arrests are expected, were prosecuted without sufficient evidence. Or if they were charged with something far less serious than what they actually did," said Tanja Arsic.

The real test is yet to come

Bojana Savovic makes a point of saying that ultimately, the success of the prosecution service won't be measured by the number of politically popular or populist arrests that are made, but by final convictions and the permanent confiscation of assets acquired through crime.

Arsic agrees and warns that conducting high-quality investigations and gathering robust evidence must take precedence over speed.

"The prosecution must not bring indictments if there is not enough evidence. That would be disastrous," she said. "If things are rushed just to achieve a result, only for the cases to end in acquittals because the prosecution failed to prove the charges against people who were at the top of the government — that would be even more disastrous."

But will that be possible within the existing structures? Savovic is not convinced that it will.

"For decades, people whose only qualification was blind obedience, reading the political climate and self-censorship were promoted in the prosecution service and the courts. Without fundamental changes in the judiciary, the police and the security structures, I see no possibility of a substantial and lasting transformation of society," she said.

The real test will come in the courtroom. The verdicts in these cases will show whether Serbia is finally breaking with its old system of power or merely replacing one set of power brokers with another.

World.title: Germany’s Gen Z protest riots spark debate on integration and bias
World.content:
Political debate about the recent Gen Z riots have raised the question: Can Germany talk about problems with integration without putting entire groups of people under suspicion?

Responses to the violent scenes that followed recent Gen Z demonstrations in Germany have revealed differences in opinion within the federal government over who or what is responsible.
