Though there is general agreement that people who committed acts of violence must be held responsible, some conservative lawmakers have largely blamed migrant groups — raising questions about whether they are identifying problems or reinforcing prejudice.

Leading Social Democrats have warned against generalizations and one CDU minister would prefer to examine the causes of the violence. Meanwhile, Gen Z's fears for the future are at threat of being overshadowed.

Police officers on duty included people from ethnic minorities Image: Andreas Arnold/dpa/picture alliance

In Frankfurt, more than 100 police officers were injured, one severely, in the street battles that erupted after the protest on Saturday (October 31). Shops were damaged and looted, too. The situation in Cologne, Hamburg and Berlin also escalated.

Earlier, tens of thousands of young people had taken to the streets across Germany in predominantly peaceful rallies. The initiative Gen Z regelt — which roughly means Gen Z takes charge — had urged young people to highlight their fears for the future and to call for better educational opportunities, affordable housing and more climate action.

CDU initially set tone of debate

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Roman Poseck, Interior Minister of Hesse, the state in which Frankfurt is located, quickly set the tone of the response. Most of those arrested were German citizens, said Poseck (CDU), but added: "This group of offenders was predominantly from a migrant background."

Dobrindt, who is from Bavaria's CSU, the sister party to Friedrich Merz's CDU, said: "There were peaceful demonstrations, which into the evening were hijacked by violent left-wing groups and migrant hooligans."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) backed the statements made by his Interior Minister. His assessment of the background of the offenders was based on "the observations of the investigating authorities and the emergency personnel on the ground," his spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said. It also matched "the images that many have seen."

The Gen Z protests across Germany were predominantly peaceful and more are planned for November 20 Image: Pia Bayer/dpa/picture alliance

Merz announced a tough approach toward the rioters. "Violence does not belong on our streets, and my government will show no tolerance here," Merz said, according to the script for a speech he was due to give at a closed-door CDU party event in Berlin on Monday (November 2). "Whoever attacks police and emergency services officers and loots shops attacks our freedom, ridicules society and the legitimate interests of young people."

Warnings against generalizations, focus on causes

The center-left Social Democrats (SPD), who are in a coalition government with the conservative CDU and CSU bloc, are in agreement on the point that criminals were involved. "It is criminals who attack and injure police officers and commit serious property damage," Defense Minister Boris Pistorius (SPD) told German public broadcaster ZDF on Sunday (November 1).

This is, however, where the similarities end. "What then are ‘migrant groups'?" said Pistorius, challenging the Interior Minister's choice of words. "Does that include people in the third generation living in Germany and who are German citizens? When do we stop drawing this distinction?" he countered. "I think that leads in the wrong direction."

The German federal government's integration commissioner, SPD politician Natalie Pawlik, followed up on Monday (November 2). "Always attributing such violent riots to migrant milieus is too simplistic," Pawlik told the German newspaper, the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung. "Because blanket generalizations about groups also affect those with migrant backgrounds who demonstrated peacefully or who were themselves on duty with the police or emergency services."

She said nothing justified the outbreak of violence and that such crimes had to be punished. However, Pawlik added that if investigations showed that certain groups, in particular, were involved, then the root causes also had to be named. "We cannot ignore difficult questions about the lack of prospects, experiences of marginalization or possible integration problems," the integration commissioner said.

Germany: Inclusive housing for migrants and non-migrants To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German Family and Education Minister Karin Prien (CDU) also wants to examine the causes of the violent behavior. She told German public radio broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that stirring resentment "would also be politically wrong." It is much more about reflecting upon reality. "If the (perpetrators) come from migrant backgrounds then that should cause us concern," Prien said.

According to Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), some 31% of the German population have a migration background. The proportion is higher in many big cities. The figure is over 50% in Frankfurt. Prien says it is necessary to examine why integration has been less successful in some groups of immigrants than others. The real challenge lies in facilitating societal participation and preventing parallel societies.

Risk of ban on Gen Z protests?

The political discussion was intensified by the Hesse interior minister suggesting a ban on further Gen Z protests. In respect of demonstrations planned for November 20, Poseck said that the right of assembly was very valuable, but social peace just as crucial. He said there had also been "massive attacks" against the police even during the demonstrations. "The organizers do not have these gatherings under control," he added.

The organizers of the demonstrations reject those accusations. They immediately distanced themselves from the violence. Germany's Family Affairs Ministry has announced that Karin Prien is due to meet with representatives from the Federal School Students Council (BSK) as well as the German Education Union (GEW) this week.

Prien herself called for younger people's interests to be taken into account more. "These are exactly the debates we need to be having, which young people are also very rightfully demanding," she told German public regional broadcaster RBB.

This article was originally written in German

World.title: Paraguay: President Pena resigns amid bank crisis
World.content:
Paraguay's President Santiago Pena has resigned amid a crisis over his ties to collapsed lender Ueno. Millions of customers' accounts are frozen, with public pension and health care funds also tied up.

Paraguayan President Santiago Pena resigned Thursday under mounting pressure over the collapse of digital lender Ueno, as lawmakers debated his removal from office.

The bank's accounts, also used to process pension payments, are frozen, leaving millions of customers unable to access their money. Ueno also held hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds.

Why did Pena face impeachment?

Pena's resignation followed the withdrawal of support by Congress President Basilio Nunez and ruling conservative Colorado Party leader Horacio Cartes.

Thirty-five opposition lawmakers and ruling-party dissidents had submitted impeachment articles in the 80-seat Chamber of Deputies, accusing Pena of conflicts of interest, misuse of pension funds and institutional cover-ups linked to Ueno.

Pena sold his shares in Ueno Holding, whose businesses include the bank, in April 2025. Lawmakers also cited two loans he received from Ueno as part of allegations of improper financial gain.

They alleged improper presidential interference in the Social Security Institute, known as IPS, and preferential treatment for Ueno. IPS manages pension and health care funds for most Paraguayan workers and held $355 million at the bank — about 9% of its investments, according to financial manager Gladys Vera.

The motion also questioned Pena's 2023 appointment of central bank chief Carlos Carvallo, who previously chaired Financiera Ueno. According to the document, the central bank approved the company's conversion into a bank just 83 days after his appointment.

What happened to Ueno Bank?

Ueno served about 2.94 million customers, roughly 60% of Paraguay's adult population.

As of last month, the bank said it held roughly $800 million in public-sector deposits — about a quarter of its total deposits — including money from the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.

People took the the streets of Asuncion on Wednesday Image: Jorge Saenz/AP Photo/picture alliance

Paraguay's central bank ordered a resolution or closure process Tuesday after finding that Ueno's solvency ratio had fallen below half the required minimum.

Ueno's app, card payments and transfers stopped working, while branches closed, leaving customers queuing outside unable to withdraw their savings.

Hundreds of employees of Ueno and other companies in its parent conglomerate protested outside the Labor Ministry Thursday, demanding unpaid wages and severance.

Retirees, depositors, students and workers had marched through Asuncion a day earlier, demanding Pena's impeachment and holding signs saying "Give us back our money."

What have authorities done?

Authorities detained eight senior executives, including founder Miguel Vazquez and bank president Juan Manuel Gustale. Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud.

Lawyers for several detainees said they needed time to review the allegations before commenting.

Pena had sought to reassure customers in a video message Wednesday, pledging legislation "that will return to every saver what they are entitled to as quickly as possible."

The crisis also forced him to cancel his attendance at the Ibero-American summit in Madrid.

Pena, a conservative economist, took office in August 2023 for a five-year term.

World.title: British comedian and actor Russell Brand found guilty of rape
World.content:
Prosecutors labeled Brand a sexual predator. He was charged in sexual assault cases spanning from 1999 to 2009.

UK comedian Russell Brand was found guilty on Thursday of one rape and three sexual assault charges. The sentences was handed by a jury in London's Southwark Crown Court.

Brand was cleared of two rapes and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Prosecutors had labeled Brand a ruthless sexual predator and brought up charges against in cases spanning from 1999 to 2009, the years where he rose in prominence from stand-up comedy in small venues to ‌becoming a television presenter and Hollywood film star.

Judge Joel Bennathan on Thursday said Brand faced a "significant" prison term, with sentencing due Monday next week.

What were the charges against Brand?

Investigative journalists from The Sunday Times and Channel 4 Dispatches published accusations in September 2023, from women who said they had been raped, sexual abused, and degraded by Brand.

The revelations encouraged four women to come forward to criminally accuse him, while another two women came forward once Brand had been charged.

Evidence at the trial revealed Brand to be a man who abused his fame to obtain sex while treating women as objects, with his entourage and showbiz bosses accused of "normalizing" sexual misconduct and looking the other way on complaints against him.

The victims accused Brand in court of forcing them into sexual activity, sometimes within seconds of them first meeting.

What has Russell Brand said?

Brand was known for risqué comedy stand-up routines and he rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show.

He also appeared in Hollywood films including "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" and "Get Him to the Greek."

Last year, Brand pleaded not guilty to the original charges and saying he was "grateful" for the "opportunity" to defend himself ahead of the trial.

"I was a drug addict, a sex addict and an imbecile, but what I never was was a rapist," he said about the charges. "I've never engaged in non-consensual activity."

Brand said the criminal case against him had a devastating impact on his life and family.

"My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations," Brand said.

He moved away from mainstream media in recent years and relocated to Florida, where he has built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.

World.title: Iran signals satisfaction, skepticism after US midterm vote
World.content:
While the Iranian regime says the US midterms will not change Washington's policy toward Tehran, some officials and commentators see the resounding Democratic victory as blowback against the Iran war.

Iran's leadership has downplayed the significance of Republican setbacks in the US midterm elections, insisting that the Democratic takeover of Congress is unlikely to alter Washington's policy toward the Islamic Republic.

"If there are still those who believe that America can be persuaded to abandon its hostility toward the Iranian nation through concessions or partisan changes in the US political system, they are gravely mistaken," Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said in a statement after the vote.

Khamenei also warned that Tehran would respond more forcefully to any future US military action.

The elections took place after months of military confrontation between Tehran and Washington, which disrupted global energy markets and raised fears of a broader regional conflict.

What defeat in US midterm elections could mean for Trump To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Tehran likely to stick to its course despite US political shift

Mohammad Sadegh Javadi Hesar, Iran-based journalist and member of the reformist party Etemad-e Melli, said the election outcome was unlikely to affect Iran's calculations.

"Iran will not change its position simply because Republicans have lost their majority," he told DW.

According to Javadi Hesar, decisions about ending the conflict will ultimately be made in Washington. Tehran, in turn, is expected to continue insisting on its previous demands for peace, such as the end of all hostilities, including in Lebanon, and the lifting of US naval blockade.

Is a vote for US Democrats a vote against the Iran war?

Others in Iran interpreted the results more positively.

Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf argued that American voters had delivered their verdict on the Iranian conflict.

"The Americans said no to war," Ghalibaf said on X, while acknowledging that rising cost of living also contributed to Donald Trump's party losing the election.

Ghalibaf also mocked US Vice President JD Vance who had acknowledged that the Iran war was the reason the Republicans lost.

"Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?" Ghalibaf wrote on X.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said Iran not only challenged the United States on the battlefield and in the Strait of Hormuz but had also dealt it a political setback in Washington.

US strikes Iran hours before midterm election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Several Iranian media outlets echoed that assessment. The news website Etelaat Online sarcastically suggested that the long-discussed "regime change" had ultimately taken place not in Iran, but in the United States.

Looking back to Jimmy Carter

Some commentators drew historical parallels to another period of US-Iran tension.

The state-affiliated Mehr News Agency compared Trump's political troubles to those of former US President Jimmy Carter, recalling the failed 1980 American military operation to rescue hostages held in Tehran.

At the time, the US deployed eight military helicopters to rendezvous with six transport planes in the Iranian desert before moving on Tehran to free the hostages. However, the aircraft encountered a sand storm and a deadly crash between a helicopter and a C-130 transport plane, killing eight Americans.

The agency argued that the 1980 episode demonstrated the limits of US military power in resolving disputes with Iran. Carter went on to lose the presidential election to Ronald Reagan later that year.

Iran released the hostages in January 1981, just minutes after Reagan was sworn in for his first presidential term.

No winds of change between Iran and US

Hardline media, however, dismissed the election's broader significance.

Tasnim News Agency, which is close to Iran's Revolutionary Guards, argued that there is little meaningful difference between Republicans and Democrats when it comes to Iran policy. According to the agency, both parties pursue similar goals toward the Islamic Republic despite differences in rhetoric.

Using a Persian proverb, Tasnim summed up its view bluntly: "The yellow dog is the brother of the jackal," suggesting that neither side should be expected to act differently toward Iran.

Diplomacy rather than escalation?

Veteran Iranian diplomat Hossein Alizadeh says the actual midterm fallout is difficult to predict, but notes US politics sends ripples out across the entire world.

"The USA is a superpower and a hegemonic power. Consequently, developments in that country are of significance to the entire world — from Mexico and Canada, through the European Union, to China, and, of course, the Middle East," he told DW.

Alizadeh is an expert in international relations who served in the diplomatic corps of the Islamic Republic for 22 years, before resigning in 2010 in protest of the 2009 Iranian post-election crackdown.

US military buildup: What message is it sending Iran? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Finland-based analyst considers another large-scale military escalation by the USA to be unlikely. While the Democrats are also opponents of the Islamic Republic, "unlike the Trump administration, they opted for a diplomatic agreement with Tehran. The 2015 nuclear deal placed Iranian nuclear activities under the oversight of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)," says Alizadeh.

He points out that the Democrats and the US allies were not in favor or attacking Iran.

"The negative repercussions of such a war have already become clear," he told DW.

This piece was originally published in German

World.title: EU court says CBD foods need approval for sale before they can be certified organic
World.content:
The EU's top court says CBD foods cannot be certified organic without approval for sale. The ruling concerns a cannabis compound whose use in food requires authorization, including before organic certification.

The European Union's top court ruled Thursday that foods containing cannabidiol, or CBD, cannot receive organic certification without first being authorized for sale in the bloc.

The court said an organic label could mislead shoppers into thinking CBD foods had been approved for sale.

What is CBD, and why does it need approval?

CBD is a compound found in cannabis, commonly extracted from hemp — cannabis varieties with low levels of THC. Unlike THC, CBD does not produce a high.

The compound is widely marketed in oils, capsules and gummies as a wellness ingredient, often with claims about sleep, stress or pain relief.

The European Commission classifies CBD as a "novel food" — a food not consumed to a significant degree in the EU before May 15, 1997. Such foods require a safety assessment and authorization before they can legally be marketed.

The court noted that CBD has not yet received that authorization, although it did not say that it was unsafe.

CBD is also found in medical marijuana, but the ruling concerns its use in food rather than medicines.

What does that mean for organic certification?

The court said meeting organic production standards did not remove the need for market authorization.

"Such certification contributes to the promotion of those products and conveys, in the eyes of consumers, a positive image of quality and approval," the court said.

The restriction also covers products intended for export outside the EU.

Medical cannabis: Helpful or overhyped? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The ruling concerns CBD-based or CBD-enriched foods that lack EU market authorization, rather than all cannabis-derived foods.

Some cannabis-derived foods, such as hemp seeds and ordinary hemp seed oil, can legally be sold and certified organic if they meet the relevant standards.

Why did the case reach the court?

France's organic farming regulator, INAO, told certification bodies that CBD-based products and CBD-enriched foods could not be certified organic. It also barred CBD as an ingredient in certified organic foods, while exempting hemp oil not enriched with CBD.

A hemp industry association challenged those restrictions before France's Council of State, which referred the case to the EU court.

The French court must now resolve the dispute in line with the EU court's interpretation.

World.title: Una nueva oleada de falsas amenazas de bomba afecta al menos a 27 aviones en Europa
World.content:
Tres aeronaves han tenido origen o destino en Madrid. Bruselas pide colaboración a los Estados para aclarar la incidencia, similar a la registrada el martes en otros siete vuelos

El tráfico aéreo en toda Europa se ha visto afectado este jueves por una nueva oleada de falsas amenazas de bomba contra más de una veintena de aviones. El episodio parece un acto coordinado en un momento especialmente turbulento en Europa, según observadores y expertos consultados. Al menos 27 vuelos con destino a ciudades europeas — y al menos tres de ellos con origen o destino en Madrid— han sufrido este jueves falsos avisos de bomba que les han obligado a realizar aterrizajes de emergencia, sin contratiempos en todos los casos. Además, tres aviones han sido desviados y varios han sido escoltados por cazas de Italia, Francia, Bulgaria y Austria.

Las incidencias, que investigan las autoridades nacionales, han afectado a aeropuertos de España, Francia, Italia, Bélgica, Bulgaria, Chequia, Rumania, Polonia, Irlanda, Dinamarca y Austria. Se producen, además, solo dos días después de que otros siete vuelos registraran falsas amenazas de bomba. Todos sobre el espacio aéreo europeo. En total, al menos 35 vuelos se han visto afectados desde el lunes.

Las amenazas se han recibido por correo electrónico en varios aeropuertos europeos. En el caso de los correos dirigidos al aeródromo de Roma llegó un mensaje firmado por Fighters of the Male State (Luchadores del Estado masculino), un grupo radical ruso de machistas y supremacistas blancos que se hizo conocido por sus campañas de odio contra las mujeres y que ha abrazado la guerra de Rusia contra Ucrania. “Vuestro régimen feminista lo recordará para siempre. La explosión se producirá en 60 minutos. Hoy vuestro cielo será rojo”, decía el correo electrónico, según relata la prensa italiana. Las autoridades del aeropuerto de Roma han confirmado que el correo, que alertaba de los vuelos procedentes de Helsinki y Dublín, estaba escrito en italiano. Rusia declaró extremista a ese movimiento en 2021, y en 2022 su nombre ya apareció en falsas amenazas de bomba contra escuelas de Montenegro, cuya autoría negó su fundador.

Fuentes de inteligencia europeas creen que el nombre de esa organización se puede estar usando como una maniobra de distracción. En cualquier caso no dudan de que la oleada de amenazas de bomba es una acción coordinada que busca no solo generar caos y angustia en los pasajeros sino también analizar la respuesta europea y el tiempo de actuación. Las autoridades nacionales no han apuntado todavía a una pista de la supuesta autoría.

La oleada de amenazas falsas coincide con otros episodios alarmantes en Europa, como los ataques cibernéticos a decenas de supermercados para alterar las temperaturas de sus sistemas de refrigeración, lo que ha llevado a la pérdida de millones de euros en alimentos. También llega después de un grave y sofisticado ataque cibernético contra el Establecimiento Francés de Sangre (EFS), que saboteó los sistemas de congelación de tres de sus principales plantas de almacenamiento biológico.

Colaboración europea

El comisario de Transportes de la UE, Apostolos Tzitzikostas, ha remarcado este jueves que es aún “demasiado pronto para sacar conclusiones sobre si los incidentes notificados están relacionados entre sí”, pero ha subrayado que Bruselas sigue la situación muy de cerca junto a la Agencia Europea de Seguridad Aérea y a los Estados miembros, que tienen las competencias de investigar lo sucedido. “Cualquier amenaza contra la población civil es inaceptable”, ha aseverado Tzitzikostas en un comunicado.

Se trata de incidentes que han afectado a varios países, y por ello la Comisión Europea ha pedido a las autoridades nacionales —responsables de evaluar las amenazas a la seguridad, investigar los incidentes e implementar las medidas de seguridad aérea pertinentes— que colaboren estrechamente con los operadores aeroportuarios, las aerolíneas y las fuerzas y cuerpos de seguridad, ha explicado el comisario griego.

Al menos tres vuelos implicados en la alerta de este jueves han sido notificados en el aeropuerto de Madrid-Barajas. Fuentes de la Guardia Civil, que han procesado las alertas, aseguran, sin embargo, a este periódico que los vuelos eran seis, no tres, informa Óscar López-Fonseca. Iberia ha confirmado que dos de sus aviones, procedentes de Milán y Roma, han recibido amenazas falsas: las alertas han llegado al aeropuerto de Barajas, se han comunicado a los comandantes y ambos aparatos han aterrizado sin incidentes hacia las diez de la mañana. Air Europa ha explicado que su vuelo a París aún no había despegado cuando llegó el aviso y que el avión ha sido evacuado e inspeccionado y, tras comprobarse que se trataba de una falsa alarma, ha despegado y ha aterrizado en París sin problemas, según han declarado ambas compañías a The Guardian. Aena, la empresa pública que gestiona los aeropuertos, ha explicado que, tras constituirse un comité de seguridad con las fuerzas de seguridad del Estado y realizarse las comprobaciones pertinentes, la amenaza de bomba ha sido descartada en todos los casos, informa Javier F. Magariño.

Un avión de Ryanair, este jueves en el aeropuerto de Sofía (Bulgaria). Stoyan Nenov (REUTERS)

Estas incidencias se suman a las que se vivieron el pasado martes en otros siete vuelos con destino a ciudades europeas: Varsovia, Sofía, Roma y Murcia. Todos recibieron amenazas de bomba, uno de los aparatos tuvo que ser desviado y se produjeron perturbaciones en varios aeropuertos, donde fueron movilizados los artificieros, aunque finalmente no fueron hallados explosivos en ninguno de los aviones. La víspera, el lunes, otro avión que volaba de Londres a Sofía había sido desviado a Budapest, escoltado por un caza húngaro, por idéntico motivo.

Por ahora, nadie ha reivindicado esas amenazas falsas y ninguno de los países afectados ha señalado a algún otro Gobierno o grupo terrorista, aunque expertos consultados por EL PAÍS sostienen que esa concentración de amenazas de bomba en cuestión de horas y un mismo espacio aéreo no puede ser casual.

Robert Jordan, del centro británico de estudios de defensa RUSI y antiguo responsable en el Ministerio de Defensa británico de las políticas para prevenir amenazas terroristas contra la aviación civil, explica por correo electrónico que la tolerancia al riesgo es muy baja: si una aerolínea no puede descartar rápidamente que un aviso es falso, actúa cuanto antes. La consultora británica de riesgos Dragonfly sostiene en un intercambio de mensajes que lo que distingue esta campaña de las numerosas falsas amenazas registradas en los últimos años en aeropuertos europeos es que parece coordinada y probablemente obra de un único grupo o de una red reducida de personas afines. Dragonfly no se aventura a señalar quién puede estar detrás de estas acciones, que hacen que las miradas de expertos se dirijan a Rusia, y señala que se trataría, en ese caso, de tácticas nuevas empleadas por Moscú. Jordan recuerda que grupos rusos e iraníes han reclutado por internet a personas para acciones similares, pero no descarta que se trate de alguien que disfruta provocando el caos.

El ministro de Defensa danés, Jeppe Bruus, ha evitado vincular estos incidentes con Rusia, pero ha afirmado a la radiotelevisión pública DR que Europa vive “una escalada de los ataques híbridos” rusos y que los europeos deben prepararse para más episodios como los de este jueves.

World.title: Koldo García asegura que acordó con el abogado del PP un millón de euros a cambio de información para hacer caer a Sánchez
World.content:
En un audio publicado por la Cadena SER, el exasesor de Ábalos afirma que el letrado le ofreció una rebaja de la pena que suponía no entrar en la cárcel

Koldo García, antiguo asesor del exministro José Luis Ábalos, asegura en un audio publicado por la Cadena SER que acordó con el abogado del Partido Popular Alberto Durán el pago de sus gastos de defensa y un millón de euros a cambio de facilitar información que sirviera para hacer caer al presidente Pedro Sánchez. En el audio enviado desde la cárcel, afirma que el abono del dinero se realizaría a través de la empresa editora de Okdiario. La abogada del exasesor, Leticia de la Hoz, ha aportado a la Audiencia Nacional dos facturas para acreditar que sus trabajos de defensa para Koldo García fueron costeados por la web ultraderechista.

“En una reunión que mantuve con el señor Durán, me planteó una rebaja de pena que suponía no entrar en la cárcel”, afirma García sobre la supuesta oferta que le hizo el letrado del PP en los casos de corrupción que afectan al Gobierno y al PSOE. “Sacar a mi familia del proceso, pagar a mi defensa y la cantidad de un millón de euros a cambio de declaraciones que afectaran a personas relevantes del Gobierno, al presidente, muy especialmente a su mujer, al expresidente Zapatero y alguno más, aun mintiendo”, añade el exasesor en el audio.

El PSOE no ha tardado en responder a estas revelaciones denunciando que, de corroborarse, serían de una “gravedad extrema”. El ministro de Justicia, Félix Bolaños, ha reclamado a Alberto Núñez Feijóo que responda a la pregunta de “si el Partido Popular ha pagado un millón al señor Koldo García para que acuse falsamente de delitos a Pedro Sánchez y al Partido Socialista“. ”Eso explicaría la cantidad de difamaciones, de mentiras, de infundios que ha tenido que sufrir Pedro Sánchez en los últimos años”, ha añadido Bolaños en una declaración ante periodistas.

Por su parte, la portavoz del PP en el Congreso, Ester Muñoz, ha desmentido la información. Muñoz ha asegurado que “no es casualidad, que es causal” que la grabación haya salido a la luz justo el día en que la UCO está registrando la casa de Ábalos en Valencia. También ha acusado a García de mentir y ha recordado que el PP pidió 30 años de cárcel para él ante los tribunales.

García, condenado a 19 años y ocho meses de prisión por la trama de las mascarillas, asegura que mantuvo dos encuentros con Durán en mayo de 2025. El exasesor, según su versión, tenía interés en contactar con el jefe de los servicios jurídicos del PP porque quería explorar la posibilidad de un acuerdo, mientras que el letrado, que dirigía la acusación popular de la causa del Tribunal Supremo que investigaba la compra de material sanitario en lo peor de la pandemia, también buscaba supuestamente reunirse cuando el acusado empezaba a estar acorralado.

Las citas tuvieron lugar, según las mismas declaraciones de Koldo García recogidas por la Cadena SER, en un despacho cerca de la sede de los populares en la calle Génova de Madrid. Fuentes consultadas por la SER apuntan que fue en la segunda reunión en la que se sentaron las bases del pacto.

“El pago del dinero ofrecido (...) se efectuaría a través de Eduardo Inda [director de Okdiario]”, afirma García en el audio. “Con posterioridad, mantuve un almuerzo con el señor Inda, en su casa, para coordinar el acuerdo económico y también acordamos el contenido de la entrevista que me iban a hacer. Lo previsto era que el contenido de la entrevista se transformara posteriormente en una declaración ante la autoridad judicial”, relata el exasesor de Ábalos.

World.title: Así se prepara la banca para los próximos años
World.content:
El avance de la inteligencia artificial en bancos como CaixaBank convive con iniciativas de inclusión como SVisual, el servicio de videointerpretación en lengua de signos.

Más educación financiera, planes acordes con la mayor longevidad de la población y digitalización inclusiva. En el horizonte, las entidades bancarias quieren pasar de un papel reactivo a otro más proactivo que acompañe, oriente y anticipe las necesidades de los clientes

La banca del futuro se imagina a menudo dominada por los algoritmos. Sin embargo, cuando se escucha a los expertos y a quienes la construyen, brota un cariz más humano: todos coinciden en que será híbrida. La tecnología es eficaz en lo cotidiano, está disponible a cualquier hora, concede una autonomía impensable hace unos años, cuando la relación con el banco tenía el rostro del trabajador y no una interfaz. Sin embargo, hay circunstancias —las decisiones más vitales— en las que se prioriza el trato personal. Son momentos en los que la conversación con alguien que orienta adquiere un valor irremplazable. Por eso, entidades como CaixaBank entienden el mañana como una suma compleja: más tecnología y más innovación sin desdeñar la posibilidad de acceder a especialistas y gestores cuando sean necesarios.

La inteligencia artificial (IA) permitirá que la relación sea más sencilla y personalizada, pronostican desde CaixaBank. Su cambio estructural consistirá en pasar de una banca principalmente reactiva, en la que el cliente busca una solución cuando surge una necesidad, a una banca con mayor capacidad para acompañar, orientar y anticiparse. Imaginan una relación en la que el banco tenga más capacidad de acompañar de forma proactiva.

Las funciones de esos modelos inteligentes ayudarán a traducir información compleja, a facilitar la comparación entre alternativas y a generar recomendaciones más adaptadas a cada perfil, como anuncian desde este banco. Como concreta Alejandro San Nicolás, docente del máster en Formación Permanente en IA para el Sector Financiero de la Universidad Internacional de Valencia (VIU), la banca conocerá mejor al usuario a través de sus hábitos, comportamientos, emociones y tendencias de consumo. Este docente añade que los entornos bancarios evolucionarán hacia una suerte de marketplace, donde el cliente podrá contratar productos, realizar compras o acceder a financiación directamente desde la plataforma digital bancaria pertinente: “El propio banco va a empezar a lanzarte ofertas basadas en tus necesidades y en lo que te gusta”, explica San Nicolás.

Las entidades financieras aspiran a esa hiperpersonalización que, como señalan desde CaixaBank, “da la oportunidad de reducir ruido y proporcionar al cliente sólo la información apropiada para su situación personal”. Por eso, insisten en que la formación en competencias digitales, la educación financiera y la prevención del fraude son también una parte crucial de ese nuevo acompañamiento.

Habla

Cómo construir una banca integradora, según CaixaBank La evolución de la interfaz Habrá una generalización del móvil como canal financiero. Las plataformas digitales seguirán en constante cambio. Evolucionará con los agentes de IA, que podrán interpretar necesidades, mantener conversaciones complejas y simplificar procesos completos. Su actuación reducirá la complejidad de gestiones que hoy requieren múltiples pasos. Una longevidad diversa Llegados a la jubilación, se generan necesidades que van más allá del dinero. Por eso, desde la entidad se trata de fomentar el ahorro desde edades tempranas, complementar ingresos en la jubilación, ayudar a optimizar el patrimonio financiero e inmobiliario o acompañar a las personas durante toda esa etapa posterior a la laboral. Un error común es considerar que todas las personas mayores son iguales, señalan desde CaixaBank. Algunos se sienten cómodos con los entornos digitales, otros prefieren la atención telefónica y algunos exigen presencialidad. El colectivo senior es especialmente diverso en cuanto a autonomía financiera y uso de canales. Atención a las necesidades específicas CaixaBank hace hincapié en la inclusión: el 94% de sus oficinas, el 99% de sus cajeros y su aplicación móvil CaixaBankNow son accesibles. Además, dispone de la Tarjeta Braille para personas con discapacidad visual, el servicio de videointerpretación en lengua de signos SVisual para clientes con discapacidad auditiva, TPV accesibles, comunicaciones en lectura fácil, una guía adaptada para ayudar en la toma de decisiones financieras y el programa Día a Día Apoyo Capacidad Jurídica. La transformación de las sucursales Las oficinas físicas evolucionarán, aunque seguirán desempeñando un papel importante. CaixaBank tiene más de 4.200, repartidas por España. Además, la entidad tiene presencia en cerca de 3.700 municipios: en 2.234 localidades con el modelo tradicional y en más de 1.420 poblaciones a través de 32 oficinas móviles. Estas permiten a clientes (y no clientes) realizar las operaciones bancarias más habituales en localidades sin oficina bancaria o con restricciones que limitan el acceso a los servicios financieros en poblaciones en las que residen más de 632.000 personas. El 70% de los usuarios tienen más de 65 años.

Mantener la confianza... ‘online’

Dar cierta credibilidad a la IA es fundamental para que su implantación sea efectiva. Pero trabajar en entornos tecnológicos plantea riesgos relacionados con la privacidad, la seguridad de los datos y la posible sensación de vigilancia excesiva, como enumera Juan Carlos López-Robles, profesor de ESIC University que imparte en ámbitos como la Informática Aplicada, las Tecnologías de la Educación y las Tecnologías Móviles e Internet de las Cosas (IoT).

Los ingredientes para que la IA tenga una buena integración, según López-Robles, son tres: que sus respuestas sean útiles, que se comprendan sin necesidad de tener un alto nivel de conocimientos específicos y que sean transparentes. “Los usuarios aceptamos mejor una recomendación cuando entendemos el porqué, el para qué y tenemos la sensación de control sobre la decisión final”. Y añade: “La confianza se construye con explicaciones claras y resultados consistentes “. Hay una necesidad de entender los criterios, de conocer las reglas del juego de algoritmos.

Los usuarios están dispuestos a compartir información cuando perciben un beneficio claro y confían en la entidad. Por eso, para CaixaBank, “la personalización solo tendrá recorrido si va acompañada de seguridad, privacidad, transparencia y capacidad de control por parte del cliente”. Un ejemplo de su compromiso es su nueva Dirección de IA y Datos, que coordina de forma transversal esta área y facilita el desarrollo de soluciones escalables, seguras y responsables. Gestiona todo el ciclo de vida de las iniciativas, desde la identificación de oportunidades hasta su diseño, implantación y supervisión. Además, integra el cumplimiento normativo y la gestión de riesgos desde las fases iniciales; se asegura de que los desarrollos sean responsables.

La IA se emplea con criterio, pero también permite al banco ser más seguro. La han incorporado a sus sistemas de defensa para reforzar las tareas de detección, análisis, actuación y para proteger los nuevos entornos. También vigila los agentes, una función que, más allá de responder a preguntas como un chat tradicional, razona, planifica y ejecuta acciones de forma autónoma para cumplir un propósito. Estos sistemas incorporan herramientas como la identificación y corrección automatizadas de vulnerabilidades, la evolución de su centro de operaciones de seguridad y el empleo de sistemas capaces de detectar indicios de actividad sospechosa, correlacionar señales, evaluar amenazas y activar medidas de protección de manera autónoma.

Sobre todo, inciden en que combinan la capacidad analítica de la IA con la supervisión y responsabilidad humanas. En esa mezcla está la virtud, secunda López-Robles: “Nadie quiere pedir cita para hacer una transferencia o revisar los movimientos de la cuenta, pero casi todo el mundo quiere hablar con una persona antes de firmar una hipoteca o una cartera de inversión”.

La atención presencial no puede desaparecer, reconocen los expertos, pero su transformación es inevitable. “Dará paso a una red mucho más reducida, orientada a un trato más personal, en un espacio con sofás y en los que le ofrecen un café”, describe San Nicolás. De ahí que sean fundamentales las citas previas; serán más puntuales, planificadas y especializadas.

Las entidades financieras se adaptan a los nuevos hábitos y refuerzan sus servicios digitales. CaixaBank aumentó en un 30% las altas digitales en el ejercicio 2025, en gran parte gracias a imagin, el banco digital del grupo dirigido especialmente a clientes jóvenes, que cuenta con alrededor de 4,3 millones de clientes. La penetración en el Grupo CaixaBank de clientes financieros de edad de entre 16 y 34 años alcanza el 42%. La tendencia online también se aprecia en los hábitos de pago. En junio, CaixaBank superó el récord histórico de pago con el móvil en España, con 139,7 millones de operaciones en un mes.

La generación de transición

¿Quiénes son los que se pueden sentir más abrumados por los cambios? San Nicolás, como experto en IA para el sector financiero, señala que los que están “en tierra de nadie”. Por ejemplo: “Los mayores de 50 años, una generación que ha visto llegar toda esta transformación cuando ya tenía gran parte de su vida financiera construida”.

La tecnología puede convertirse en una nueva forma de exclusión, advierte López-Robles, profesor de ESIC. “A medida que aumente el número de personas mayores, la clave no será ofrecer más tecnología, sino hacerla accesible, dinámica, sencilla y fluida”, sostiene. Es uno de los motivos que lleva a CaixaBank a ir más allá de la jubilación, que les mueve a planificar una etapa de la vida cada vez más larga y diversa y apostar por un acompañamiento integral. Para López-Robles, el objetivo que se deben proponer las entidades es construir una banca “no solo más digital, sino más inteligente, más sencilla y, sobre todo, más relevante para cada cliente”.

World.title: En el contrato anual con el inquilino hay una cláusula para que mis hijos recuperen la casa. ¿Aplica la prórroga de dos años?
World.content:
Pregunta. Tengo un piso alquilado que cumple el contrato anual el 31 de diciembre. Cuando renovamos el año pasado, incluimos una cláusula por la que se rescindiría dicho contrato si uno de nuestros dos hijos lo necesitaba. El inquilino aceptó las condiciones. Queremos saber si obligatoriamente tiene que estar dos años más, aunque nuestros hijos lo necesiten, avisando con los plazos legales. C. Sisamon

Respuesta. Entiendo que se está refiriendo a la prórroga extraordinaria de dos años prevista en la disposición final quinta del Real Decreto-ley 29/2026, de 6 de octubre, por el que se adoptan medidas urgentes para la protección de la función social de la vivienda y la ampliación de la oferta de vivienda asequible. Este Real Decreto entró en vigor el 7 de octubre de 2026.

Si el contrato de arrendamiento al que se refiere en la consulta tiene una duración de un año (actualmente denominado contrato temporal o de temporada) y no es de vivienda habitual, no se encontraría dentro de los supuestos en los que puede solicitarse la citada prórroga extraordinaria de dos años. Por tanto, el compromiso de desalojo pactado en favor de los hijos del arrendador debería ser respetado por la parte arrendataria. Además, dicha prórroga extraordinaria no resulta aplicable a los contratos temporales.

No obstante, conviene realizar una precisión importante. Si, tal y como parece desprenderse de la consulta, se vienen formalizando contratos de un año de duración, no prorrogables, sobre la misma vivienda y con los mismos arrendatarios, debe tenerse en cuenta que, si el Real Decreto es finalmente convalidado por la Diputación Permanente, el próximo contrato de temporada que se suscriba (en principio en diciembre de 2026) deberá recoger de forma expresa y obligatoria la causa concreta que motiva el desplazamiento temporal del arrendatario y que justifica la temporalidad del arrendamiento. Asimismo, corresponderá al arrendador acreditar la existencia de dicha causa.

En caso de no poder demostrarse la necesidad temporal que justifica este tipo de contrato, el artículo 7.2 de la Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos, en su redacción dada por el Real Decreto, establece que esta circunstancia “lo privará de su naturaleza temporal y comportará su sumisión al presente título en las mismas condiciones que los contratos de arrendamiento de vivienda habitual, con efectos retroactivos a la formalización del contrato”.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Unfair rent clauses: why thousands of tenants may get money back
World.content:
Did you know that, as a renter, you may be entitled to money back? Read on to see if you qualify.

It all centres on unfair clauses regarding rent increases and recent legal rulings – to the benefit of renters.

Dutch courts, including the Supreme Court, have ruled that a clause in private-sector leases allowing an annual rent increase in line with the Consumer Price Index (consumentenprijsindex, CPI) plus a surcharge of up to 3% is, as a rule, not unfair.

A higher surcharge, though, may be deemed unfair: in December 2025, the Amsterdam Court of Appeal held a surcharge of up to 5% unfair.

“If you believe you paid too much based on an unfair rental clause, you can claim money back,” says Robert Berendsen, founder of Mr. Berendsen Advocaten in Amsterdam. “Many tenants don’t realise they have strong protections in this tight housing market.”

The high court rules

When the Supreme Court made that ruling in November 2024, it set a legal precedent: the CPI and the additional surcharge can be split, meaning that even if the CPI is legal, the surcharge can be seen as unfairly burdensome.

“Until then, that was deemed legally impossible,” says Berendsen of the fair-unfair division. “There was huge interest in the outcome of this case. Hundreds of thousands of tenants may be owed money. Which means potentially hundreds of millions of euros paid out. It has a huge economic impact.”

Most affected would be landlords, housing associations and investors, who would have to return the money.

DIY

Berendsen advises tenants to check their leases and see what surcharge on top of inflation the rent increase clause allows. If it’s more than 3%, enter your data into your AI program of choice and let modern technology do the rest.

“Enter the start date of your lease, the initial rent excluding service charges and every annual increase,” says Berendsen. “Then ask: ‘suppose the rent had only been increased with inflation each year, without the surcharge. What would the rent be today, and how much did I overpay?’”

Only the surcharge can be reclaimed; the inflation increases stand.

“If you believe you are owed money for the unfair surcharges only, write a letter to your landlord. If they don’t react or decline, says Berendsen, you (the tenant) can take the claim to the subdistrict court (kantonrechter). In all cases concerning a lease, even those brought by a landlord, the court must check whether the surcharge clause is unfair, even if the tenant does not raise the issue.”

The future

In July 2026, the Amsterdam District Court referred questions regarding “the splitting of the rent change clause and whether the clause is unfair or not” to the Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg in the cases of 19 tenants seeking a refund.

While any decision is likely years away, Berendsen advises tenants not to worry. “The Supreme Court’s ruling is the starting point for tenants; I do not expect the EU court to make their position worse,” he says.

“The idea behind the rules is that tenants operate in a tight market, and it’s not reasonable to expect them to vacate their rental homes if they don’t agree with rent increases,” says Berendsen. “Tenants must be protected from unfair practices.”

If you want legal help from an actual person, contact Mr. Berendsen Advocaten.

World.title: KLM to cut 5,000 jobs amid high fuel prices and global unrest
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

National airline KLM is slashing around 5,000 jobs, almost 15% of its workforce, in a move the company says is necessary to survive.

CEO Marjan Rintel announced in a press release on Thursday that without serious action the airline, which was founded in 1919 and is one of the oldest in the aviation industry, could fold.

High fuel prices and global unrest are major factors in pressure the company is facing.

KLM was effectively taken over by Air France in 2004, though the Dutch brand kept its own name and management. Of the jobs being cut, 2,000 will be moved to the Air-France KLM group.

Labour unions have expressed concern about the move, with FNV and CNV saying workers are footing the bill for a major corporation.

KLM says compulsory layoffs likely won’t be needed, and that voluntary departure schemes and not replacing staff who leave will help make the needed cuts.

World.title: Human rights orgs cut ties with ICC under US sanctions pressure
World.content:
At least 20 human rights organizations have ended or considerably reduced cooperation with the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague over US-imposed sanctions against the court and its employees, and that may just be the tip of the iceberg.

So found investigative journalism platform Investico and German daily Süddeutsche Zeitung after surveying 100 non-profit organizations, including big names like Human Rights Watch and the Center for Constitutional Rights.

The Trump administration has declared war on what it calls a “rogue court”, sanctioning judges, prosecutors, human rights organisations and, in October, the court as a whole.

“They want more power, and they want it at the expense of our sovereignty as a nation,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote on X at the time.

“And President Trump will never allow the ICC to prosecute Americans… We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources, and crippling their ability to operate against us. The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC.”

ICC employees have faced visa restrictions, a loss of access to their American property and financial assets and seen their accounts with American financial service institutions cut as a result of the sanctions, with one judge saying she lost access to all her American credit cards earlier this year.

Human rights organizations

While human rights organizations don’t work directly for the court, they provide valuable information in criminal cases, including eyewitness testimony and local law knowhow.

“They are a very important part of our work,” former Chief Prosecutor Fatou Bensouda told Investico. “They do not conduct investigations on our behalf, but they do provide us with leads, which help us find ways to substantiate evidence.”

Bensouda worked at the ICC until 2021 and was herself sanctioned by the US in 2020, which froze her American assets.

Chilling effect

Some organizations not directly covered by the sanctions have also stopped cooperating with the ICC.

“We cannot accept the risk of being sanctioned ourselves and that all our other work is at risk,” a German NGO told the researchers.

Save the Children Netherlands also says it is struggling to find new ways of working with the court.

As the host country of the ICC, the Netherlands is obliged to protect the court’s work from “interference”. But a spokesperson for the foreign affairs ministry told Investico that the country bears “no special responsibility as a host country” to protect NGOs from the consequences of sanctions.

Midterm elections

While Democrats won control of the US House and Senate in this week’s midterm elections, that won’t change the current sanctions.

“That foreign policy is firmly in the hands of the White House,” legal historian Iva Vukušić from Utrecht University told Dutch News. “But the election results may distract the White House with domestic issues and investigations against them and whatnot. It also changes the mood of invincibility of the White House and that may hold them back a bit.”

World.title: Half of rental agents willing to exclude foreign tenants: study
World.content:
Almost half of rental agents contacted for a government-commissioned study were willing to discriminate against potential tenants with foreign roots, researchers have found.

The study, conducted by the Verwey-Jonker Institute, used actors posing as landlords to phone rental agents and ask them if they could avoid renting to “foreigners; Moroccans, Turks or Poles”.

They found that 97 out of 200 agreed outright with the request. Another 30% didn’t refuse, mostly saying it was up to the landlord, and only 20% said no.

“Expat” privileges

In 36 of the cases, agents distinguished “expats” as good foreign tenants, describing them as highly educated and well paid, with reliable employers. Some also said they tend to leave after a while, which they presented as a way around the 2024 ban on most temporary leases.

“Let me put your mind at rest, neither do we,” one agent told an actor who said they did not have a good feeling about foreigners. “The foreigners we usually talk about are the expats, who just come here to work for the big companies.”

Another said: “Officially we’re not allowed to discriminate, of course, but if you say you don’t want people from certain types of countries, I don’t need to put them forward to you.”

Moroccan-sounding names

In separate tests on 1,662 listings on the rental site Pararius between December and May, applicants with Moroccan-sounding names were invited to viewings less often than otherwise identical applicants with Dutch-sounding names.

For men, there were 14% of cases where only the Dutch-named applicant got an invitation, and 16% for women. Last year’s monitor found no significant discrimination against any group for the first time. The researchers found none this year against Polish-sounding names or same-sex couples.

Findings of the investigations were sent to MPs on Wednesday.

World.title: Back to class: cabinet seeks to train civil servants as teachers
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

A majority of MPs are seeking to have soon-to-be-redundant civil servants at the education, culture and science ministry (OCW) retrained as teachers.

The VVD will bring the proposal, which also has the backing of political parties D66, CDA, JA21 and 50Plus, the to the cabinet Thursday.

VVD MP Arend Kisteman believes the plan will “kill two birds with one stone”.

“The announced cuts are a great opportunity to have these enthusiastic people voluntarily retrained for a job in education at the expense of the government,” Kisteman told broadcaster NOS.

The cabinet plans to eliminate 25,000 civil servants over the next nine years, a cut of some 16% by 2035. The OCW will not be spared.

Supporters say retraining already enthusiastic education workers as teachers will help alleviate chronic teacher shortages nationwide, especially in the country’s big cities.

But similar past initiatives have gotten low marks over schools’ reluctance to hire people with little to no classroom experience and civil servants’ reluctance to take salary cuts.

World.title: Disgruntled estate agents plan rival to property site Funda
World.content:
A group of disgruntled real estate brokers is starting a rival online real estate marketplace to the dominant Funda, saying it is “building a platform in which the broker is no longer a cash cow but is at the helm.”

The new platform, called Homek, is expected to launch in March 2027. For now, it’s appealing to brokers to join the platform, with RTL Z reporting that it won’t launch until at least 1,000 agents have bought in or the foundation has raised €1 million.

The increasing price of placing a property on Funda is one of the irritants that led the brokers to start the rival site.

“Homek is the fair, transparent alternative to Funda, without expensive packages or paid priority,” says Homek’s website, which currently doesn’t list any properties for sale or rent.

Only certified brokers affiliated with industry associations can use Homek, unlike Funda, where unaffiliated real estate agents who meet the site’s conditions can place properties.

Brokers on Homek will also share in the profits.

“The high placement costs and priority paid at Funda require an alternative: a housing platform where real estate agents themselves are in charge,” says Homek’s website. It promises “fair rates, equal opportunities and control for the affiliated brokers and offices.”

Supply problems

Funda was established in 2001 by the brokers’ association NVM.

“As brokers, we came up with Funda ourselves,” says Toine Naber, former chairman of the NVM branch in West-Brabant and a past member of Funda’s advisory board. “With Homek, we get the chance to do it again, but this time without giving away control of our own future.”

Sven Heinen, who is slated to be chairman of the Homek Foundation, told RTL Z he recognises that to become successful, Homek must have the goods to offer home buyers or renters.

“In the past, there have been plenty of competitors of Funda who wanted to take a piece of this market, but they all stalled because the supply was too limited,” Heinen says. “Only when many real estate agents join us and share their housing supply…can we become a serious competitor of Funda.”

Heinen says that within 48 hours, they’ve already raised €200,000.

Funda says it’s not worried about the competition for now. “In a healthy market, there is competition, and sometimes new players join,” spokesperson Claire Verhagen told RTL Z. “We look forward to that with confidence.”

World.title: Coalition parties ready to vote against each other on tax plans
World.content:
The ruling coalition parties have signalled they could vote against one another on amendments to the 2027 tax plan before parliament votes on it next week, after a debate that went ran late into Wednesday night.

Prime minister Rob Jetten’s centrist social-liberal D66 and the centrist Christian Democrat CDA said they could back opposition amendments even if their coalition partner, the right-wing liberal VVD, voted against them, broadcaster NOS reported.

“It is not an unthinkable situation,” D66 finance spokesman Henk-Jan Oosterhuis said after repeated questions from MPs. “The coalition is not a merger party.” CDA MP Inge van Dijk said split voting was “certainly not the intention” but did not rule it out.

Senate hurdle

The tax plan sets income tax rates and other levies for next year, and must be passed in time for the tax office to bring in the changes. If it fails, the cabinet will almost certainly fall, NRC reported.

Earlier this week the cabinet offered about €350 million in concessions to opposition parties on the left and right, which have formed rival blocs and demanded that the coalition choose between them.

The coalition holds 66 of the 150 seats in parliament. It now looks likely to win next week’s vote with the help of the ChristenUnie, 50PLUS and the group led by former PVV MP Gidi Markuszower. But that is not enough in the senate, where it needs the support of either Pro and Volt or the BBB.

Left-wing parties attacked the coalition for relying on Markuszower, after MPs, including the coalition parties, voted earlier this year against deals with politicians who call for violence against refugees. Markuszower had said Palestinian refugees should be stopped “with maximum violence”, the Volkskrant reported. Pro, Denk and the PvdD said extra police funding credited to him amounted to buying his support.

Oosterhuis said there was “no agreement” with Markuszower, but added: “If Mr Markuszower wants to support the tax plan, I am not going to ask him to vote against it.”

Wealth tax offer

The Pro and Volt alliance used the debate to table an amendment that would shift €1.5 billion of tax from workers to the wealthiest. Income tax would be lowered, paid for by a higher tax rate on the largest fortunes, higher tax on business owners’ income from their companies and an end to tax breaks on passing on family businesses.

The VVD’s Wendy van Eijk said it was “unthinkable” that any coalition party would back the proposal “in this form”, and that her party would not support higher taxes on wealth.

Parliament votes on each amendment before voting on the plan as a whole. That means the VVD could vote against a wealth tax rise but still back the final plan, if D66 and the CDA help the amendment through.

MPs vote on the tax plan on November 12, and the senate in the week before Christmas.

World.title: Sunny end to week, but near-freezing nights ahead
World.content:
Thursday and Friday will be sunny and dry across the Netherlands, but temperatures won’t rise past 10° and could drop close to freezing overnight, according to the KNMI forecast issued at 6am on Thursday.

The national weather institute KNMI said Thursday afternoon would bring plenty of sunshine, with a high of around 10°. Wind from the east will make it feel colder.

Thursday night will stay dry. Temperatures will fall to near freezing in the east, and stay at about 6° on the Wadden islands. Fog is possible in the far southwest.

Friday will be sunny and dry again. Highs will range from 8° in the far north to 12° in the southeast. Clouds will build in the southwest late in the afternoon.

Saturday may start with fog, mainly in the south and southwest, and some frost is possible inland, the KNMI said.

World.title: Chinese fashion platform Shein to invest €500 million in Polish logistics hub

Chinese fast fashion platform Shein has announced a €500 million (2.2 billion zloty) investment to expand its logistics centre in Poland, a move it says will create around 2,000 new jobs by the end of this year. The announcement comes amid growing controversy over the impact of Chinese e-commerce platforms on European businesses and follows a recent decision by the European Union to introduce a special fee on low-value parcels sent from outside the EU and European Free Trade Area. SHEIN investește 500 mil. euro în Polonia. Extinde hub-ul logistic europeanhttps://t.co/WNbib4dFta pic.twitter.com/KiI1AB4wFM — Cristi Dorombach (@piticu21) November 4, 2026 The investment will expand Shein’s existing logistics facility in Magnice, near the city of Wrocław in southwestern Poland, which has been operating since 2022. The expansion will bring total employment at the site to around 10,000 by creating 2,000 jobs in logistics, supply chain management, technology and warehouse operations, according to local news service Wroclaw.pl. The facility will also host 6,500 autonomous robots for sorting items. Shein says that the move will help it cut delivery times in Europe, allowing some orders to arrive within 48 hours. “This investment in Poland clearly demonstrates our commitment and belief in the potential of the European market,” said Leonard Lin, the firm’s global head of public affairs. “Poland has become one of the pillars of our operations in Europe,” he added. “This latest investment is a testament to our confidence in the country’s potential, the competencies of its workforce, and its business environment.” The expansion comes as Shein faces a tougher trading environment in Europe. Its sales in the region fell by 13.9% year-on-year to $3.77 billion in the second quarter, while net profit dropped by 67%. The decline comes as the EU steps up efforts to curb the influx of low-cost imports from Chinese platforms such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress, which European retailers say pose unfair competition. In July, the bloc introduced a €3 fee on parcels worth less than €150. From 1 November, a further €2 handling fee was added to all imported parcels, regardless of their value, to cover customs processing costs. China overtook Germany to become Poland’s biggest source of imports for the first time in July, ending a period of around 35 years in which Germany had consistently held top spot https://t.co/U6rQwfEJ7I — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 16, 2026 Shein has also faced accusations of labour-law violations at its facilities in China, including concerns that it may use cotton produced through forced labour. The company disputes many of the allegations, saying that it prohibits forced and child labour and regularly inspects working conditions at its suppliers. China is an increasingly important trading partner in Poland. In July, it overtook Germany to become Poland’s largest source of imports for the first time, driven by rising purchases of cars, computer hardware and consumer goods. Poland has detained and charged six people – five Poles and one Russian – suspected of running an operation to illegally supply Russia with military components. Investigators say that over 2 million zloty (€450,000) worth of equipment was smuggled into the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. The arrests, which took place on 21 October and 2 November, were announced on Thursday morning by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) and National Prosecutor’s Office. 🚨 ROSYJSKI WYWIAD. PRZEMYT CZĘŚCI DO PRODUKCJI UZBROJENIA. 6 ZATRZYMANYCH.@ABW_GOV_PL rozbiła grupę podejrzaną o działalność na rzecz rosyjskich służb specjalnych. 🔴6⃣ osób zatrzymanych, 🔴2⃣1⃣przeszukanych lokalizacji, 🔴 4⃣osoby z zarzutami szpiegostwa – wszystkie trafiły… pic.twitter.com/L90n3rf5rY — ABW (@ABW_GOV_PL) November 5, 2026 Prosecutors report that all six suspects have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group that sought to export weapon components from Poland to Russia in violation of a ban on such trade. Four of the suspects have also been charged under Poland’s espionage law, accused of acting on behalf of Russian intelligence in return for financial benefits. Those four individuals have been placed in pretrial detention. The other two were released with preventative measures put in place. The ABW says that the criminal group “illegally supplied Russia with significant quantities of military components, including those used in the production of ammunition and weapons systems”. “This type of activity may lead to the strengthening of the Russian arms industry and the military capabilities of the Russian Federation, and thus pose a serious threat to Poland’s security and interests,” wrote the agency. Prosecutors say that the group operated at least between June 2023 and December 2025 in Poland, Lithuania and Russia. Members were responsible for procuring goods and transporting them to Kaliningrad, which borders Poland and Lithuania. “Vehicles equipped with hidden compartments were used to transport the goods,” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The suspects repeatedly crossed the Polish-Russian border, and some of the transports were intercepted by Polish border guards.” Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, revealed that the six suspects include five Polish citizens, aged 25 to 52, and one Russian woman, aged 37. Onet, a leading news website, reports, based on unnamed sources, that the Russian citizen acted as a liaison between the group and the foreign intelligence agency behind the operation. Funkcjonariusze @ABW_GOV_PL zatrzymali 6 osób podejrzanych o udział w zorganizowanej grupie przestępczej działającej przeciwko Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej. Wśród zatrzymanych jest pięciu Polaków w wieku od 25 do 52 lat i 37-letnia Rosjanka. 🛑 Sąd – pod zarzutem szpiegostwa -… — Tomasz Siemoniak (@TomaszSiemoniak) November 5, 2026 Poland has seen a huge rise in espionage cases in recent years. The ABW launched 48 investigations related to espionage last year, more than twice as many as in 2024. In those two years taken together, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined. Last month, a Polish man was jailed for five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of an airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. In July, a Russian married couple with refugee status in Poland were convicted of working as spies on behalf of Moscow. In October, a member of Poland’s military reserve, who holds both Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, was detained on suspicion of espionage. World.title: Polish far-right leader Braun to face second trial
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun will again stand trial, after prosecutors filed an indictment against him for a series of anti-Ukrainian, anti-Jewish, anti-LGBT and anti-EU acts committed during his presidential election campaign last year. Braun is already separately on trial for a number of other alleged crimes, including an attack on a Jewish religious ceremony in parliament. He is also facing further charges for a range of other alleged offences. Grzegorz Braun stanie przed sądem. Prokuratura Okręgowa w Warszawie skierowała dziś akt oskarżenia za zuchwałą kradzież flag Ukrainy w Białej Podlaskiej i Unii Europejskiej w Katowicach, zniszczenie wystawy LGBT w Sejmie oraz zniesławienie organizatorów akcji Żonkile i Muzeum… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 4, 2026 On Wednesday, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw announced that it had indicted Braun for four alleged crimes. It was able to do so after the European Parliament, where Braun sits as an MEP, stripped him of immunity earlier this year. One of the charges, for criminal defamation, stems from Braun’s claim, during a televised presidential debate in April last year, that the yellow paper daffodils distributed each year in Warsaw to mark the anniversary of the 1943 Jewish Ghetto Uprising against German Nazi rule are “symbols of shame”. Prosecutors say that Braun’s words were “extremely xenophobic, manipulative and aggressive”, and that they defamed the organisers of the daffodil campaign, in particular the POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews in Warsaw. During the same debate, Braun also warned about the “Judaisation” of Poland, saying that “Jews have far too much say in Polish affairs”. That prompted protests by some of his opponents, one of whom filed a notification to prosecutors. Two other charges relate to thefts of flags. In one incident, Braun and his supporters removed a Ukrainian flag hanging outside city hall in the town of Biała Podlaska during a campaign event. In another, he removed a European Union flag from the industry ministry in the city of Katowice and set it on fire. Braun regularly rails against what he calls the “Ukrainisation” of Poland, warning of the supposed dangers of having so many Ukrainian refugees and migrants in the country. He is also a vocal critic of the EU. On those and other issues, Braun’s rhetoric often echoes Russian propaganda. The final charge, of destruction of property, relates to an incident in June 2025, when Braun vandalised an exhibition about the LGBT+ community in the Polish parliament. He regularly condemns what he calls the “perversions” of LGBT+ people, and has called for homosexuality to be criminalised. The European Parliament has again stripped Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face charges of denying Nazi crimes. The decision marks the sixth time it has lifted Braun’s immunity, and the second time for charges of Holocaust denial https://t.co/O9FN1YbchE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 16, 2026 The charges Braun faces carry prison sentences of up to five years in the case of destruction of property, and up to one year in the case of criminal defamation and theft. Additionally, the deputy leader of Braun’s Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party, Roman Fritz, was indicted for assisting in the theft of the EU flag, while four other men (who have not waived their right to anonymity under Polish law) were indicted for their alleged roles in stealing both the EU and Ukrainian flags. All four incidents for which Braun has been indicted took place when he was campaigning for the May 2025 presidential elections, in which he finished a surprise fourth, with 6.3% of the vote. Since then, KKP has continued to perform strongly in polls, with its support currently standing at around 9%. If it obtained that kind of result at next year’s parliamentary elections, it would be likely to play a major role in deciding what kind of government could be formed. Our essential guide to Poland's parliamentary elections, which will take place one year from now. How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026 Much of Braun’s political brand has been built around provocative statements and actions. The politician is already on trial for his attack on a Jewish Hanukkah ceremony taking place in parliament, at which he put out the candles with a fire extinguisher. In their statement on Wednesday, the Warsaw prosecutor’s office noted that the latest hearings in that trial had been cancelled after Braun presented a medical certificate justifying his absence. However, the prosecutors pointed out that, last Friday, the day that the hearings had been due to begin, Braun attended a protest by opposition supporters outside the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw, which that evening had been taken over by government-backed judges. Braun was pictured “jostling with police riot police, addressing the crowd and giving interviews”, showing “no signs of health problems that would prevent him from attending the hearing”, wrote the prosecutors. They have therefore asked the court to investigate the doctor who issued the medical certificate.
