Polish political leaders have reacted to the results of Tuesday’s US midterm elections, in which the Democrats won control of both houses of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republicans. The outcome was welcomed by Poland’s ruling coalition, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk declaring that “democracy won”. The response was more muted from the right-wing opposition and the office of conservative President Karol Nawrocki, who is a Trump ally. 🚨 🇺🇸 Tusk gives Trump some great advice. But will the US president listen? Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk urged the US president to seek compromises after the Republicans' defeat and not to rely on vetoes as his main way of governing. Trump had earlier threatened to become… pic.twitter.com/s3E6G5zIQT — NEXTA (@nexta_tv) November 4, 2026 Tusk addressed the election results on Wednesday afternoon local time at a press conference alongside his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš. “Today, democracy won in America,” said a smiling Tusk. “I love democracy; it is a beautiful thing.” “As President Donald Trump himself said just after the election, the Democrats did a good job, and I really could not agree more with him this time,” added Tusk. “I hope that the result will stabilise the situation also in our region.” Although the United States remains Poland’s most important security partner, Tusk’s government – a broad, pro-EU coalition that ranges from left to centre right – has at times had uneasy relations with the Trump administration. It has been critical of Trump’s conciliatory approach towards Russia, his often tough stance on Ukraine, as well as his pursuit of US control over Greenland. Meanwhile, the head of the parliamentary caucus of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, Zbigniew Konwiński, told broadcaster Polsat News that “personally, I was happy with the Democrats’ victory”. “We know how Donald Trump behaves, how volatile he is in his political declarations, how he can sometimes put Ukraine in a more difficult position than Russia, so I would rather look for the positives in what happened,” said Konwiński. “If we look at recent years, the more Democrats, the stronger the Democrats, the better for Poland,” he added. .@Konwinski_PO: Cieszę się z wygranej Demokratów w USA, bo to lepszy scenariusz dla Polski. @marcinfijolek pic.twitter.com/gJ3TnlMn0l — Graffiti_PN (@Graffiti_PN) November 4, 2026 The speaker of Poland’s parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is also the leader of one of KO’s junior coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), has clashed with the US ambassador to Poland twice this year over Czarzasty’s criticism of Trump. Today, Czarzasty shared and commented on a social media post by Trump, published in the wake of the Democrats’ victory, in which the US president showed an image of his signature red cap with the word “VETO” on it. “Where have I heard this before?” wrote Czarzasty, referring to the fact that Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills passed by parliament, where Tusk’s coalition has a majority. Czarzasty then went on to list a series of characteristics that he suggested both Trump and Nawrocki share, including “arrogance”, “lack of respect for women”, a “suspicious past”, “transactional exploitation of their position”, and “admiration for politicians with fascist tendencies”. Skąd ja to znam? Arogancja. Buta. Nieuzasadniona pewność siebie. Brak szacunku dla kobiet ( a to popchnę jakąś dwojga nazwisk, a to zakpię prymitywnie). Dziwna przeszłość. Instrumentalne traktowanie dziennikarzy. Pieniądze za spotkania. Transakcyjne wykorzystywanie funkcji.… pic.twitter.com/ryT2BMOZb2 — Włodzimierz Czarzasty 📚📖 (@wlodekczarzasty) November 4, 2026 Nawrocki has closely aligned himself with Trump. During last year’s Polish presidential election campaign, Trump invited Nawrocki for a private meeting at the White House. His then-homeland security secretary, Kristi Noem, visited Poland to endorse Nawrocki. Nawrocki himself has not thus far commented on Tuesday’s midterm election results. However, Marcin Przydacz, the head of the president’s International Policy Bureau, did address the issue in a social media post. “As predicted, in the US midterm elections voters decided on change,” wrote Przydacz. “Poland will continue its good cooperation with the US, because it is our ally, and collaboration is in our mutual interest.” Przydacz also added that the results were “a reminder for Tusk” that “no government lasts forever”. In Poland, too, “the moment will come when voters will decide on change – and it might be quite soon”, added Przydacz, in a nod to next year’s Polish parliamentary elections. Zgodnie z przewidywaniami w wyborach połówkowych w USA wyborcy zdecydowali o zmianie. Wcześniej wygrywali Republikanie, dziś Demokraci. Polska będzie kontynuować dobrą współpracę z USA, bo jest to nasz sojusznik, a kooperacja jest w naszym wspólnym interesie. O tym, kto sprawuje… — Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) November 4, 2026 Tusk’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, meanwhile, used the US election results to revive his long-running feud with Elon Musk, who is no longer part of the Trump administration but donated enormous amounts of money to support the Republicans ahead of the midterms. Last year, Musk and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio criticised Sikorski after he suggested that Musk had threatened Ukraine. In a post on his social media platform, X, Musk told Sikorski to “be quiet, small man”. On Wednesday, Tusk shared a screenshot of a tweet he had published last year, after Musk left the Trump administration, in which Sikorski wrote: “See, big man, politics is harder than you thought.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: International Commission of Jurists criticises takeover of Polish constitutional court
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) has criticised the takeover of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) by a group of government-backed judges. It says that the move “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”. However, the ICJ, a Swiss-based NGO led by judges, lawyers and academics from around the world, also chastised Poland’s opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, for his role in the crisis surrounding the TK, in particular his refusal to swear in judges elected by parliament. 🚨#Poland’s constitutional crisis must be resolved through the rule of law. The ICJ urges all authorities to respect judicial independence, follow lawful procedures, and comply with European court rulings. 🔗More information: https://t.co/NWmca9mpUx — ICJ (@ICJ_org) November 3, 2026 On Friday, eight judges who were elected to the TK this year by the government’s parliamentary majority effectively took over the tribunal. They announced that the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been suspended for failing to properly fulfil their duties. Meanwhile, large numbers of riot police were deployed outside the court, holding back protesters, including opposition politicians, and preventing Święczkowski and Sochański from entering the grounds. Święczkowski denounced the takeover of the court as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the tribunal’s remaining six judges, who, like him, were appointed under the rule of the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which brought the TK under its political influence. Nawrocki has likewise denounced the actions of the government-backed judges. In the early hours of Saturday, he dramatically forced his way into the court, where he clashed physically and verbally with the judges who had taken over the TK. During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court. The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026 In a statement on Tuesday, the ICJ expressed regret that the latest developments have “deepened the crisis over the tribunal”. It called on Polish “state institutions to seek solutions…that comply fully with the rule of law, including the principle of the independence of the judiciary”. The ICJ’s secretary-general, Santiago Canton, noted that Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of the eight TK judges elected by parliament this year. That “violates international standards and is contrary to the interim measures indicated by the European Court of Human Rights”, said Canton. In May, the ECHR issued an interim order for all judges elected by parliament to be allowed to serve on the court. However, that has been ignored by Nawrocki and Święczkowski, who argued that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision. The ICJ also noted that the roots of the crisis at the TK date back a decade, to the time when the PiS government took actions – including unlawfully appointing judges to the tribunal – that rendered the court illegitimate. “At the same time,” continued Canton, “the suspension of the president and vice-president of the tribunal without a fair and appropriate procedure established by law, carried out with the involvement of the police, contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary.” In its statement, the ICJ added that “criminal and disciplinary proceedings must respect all the guarantees of a fair trial and must never be used as a means to change [a court’s] composition”. Later on Tuesday, after the ICJ had issued its statement, the eight government-backed judges held their first general assembly, at which they moved forward with disciplinary proceedings against Święczkowski and Sochański. The justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, has also submitted six requests to the TK to lift Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution so that he can face charges for a range of alleged crimes relating to both his time as chief justice and his previous role as a senior prosecutor under the PiS government. Skierowałem do Trybunału Konstytucyjnego kolejny, szósty już wniosek o uchylenie immunitetu Bogdanowi Święczkowskiemu, dołączając go do pięciu wniosków przekazanych w piątek. Dzisiejsza sprawa dotyczy zakupu systemu szpiegowskiego Hermes w czasie, gdy pełnił funkcję Prokuratora… — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 3, 2026 The takeover of the TK has also stirred controversy among Polish legal experts. The issue has even caused an unprecedented split at the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a well-respected NGO. On Saturday, the HFPC’s management board issued a statement, signed by its president, Maciej Nowicki, saying that it “sees no clear legal basis” for the actions taken on Friday by the government-backed judges to suspend Święczkowski and take control of the tribunal. It warned that the situation “set a dangerous precedent” and “does not contribute to fixing the tribunal”. However, HFPC also made it clear that the crisis at the court dates back a decade and reiterated its view that Nawrocki “has no right to block or invalidate the election [of judges] by parliament”. That statement prompted six of the eight members of HFPC’s council – a separate body from the management board – to resign. Those to depart included a former chief justice of the TK, Andrzej Rzepliński, and a former deputy human rights commissioner, Hanna Machińska. Machińska announced their resignation in a social media post. She said that the reason for her decision had been the management board’s statement, “with which I disagree”. Speaking later to broadcaster TVN, Machińska said that “we believe that the legal basis [for the TK takeover] was clearly defined”. Poland’s government, including Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has also argued that the takeover of the tribunal was necessary to ensure that legally appointed judges can take up their seats and that the court’s legitimacy can be restored. However, on Tuesday evening, Tusk shifted to a more conciliatory tone, offering to hold a one-on-one meeting with Nawrocki to discuss the crisis around the Constitutional Tribunal and “try to find solutions that will protect Poland from any political upheaval”. World.title: Disputed Polish constitutional court holds first meeting after takeover by government-backed judges
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. The group of eight government-backed judges who last week took control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) have held a meeting at which they made a number of key decisions, including moving forward with disciplinary proceedings against the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski. However, the situation is mired in controversy and uncertainty. Święczkowski and the opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, do not recognise the judges who are now claiming control of the court, describing their actions as a “coup d’état”. Meanwhile, there are doubts as to whether today’s general assembly even had a valid quorum, given that the chief justice and six other judges appointed under the former government did not attend. PILNE: Zgromadzenie Ogólne Sędziów TK przyjęło, że kworum to osiem osóbhttps://t.co/SYEf9Ead3L — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 3, 2026 The meeting was called by Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who on Friday declared that Święczkowski and the deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been suspended for failing to fulfil their duties. Korwin-Piotrowska said that she herself, as the longest-serving judge on the court, was taking control. Large numbers of riot police were deployed outside the court, holding back protesters, including opposition politicians, and preventing Święczkowski and Sochański from entering the court. However, Nawrocki himself did enter the premises, where he clashed physically and verbally with Korwin-Piotrowska. For a general assembly of the TK to be valid, two thirds of the court’s judges need to be present. Normally, given that the tribunal has 15 positions, that would mean at least 10 judges being present. However, only eight judges attended today’s meeting. They were all appointed to the TK by the government’s parliamentary majority this year. But Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of them, meaning that their legal status has become disputed. The TK’s seven other judges, including Święczkowski and Sochański, were all appointed to the court under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under its political control, including by unlawfully appointing three judges. None of them attended Tuesday’s general assembly. Nevertheless, the eight judges present at the meeting, which was broadcast live for the first time in the TK’s history, decided that a quorum had been reached. They did so on the basis that three of the TK’s judges were not authorised to attend: Święczkowski and Sochański, because they are suspended, and Jarosław Wyrembak, because he inherited his position from one of PiS’s unlawfully appointed judges. That meant only 12 judges were authorised to attend, and two thirds of that number is eight, meaning that a quorum had been reached. Zgromadzenie Ogólne TK: JEST KWORUM! 👏 Według przedstawionej interpretacji liczy się je od 12 uprawnionych osób. 2/3 × 12 = 8. Prawo i matematyka.👏 pic.twitter.com/77v2ep9HbT — Pani Prezes 👠 (@PaniNaSzpilkach) November 3, 2026 Once that issue was agreed, the eight judges present proceeded to decide upon a number of key issues. First, they adopted a draft budget for the TK for 2027, something that Święczkowski had been unable to achieve, which was used as an argument for his ousting. Second, they drew lots to decide which of the TK’s judges would sit on disciplinary panels for Święczkowski and Sochański in relation to their suspension from the court. However, some legal experts have expressed doubt as to whether a legal quorum was established at today’s meeting. Ryszard Piotrowski, a prominent constitutional scholar, called the meeting “illegal”, reports news website Onet. Przemysław Rosati, the president of the Supreme Bar Council, also expressed his doubts. Obniżenie progu kworum na skutek zawieszenia prezesa i wiceprezesa otwiera puszkę Pandory. To jest mechanizm, który pozwala dowolnie obniżać kworum na Zgromadzeniu Ogólnym TK – wystarczy, że prezes zawiesi 10 sędziów i będzie mógł na Zgromadzeniu podejmować decyzję w trzy osoby.… — Marcin Matczak (@wsamraz) November 3, 2026 Święczkowski himself rejected the legitimacy of what he called a “social gathering”, saying that Korwin-Piotrowska is a “usurper” who has no right to call a general assembly at all, reported Polsat News. Shortly before the meeting at the TK, Nawrocki also met with the prime minister, Donald Tusk, for the first time since the crisis at the court broke out last Friday. They had convened at the presidential palace for a meeting of the National Security Council that Nawrocki had called before the TK crisis. During public remarks broadcast before the confidential meeting got underway, Nawrocki accused the government of “illegally taking over the Constitutional Tribunal”. He added that Tusk “bears full responsibility for…all these illegal actions”. Grubo! Karol Nawrocki do Tuska: „Pełną odpowiedzialność za wszystkie nielegalne działa w Trybunale Konstytucyjnym ponosi jeden człowiek, który jest obecny – premier Donald Tusk” pic.twitter.com/WMPnWTZIKt — chrzanik (@chrzanikx) November 3, 2026 Tusk and his government have argued that the source of the crisis is, in fact, Nawrocki’s refusal to swear in judges appointed by parliament, as he is required to do, and then Święczkowski’s resultant refusal to accept those judges onto the court. They also note that the TK has not been legitimate for a decade, since PiS unlawfully appointed judges and brought the court under its political influence. Speaking to broadcaster TVN on Tuesday before the general assembly, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said that the actions being undertaken by Korwin-Piotrowska are the only way “to rebuild the independence of the tribunal”. World.title: Poland has EU’s second-highest electricity prices accounting for cost of living
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland had the second-highest household electricity prices in the European Union in the first half of 2026 after adjusting for differences in the cost of living, new Eurostat data show. Prices in Poland were also among the fastest-rising in the bloc. Poland’s relatively high electricity costs reflect the country’s continued reliance on coal, which results in EU charges for carbon emissions, and its taxes and levies, which make up the largest share of household electricity bills anywhere in the EU. In nominal terms, Polish households paid €29.99 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh) for electricity in the first half of 2026. This was the seventh-highest price among the EU’s 27 member states and above the bloc-wide average of €28.32. Ireland (€38.71 per 100 kWh) had the highest prices, followed by Germany (€36.18) and Belgium (€35.75). The lowest costs were recorded in Hungary (€11.39), Malta (€12.68) and Bulgaria (€13.41). However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in the cost of living, Poland ranked second in the EU, at 41.12 PPS per 100 kWh. Only Romania had higher prices, at 46.89 PPS. The lowest prices when measured in PPS were recorded in Malta (13.75), Hungary (14.7) and Luxembourg (15.47). Poland’s electricity prices, in PPS terms, rose by 10.7% compared with the second half of 2025, which was the second-biggest increase in the EU after Finland. They were also up 17.6% compared to the first half of 2025, the fourth-largest rise in the bloc. One reason why electricity prices in Poland remain high is the country’s continued reliance on coal, which last year generated just over half of power, by far the highest proportion in the EU. Almost all coal used in Polish power plants is mined domestically and is among the most expensive in the world to extract. Additionally, burning it also produces high carbon emissions, which power generators must pay for under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS). These costs contribute to the high taxes and levies included in household electricity bills, which accounted for 39% of the final price in Poland in the first half of 2026. This was the highest share in the EU, ahead of Germany (23.6%) and well above the bloc-wide average of 18.6%. “In Poland, only one-third of our electricity generation is carbon-free. We have to pay for the rest – often dearly,” noted Polish energy journalist Jakub Wiech, commenting on the data. Without taxes and levies, the nominal price of electricity in Poland would have been just under €16 per 100 kWh, below the EU average of €20.27. However, Bartłomiej Orzeł of the Project Tempo think tank notes that electricity prices in Poland would, in fact, be even higher were it not for the huge state subsidies paid to support the unprofitable coal mining sector, which amount to billions of zloty a year but also shield end consumers from the full cost of extracting coal. He told news website Interia that mines actually sell coal to power stations at a price below the cost of extraction. Poland will from next month be the last remaining EU country still mining hard coal, after the Czech Republic – the only other producer – announced the closure of its last mine https://t.co/0sfMDQb19N — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026 According to Wiech, the high tax burden also reflects the costs of transforming Poland’s energy sector while continuing to support coal-fired power stations and the state budget. He says Poland needs “on the one hand, to fund the accelerated but delayed transformation and modernisation of the electricity sector; on the other hand, to maintain the fleet of coal-fired power stations; and thirdly, to contribute to the state budget”, which is struggling with persistently high deficits. Wiech expects, however, that politicians will come under pressure to reduce electricity bills ahead of next year’s parliamentary election. He says they may be tempted to “interfere with electricity bills” and that “it is therefore quite likely that certain charges (e.g. the distribution charge) will be reduced in 2027”. Komisja Europejska wrzuciła dane o cenach prądu za I półrocze 2026 roku i – boy, oh, boy – niesamowita jest to lektura. Na początek mocne uderzenie: w ujęciu standardu siły nabywczej polskie gospodarstwa domowe mają drugie najwyższe ceny prądu w całej Unii Europejskiej.… pic.twitter.com/yKvt5251i7 — Jakub Wiech (@jakubwiech) November 1, 2026 Energy prices and the wider energy transition have already become increasingly politicised this year, with the right-wing opposition criticising EU climate policies. The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, recently called for Poland to unilaterally withdraw from ETS, claiming that it treats “Poles as a cash machine for the absurd leftist climate policy of the EU”. Opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has twice attempted to call national referendums on rejecting EU climate policy, but in both cases his proposals were rejected by the more pro-EU government’s majority in parliament. Poland's right-wing opposition wants to withdraw from the EU Emissions Trading System, saying it makes Poles "a cash machine for absurd leftist climate policies"@PStrzalkowski explains what costs ETS really brings, and what prospects there are for reform https://t.co/UxpMWpG1pE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 4, 2026 However, when PiS was in power from 2015 to 2023, it recognised the need to move Poland away from coal and towards a mix of renewables and nuclear. Solar energy installations boomed under the PiS government, and the overall share of renewables in the energy mix rose from around 9% in 2015 to a record 29% in 2024. The current government has continued with PiS’s plans to shift towards nuclear and renwables. This year, Poland’s first offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea began generating electricity, with a number of other offshore projects set to follow. Poland’s national energy and climate plan, approved in June, envisages coal accounting for 0-5% of the energy mix by 2040. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). World.title: Polish journalist held at Ukraine border and handed three-year entry ban
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A prominent Polish journalist and commentator, Łukasz Warzecha, has been prevented from entering Ukraine and handed a three-year ban on crossing into the country. Warzecha, who is primarily associated with right-wing weekly Do Rzeczy, says he was told that the decision had been made for “security reasons”. Polish journalist Łukasz Warzecha was travelling to Kyiv on a study visit jointly organised by Poland’s @MieroszewskiPL Centre and the Ukrainian Institute @UA_Institute an institution affiliated with Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry. According to head of @MieroszewskiPL Dr Łukasz… https://t.co/Tawp2hEJ5u — Sławomir Dębski (@SlawomirDebski) November 2, 2026 Warzecha had been due to join a study visit to Ukraine for Polish journalists organised by the Mieroszewski Centre, a Polish state institution, and the Ukraine Institute, a Ukrainian public body affiliated with the foreign ministry. The head of the Mieroszewski Centre, Łukasz Adamski, revealed that the list of journalists attending the tour had been agreed between the two organisers and forwarded to the relevant Ukrainian state authorities, who previously raised no objection. However, on Monday afternoon, Warzecha announced on social media that he had been held at the Ukrainian border and told to wait in a room. The journalist remained there for over seven hours before being informed that he was banned from entering Ukraine for three years. Proszę państwa, oto miś. Miś jest bardzo grzeczny dziś. pic.twitter.com/aVEUnkGhM7 — Łukasz Warzecha (@lkwarzecha) November 3, 2026 Adamski revealed that his organisation had sought to intervene with the foreign ministries of both countries, but to no avail. Warzecha said on social media that he had been told the decision, which was issued by the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), was made due to “security reasons”. Adamski commented that, while he “recognises Ukraine’s sovereign right to decide whom to grant entry…restricting journalists’ work on state security grounds…creates fertile ground for unfriendly commentary”. At the time of writing, there had been no comment from the SBU regarding its decision to issue an entry ban against Warzecha. In his journalistic work, Warzecha has at times been critical of Ukraine, for example over its honouring of historical nationalist figures, and has called for a reduction in social benefits given to Ukrainian refugees in Poland. However, those views are within the Polish mainstream. Warzecha has also voiced support for Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. In February 2023, on the first anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion, he expressed satisfaction that Ukraine defended itself so effectively. However, Do Rzeczy, with which Warzecha has been associated for around a decade, has taken a tougher position on Ukraine. In 2024, its front cover warned of the “Ukrainisation of Poland”, a phrase often used by the far right to warn against the growing presence and influence of Ukrainians. OKŁADKA "Do Rzeczy" nr 35: Ukrainizacja Polski. Raport "Do Rzeczy" o groźnym procesie pic.twitter.com/SUYy1GhIat — DoRzeczy (@DoRzeczy_pl) August 25, 2024 Speaking to Do Rzeczy after the ban against him was issued, Warzecha said he had “wanted to confront my own views with open-minded politicians and opinion leaders in Ukraine. Unfortunately I was not given the opportunity to do so”. Ukraine’s decision was criticised by Andrzej Śliwka, an MP from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party. He asked if Warzecha had been banned “because he dared to criticise Ukrainian corruption, the confrontational policy toward Poland, and the distortion of history”. “One can agree with editor Warzecha or not, but such a decision demands explanations and a firm response from Polish authorities,” wrote Śliwka. At the time of writing, Poland’s government had not commented on the case. Polski dziennikarz, red. Łukasz Warzecha, otrzymuje od ukraińskich służb trzyletni zakaz wjazdu na Ukrainę. Dlaczego? Czy dlatego, że odważył się krytykować ukraińską korupcję, konfrontacyjną politykę wobec Polski i zakłamywanie historii? Można zgadzać się z red. Warzechą albo… https://t.co/JvuhLL9O8F — Andrzej Śliwka 🇵🇱 (@SliwkaAndrzej) November 2, 2026 Adamski said that the visit to Ukraine had been arranged specifically with the aim of “representing diverse editorial perspectives”. The Mieroszewski Centre last month arranged a similar visit for Ukrainian journalists to Poland. The aim was “to enable Polish journalists to gain direct knowledge of the situation in Ukraine, engage in conversations with representatives of various communities, and achieve a better understanding of the challenges facing Ukrainian society”, wrote Adamski. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing extensive military, humanitarian and diplomatic support. However, there have also been regular tensions between the two countries, in particular over their difficult shared histories. This year has seen the two sides clash over the unresolved issue of large-scale massacres during World War Two. World.title: Two-Michelin-Starred Austrian Chef Comes to Prague for Exclusive Dinner
World.content:
Prague’s Zlatá Praha restaurant will host an exclusive four-hands dinner bringing together two-Michelin-starred Austrian chef Andreas Döllerer and Maroš Jambor for one evening of contemporary fine dining.

The special collaboration will see the two chefs create a bespoke menu combining their individual culinary styles, seasonal ingredients and modern interpretations of gastronomy.



Based in Golling, Austria, Andreas Döllerer is one of the country’s most acclaimed chefs.

His restaurant, awarded two Michelin stars, is known for its distinctive approach to Alpine cuisine, which reinterprets traditional regional ingredients and culinary influences through contemporary techniques.

For the occasion in Prague, Döllerer will join forces with Maroš Jambor, creating a menu that brings together their respective approaches to fine dining.

The four-hands concept offers guests the opportunity to discover the work of both chefs through a single, specially designed dining experience.

The exclusive menu is priced at CZK 6,000 per person and includes a welcome drink and water. Guests can also opt for a wine pairing at an additional CZK 2,500 per person.

The event requires full prepayment. Reservations are available online.

World.title: American Man Suspected of Racist Assault at Prague’s Želivského Stop
World.content:
Police are investigating an alleged racist assault at the Želivského tram and metro stop in Prague’s Vinohrady district after an English-speaking man reportedly attacked a passerby and damaged his phone.

The suspect has since been identified, although police have not confirmed reports linking him to an American previously detained in Russia.

The incident took place on the morning of November 4 on Vinohradská Street, close to the Želivského stop.



According to the victim, an Arab man who has lived in the Czech Republic for several years, the confrontation began when a stranger started shouting racist remarks in public.

The man allegedly called for the deaths of Black people, Jews and Arabs.

The victim challenged the statements, telling the stranger that racist abuse and threats against people because of their background were unacceptable.

He then began recording the encounter on his mobile phone, fearing that the situation could turn violent.

“I started recording in case I was attacked—and, unfortunately, that is exactly what happened,” he later wrote in the Facebook group Vinohradská parta.

Footage of the confrontation shows the alleged attacker directing insults at the victim. At one point, he raises his phone and says, “Hello, Trump?” He also appears to threaten the other man with death before the confrontation turns physical.

The suspect then allegedly grabbed the victim’s mobile phone and threw it into the road. According to the victim, the device was struck by a passing truck. Although he managed to recover it, the phone was damaged.

The victim said he had reported the incident to the police and called on local residents to help identify the alleged attacker.

“I am dealing with this through the police, but the perpetrator has vanished. Let’s find him and show that violence and racism have no place in Vinohrady,” he wrote.

The original Facebook post containing the video was subsequently removed. The victim suggested that its disappearance might have been connected to the ongoing police investigation.

Police later confirmed that they were dealing with the case as a suspected criminal offence.

“We are handling the matter as a suspected criminal offense, and we have identified the suspect,” police spokesperson Eva Kropáčová told Czech tabloid Blesk.

Suspect reportedly linked to Russia

The investigation has also raised questions about the man’s identity.

The suspect could be an American citizen who previously faced criminal proceedings in Russia and was ordered by a Russian court to undergo compulsory psychiatric treatment.

The man was reportedly accused of assaulting a female police officer in Russia. Media reports have also suggested that he holds Czech citizenship and travelled from Russia to Prague, where he is currently staying.

However, Czech police have not confirmed whether the individual identified in connection with the Želivského incident is the same American mentioned in the Russian case.

World.title: Fake Apartments and Rental Scams Target Students in Prague, Police Warns
World.content:
Prague Police are warning about a growing number of rental fraud cases, with international students among the groups most vulnerable to fake apartment listings.

Leaving everything you know behind is the beginning of a new chapter. A new city. A new home. A new life.

After weeks of searching, you finally have the keys to your apartment in Prague. You climb the stairs of an old building, find the right door and put the key in the lock.

But it will not turn.

You try again. You check the address, look at the contract and reread your messages with the supposed landlord. Everything appears to be in order, except for one crucial detail: the apartment was never yours.

The address exists. The building is real. But the home you thought you had rented does not belong to you.



A Key That Opens No Doors

Rental scams are an increasingly common problem in Prague’s housing market, with international students among the most vulnerable targets.

Many arrive in the Czech capital without knowing the local rental system or having the opportunity to view an apartment in person. The pressure to secure accommodation before the start of the academic year can also make students more vulnerable to convincing-looking fraudulent listings.

In 2024, Czechia ranked ninth among Erasmus+ programme countries for incoming higher education mobility, with approximately 17,000 arrivals, according to Dům zahraniční spolupráce.

The growing number of international students in Prague has also increased the demand for accommodation.

Charles University, one of the city’s largest universities, has repeatedly warned prospective international students about rental fraud. According to its 2024 annual report, the university had 11,455 international students from 139 countries, out of a total student population of more than 54,000.

The university advises students to watch out for several warning signs, including requests for deposits or other payments before a contract has been signed, pressure to finalise an agreement unusually quickly, and landlords who claim to be living abroad.

Offers that appear too good to be true should also raise suspicion.

Three Cases, Nearly CZK 150,000 in Losses

Prague Police have also warned about an increasing number of rental fraud cases involving apartments.

In mid-January, three cases were reported within a single week, resulting in combined losses of nearly CZK 150,000, or approximately €6,000.

One increasingly common method involves collecting deposits from prospective tenants for apartments that are never actually rented out. In some cases, fraudsters advertise properties they do not own or have no right to rent.

Police have not ruled out the possibility that the suspect involved in the January cases may be connected to other similar incidents, meaning the number of victims could be higher.

For international students, the consequences can be particularly severe.

Police and universities therefore advise prospective tenants to verify listings carefully, avoid sending money before signing a contract and viewing the property, and remain cautious of unusually cheap offers or landlords who create pressure to pay quickly.

World.title: Frank Sinatra & Friends Live Show Brings Las Vegas Classics to Prague
World.content:
Fans of Frank Sinatra and the golden age of Las Vegas entertainment will have a chance to relive the era this Christmas.

The Frank Sinatra & Friends Live Show will arrive in Prague on December 29, bringing its tribute to the legendary Rat Pack to O2 Universum.



Originally created to mark the 100th anniversary of Frank Sinatra’s birth, the international production features Stephen Triffitt, George Daniel Long and Mark Adams, three performers known for their portrayals of Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin and Sammy Davis Jr.

All three previously starred in the acclaimed The Rat Pack Live from Las Vegas, performing for nearly a decade in London’s West End. Their careers have also taken them to stages alongside prestigious orchestras, including the BBC Concert Orchestra, the London Symphony Orchestra and the Amsterdam Metropole Orchestra.

The trio has since taken the show around the world, recreating the music, humour and spontaneous stage chemistry that made the original Rat Pack one of the most celebrated entertainment acts of its time.

The Prague performance will feature more than just the three leading artists. They will be joined by the Golddiggers, a trio of singers and dancers whose costumes and choreography add a classic Las Vegas revue atmosphere to the production. The show will also feature a special appearance by Nancy Sinatra.

The programme includes classics such as Fly Me to the Moon, My Way, New York, New York, Strangers in the Night and more.

Combining live music, comedy and theatrical performances, the production aims to recreate the atmosphere of the Las Vegas stages that defined an era of popular entertainment.

World.title: Beyond the Usual Order: 7 Prague Restaurants to Try on Bolt Food
World.content:
We all have one. The order you place without thinking. Same app, same five restaurants, same Thursday night. It is comfortable, it is reliable, and if we are honest, it is getting a little boring.

Prague’s food scene runs far deeper than the places that sit at the top of your feed. Tucked into Nusle side streets, Dejvice corners and the quieter end of Libeň are small kitchens with loyal regulars, big personalities and dishes worth crossing the river for.

The good news? You don’t have to cross the river. They deliver.

So as the evenings get darker and the sofa gets more convincing, we asked Bolt Food to point us towards the city’s hidden gems. Here are seven places worth adding to your rotation, from an Aussie pub in Vinohrady to a half-metre pizza you will want to share (or not).

For when you miss home (or just miss a proper pie).

On Vinohradská street sits what bills itself as Prague’s only Australian restaurant. The menu reads like a trip home: a whole section of beef, chicken and vegetarian pies, a chicken parmy, a proper schnitty, fish and chips and, for the curious, a bag of “Skippy’s” kangaroo jerky. Wash it down with something from the Aussie bottled beer list.

Can’t make it in? The pub classics travel well. A pie with a side of gravy and the match on your own TV is a very respectable Sunday.

What to order: the Melbourne Pie, the most popular pie on the menu, with gravy on the side. Or the chicken parmy if you’re properly hungry.

For when you want a pizza with a story

During lockdown, half of Prague learned to bake sourdough bread. Pavel Petřík went for sourdough pizza instead. A few years, many pop-ups and one very customised electric cargo bike later (yes, it carries a pizza oven that runs hotter than 500°C), Pizza Bici has a permanent home on Na Hutích in Dejvice.

The shop is decorated with vintage bike parts, and the sourdough dough is the star. The menu is short and built for takeaway, with picks like the Marinara Sprint, a Mortadella & Pistachio and the spicy Diavola Express.

What to order: the Mortadella & Pistachio for something different, the Diavola Express if you like heat.

For flatmate nights and office Fridays

Yes, a second pizza place. But this one comes with a measuring tape. Near the Žluté lázně riverside, Pizza Napoletana bakes proper Neapolitan pies with San Marzano tomatoes and Sabelli mozzarella, plus its party trick: pizza by the half metre.

The mezzo metro pizzas are built for sharing (in theory). The Margherita D.O.P. comes with buffalo mozzarella, the Parma version with cured ham and rocket, and the Carciofara is a little wild, with artichoke cream, salsiccia, pistachios and crispy potato. Prefer your own pizza? The classic 32 cm range covers everything from marinara to quattro formaggi.

What to order: one half-metre pizza for the table, and a slice of torta caprese for whoever wins the last piece.

For when Tex-Mex just won’t cut it

If you have ever lived somewhere with a serious taco scene, you know the difference between Mexican food and “Mexican-style” food. Alambre, on náměstí Bratří Synků in Nusle, is firmly in the first camp: modern, casual and easy to love.

The menu leans into the dishes taco lovers actually crave: tacos al pastor, loaded nachos, quesadillas and the house namesake, Alambre Camarón. The real headliner, though, is the birria de res quesadilla.

What to order: birria quesadilla, no debate. Add tacos al pastor if you are feeding two.

For the hummus purists

Supermarket hummus is fine. Then you try the real thing and there is no going back. Tahini on Nuselská street calls itself the home of legendary hummus, with Israeli roots and, lately, an Indian twist on the menu too.

Start with the classic hummus plates, topped with anything from falafel and chicken shawarma to sabich or a full shakshuka. Feeling adventurous? Check the daily specials, which have included mezze spreads and hummus with lamb kebab.

What to order: Hummus & Sabich, or Hummus & Shakshuka on a slow weekend morning.

For proper American-style burgers

Out on Sokolovská, far from the burger joints of the centre, Hadog has quietly built a loyal following. Expect 200 g beef patties, melted cheese and sauces with a kick, like the Chipotle burger with smoked cheese, bacon, BBQ sauce and chipotle mayo.

Smash fans should head straight for the Smash Juicy Lucy, one of the most popular picks on the menu. Any burger can come in a gluten-free bun or with a Beyond Meat patty, so nobody gets left out of burger night.

What to order: the Smash Juicy Lucy, or the Chipotle burger if you like it smoky.

For when you can’t decide which Asian cuisine you’re craving

Small room, fresh flowers on the tables, big portions. Bento Café & Bistro in Holešovice is the kind of neighbourhood spot locals tend to keep to themselves.

The menu hops across Asia, from Vietnamese bun nem to udon noodles and a red curry ramen that regulars rave about.

It is exactly what you want on a grey November evening: something warm, something fresh and a little bit of everything. Don’t skip the homemade passion fruit lemonade.

What to order: red curry ramen on a cold night, bun nem when you want something lighter.

Your new rotation, sorted

An Aussie pie in Vinohrady, sourdough from a cargo-bike pizzaiolo, birria in Nusle and ramen in Holešovice. Prague tastes a lot more interesting once you look past the usual suspects.

All seven are available on Bolt Food, so the only thing you need to explore is the app. Open Bolt Food, search for any of the names above and try something new this week. Your Thursday-night order will forgive you.

Ordering more than once a week? Then Bolt Plus is worth a look. Members get free delivery from Bolt Food partner restaurants marked with a “+” in the app, on orders over 170 CZK (delivery discount up to 45 CZK), with no promo codes to type in.

The membership covers your rides too, with cashback on every trip and up to three free cancellations a month. And the first month is free, so you can test it on your new hidden gems before deciding.

World.title: Your Next Weekend Away: A Renovated Neoclassical Spa Hotel in Františkovy Lázně
World.content:
The hotel, housed in a 1918 Neoclassical building, has renovated its rooms, restaurant and wellness facilities.

Františkovy Lázně, one of the Czech Republic’s best-known spa towns, is offering visitors a renovated accommodation option following an extensive refurbishment of the five-star Harvey Spa Hotel.



Located in the town’s park zone in western Bohemia, the hotel occupies a Neoclassical building dating back to 1918. The recent renovation covered all 105 rooms, as well as the lobby, corridors and restaurant, updating the interiors while retaining the building’s historic character.

The hotel is situated next to the town’s central park, within walking distance of its main colonnades and mineral springs. Glauber I Spring, one of the town’s traditional drinking cure springs, is located in the nearby park by Swan Lake.

Spa treatments and wellness facilities

The hotel offers a range of spa treatments, massages and wellness services, alongside a relaxation pool, sauna and fitness centre. Guests can combine traditional spa procedures with recreational facilities during both short stays and longer wellness programmes.

The property also features a restaurant and BAR 222, which has been renovated as part of the wider refurbishment.

Františkovy Lázně has a long history as a European spa destination, attracting visitors with its mineral springs and therapeutic treatments for more than 200 years. In 2021, the town became part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing Great Spa Towns of Europe, together with ten other historic spa towns across seven countries.

Its compact centre, historic colonnades and landscaped parks make it suitable for visitors looking to explore the town on foot. The surrounding region also offers opportunities for walking and excursions beyond the spa centre.

Staying at Harvey Spa Hotel

The hotel has 105 air-conditioned rooms, all refurbished as part of the renovation. You can book your room directly here.

Its location directly beside the central park also means guests can reach the town’s main spa attractions on foot, while the hotel’s five-star facilities make it possible to combine accommodation with spa treatments and wellness services during the same stay.

World.title: Christmas Charity Market Brings Gifts and Flavours from 50 Countries to Prague
World.content:
One of Prague’s best-known international Christmas events will return this November, bringing gifts, food and traditions from nearly 50 countries under one roof.

The DSA International Christmas Charity Market 2026 will take place on Saturday, November 21, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. at the Hilton Prague Atrium.



Organised by the Diplomatic Spouses Association (DSA) together with Prague’s international diplomatic community, the annual event allows visitors to shop for Christmas gifts while supporting Czech charities.

Stalls representing almost 50 countries will offer a wide range of products, including traditional sweets and spices, gourmet food, handicrafts, toys, glassware, porcelain, cosmetics, fashion accessories and Christmas gifts.

The market is held under the patronage of First Lady Eva Pavlová and regularly attracts thousands of visitors.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by DSA Prague (@dsa_prague)

Shopping for a Good Cause

The event also serves as one of the DSA’s main fundraising initiatives. Money raised through the market, together with donations and sponsorship, is distributed to Czech charitable organisations.

Earlier this year, the association awarded a total of CZK 1.32 million to 16 Czech charities during its Grant Award Ceremony in June.

According to Jana Muranska, President of the Diplomatic Spouses Association, the event is intended to bring together Prague’s international community while supporting organisations working across the Czech Republic.

“The Christmas Charity Market is about much more than Christmas shopping,” Muranska said. “It brings together people from across the world in a spirit of friendship, generosity and solidarity.”

World.title: “The Art of James Cameron” to Open at Prague’s Municipal House in April 2027
World.content:
An exhibition dedicated to filmmaker James Cameron will open at Prague’s Municipal House (Obecní dům) on April 29, 2027, bringing more than 300 items from the director’s archive to the Czech capital.

Titled The Art of James Cameron, the exhibition will run until October 3, presenting original drawings, paintings, film props, costumes and photographs connected to the Canadian director’s career.



Visitors will also see examples of 3D technologies developed or adapted for his films, alongside multimedia installations and audio commentary in which Cameron discusses his artistic development.

The collection will cover several decades of his work, from early sketches and storyboards to the technical innovations behind some of Hollywood’s biggest productions, including The Terminator, Aliens, Titanic and the Avatar films.

Although Cameron is widely recognised for pushing the technical boundaries of cinema, the exhibition will focus on his work as an artist and illustrator.

His creative process often began with pencil and paper, with early sketchbooks filled with imaginary creatures, futuristic machines and visions of distant worlds.

The exhibition will also explore recurring themes in his films, including the threat of nuclear catastrophe and the risks posed by rapid advances in artificial intelligence.

Cameron made his feature-film debut in 1981 with the action horror film Piranha II. His breakthrough came three years later with The Terminator, followed by Aliens in 1986. He continued to explore science fiction with The Abyss (1989), which follows a team investigating an underwater encounter with an unknown form of life.

His biggest success at the time came with Titanic (1997). The film won 11 Academy Awards and became one of the highest-grossing productions in cinema history, earning approximately $1.85 billion worldwide.

World.title: Equippers Church Budapest: A growing international community bringing nations together in the heart of Budapest
World.content:
Have you heard of Equippers Church Budapest? This relatively young international church community has recently found a permanent home in the city and celebrated its fifth anniversary with a special event.

Today, Equippers is a thriving and rapidly growing community, representing more than 40 nationalities. Ukrainians, Russians and Belarusians worship side by side, while people from Mexico, Sweden, South Africa, China, Argentina, Jamaica, Jordan, New Zealand, Brazil, Pakistan, India, the United States and, of course, Hungary come together to pray for one another, their countries and their personal lives.

Over the years, Equippers has become a meeting place for international students and young people, while remaining open to people of all ages. The church is known for its contemporary worship music, welcoming atmosphere and modern approach to sharing the Gospel, which also takes its message out into the streets and public squares of Budapest.

Photo: Equippers Church Budapest

Despite its relatively short history, the church has already become a mission base for visiting teams from every continent. One of its upcoming highlights is a 50-member Christmas carol choir from the United States, currently preparing to perform at several Christmas markets across Budapest and bring a festive musical experience to the city.

The global Equippers movement originated in Auckland, New Zealand, while its flagship European church, with a congregation of more than 1,500 people, is located on the outskirts of London in the United Kingdom.

The name Equippers reflects the movement’s vision: to equip people for life as God intended, guided by the teachings of Scripture. In Budapest, the church is led by Pastor Miro Toth, who originally comes from Slovakia, together with his wife, Marta, and their son, Tobias. The pastoral family is committed to building a lasting community and making a positive contribution to life across the city.

Photo: Equippers Church Budapest

With its new permanent venue, Equippers Budapest now holds both morning and evening Sunday services. Alongside its weekly gatherings, the church is developing smaller communities, outreach initiatives and programmes aimed particularly at connecting with young people, both in Budapest and elsewhere in Hungary.

Equippers is about more than Sunday services. It is about building relationships across cultures, supporting one another, sharing faith and offering hope and practical help to those who need it.

In an increasingly international city like Budapest, Equippers Church aims to provide a place where people from different backgrounds can find a sense of belonging, build friendships and discover a shared spiritual home.

“At the heart of our church is a mission to be a community that welcomes God’s presence, welcomes people, and sees lives transformed for the better. Whether you are visiting the city, staying here temporarily for work or studies, or have made Budapest your home, we would be honoured to welcome you to one of our Sunday services.”

World.title: V4 summit: Leaders all back EU enlargement but remain divided over Ukraine
World.content:
The leaders of the Visegrád Group (V4) have called for closer regional cooperation and further European Union enlargement, while acknowledging differences over the war in Ukraine. Hungarian President András Baka said Hungary wanted to become an even more committed partner in building a common Europe following the country’s recent elections.

The four countries – Hungary, Slovakia, Czechia and Poland – met in Trenčín, Slovakia, on 4–5 November for a summit marking 35 years since the V4 group’s establishment. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also attended the talks, which covered EU enlargement, European security, Ukraine and energy prices.

EU enlargement must be based on merit

Speaking after the meeting, Baka said EU enlargement was in the interests of all four Visegrád countries. He described it as a strategic investment in Europe’s peace, security, stability and prosperity.

However, he stressed that accession must be based on merit, with all candidate countries assessed consistently according to the same principles and conditions. This approach, he said, served the long-term interests of both the candidates and the EU.

Slovak President Peter Pellegrini also backed enlargement, identifying Montenegro as the most advanced candidate country. He suggested that it could join the EU in 2028 if it fulfils the necessary requirements.

The V4 leaders are open to changes to the accession process, Pellegrini said, but want to preserve the right of existing member states to veto decisions on admitting new members.

Photo: Anadolu Agency

Different views on Ukraine, but winter support pledged

The war in Ukraine remains an area of disagreement within the V4. Czech President Petr Pavel called for a strong and united European response and said sanctions against Russia should remain in place.

Pellegrini urged a diplomatic solution to the conflict, with the EU playing a role in efforts to achieve peace. The leaders also agreed that their countries would continue helping the Ukrainian population through the winter, including by providing technical equipment and supporting the construction of shelters.

Baka highlighted the rights of the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia, western Ukraine, as a key issue for Hungary. He welcomed steps that could help enforce minority rights and restore trust between Hungary and Ukraine.

Energy prices and industry among key concerns

Affordable energy and the competitiveness of European industry were also major topics at the summit, Index writes. Pellegrini warned that high energy prices threatened industries that play a significant role in the V4 economies and called for swift EU action.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki argued that the V4 countries should have a greater influence on EU decision-making. Despite their differences, he said, they should work together to represent their shared economic interests. He also called for EU climate policy to take account of member states’ energy security and economic needs.

Baka said close relations between neighbouring countries were particularly important in the face of Europe’s security challenges. He expressed hope that V4 cooperation would continue to contribute to the development and security of both the region and the wider continent.

The summit was also an opportunity for the four presidents to reaffirm their commitment to continued cooperation, even where their positions do not fully align.

World.title: Air France-KLM to operate 48 weekly flights from Budapest this winter!
World.content:
Air France and KLM will maintain their usual capacity on routes connecting Budapest with Paris and Amsterdam during the winter 2026–2027 schedule. The two airlines will operate a combined 48 flights a week between the Hungarian capital and the two major European aviation hubs until the end of March.

The winter timetable began with the switch to winter time and runs until late March 2027. Across its wider network, the Air France-KLM Group is increasing capacity on several routes to meet demand during the winter travel season, AIRportal.hu reported.

Air France expands routes to the Americas and Asia

Air France will operate around 725 flights a day to nearly 170 destinations in 78 countries. Compared with the previous winter season, the airline is increasing capacity by 6% to North America, 3% to South America, 2% to Asia and 5% to the Iberian Peninsula.

Its North American network will include 23 destinations. Las Vegas will remain available throughout the winter, while flights to Orlando will operate daily during peak periods. The airline is also increasing services to the Caribbean, where demand is growing.

Brazil is a particular focus in South America. From 21 December, Air France will operate two daily flights to Rio de Janeiro and one daily service to Fortaleza.

In Asia, the airline is adding capacity to popular winter holiday destinations, including Phuket, Bangkok and the Maldives. It is also introducing daily flights between Paris and Kilimanjaro in Africa during the winter season.

Free high-speed Wi-Fi on regional flights

Passengers will also benefit from free, high-speed Wi-Fi on Air France’s regional services during the winter season.

Another development concerns the airline’s La Première first-class cabin. The exclusive product, available on Boeing 777-200ER aircraft, will also be bookable on flights to Boston, Houston and New York-Newark.

If you missed it: Bomb threats on European skies: at least 10 flights alerted this week

KLM strengthens its European network

KLM will operate flights to 164 destinations in 64 countries from its Amsterdam hub during the winter schedule. Alongside North America and the Caribbean, the Dutch airline is placing greater emphasis on routes in northern and southern Europe.

Minneapolis and San Diego will remain part of its winter network, while services to Panama City, São Paulo and Curaçao will increase.

In Europe, KLM is adding flights to Rovaniemi and Kittilä in Finnish Lapland, as well as to Basel and Florence.

Budapest retains 48 weekly connections

For passengers travelling from Budapest, the main news is that the group is maintaining its established flight capacity.

Air France will operate 22 flights a week between Budapest and Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport, while KLM will provide 26 weekly services between Budapest and Amsterdam Schiphol.

Together, the airlines will therefore offer 48 flights a week connecting the Hungarian capital with two of Europe’s major aviation hubs until the winter timetable ends in late March 2027.

World.title: Budapest suburban rail disrupted this weekend: H8 shortened, H9 suspended
World.content:
Budapest’s suburban railway services will be affected by maintenance work on 7 and 8 November, with changes to the H8 Gödöllő and H9 Csömör HÉV lines, the Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) has announced.

Budapest suburban railway undergoes maintenance

According to their statement, the H8 service will operate on a shortened route, running only between Kerepes and Gödöllő. Meanwhile, the H9 line will be suspended entirely on Saturday and Sunday.

Replacement buses will operate to help passengers reach their destinations. Buses marked H8 will run between Örs vezér tere and Kerepes, while H8A services will connect Örs vezér tere with Cinkota. An express replacement bus, designated H8E, will also operate between Örs vezér tere and Kerepes. However, it will not stop at Kistarcsa hospital station.

Passengers travelling on the suspended H9 line will be able to use replacement buses running between Örs vezér tere and Csömör. These services will bypass Cinkota alsó station. The changes are expected to affect weekend journeys for commuters and other passengers using the suburban railway network.

Updated timetables and journey-planning information are available through BudapestGO and the BKK website at bkk.hu/menetrendek.

World.title: Bomb threats on European skies: at least 10 flights alerted this week
World.content:
Another wave of bomb threats targeting passenger aircraft across Europe has disrupted air travel, with more than ten flights reportedly affected on Thursday alone. Several planes were diverted to airports other than their intended destinations, while security teams launched inspections following emergency landings.

Bomb threats on European flights all week

Among the affected services was an Aer Lingus Airbus A320 travelling from Dublin to Rome. The aircraft declared an emergency and diverted to Évreux military airbase in northern France, landing around 90 minutes after take-off. The plane was escorted by fighter jets.

A passenger told the Daily Mail that panic broke out on board after the diversion. The pilot initially cited a technical issue before passengers were informed after landing that the aircraft had received a security threat, which was reportedly not considered credible.

A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome also received a bomb threat. Italian fighter jets escorted the aircraft to Rome’s Fiumicino Airport, where it landed at its original destination. In Romania, nearly 200 passengers were evacuated from a Wizz Air aircraft arriving from Milan at Bucharest’s Henri Coandă International Airport. The Romanian Intelligence Service’s bomb disposal team began examining the plane.

A LOT Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Brussels was also inspected. No explosive device was found, after checks were carried out by crew members during the flight and by specialists following its arrival. Czech police reported threats against four aircraft heading to Prague. Authorities assessed the threats as low-risk, but confirmed that bomb disposal experts would examine the planes after landing.

Diversions across the continent

According to the BBC, other affected flights included Wizz Air services from Milan to Warsaw and Bucharest, Ryanair flights from Copenhagen and Madrid to Sofia, and a London-to-Sofia Ryanair service diverted to Plovdiv.

The latest incidents follow a series of similar alerts earlier in the week. On Tuesday, at least seven European flights reportedly received bomb threats, prompting diversions and security checks. Several airports were temporarily closed amid the disruption. The wave began on Monday, when a Wizz Air flight from London to Sofia was diverted to Budapest. A Hungarian Gripen fighter jet escorted the aircraft during its landing.

Although some earlier threats were later found to be false, the repeated incidents have prompted heightened security measures across several countries. Authorities continue to inspect affected aircraft, while the alerts have raised concerns over the safety and reliability of European air travel. So far, no explosive devices have been confirmed in the incidents described in the reports.

World.title: Were you misled too? Major Hungarian supermarket chain fined millions – Here’s what went wrong
World.content:
Hungary’s Competition Authority (GVH) has fined supermarket chain Auchan HUF 68.9 million (approximately EUR 190,000) for misleading customers in several coupon promotions. The retailer failed to clearly communicate important conditions for obtaining and redeeming the discounts, including minimum spending requirements and the need for an active loyalty card.

The GVH launched an investigation in July 2025 into Auchan’s promotional campaigns advertised between 1 April 2024 and 12 February 2025. The authority found that the company had omitted significant information about the conditions attached to its coupons in three separate campaigns, each lasting around a month.

The promotions were advertised through various channels, including national television. However, customers were not adequately informed that they had to meet additional requirements to receive or use the discounts.

Minimum spending and loyalty card requirements were not clear

According to the GVH, the omitted information included the fact that customers had to spend a certain amount to qualify for the coupons. They also needed an active Auchan loyalty card, known as the Bizalomkártya, to redeem them.

The authority also identified differences between the rules applying to Auchan’s hypermarkets and supermarkets, as well as varying redemption periods for individual coupons. These conditions were not communicated clearly enough in the promotional materials.

The GVH’s Competition Council concluded that Auchan had engaged in unfair commercial practices and imposed a fine of HUF 68.9 million.

The authority took several mitigating factors into account when determining the penalty. Auchan admitted the infringement, waived its right to appeal and committed to improving its compliance programme.

The GVH also reminded businesses that whenever they advertise coupons or other discounts, they must provide consumers with complete information about the conditions for obtaining and using the offers at the same time as the  itself.

Auchan now fully owned by Hungarian investor

The fine comes as Auchan Hungary has undergone a major ownership change. In June 2026, the company became fully owned by businessman Dániel Jellinek’s Indotek Group.

Indotek had acquired a 47% stake in Auchan Hungary in November 2024, following a lengthy process lasting around four years. The deal already gave the Hungarian investor full management control of the retailer, despite the remaining ownership stake.

Auchan operates 25 stores across Hungary.

World.title: Hungary’s former central bank governor Matolcsy to remain in detention due to concerns about destroying evidence
World.content:
Hungary’s former central bank governor, György Matolcsy, will remain in custody after a Budapest court upheld his pre-trial detention in a major investigation linked to the National Bank of Hungary (MNB) scandal.

The court cited concerns over potential flight, interference with evidence and the risk of further criminal activity, while also pointing to Matolcsy’s extensive personal and business connections.

Matolcsy’s connections and his son’s disappearance

The Budapest-Capital Regional Court rejected appeals against the detention of Matolcsy and two other suspects, confirming the initial ruling that ordered their imprisonment until 23 November 2026. In its decision, the court highlighted the suspects’ financial resources, international mobility and alleged close family, economic and personal relationships as factors increasing the risk of them becoming unreachable by authorities.

The concerns are further heightened by the whereabouts of two alleged members of the suspected group, who are currently abroad at unknown locations. They are identified as Ádám Matolcsy, the former central bank governor’s son, and György Stofa. International arrest warrants have reportedly been issued for both individuals. The court argued that the extensive network of relationships surrounding the suspects could facilitate their escape or allow them to influence the investigation indirectly.

Evidence destruction fears deepen the investigation

The court also expressed serious concerns about potential interference with evidence in the ongoing MNB investigation. According to its statement, investigators are still analysing substantial quantities of seized electronic data and documents, identifying additional individuals and conducting witness interviews. Further questioning of existing suspects may also be necessary.

The court said concrete circumstances supported the risk of evidence being compromised. Investigators reportedly discovered documents connected to the criminal proceedings within the interests of one suspect, while circumstances suggesting the possible destruction of evidence had also emerged. The investigation has additionally uncovered documentary evidence, witness statements, audio recordings and transcripts, as well as IT data concerning the creation and alleged backdating of documents.

Why Hungary’s court rejected the bail

The court ruled that neither bail nor house arrest with electronic monitoring would sufficiently protect the investigation. According to the judges, restricting a suspect’s physical movements would not prevent indirect communication, electronic contact or attempts to influence witnesses and evidence through other individuals. A contact ban was also deemed insufficient, given that the full circle of people potentially involved in the proceedings remains unknown.

Matolcsy’s former position as central bank governor and his previously unblemished criminal record were not considered sufficient to eliminate the risk of reoffending. The court pointed to his suspected informal leadership role within an organised group, alongside long-established economic and personal relationships, as grounds for maintaining detention.

The ruling does not constitute a finding of guilt. The investigation into the MNB scandal remains ongoing, with authorities continuing to examine the alleged financial misconduct and the potential involvement of further individuals.

World.title: Hungary’s Magyar government ends Orbán-era subsidy programme for Republika Srpska
World.content:
Hungary’s new government has stopped a 2026 agricultural machinery spubsidy programme reserved exclusively for Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Serb-majority entity, Republika Srpska. The scheme was part of a EUR 100 million support package announced by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Milorad Dodik in 2022, but its future – and the fate of the remaining funds – remains unclear.

Subsidy programme that Viktor Orbán started ends now

According to Radio Free Europe’s Balkan Service, the Progressus Foundation, which administered the programme in Republika Srpska, announced on 16 October that it was suspending the latest grant call after the new Hungarian government halted its funding.

The call, launched on 13 March 2026, was open for only five days due to exceptionally high interest. A total of 1,025 applications were submitted from Republika Srpska and the Brčko District. Farmers could have received grants ranging from EUR 2,500 to EUR 25,000, but applicants will now be informed that the call has been cancelled.

Neither the Hungarian government nor the Central European Economic Development Network (CED), which managed the programme on Hungary’s behalf, had explained the decision or clarified whether the funding could resume by the time Radio Free Europe published its report.

More than EUR 28 million already spent

The programme was announced in 2022 by then Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and Milorad Dodik, at the time the president of Republika Srpska. Although the wider package was worth EUR 100 million, at least EUR 28 million had been spent on agricultural machinery, equipment and tools by the end of the first two rounds in 2022 and 2023.

Farmers in Republika Srpska contributed an additional EUR 12.9 million of their own money, bringing the total value of purchases to more than EUR 39 million. In total, 1,959 projects were approved.

The scheme did not provide farmers with cash grants directly. Instead, they could apply for support to purchase machinery and equipment manufactured exclusively in Hungary, provided they covered at least 30% of the investment themselves. They also had to pay Bosnia and Herzegovina’s 17% import VAT.

Farmers left disappointed as questions remain

Some farmers had already set aside their own money for the latest round. Slaviša Simojlović, a farmer from Bijeljina, told Radio Free Europe that he had secured around EUR 8,000 for new machinery and expected the foundation to return the money he had invested if the programme was cancelled.

The president of Republika Srpska’s Association of Agricultural Producers, Stojan Marinković, said farmers were disappointed, particularly after benefiting from the first two rounds.

However, the programme’s economic purpose has also been questioned. Admir Čavalić, a professor at the Faculty of Economics in Tuzla, told Radio Free Europe that the scheme was not a conventional development grant, as farmers could only buy Hungarian-made products and had to contribute their own money. He argued that it could also be viewed as a way of promoting Hungarian exports.

The end of an Orbán-Dodik partnership?

The programme was part of broader economic and political cooperation between Orbán and Dodik, which included a EUR 126 million loan from Hungary’s state-owned EXIM Bank to Republika Srpska in 2022, as well as planned energy and infrastructure investments.

Dodik left the entity’s presidency in 2025 after a final court ruling sentenced him to one year in prison and barred him from holding public office for six years.

The cancellation of the 2026 agricultural programme marks another change in Hungary’s relationship with Republika Srpska following the change of government in Budapest. However, it remains unknown what will happen to the unspent portion of the original EUR 100 million package or whether any of the other planned projects will continue.
