While the ICJ has no means of enforcing its decisions, a ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would heap more international pressure on its military junta and be seen as justice for hundreds of thousands of Rohingya.

Legal experts are closely watching the verdict from the ICJ, which rules in disputes between countries, for clues as to how the court might rule in the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.

Myanmar has always denied carrying out a genocide against the Rohingya, arguing its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

The crackdown by the Myanmar military and Buddhist militias forced hundreds of thousands of Rohingya to flee to neighboring Bangladesh, bringing with them harrowing accounts of gang rape and mass executions.

More than 1 million Rohingya still live across the border in Bangladesh, in the world’s largest refugee settlement.

‘Collective conscience’

During hearings on the case in January, Gambian Justice Minister Dawda Jallow told the court the Rohingya had suffered “the most horrific violence and destruction one could imagine.”

“It is not about esoteric issues of international law. It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings,” said Jallow.

“The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction,” added the minister.

Gambia brought the case to the ICJ under the terms of the UN Genocide Convention, which allows any state to sound the alarm if it suspects genocide is being committed.

The alleged violations of the convention “are a stain on our collective conscience and it would be irresponsible to pretend that it is not our business,” Jallow said.

Myanmar retorted at the hearing that the allegations were “unsubstantiated.”

“Emotional language and blurry factual pictures are not a substitute for a rigorous presentation of facts,” said Ko Ko Hlaing, a minister in the President’s Office.

In a previous hearing in 2019, then-de facto civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi herself addressed the court, housed in the iconic Peace Palace in The Hague.

The Nobel peace laureate said the case risked reigniting the crisis that led to the Rohingyas’ expulsion and there was no “genocidal intent” behind the crackdown.

Aung San Suu Kyi, 81, will not be attending the verdict, however. She has been detained in Myanmar’s capital Naypyitaw since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.

The ICJ has already made one ruling in this case, ordering Myanmar in 2020 to “take all measures within its power to prevent the commission of all acts” described by the Genocide Convention.

These acts included “killing members of the group” and “deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part.”

ICJ judges also threw out a challenge to its jurisdiction by Myanmar, ruling that it did have the power to decide on the genocide question.

The ICJ is not the only court looking into possible crimes against the Rohingya.

In 2024, the chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, also based in The Hague, asked judges for an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s junta chief Min Aung Hlaing over alleged crimes against humanity.

A case is also underway in Argentina, under the principle of universal jurisdiction, the idea that some crimes are so heinous they can be heard in any court.

World.title: China’s Myanmar Policy at Crossroads After 5 Years of Failure
World.content:
China’s Myanmar policy rests on a central assumption: that the military remains the country’s decisive political and military force. That assumption may have been valid in previous eras, but Myanmar’s post-coup reality demonstrates Beijing has overestimated the military while underestimating the revolutionary movement that has emerged since 2021.

The revolutionary forces factor

Throughout Myanmar’s civil war since 1948, and again after the 1988 pro-democracy uprising, successive revolutionary movements have failed to establish dominance, leaving most of the country in control of the military. Beijing has shaped its Myanmar policy accordingly, viewing the military as the guarantor of stability in an otherwise fractured nation.

Yet Myanmar after the 2021 coup bears little resemblance to either of those earlier periods.

The political and military balance has shifted dramatically. The Kachin Independence Army (KIA), Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), Arakan Army (AA), Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), and Chin and Karenni resistance forces have emerged as formidable military actors capable of seizing and controlling large swaths of territory.

Even the Karen National Union (KNU), weakened by decades of internal splits and defections since the 1990s, has regained momentum, recapturing numerous military bases and inflicting significant losses on regime forces.

Meanwhile, armed resistance has spread into the Bamar-majority heartland, posing an unprecedented challenge to central rule.

The National Unity Government (NUG) and its People’s Defense Forces (PDFs) have emerged as a major parallel authority, reinforced by cooperation with ethnic armed organizations.

China’s Special Envoy for Asian Affairs Deng Xijun has reportedly warned the United Wa State Army (UWSA) that the NUG will never be a genuine rival to Myanmar’s military. That judgement has historical precedent. Revolutionary movements that emerged after 1948 ultimately failed because of military and political mistakes coupled with weapons and funding shortages. Likewise, the National Coalition Government of the Union of Burma (NCGUB) and the All Burma Students’ Democratic Front (ABSDF), which emerged after the 1988 uprising, never threatened military dominance.

Beijing has calculated that the NUG and PDFs will follow suit and collapse.

But today’s realities point in the opposite direction. Plagued by systemic corruption, declining battlefield effectiveness and shrinking troop numbers, the military has lost support among the Bamar majority amid growing public revulsion over its war crimes against civilians.

Resistance movement: Past and present

The post-1988 NCGUB enjoyed political leadership but little organizational structure on the ground. By contrast, NUG networks extend deep into local communities.

Meanwhile, the ABSDF lacked the strength to operate effectively in Myanmar’s heartland and depended on ethnic armed organizations for refuge. Today’s PDFs and Spring Revolution forces operate independently across Sagaing, Mandalay, Magwe, Bago and Tanintharyi regions, also pushing into Ayeyarwady Region and conducting urban guerrilla warfare in Yangon.

Their military expansion has been matched by broad support among rural Bamar communities. Ethnic armed organizations, meanwhile, increasingly credit PDFs and other Spring Revolution groups with contributing to their own battlefield successes. That combat strength is supported by a centralized command chain and disciplined organization. Battlefield setbacks and defections in 2025 barely dented the movement’s momentum and never matched the mass desertions seen within the Myanmar military in recent years.

While resistance forces still face constraints in weaponry and logistics, by historical standards they remain well equipped.

Also, while the NCGUB and ABSDF were bound by ideology, the link between the NUG and PDF is institutional and operational.

While the NCGUB and ABSDF subsided into political opposition groups within five years, the NUG and PDF remain a formidable military force — arguably the strongest and most expansive resistance movement in modern Myanmar history.

As such, China’s assessment that the NUG and its armed wing are not a serious rival to the military no longer reflects realities on the ground. In today’s Myanmar, it is impossible to understand the conflict without including the NUG and PDF in the equation.

Democracy and China’s concerns

If Beijing has underestimated the military significance of revolutionary forces, it also remains wary of their political agenda — particularly their commitment to democracy.

Yet democracy is hardly an alien concept in China. During its own revolutionary era, the Chinese Communist Party described its struggle as a “people’s democratic revolution” and promoted Mao Zedong’s concept of a “New Democracy.”

The fight against military dictatorship naturally carries democratic aspirations. But that does not mean importing a Western political model wholesale, nor would such a model be easily transplanted.

Myanmar’s revolutionary forces recognize the critical importance of relations with neighboring China. After all, long-term economic engagement with Beijing was also a cornerstone of National League for Democracy (NLD) government’s foreign policy.

New alliances

Chinese pressure has sidelined two major ethnic political and military alliances, namely the Federal Political Negotiation and Consultative Committee led by the UWSA and the tripartite Brotherhood Alliance. Yet new revolutionary coalitions have emerged.

One is the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF), which brings together the NUG and major armed organizations including Kachin, Chin, Karen and Karenni forces. Another is the Spring Revolution Alliance (SRA), which unites anti-regime forces that emerged after the coup. Both alliances pursue political and military objectives, and coordination between them appears to be steadily improving.

The Arakan Army — which controls most of Rakhine State and remains the biggest thorn in the regime’s side — is forging deepening ties with both groupings.

The trajectory of once-isolated resistance organizations is thus becoming increasingly interconnected, gradually evolving into a broader political and military bloc. These organizations are indispensable not only to achieving peace and nationwide stability, but also to safeguard long-term China-Myanmar relations and Chinese interests in the country.

Weaknesses of revolutionary forces

The resistance continues to suffer gaps in institutionalization, chain of command, logistics and weapons supply, and unification. Yet these are offset by substantial public support, a reputation largely unstained by atrocities, and high internal morale.

Most revolutionary groups also refrain from the systemic corruption that characterizes regime rule. Those who do profit from drug trafficking or online scam operations remain exceptions rather than the norm.

Close public scrutiny and critical supporters generally ensures that revolutionary misrule is generally harder to conceal and easier to correct. Myanmar’s military, by contrast, exhibits many of the opposite traits and has also repeatedly failed to unite the country’s ethnic communities or deliver lasting stability.

China’s Myanmar policy vs Myanmar’s reality

Taken together, these developments expose two fundamental errors in China’s reading of post-coup Myanmar.

While Beijing justifiably views the military as a key actor in Myanmar’s future, it overestimates its ability to achieve stability in the face of an increasingly entrenched and unified armed resistance. A military-centric policy no longer reflects a landscape transformed since the 2021 coup.

The second error lies in the timing of Beijing’s intervention. China moved to shore up the regime as Min Aung Hlaing faced mounting pressure from battlefield defeats, economic crisis and growing dissent within the military.

Had Beijing waited for his removal before backing the regime, more pragmatic figures may have taken the military helm.

Instead, China’s hasty support strengthened hardliners around Min Aung Hlaing while sidelining moderates and internal critics. In effect, Beijing’s scramble to preserve the military prolonged the rule of a failing strongman. Desperate to salvage his diminished authority and prestige, Min Aung Hlaing has vowed to reclaim all territory lost to revolutionary forces. As such, the civil war looks set to escalate rather than ease.

China’s policy has yielded gains for the regime, most notably by pressing ASEAN countries to reengage with Naypyitaw. But it has come at the cost of entrenching Naypyitaw’s hardliners, the root cause of instability.

The generals’ flawed policies and spiraling military spending have opened the door to economic collapse and poverty, while systematic corruption has fueled narcotics trafficking and online scam networks.

Despite China’s support, they have failed to achieve the military, political, and economic stability that Beijing craves.

Time for a policy shift?

Recent developments suggest Beijing may already be reassessing its Myanmar strategy. While China remains Myanmar’s largest foreign investor, new investment in fiscal 2025-26 fell to just US$ 158.2 million. Large-scale Chinese investment and lending failed to materialize even after the junta rebranded as a pseudo-civilian government in April.

Meanwhile, China’s Special Envoy Deng Xijun has broken off from frequent visits to Myanmar, where he has not been seen since March. Likewise, Chinese Ambassador Ma Jia, who regularly met Min Aung Hlaing and senior regime officials after taking up her post in August 2024, last met the junta chief in Naypyitaw on April 6, 2026.

The Chinese Communist Party regularly evaluates its policy outcomes. As pragmatists, Chinese leaders place considerable emphasis on results.

In Myanmar’s case, Beijing’s objective remains unchanged: stability. Yet stability remains elusive even as China’s core interests — including Belt and Road development and multibillion-dollar border trade — continue to face severe disruption. Under such circumstances, Beijing cannot afford to proceed with the status quo. While China’s core aim in Myanmar is unlikely to change, its strategic assumptions and methods must adapt.

Thet Htar Maung is a political analyst.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Jordan Focus on Security, Trade and Regional Stability
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Jordan discussed regional and global security challenges, as well as ways to expand bilateral cooperation during talks between President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and King Abdullah II Bin Al Hussein in Astana on Nov. 5, reported Akorda.

Tokayev described the Jordanian king’s official visit as a sign of the strong ties of friendship, mutual respect and solidarity between the two countries.

“Jordan is a time-tested and reliable partner of ours in the Arab world. In recent years, our cooperation has gained new momentum. We highly value the strong political dialogue between us, which is maintained at various levels,” Tokayev said.

He noted that the previous year had marked an important milestone in bilateral relations, with reciprocal high-level visits and the signing of a joint statement and numerous agreements between government agencies and business representatives.

Tokayev emphasized Kazakhstan’s commitment to implementing the agreements and expanding cooperation in areas of mutual interest. He described economic engagement as a key driver of bilateral relations and pointed to opportunities to strengthen cultural and humanitarian ties through academic and scientific exchanges and tourism.

The president also highlighted the countries’ shared approaches to international and regional issues and praised King Abdullah II’s contribution to strengthening bilateral ties and bringing the two nations closer.

Tokayev commended Jordan’s role in promoting peace and stability in the Middle East and beyond, as well as the king’s initiative to launch the Aqaba Process more than a decade ago.

“Kazakhstan highly values the Aqaba Process. It is a great honor for us to co-host the first meeting in this format in Central Asia,” Tokayev said.

He said the summit’s focus on artificial intelligence security was particularly timely and expressed confidence that it would present the Central Asian region’s perspective and give fresh impetus to joint efforts to promote peace and security.

King Abdullah II thanked Tokayev for the warm welcome and said the two countries shared longstanding relations, mutual respect and a commitment to strengthening peace and stability.

“As you mentioned, last year’s exchange of visits gave a significant boost to bilateral relations. We intend to continue implementing the agreements reached and expand cooperation in key areas, including trade, investment, tourism, technology and defense,” he said.

King Abdullah II also expressed appreciation for Kazakhstan’s role in organizing a new round of Aqaba Process meetings, describing the initiative as evidence of the two countries’ shared commitment to addressing regional and global security challenges.

He reaffirmed Jordan’s interest in expanding cooperation with Kazakhstan on regional security and countering terrorism and extremism.

State honors highlight Kazakhstan-Jordan ties

The two leaders also exchanged state awards in recognition of their efforts to strengthen ties between Kazakhstan and Jordan.

Tokayev presented King Abdullah II with Kazakhstan’s Order of Al-Farabi, citing his contribution to strengthening friendship between the two countries.

Tokayev noted that the award is named after the renowned Eastern philosopher whose legacy continues to inspire generations.

“Al-Farabi holds a special place in the hearts and minds of the entire Arab world. His enduring ideas of wisdom, harmony and unity continue to unite our cultures. We highly appreciate your tireless efforts to support these noble values. It is especially symbolic that you have become the first recipient of this order. I consider this a historic event,” Tokayev said.

King Abdullah II, in turn, presented Tokayev with Jordan’s highest state honor, the Order of al-Hussain ibn Ali, as a sign of respect and political trust between the two countries.

Tokayev thanked the king for the award, describing it as a symbol of the strong friendship and mutual respect between the two nations.

“It is a great honor for me to receive the highest award of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan. This order bears the name of the founder of your noble dynasty. His legacy, based on honor, faith and dedication to his people, continues to inspire many generations,” Tokayev said

He added that he viewed the award not only as recognition of his personal achievements but also as a testament to the close and strengthening ties between Kazakhstan and Jordan.

World.title: Narxoz Conference Explores Central Asia’s Path to Stronger Regional Cooperation
World.content:
ASTANA – Central Asia’s role in shaping global governance, strengthening regional cooperation and advancing sustainable development was the focus of an international conference hosted by Narxoz University on Nov. 4 in Almaty, the university’s press service reported.

The Mind for Peace conference examined how education, academic diplomacy and regional partnerships can contribute to peace, justice and stronger institutions.

The conference brought together representatives of diplomatic missions, international organizations and academia to exchange views and explore common approaches to regional and global issues.

Opening the event, Narxoz University President Kanat Kozhakhmet said the conference was taking place amid major geopolitical and technological changes.

He emphasized that peace, stability and mutual trust are essential not only as political priorities but also as conditions for sustainable development.

Kozhakhmet also reaffirmed Kazakhstan’s support for multilateral cooperation and the central role of the United Nations in international affairs.

Anara Dutbayeva, an adviser to the representative office of Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry in Almaty, highlighted the importance of a coordinated regional voice and the development of C5+ cooperation, a format connecting the five Central Asian countries with external partners. She pointed to opportunities for cooperation in trade, transport connectivity, artificial intelligence regulation and water management.

Dutbayeva also emphasized the importance of peaceful and inclusive societies, access to justice and accountable institutions. Achieving these goals requires cooperation among governments, international organizations, universities and civil society, she said.

European Union Ambassador to Kazakhstan Aleška Simkić highlighted the importance of advancing regional cooperation through the C5+ format. She expressed hope that Central Asian countries would eventually achieve a level of integration that could support the establishment of supranational institutions.

According to Simkić, such a body could facilitate the EU’s engagement with the region as a whole, rather than requiring separate negotiations with individual countries. It could also help address issues related to legal frameworks, cooperation and logistics.

Su Fangqiu, China’s consul general in Almaty, described the conference as timely amid major global transformations. He linked discussions on global governance to four initiatives proposed by Chinese President Xi Jinping: the Global Development Initiative, Global Security Initiative, Global Civilization Initiative and Global Governance Initiative.

Su Fangqiu highlighted Central Asia’s growing international standing, Kazakhstan’s achievements over the past 35 years and expanding cooperation between China and the region. He pointed to the China-Central Asia mechanism, established three years ago, as a framework for strengthening regional cooperation and building a closer community with a shared future.

Participants also explored the possibility of establishing a U.N. University presence in Central Asia, particularly in Kazakhstan. The proposed initiative could support research, education and expert dialogue on global governance, sustainable development and emerging technologies.

Conference sessions examined C5+ cooperation in public administration, water management, energy, climate, digital connectivity, artificial intelligence and human mobility. Another track focused on the universities’ role and academic diplomacy in promoting international dialogue and peace.

Aizhan Smailova-Schmidt, Director of the Institute for Global Dialogue and Multilateral Studies, emphasized that education and critical thinking underpin peace and effective institutions.

She highlighted investment in education, youth leadership and international exchanges as contributions to a more peaceful and sustainable future, describing the conference theme as an expression of Central Asia’s shared responsibility.

The conference also featured a youth program that allowed students and emerging professionals to discuss regional challenges through BirliNk C5+, a Narxoz initiative. The university also inaugurated its International Students Sustainability Club to expand student engagement in sustainable development.

World.title: Kazakh Prosecutor General Keeps Mangystau Military Investigation Under Oversight
World.content:
ASTANA – More than 300 people have been questioned and over 30 forensic examinations and expert studies have been conducted as part of an investigation into the deaths of servicemen during a military exercise in the Mangystau Region, the Prosecutor General’s Office press service reported on Nov. 5.

The Interior Ministry’s military investigative authorities are investigating the case, which remains under the special oversight of the Prosecutor General’s Office. Investigators have carried out a series of measures to establish the full circumstances of the incident.

Eight officials have been detained with court authorization on suspicion of negligence and violating navigation safety rules. They include the commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces’ Naval Forces, his first deputy and deputy for combat training, the commanders of two military units, a marine battalion and company, and the boat’s captain.

Investigative procedures are expected to be completed soon, after which participants in the criminal proceedings will be given access to the case materials.

World.title: Kazakhstan Advances in Global Digital Rankings as AI Infrastructure Expands
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has improved its standing in several international digital development rankings, with progress in artificial intelligence readiness and e-government services highlighting the country’s growing role in the global technology landscape.

According to Oxford Insights, Kazakhstan ranked 60th out of 195 countries in the 2025 Government AI Readiness Index, climbing 16 places from the previous year. The result reflects the country’s progress in preparing to introduce artificial intelligence into public administration and the economy.

A 2026 study by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) also placed Kazakhstan among emerging economies that outperform many comparable countries in AI readiness. However, the report noted that the country still needs to narrow the gap with advanced economies in areas such as regulation and innovation.

Kazakhstan has also maintained a strong position in digital government services. The United Nations E-Government Survey 2024 ranked the country 24th out of 193 countries for e-government development and placed it among the world’s top 10 countries in the Online Services Index.

Meanwhile, the 2025 Network Readiness Index, prepared with the participation of the Portulans Institute, ranked Kazakhstan 65th among 127 economies. The country performed relatively well in the impact of digital technologies and the quality of governance, while technological development remains an area requiring further investment.

These rankings point to a solid foundation for digital transformation, but sustaining progress will require greater investment in technology, research and development, and digital skills.

The potential applications of artificial intelligence extend beyond the technology sector. In energy, AI can help predict equipment failures and reduce downtime; in manufacturing, it can optimize production; in logistics, it can improve transport efficiency; and in agriculture, it can support more effective resource management.

Kazakhstan’s longer-term challenge is to move beyond exporting raw materials and energy towards developing products and services with higher added value. The ability to turn international interest in AI and computing infrastructure into domestic innovation, new jobs and competitive digital exports will determine the economic impact of the country’s digital transformation.

World.title: IFC Invests $ 33 Million to Modernize Agricultural Services in Central Asia
World.content:
ASTANA – Eurasia Group has secured $33 million in financing from the International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, to expand agricultural machinery distribution, maintenance and farmer training networks in Kazakhstan and the Kyrgyz Republic. The investment aims to increase agricultural productivity, strengthen food security and support an estimated 1,600 jobs across the two countries.

The financing will support the construction of four modern, energy-efficient service and distribution centers: three in Kazakhstan, in Astana, Pavlodar and Petropavlovsk, and one in Bishkek. The latter will be the Kyrgyz Republic’s first dedicated John Deere service center.

IFC is initially committing $18 million, including $15 million for Kazakhstan and $3 million for the Kyrgyz Republic. An additional $15 million may be made available to support the group’s further expansion in Kazakhstan.

Agriculture is central to Central Asia’s economies and rural livelihoods. However, many farmers continue to rely on aging, fuel-inefficient machinery that limits yields and raises operating costs. The project is expected to support around 1,600 full-time-equivalent direct and indirect jobs in local economies. It will also promote productivity through training and the transfer of new technologies.

Eurasia Group, a leading distributor and the region’s exclusive John Deere dealer since 2002, employs more than 600 people. By bringing service facilities closer to farming communities, the project is expected to reach around 1,700 additional farmers and improve their access to modern machinery.

“With IFC’s support, we will bring reliable equipment and maintenance closer to farmers while investing in skills, knowledge, and digital tools to help them succeed,” said Mustafa Sahin, president & CEO of Eurasia Group AG

“Modern farm services can help Central Asia’s farmers increase productivity, strengthen rural livelihoods, and better manage changing weather conditions. Through this partnership, farmers will gain better access to modern equipment, training, and support to improve yields and create jobs in rural communities,” said Wagner Albuquerque de Almeida, IFC’s regional industry director for manufacturing, agribusiness and services in the Middle East and Central Asia.

The project also includes climate and education initiatives. All four new service centers will be certified under IFC’s EDGE (Excellence in Design for Greater Efficiencies) green building standard. The certification is expected to help reduce energy consumption at the facilities by 20% and avoid an estimated 1,674 metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions annually.

World.title: Kazakhstan Strengthens Export Push with New Istanbul Trade Office
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has opened a QazTrade office in Istanbul to help domestic manufacturers enter the Turkish market and find business partners in other countries, Kazinform reported on Nov. 4.

The office aims to promote Kazakh products in Türkiye and expand export opportunities for local businesses. It will connect Kazakh manufacturers with Turkish companies, allowing potential buyers and distributors to view product samples, learn about producers, hold negotiations and establish direct business contacts.

The initiative is another step toward strengthening trade and economic ties between the two countries. The expansion of bilateral trade and investment was also discussed during a meeting between Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in Ankara on Oct. 28.

The opening comes as bilateral trade continues to grow. From January to September 2026, trade between Kazakhstan and Türkiye increased 62.1% from the same period last year, reaching $6.33 billion. Kazakh exports rose 91% to $5.3 billion, while imports from Türkiye totaled $1.03 billion. Türkiye is Kazakhstan’s fourth-largest trading partner by trade volume.

Yenisan Companies Group is QazTrade’s partner in the project. The Turkish company provided the office and exhibition space and will help connect Kazakh businesses with local companies and support joint initiatives.

The office features meeting rooms and a permanent showroom displaying products from Kazakh manufacturers. The selection includes flour, pasta, cereals, rice, lentils, peas, sunflower and flaxseed oil, powdered milk, camel milk products, traditional dairy products, honey, jam, confectionery, chocolate, beverages, syrups and tea, as well as clothing and accessories.

The exhibition showcases the potential of Kazakhstan’s food and light manufacturing industries.

The office will also explore opportunities beyond Türkiye. QazTrade and Yenisan Companies Group are considering ways to supply Kazakh products to Syria, Iraq, Iran and Afghanistan. Their plans include developing warehouse and terminal infrastructure, attracting investment and introducing new technologies.

One potential project is a logistics and warehouse complex to support exports. It could simplify the storage and distribution of goods, expand logistics options for Kazakh companies and make it easier for them to access markets across the region.

World.title: Kazakhstan Proposes UN Cybercrime Center in Astana
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan has proposed establishing a United Nations regional center to combat cybercrime in Astana, as representatives from 27 countries and international organizations gathered in the capital on Nov. 4-5 to discuss cross-border investigations, digital fraud and new tools to counter online criminal networks.

According to the Astana office of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), the proposed center would help authorities identify links between international criminal networks, analyze emerging threats and adopt new investigative technologies. It would also provide specialized training for law enforcement and judicial personnel and support joint cyber exercises.

The initiative has received support from UN leadership, while Kazakhstan and UNODC are developing the concept for the center. According to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the necessary infrastructure is already in place.

International cooperation against cybercrime

The International Conference on Combating Cybercrime, jointly organized by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs and UNODC with support from the International Criminal Police Organization (INTERPOL), brought together law enforcement officials, digital security experts, financial institutions and technology companies from Asia, Europe, Africa, the Middle East and the United States.

Addressing the conference, Minister of Internal Affairs Yerzhan Sadenov said criminal groups are increasingly using artificial intelligence, voice and image impersonation technologies, anonymous online platforms and cryptocurrencies to carry out fraud and conceal illicit transactions.

“Cybercrime knows no borders. A criminal may be in one country, the victim in another, and the stolen money can pass through bank accounts in several countries in a matter of minutes. That is why we need to act together,” said Sadenov.

He also proposed making the Astana conference an annual event to maintain regular dialogue among international partners.

UNODC Regional Representative for Afghanistan, Central Asia, Iran and Pakistan Oliver Stolpe welcomed Kazakhstan’s proposal for a regional center, noting that tackling cybercrime requires involvement beyond law enforcement.

“Cybercrime is evolving rapidly, and our response must evolve even faster. No country can meet these challenges alone. Success depends on cooperation among governments, law enforcement and judicial authorities, the private sector, academia, civil society and international organizations,” said Stolpe.

Expanding international legal cooperation

Kazakhstan has expanded its participation in international agreements governing cybercrime investigations and access to electronic evidence.

On Sept. 30, Kazakhstan ratified the Council of Europe’s Convention on Cybercrime, commonly known as the Budapest Convention, which establishes mechanisms for investigating cybercrime and obtaining electronic evidence across borders.

Kazakhstan was also among the first countries to sign the United Nations Convention against Cybercrime in October 2025, with ratification currently underway. Adopted by the UN General Assembly in December 2024, the treaty establishes a global framework for international cooperation in cybercrime investigations.

As of Nov. 4, the convention had 96 signatories, including the European Union, but only three countries – Azerbaijan, Qatar and Vietnam – had ratified it. The agreement requires 40 ratifications to enter into force.

Beyond these legal frameworks, Kazakhstan has stepped up cooperation with foreign law enforcement agencies to dismantle fraudulent call centers, including those operating abroad, investigate the illegal trade in personal data and trace stolen funds.

Authorities have also expanded cooperation with major technology platforms, including Google, Meta and TikTok, to identify online fraud schemes.

According to the ministry, measures taken over the past two years have contributed to a 21% decline in online fraud cases in Kazakhstan. Current prevention efforts focus on detecting scams before financial losses occur, improving digital literacy and protecting people particularly vulnerable to online fraud.

Cybercrime specialists demonstrate new technologies

The conference featured an international hackathon supported by INTERPOL, bringing together 38 specialists from 13 countries and representatives of 20 regional cybercrime units within Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Internal Affairs. Participants demonstrated technical solutions designed to detect cybercrime and assist investigations, while an accompanying exhibition showcased digital security technologies developed in Kazakhstan and abroad for law enforcement agencies and financial institutions.

The conference participants also adopted a joint statement outlining priorities for future cooperation, including faster exchanges of information and electronic evidence, improved investigative methods and specialized training. The statement also identified cybercrime prevention, technology sharing and stronger international partnerships as areas for joint action.

World.title: Beyond Memorandums: How Cyberport and Central Asia Are Building Startup Bridge
World.content:
HONG KONG – Hong Kong’s Cyberport is looking to deepen its ties with Central Asia as technology hubs in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan seek to connect their startup ecosystems with international markets, investors and partners. In two separate interviews with The Astana Times on Nov. 4 as part of Cyberport Venture and Capital Forum, Eric Chan, Cyberport’s chief public mission officer, and Shakhzod Narzullaev, head of product-market fit at IT Park Uzbekistan, outlined complementary approaches: Hong Kong offers an established technology and financial ecosystem, while Central Asian partners can help startups move across neighboring markets and build a wider regional presence.

Wholly owned by the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region government, Cyberport is home to more than 2,400 companies, including 30 listed companies, 10 unicorns and more than 500 AI and data science startups. Companies in its ecosystem have expanded into 36 markets worldwide.

Chan said the regulatory environment should make room for experimentation, particularly when technology companies work with financial institutions. Rather than simply telling companies what they cannot do, regulators should create controlled environments in which businesses can test new solutions and develop them in cooperation with established financial institutions.

AI is now driving a larger share of the hub’s work. Chan said Cyberport initially supported companies using generative AI to develop and fine-tune large language models, but the focus is increasingly shifting toward redesigning business processes.

“What I can see is that people are getting a lot more serious and the scale of those projects is a lot bigger,” he said, explaining that companies are moving beyond testing individual applications toward integrating AI into their operations.

“It’s not a matter of whether we should do it. It’s a must, it’s an imperative now,” Chan said.

He also stressed that AI adoption cannot be separated from risk management, cybersecurity, governance and ethical considerations, adding that AI should be more accessible beyond the business community. Through its “AI for All” initiative, it plans to reach students, parents, older people and disadvantaged communities.

“AI should be democratized for everyone. It should not be concentrated for just a few who can afford it,” Chan said.

Talent is another part of Hong Kong’s proposition. Chan pointed to the city’s 12 universities and what he described as the “free flow of talent,” funding and data.

“At the end of the day, we are grooming talent for the globe, not just for Hong Kong or any other countries,” he said, noting that international exposure can benefit both companies and specialists who eventually return to their home markets.

Cyberport’s Central Asia strategy: partnerships before offices

Cyberport’s engagement with Central Asia has developed through visits to technology hubs in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, Chan said. In June 2026, during Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee’s visit to Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, Cyberport signed memorandums of understanding with Astana Hub and IT Park Uzbekistan. The agreements cover technology transfer and cooperation in AI, fintech, smart city solutions and Web3, alongside support for overseas expansion and international market access. IT Park Uzbekistan and Cyberport are also discussing exchanges of projects and potentially investments, although a detailed plan has yet to be finalized, according to Narzullaev.

Chan said Cyberport does not intend to establish a permanent office in every market, preferring to build relationships with established local organizations.

“Since we may not be able to afford to have people in every country, every jurisdiction, what we do is we find a good partner, a good strategy partner,” he said.

The model is intended to be reciprocal. Cyberport wants to help Central Asian startups find investors, customers and business partners in Hong Kong, while its partners can support Hong Kong companies entering their markets. He believes international expansion is essential even for companies operating in an established ecosystem such as Hong Kong.

“Anyone has the aspiration to become the next unicorn. Not just the unicorn from Hong Kong, but the unicorn of the world. They have to operate in multiple markets,” he said.

For head of product-market fit at IT Park Uzbekistan Narzullaev, regional cooperation starts with a question of scale. Individual Central Asian countries can compete with one another to attract investment, he said, but presenting themselves separately to global markets can limit their visibility.

“Why can’t we present ourselves as Central Asia when we go to the global market? And why don’t we do it together?” he said.

The Central Asian Innovation Hubs initiative, developed with Kazakhstan, gives the countries a shared brand at international events, where they present startups together rather than compete for visibility. Narzullaev said Tajikistan was now joining the initiative. The partners have also developed a shared hub in China where founders can work, hold meetings and connect with local businesses. For startups entering an unfamiliar market, he said, having a place and a network to turn to can make a significant difference.

Narzullaev also challenged the assumption that Silicon Valley should automatically be the first destination for every startup seeking venture capital. Deep-science projects requiring very large initial investments may need to look to the United States, he said, but companies seeking more modest early-stage funding could find opportunities closer to home.

“If your startup needs $500,000, up to $3 million to $5 million, you can easily find this money in our regions,” he said.

In his assessment, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan currently have more venture capital available than investment-ready projects, making the region an attractive option for founders who are prepared to develop their products and build teams before approaching investors.

He was also refreshingly blunt about the practical value of memorandums. IT Park Uzbekistan has signed about 70 memorandums with organizations in different countries, he said, many of which risk becoming little more than documents and photographs without concrete obligations.

“We want to remove it altogether,” he said, describing the need to move away from symbolic agreements toward partnerships with measurable results.

IT Park Uzbekistan is therefore working on a proposed Global Growth Alliance that would bring technology parks, investors and other startup-support organizations into a functioning international network. He said the initiative could develop into an annual forum, with the first global summit planned in Uzbekistan in May 2027.

Narzullaev described the idea of working with international partners such as Cyberport as creating an “IT embassy of Uzbekistan” in Hong Kong, allowing Uzbek startups to have a local base without requiring IT Park to establish a separate office and maintain its own staff and infrastructure.

“It is not logical to go to all the countries and open an office there. But Hong Kong is an interesting region for us and we can be part of it,” he said.

He said rather than treating Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan as competing destinations, Narzullaev views them as interconnected markets within a wider regional opportunity.

“If Kazakhstan grows, Uzbekistan grows. If Uzbekistan grows, Kazakhstan grows,” he said.

For Narzullaev, that is ultimately the logic behind building partnerships across the region: a startup’s success in one Central Asian market can create opportunities in another, making the region more attractive to international companies and investors as a whole.

World.title: Russia declares Georgian opposition party Droa ‘undesirable organisation’
World.content:
Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office has designated the Georgian opposition party Droa an “undesirable organisation”, citing its “strongly anti-Russian stance”.

According to the Prosecutor General’s Office press service, Droa representatives oppose the normalisation of political, economic, cultural and humanitarian relations between Georgia and Russia. They also call for the reinstatement of visa requirements for Russian citizens and an end to direct flights between the two countries.

The Prosecutor General’s Office also accuses the party of considering Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) territories occupied by Russia, and of accusing Moscow of violating international law and Georgia’s sovereignty.

According to the Prosecutor General’s Office, Droa’s activities are aimed at “exposing links between Georgia’s ruling elite and Russia”, dismantling the country’s one-party system and promoting faster integration with the European Union.

The Russian authorities also criticised the party’s leader, Elene Khoshtaria, who accuses the ruling Georgian Dream party of pursuing a pro-Russian course and attempting to isolate Georgia from the European integration process.

The Russian Prosecutor General’s Office also says Droa supports the Ukrainian authorities and advocates Georgia’s accession to the “Carpathian Eight”, a regional and economic cooperation format for countries in Central and South-Eastern Europe linked to the Carpathian region.

Droa’s response

Droa, in turn, says Russia’s accusations concern precisely the positions and activities that the party considers part of its efforts to defend Georgia’s national interests.

The party listed six reasons why it believes the Russian authorities designated it an “undesirable organisation: recognising Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region as territories occupied by Russia; exposing secret links between Georgian Dream and Russia; working to end the one-party system in Georgia; supporting faster integration with the European Union; backing the Ukrainian authorities and cooperation between Georgia and Ukraine; and Elene Khoshtaria’s statements accusing Georgian Dream of pursuing a pro-Russian course and obstructing European integration.

“We are taking this opportunity, which we consider an honour, to reiterate: Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region are Georgia! Glory to the heroes! Ivanishvili’s regime is Russian! We will put an end to Ivanishvili’s Russian regime in Georgia! Georgia will become a member of the European Union and NATO!” the party said in a statement.

What is the “Carpathian Eight”?

The “Carpathian Eight” mentioned in this context is a new regional cooperation initiative unveiled by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at a summit in western Ukraine on 18 September.

The initiative aims to deepen trade, energy, logistics and security cooperation among countries in Central and Eastern Europe. Its members are Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria, Hungary and the European Union.

At the summit, Zelensky said the Carpathian region could play an important role in supplying energy to the European Union rather than serving merely as a transit corridor. He added that stronger regional cooperation could also help reduce Europe’s dependence on Russian energy resources.

According to Zelensky, the new format will strengthen ties between the countries and provide an additional, robust framework for cooperation at EU level.

About the Droa party

Droa (“It’s Time!”) is a pro-Western, pro-European opposition party in Georgia. Former State Minister for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration Elene Khoshtaria founded it in 2021.

The party’s political agenda focuses on Georgia’s European and Euro-Atlantic integration, strengthening democratic institutions, fighting corruption and countering Russian influence.

Droa is a vocal critic of Georgian Dream’s policies and accuses the authorities of pursuing a pro-Russian course and obstructing the country’s European integration.

Droa emerged as a political movement in March 2021 and registered as a political party in August that year. Before founding it, Khoshtaria left European Georgia, which she had joined after the 2020 parliamentary elections. Earlier, she had been a member of another opposition party, the United National Movement.

From 2007 to 2012, under the previous government led by Mikheil Saakashvili, Khoshtaria served as First Deputy State Minister of Georgia for European and Euro-Atlantic Integration. From 2016 to 2022, under the current government, she was a member of parliament.

In the 2024 parliamentary elections, Droa ran as part of the opposition Coalition for Change, which also included the Akhali and Girchi – More Freedom parties.

Droa has actively participated in anti-government protests and criticised decisions by Georgian Dream, including the suspension of the country’s EU accession process.

Elene Khoshtaria is currently in prison. In September 2025, authorities arrested her for writing “Russian Dream” on an election campaign banner belonging to Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze. In March 2026, a court sentenced her to one year and six months in prison for damaging property belonging to another person.

Elene Khoshtaria
