World.title: Election watchdogs warn that new amendments to Georgia’s Election Code will undermine trust in election results
World.content:
Three leading election watchdogs in Georgia – the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA), Transparency International Georgia and the International Society for Fair Elections and Democracy (ISFED) – have criticised the amendments to the Election Code proposed by the authorities.

The organisations say the proposed legislation would significantly restrict the right to challenge election results in court, weaken oversight of the electoral process and further centralise the powers of the election administration.

They identify the proposed change to the procedure for challenging the CEC’s final results protocol as one of the most problematic amendments. Under the new rules, the protocol could only be challenged in court to correct mechanical and technical errors.

“Such a restriction at the stage of finalising election results rules out disputes over systemic violations and their cumulative impact on the outcome,” the organisations warn.

They explain that the systemic nature and scale of electoral violations can only become apparent through a joint analysis of data from different polling stations and the electoral process as a whole. Therefore, the possibility of challenging results at individual polling stations cannot replace full judicial scrutiny of the final election results.

The organisations also criticise the abolition of mandatory recounts at five polling stations, selected at random by district election commissions. In their view, this change will reduce the transparency of the electoral process and further undermine public trust in the official results.

Another controversial amendment concerns the registration of election observer organisations. Under the proposed rules, the authority to make decisions on registration would rest solely with the chair of the election commission. The organisations warn that this approach increases the risk of subjective and politically motivated decisions, as other commission members, including representatives appointed by political parties, would no longer have a say in the process.

The watchdogs also raise concerns about shorter deadlines for registering election observers and media representatives ahead of the second round of voting. They believe this could hamper the work of electoral stakeholders, observers and journalists.

The organisations have also criticised changes to the rules governing the allocation of free airtime for election campaign advertising. They say the proposed restrictions could further widen the gap between the ruling party and opposition parties, undermining political pluralism.

GYLA, Transparency International Georgia and ISFED note that the authorities did not hold public discussions or consult interested parties before drafting the legislative initiative. According to the organisations, this runs counter to electoral standards set by the Venice Commission.

The watchdogs also view the initiative in the context of the legislative practices that have taken hold in Georgia in recent years. They say legislation is increasingly tailored to serve the interests of the ruling group, while mechanisms for public oversight are steadily weakening.

“Without effective oversight and accountability, the state loses public trust and, instead of protecting the common interest, becomes a system that serves narrow group interests,” the organisations say.

What exactly will change in the Election Code?

The ruling Georgian Dream party has introduced amendments to the Election Code in parliament. Under the proposed changes:

● District election commissions will no longer compile final election results: Precinct election commissions will send their final results protocols directly to the Central Election Commission (CEC), which will compile the definitive results.

● The grounds for challenging the CEC’s final results protocol will be restricted: A challenge will only be admissible if the protocol incorrectly or incompletely records data from precinct election commissions or final court rulings on electoral violations. Courts will reject claims based on any other grounds.

● Mandatory random recounts at five polling stations will be abolished: Previously, district election commissions had to recount the votes at five randomly selected polling stations within six days of the election.

● The deadline for finalising election results will be shortened: The CEC will have a maximum of 15 days to finalise the results of all elections. Previously, the deadline for parliamentary elections and elections in Tbilisi was 26 days.

● The deadline for financial reporting by the winning party will be shortened: A party that, according to preliminary results, receives the legally required number of votes will have to submit a report on its election campaign spending to the State Audit Office within five days. Previously, the deadline was 12 days.

● The consequences of financial violations by electoral contestants will change: If the State Audit Office identifies a serious violation that could have affected the election results, the CEC will be able to apply to the court and finalise the results without counting the votes cast for the party concerned.

● Broadcasters and newspapers will be prohibited from reallocating unused party advertising time: If an electoral contestant does not use its allocated advertising time, the broadcaster or newspaper will no longer be allowed to give that time to another party.

● Requirements for political advertising will be tightened: The name and number of the electoral contestant must appear on screen during the final second of an advert. Broadcasters will be prohibited from airing adverts that fail to meet this requirement.

Amendments to Georgia’s Election Code

World.title: Birth rate hits lowest level since 1950: why has number of newborns in Azerbaijan fallen by 42% in 10 years?
World.content:
Declining birth rates in Azerbaijan

In 2025, 95,875 children were born in Azerbaijan. According to the State Statistics Committee, this was the lowest annual figure since 1950. By comparison, 166,210 children were born in the country in 2015. This means the number of newborns fell by 42% over the decade.

The decline in births has continued this year. In the first half of 2026, the number of births fell by 10.6% compared with the same period last year. Between January and August, 56,404 children were born, while the birth rate dropped from 9.3 to 8.2 per 1,000 people.

However, opinions differ on how serious the situation is. Bahar Muradova, chair of the State Committee for Family, Women and Children Affairs, said the situation had not yet reached a critical level. Economist Natig Jafarli, by contrast, believes that “the country is heading towards a demographic catastrophe”. The key question is:

Is this a temporary decline, or are families genuinely choosing to have fewer children while the government fails to take the necessary steps to reverse the trend?

What do the statistics show?

Indicator 2015 2025 Number of births 166 210 95 875 Average number of children per woman 2,1 1,4 Urban areas 2,0 1,2 Rural areas 2,2 1,6 Natural population increase 111 513 36 041 Registered marriages 68 773 48 546 Divorces 12 764 20 675 Population aged 20–29 1.84 million 1.34 million

Source: State Statistics Committee

Azerbaijan’s population is still growing. As of 1 July 2026, it stood at 10,273,000. However, the rate of growth is slowing. To maintain a stable population in the long term, each woman needs to have an average of 2.1 children. Azerbaijan’s figure has remained below this level since 2016.

According to calculations by the State Statistics Committee, in 2025 the female population’s replacement rate stood at around 61% of the level needed to replace generations. Between January and August 2026, natural population growth amounted to just 16,213 people.

The decline in birth rates is also uneven. In urban areas, women have an average of 1.2 children, compared with 1.6 in rural areas. In the first half of 2026, the overall birth rate stood at 8.0 per 1,000 people. In the Mountainous Shirvan economic region, it reached 10.1, while in the Lankaran-Astara economic region it stood at 9.9.

A temporary decline or a long-term trend?

Two distinct demographic processes lie behind the falling birth rate.

The first stems from the consequences of the 1990s. In 1991, 190,353 children were born in Azerbaijan. By 2001, that figure had fallen to just 110,356. The smaller generation born during the years of war and economic crisis has now reached the age when people typically start families and have children. Over the past decade, the population aged 20–29 has fallen by around 27%. This factor alone would have been enough to reduce the number of births.

However, the impact of this demographic wave may begin to ease. Birth rates started rising again in the mid-2000s, and today the number of teenagers aged 15–19 is significantly higher than the number of young people aged 20–24: 817,000 compared with 672,000. In the coming years, more people will reach the age at which they typically start families.

The second process cannot be explained by demographic fluctuations alone: the average number of children per woman has fallen from 2.1 to 1.4. In other words, not only are there fewer potential parents, but they are also having fewer children. If the next generation maintains the current birth rate, the number of newborns may not increase significantly.

Marriage statistics also point to this trend. In 2013, Azerbaijan recorded 86,852 marriages, compared with just 48,546 in 2025. In the first half of this year, the number of marriages fell by a further 22.5%. Meanwhile, the average age at which women marry for the first time has changed little over the past decade, rising from 23.6 to 24.1. This suggests that the main change is not that people are marrying later, but that fewer marriages are taking place. It is worth noting that these statistics cover only officially registered marriages.

“A change in mindset” or housing problems?

Bahar Muradova, chair of the State Committee for Family, Women and Children Affairs, believes the decline in births has more to do with changing attitudes. She expressed confidence that the situation in Azerbaijan would not reach a critical level and compared the trend with developments in developed countries.

The statistics partly support this comparison. According to Eurostat, the average fertility rate in the European Union stood at 1.34 children per woman in 2024. However, Azerbaijan’s figure fell from 2.1 to 1.4 in just ten years. The country’s birth rate has therefore reached a level comparable to that of the EU, although household incomes remain significantly lower than in Europe.

Economist Natig Jafarli, by contrast, links the problem to economic factors. He identifies limited access to housing and high property prices as major causes. He also points to growing emigration among young people of reproductive age.

It is difficult to assess the impact of migration on birth rates. According to official statistics, 2,000 people left Azerbaijan to take up permanent residence abroad in 2025, while 3,400 moved to the country. However, these figures cover only registered cases of permanent relocation and do not capture the scale of emigration Jafarli describes.

Access to kindergartens is another problem. According to a report by the Cabinet of Ministers, only 38.7% of children aged one to five have access to pre-school education. The government’s target for 2026 is 50%.

What measures is the government proposing?

According to the State Social Protection Fund, mothers who are not in employment receive a one-off payment of 600 manats following the birth of a child. Between January and October this year, the fund awarded this benefit to 72,655 recipients.

Working parents who take parental leave receive a monthly allowance of 44 manats until the child reaches 18 months, and 28 manats from 18 months to three years. Women who give birth to and raise five or more children receive 140 manats per child. A total of 2,939 women receive this benefit.

Azerbaijan does not provide a universal monthly child benefit. Sociologist Uzeyir Shafiyev says the authorities abolished such payments in 2006 after introducing targeted social assistance. He proposes reinstating child benefits and revising the criteria for recognising families as large.

“It would make sense to lower the minimum number of children required for a family to qualify for large-family status from five to three,” the sociologist says.

Akif Nasirli, head of the Centre for Liberal Economists, also sees child benefits as a long-term investment in improving the demographic situation.

However, MPs have differing views on the issue. Gunay Agamali, an MP and chair of the Ana Vatan party, argues that child benefits could encourage a sense of entitlement among parents:

“When deciding to have a child, families should not expect the state to be obliged to provide them with something in return.”

Expert Ilgar Huseynli disagrees: “There is no reason to associate this with laziness.”

MP Razi Nurullayev also believes it is wrong to reduce the problem of falling birth rates solely to child benefits. He proposes a comprehensive programme that would include preferential mortgages and better access to kindergartens.

The government has yet to announce any plans to reinstate child benefits.

When will the effects become tangible?

The effects of falling birth rates are already being felt in the education system. In March, Ali Ahmadov, First Deputy Speaker of the Milli Majlis, told parliament that 1.5–1.6 million pupils attended schools in 2015. However, if the current trend continues, that figure could fall to one million within a few years. This would put around 50,000 teachers’ jobs at risk. At the start of the 2024–2025 academic year, Azerbaijan had 146,381 teachers. In other words, roughly one in three could be affected.

In the longer term, falling birth rates could also affect the labour market and pension system. The number of children under five fell from 851,000 in 2015 to 539,000 at the beginning of 2026. Jafarli believes that “pension funding will become one of the main items of state budget expenditure”. He warns: “If we do not take action today, it will be too late tomorrow.”

If the birth rate recorded between January and August continues through the end of the year, around 85,000 children will be born in Azerbaijan in 2026. By comparison, 90,280 children were born in 1950, which until recently was the lowest annual figure in the State Statistics Committee’s records.

Declining birth rates in Azerbaijan

World.title: Abkhazia’s ‘MP budgets’: why do ‘servants of the people’ receive $100,000 in public funds every year?
World.content:
A debate has erupted in Abkhazia over so-called “MP budgets”. Each of the 35 MPs receives 10 million roubles (around $100,000) from the state budget every year. For the past three years, parliament and the government have agreed to allocate this money to local infrastructure and maintenance projects in the constituencies where the MPs were elected.

The MPs themselves say the funds allow them to address problems in their constituencies quickly, such as repairing water pipes, paving rural roads and building playgrounds.

Those who oppose the scheme, however, describe it as outright corruption.

According to Daut Khutaba, head of parliament’s committee on legislation, MPs have reached an agreement with the government. Each MP can now decide how to spend up to 10 million roubles on construction and repair work in their constituency, consulting local voters or town and village administrations.

“Thanks to this agreement, over the past three years I have secured the construction of more than 2.5 kilometres of fencing in the Pitsunda Nature Reserve, at a cost of around 20 million roubles, as well as the laying of more than a kilometre of roads,” says Khutaba, who represents the Pitsunda constituency.

Abkhaz journalist Inal Khashig believes that giving individual MPs a separate budget for municipal spending will eventually turn parliament into a closed club and undermine the rotation of elected representatives:

“Under this system, any MP running in the next election has a significant advantage over other candidates. In voters’ eyes, they have already ‘invested’ in their constituency by repairing water pipes, laying gravel on rural roads or replacing light bulbs in street lamps.

“At first glance, this may seem like a worthy initiative: listening to voters and quickly addressing local infrastructure problems. But ultimately, this small handout – or, more accurately, an undisguised form of electoral bribery – will effectively give incumbent MPs a lifetime position, unless, of course, they decide not to stand for re-election.”

According to well-known blogger and civic activist Tengiz Jopua, the “MP budget” effectively violates the fundamental principles of parliamentarism and a democratic state governed by the rule of law.

“In a civilised country, the same rules apply to everyone. There are dedicated institutions people must approach, along with established procedures for submitting applications, reviewing them and allocating funds.

“The money allocated to [MPs] comes from the state budget. It is our money – taxpayers’ money – and belongs to the people as a whole, not to the state, prime ministers, presidents or MPs. That is why I believe this way of distributing public funds is wrong,” Jopua said, expressing his firm opposition to the scheme.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: ‘Factual inaccuracies and misjudgements’ – Georgian Foreign Ministry responds to European Commission report
World.content:
In response to the European Commission’s critical enlargement report, Georgia’s Foreign Ministry said the document contained factual inaccuracies and flawed assessments. It argued that these reinforced anti-Georgian narratives and narrowed the scope for constructive engagement between the European Union and Georgia.

The Foreign Ministry says the report wrongly describes the Georgian authorities’ actions as “state capture”. It argues that governing the country is the duty of a government elected by an overwhelming majority in a democratic society.

“It is concerning that the European Commission’s report, through factual inaccuracies and flawed assessments, reinforces anti-Georgian narratives. This, in turn, narrows the scope for constructive engagement and dialogue between the European Union and Georgia,” the ministry said in a statement.

The ministry claims that the European Union held no meetings with Georgia at any level during the reporting period, despite the Association Agreement providing for them. It says this resulted from the suspension of dialogue with the Georgian side following the European Council’s conclusions of 27 June 2024. According to the ministry, this has limited the European Commission’s ability to assess Georgia’s progress objectively.

The ministry also argues that the report’s selective analysis of legal issues encourages their politicisation, undermines the rule of law and amounts to an attempt to interfere in the country’s internal affairs.

It further says that describing Georgian politicians’ responses to actions targeting Georgia as “hostile rhetoric” infringes on freedom of speech and damages the partnership between Georgia and the European Union.

“Although the enlargement report on Georgia has largely served to voice biased assessments and reinforce political speculation, the Georgian side will examine the European Commission’s report in detail and submit substantiated comments to the Commission,” the statement said.

The Foreign Ministry insists that Georgia’s leadership remains ready to engage in open and constructive dialogue with the European Union, based on mutual respect.

What does the European Commission’s 2026 report say?

According to the European Commission’s 2026 enlargement report, the state of democracy in Georgia has deteriorated further. The document sets out several key criticisms of the country’s government:

● Democratic backsliding and concentration of power: The European Commission says democratic institutions are weakening, political and civil liberties are being restricted, and the government is increasingly concentrating power in its own hands.

● Attempt to ban opposition parties: The Commission believes the proposal to ban five opposition parties threatens the country’s democratic foundations and raises further concerns about the use of the judiciary for political purposes.

● Electoral environment: The authorities have failed to carry out fundamental electoral reform. According to the report, the 2025 municipal elections took place in a polarised and repressive environment, marked by voter intimidation, pressure and legislative changes that gave the ruling party an advantage.

● Restrictions on civil society: The European Commission is concerned about the use of criminal proceedings and charges such as sabotage and assisting hostile activities by foreign organisations against civil society representatives. In the Commission’s assessment, this runs counter to democratic pluralism.

● Judicial independence: For the third consecutive year, the European Commission has recorded a deterioration in the judiciary. According to the report, judicial independence and impartiality have been undermined, while legal changes have increased the risk of state capture of the system. The Commission also criticised the harsh sentences imposed on demonstrators.

● Corruption and de-oligarchisation: The Commission says there has been no progress in tackling corruption. Georgia has had no anti-corruption strategy since 2020, and the authorities have taken no steps towards de-oligarchisation. The report also points to the role of oligarchic influence in facilitating state capture.

● Failure to meet visa-free travel requirements: Georgia has made virtually no progress on the European Commission’s previous recommendations, which concerned the protection of fundamental rights, combating discrimination and fighting corruption. As a result, the Commission has activated the revised visa suspension mechanism.

● Relations with Russia and sanctions: Georgia’s alignment with the EU’s foreign policy has fallen from 40% to 38%. The country has not joined most of the sanctions imposed by the EU on Russia, Belarus and Iran. The report also notes an increase in the number of direct flights to Russia.

● EU financial assistance: In response to democratic backsliding, the EU suspended €121.3 million in bilateral funding for the Georgian government in 2024. Georgia’s participation in new EU programmes under the Association Agreement has also been suspended.

● Anaklia port project: The European Commission notes that the project has become fully state-owned, construction work was suspended for several months, and budget funding for the project fell by 60% during the reporting period.

The European Commission’s report on Georgia

World.title: Baku says there is “no war” with Armenia, yet allocates 20.8% of its state budget to defence and national security. What will money be spent on?
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s defence budget

On 4 November, the Milli Majlis Committee on Economic Policy, Industry and Entrepreneurship discussed Azerbaijan’s draft state budget for 2027. The document allocates 8.816 billion manats (approximately $5.19 billion) to defence and national security, accounting for 20.8% of total budget expenditure.

On 2 October, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev told a congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP):

“Today, there is no conflict or war between Azerbaijan and Armenia. The situation along the border is calm.”

However, in the same speech, Aliyev described strengthening the country’s military capabilities as “one of the main tasks”. Azerbaijan and Armenia have yet to sign a peace agreement. Baku has made amendments to Armenia’s constitution a condition for signing one.

We reported on the revenue side of the budget in September. Now we turn to the other side of the equation:

If there is no war, why is one-fifth of the state budget going to defence and national security? And what do we know about its largest spending item?

What do the figures tell us?

In 2023, Azerbaijan spent 5.85 billion manats (approximately $3.45 billion) on defence and national security. The figure rose to 6.56 billion manats (approximately $3.86 billion) in 2024 and reached 8.07 billion manats (approximately $4.75 billion) in 2025. The 2026 budget allocated 8.72 billion manats (approximately $5.13 billion) to these areas, while the 2027 draft budget provides for 8.82 billion manats (approximately $5.19 billion).

Over four years, spending has increased by roughly 50%, although the rate of growth is slowing. In 2025, the increase stood at 23%, while the government forecasts growth of just 1.1% in 2027. Meanwhile, an earlier medium-term government plan projected a reduction in defence and national security spending to 7.97 billion manats (approximately $4.7 billion) by 2030.

Despite the slower growth, spending remains substantial. In 2027, defence and national security will rank as the second-largest item in the state budget, after economic activity. The government plans to allocate 5.1 billion manats (approximately $3 billion) to education and 2.08 billion manats (approximately $1.23 billion) to healthcare. Combined, spending on these two sectors will be 1.6 billion manats (approximately $942 million) lower than the allocation for defence and national security.

Per capita, defence and national security spending will amount to around 858 manats (approximately $505), compared with just 203 manats (approximately $120) for healthcare. Meanwhile, state budget expenditure will exceed revenue by 3.15 billion manats (approximately $1.85 billion).

The same pattern can be seen in 2026. According to the Finance Ministry, the government allocated 5.25 billion manats (approximately $3.09 billion) to defence and national security in January–September, compared with 3.12 billion manats (approximately $1.84 billion) for education and 954 million manats (approximately $562 million) for healthcare.

High military spending is not unique to Azerbaijan. According to a report by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), military expenditure accounted for 6.5% of Azerbaijan’s GDP in 2025 and 6.1% of Armenia’s. The global average stood at 2.5%. Azerbaijan and Armenia ranked sixth and seventh worldwide, respectively, by military spending as a share of GDP. In terms of the increase in this indicator, Azerbaijan ranked second after Ukraine, with a rise of 1.4 percentage points.

Defence spending will rise from 2.99 billion manats (approximately $1.76 billion) in the 2026 budget to 3.37 billion manats (approximately $1.99 billion) in the 2027 draft. At the same time, funding for “special defence projects and measures” will fall from 4.5 billion to 4 billion manats (approximately $2.65 billion to $2.35 billion). Spending on national security will decrease from 520 million to 480 million manats (approximately $306 million to $282 million), while funding for the border service will increase from 540 million to 550 million manats (approximately $318 million to $323 million). Other expenditure will rise from 160 million to 410 million manats.

The largest allocation goes to “special defence projects and measures”. In 2025, Azerbaijan spent 4.58 billion manats (approximately $2.7 billion) on these projects, accounting for 57% of total defence and national security expenditure. For comparison, in 2023, according to Ziyafat Asgarov, chairman of the parliamentary defence committee, spending on this item reached 2.07 billion manats (approximately $1.22 billion), even after the government added another 1 billion manats (approximately $588.3 million) through a budget revision.

In 2027, this item’s share will fall to 45%, as funding for special defence projects decreases while spending on the armed forces rises by 12.7%. However, the government may revise the allocation during the year, as it did in 2023 following budget amendments.

The draft budget describes the purpose of this funding only in general terms: strengthening defence capabilities and providing the armed forces with equipment and supplies. It says the authorities allocate the money “in accordance with the assigned tasks and signed contracts”.

In the Finance Ministry’s 2026 “Budget for Citizens” document, the government classifies funding for these projects as capital expenditure. The allocated 4.5 billion manats exceed the amount earmarked for the reconstruction of Karabakh and Eastern Zangazur (approximately $2.06 billion) by 1.3 times. They also amount to almost ten times the spending on targeted social assistance (approximately $273.5 million).

However, the 2026 budget law provides no detailed breakdown of this spending category. The document does not identify the contracts involved, the suppliers or the types of weapons the government plans to purchase. By comparison, the “Budget for Citizens” separately lists 35 million manats (approximately $20.6 million) for military personnel’s housing and 15.5 million manats (approximately $9.1 million) to compensate them for rental costs. In 2027, the combined allocation for these two items will fall from 50.5 million to 29.7 million manats (approximately $29.7 million to $17.5 million).

Many countries classify details of military procurement as secret. However, media outlets sometimes report on individual contracts. For example, in October, Israeli company Elbit Systems announced a $235 million contract to supply multiple-launch rocket systems, but did not disclose the buyer. Israeli publication Calcalist reported that Azerbaijan had placed the order, although the company did not confirm this information. Media reports put the cost of Azerbaijan’s purchase of JF-17 fighter jets from Pakistan at $1.6 billion.

Thus, almost a tenth of the state budget goes towards a single spending category whose detailed breakdown remains closed to the public.

How do the authorities justify this spending?

In September, Prime Minister Ali Asadov said that defence and national security spending would remain “as always” one of the largest items in the budget. He also noted that 44% of budget expenditure served social purposes.

President Ilham Aliyev cited two reasons why Azerbaijan needs to strengthen its military capabilities. The first concerns Armenia. Despite the initialling of a peace agreement and the start of trade between the two countries, Aliyev referred to historical events and said: “…we must remain vigilant and be ten times stronger than them at all times, every single day.”

The second reason, he said, involves wars and conflicts in neighbouring regions. According to Aliyev, new sources of conflict are emerging “in the North, in the South and in the Middle East”, while no international mechanisms exist to stop them. The president therefore believes Azerbaijan must have enough military power to ensure that “no one would even think of staging any provocation against Azerbaijan”.

Aliyev acknowledged that the country also had “other needs”, including the reconstruction of Karabakh and improving people’s living standards. However, he added: “But if we cannot defend ourselves, then every other project we undertake will lose all meaning.”

Economist Khalid Kerimli shares a similar view: “We cannot expect stability in this area for now. On the contrary, tensions are likely to increase.”

What does “ten times stronger” mean in figures?

Armenia’s draft 2027 budget allocates approximately 616.5 billion drams, or around $1.7 billion, to its Defence Ministry. This represents a 9.5% increase on 2026, when the government cut the defence budget to 563 billion drams. The allocation will therefore almost return to its 2025 level. Azerbaijan, meanwhile, plans to spend 8.8 billion manats, or around $5.2 billion, on defence and national security.

Azerbaijan’s allocation is therefore roughly three times larger than Armenia’s. However, the Azerbaijani figure also includes spending on national security and the border service.

Armenian political analyst Suren Surenyants believes that Baku wants to consolidate the political gains it made through its military superiority, as the current balance of power cannot last indefinitely. At the same time, he says there is not yet sufficient evidence to conclude that Azerbaijan is preparing for another military escalation.

Despite the initialling of a peace agreement, neither country plans to reduce military spending in 2027. Armenia will increase its allocation by 9.5%, while Azerbaijan will raise its spending by 1.1%.

Will signing a peace agreement lead to lower military spending? Aliyev’s words following his statement about the need to be “ten times stronger” suggest the opposite: “It will remain as it is today, tomorrow as well.”

After parliamentary committees review the draft budget, the Milli Majlis will debate it in a plenary session. The 2026 budget law did not provide a detailed breakdown of the 4.5 billion manats allocated to “special defence projects and measures”.

Azerbaijan’s defence budget

World.title: Georgia must adopt European laws if it wants to join EU – ambassador
World.content:
Georgia’s EU accession

According to EU Ambassador to Georgia Pawel Herczynski, the EU accession process is based not on a candidate country’s own assessment of its progress, but on the European Union’s evaluation. In other words, it is the EU that assesses the progress made by a candidate country, not the other way around.

Herczynski made the remarks in response to a statement by Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, who said at an EU enlargement summit that the Georgian authorities were optimistic about a possible change in the EU’s approach towards Georgia.

“This is a simple truth and the foundation of EU enlargement: the European Commission assesses Georgia, not the other way around. The accession process is based on a voluntary application. By applying for EU membership, a country agrees to be monitored and assessed by the European Commission,” Herczynski said.

According to the ambassador, some candidate countries take EU accession seriously. He named Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine and Moldova as frontrunners in the accession process.

At the same time, Herczynski said, some countries express an interest in joining the EU but are in fact moving away from the European path and reversing the progress they have made.

“This is extremely regrettable, but it is the sovereign decision of each candidate country,” he stressed.

The EU ambassador also said that if Georgia wanted to join the EU, it should adopt European legislation rather than American, Russian, Chinese or other countries’ laws.

Herczynski was particularly critical of the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence, which he said was incompatible with EU legislation.

According to the ambassador, the EU had warned the Georgian authorities about this as early as 2023. At the time, the ruling party withdrew the repressive law, after which Georgia was granted EU candidate status at the end of the year. However, the authorities soon reintroduced the same legislation in parliament.

“We said loudly and clearly, including myself: ‘Please don’t do this. This law is not compatible with EU legislation.’ And we also said loudly and clearly that there would be consequences. The Georgian government decided to continue down this path. Then came another law, and another law, each one widening the gap between the European Union and Georgia,” Herczynski said.

According to the ambassador, Georgia is free to decide which laws to adopt, but a country seeking to join the European Union must implement EU legislation.

Herczynski also responded to Irakli Kobakhidze’s calls for dialogue, noting that the EU supports dialogue but that Georgia’s ruling party had stripped it of any substance over the past three years.

According to the ambassador, democratic backsliding, pressure on civil society, threats to ban political opposition groups, actions against independent media and a daily campaign to discredit the European Union were preventing the resumption of dialogue.

“The European Union is built on dialogue. Dialogue is part of our DNA. Behind me, you can see the flags of the 27 EU member states. We constantly negotiate and compromise to reach consensus. As the EU, we fully support dialogue. The problem is that over the past three years, the ruling party in Georgia has rendered this dialogue meaningless,” Herczynski said.

He questioned what exactly the EU and the Georgian authorities could discuss when the ruling party was talking about the “deep state” and the “global war party”, as well as drawing parallels between the European Union and the Soviet Union.

“Do you expect serious representatives of EU institutions to start discussing the definition of the ‘deep state’? Do you expect us to engage in dialogue about the ‘global war party’? This smear campaign must stop for dialogue to resume,” he said.

Pawel Herczynski

The EU ambassador also addressed the ongoing proceedings in Georgia’s Constitutional Court concerning a request to ban opposition parties. Herczynski said the European Union was following the process with great concern.

According to him, attempts to ban opposition parties threaten the foundations of democracy in Georgia. He also reiterated the European Commission’s position, expressed several days earlier by EU Commissioner Marta Kos.

Herczynski said that if the authorities attempted to ban opposition parties that had passed the electoral threshold in the last parliamentary elections, it would be an unprecedented case in the history of the Council of Europe.

“I do not want to speculate about something that has not yet happened. We are following the proceedings in Georgia’s Constitutional Court with great concern. Attempts to ban the main opposition parties through a lawsuit in the Constitutional Court threaten the foundations of democracy in the country,” he said.

According to the European Commission’s enlargement report of 4 November 2026, Georgia’s EU integration process remains suspended, while the situation in the country has deteriorated further compared with the previous year.

The European Commission assessed that the Georgian authorities had taken no steps during the reporting period to implement the nine steps set out for the country to advance its EU accession process.

The report highlights the weakening of democratic institutions, restrictions on political and civil liberties, problems with judicial independence, attempts to ban opposition parties and a lack of progress in tackling corruption.

The Commission also points to Georgia’s incomplete alignment with sanctions against Russia, an increase in direct flights to Russia and the presence of Georgian companies on EU sanctions lists.

Consequently, due to continued democratic backsliding, the European Commission is no longer issuing new recommendations on accession negotiation chapters, except in areas relating to fundamental reforms.

World.title: Armenian businessman Samvel Karapetyan detained while under house arrest
World.content:
Samvel Karapetyan detained following search

Prominent Armenian businessman Samvel Karapetyan, founder of the Tashir Group and leader of the opposition Strong Armenia party, has been detained.

A criminal investigation has been launched against Karapetyan and 35 others. They are suspected of:

Causing particularly large-scale financial damage to Electric Networks of Armenia (ENA).

Embezzling entrusted property.

Money laundering on a particularly large scale.

The total damage allegedly caused to Electric Networks of Armenia exceeds 64.585 billion drams (more than $180m).

Armenia’s Investigative Committee said the alleged offences were committed between 2016 and 2024 by a group of individuals led by “S.K.”. Investigators are examining four alleged criminal episodes in the private sector.

The committee said the alleged crimes had been uncovered following extensive investigative work and on the basis of information obtained from the National Security Service, the Interior Ministry and the State Revenue Committee.

Billionaire Samvel Karapetyan was already under house arrest in connection with a separate criminal case. In June 2025, he was charged with publicly calling for the seizure of power and the overthrow of the constitutional order. Several months later, another criminal investigation was launched, and Karapetyan faced additional economic crime charges, including money laundering. In July 2026, criminal proceedings were also initiated against his nephew, Narek Karapetyan. He is accused of coercing people into attending gatherings and money laundering on a particularly large scale. The court imposed bail of 1 billion drams ($281,000) and a ban on leaving the country.

Searches began early in the morning

Armenia’s Investigative Committee began conducting searches early in the morning at the homes of Strong Armenia party leader Samvel Karapetyan and his nephew Narek Karapetyan, who heads the parliamentary faction of the same name.

“Searches are also being carried out at other addresses linked to the Karapetyan family,” party spokeswoman Aghavni Sukiasyan said.

The Investigative Committee later confirmed the information, specifying that simultaneous searches were being conducted at 65 locations. It emerged that the searches were being carried out by the Main Department for the Investigation of Economic Crimes as part of a criminal investigation.

Investigative Committee reveals details of alleged crimes

Several hours after the searches, Armenia’s Investigative Committee released details of the case under investigation:

“Members of a criminal group operating under the leadership of S.K. – including certain members of the Board of Directors of Electric Networks of Armenia CJSC, the company’s general director, his deputy and other senior officials – abused their powers in managing the company’s day-to-day operations with the aim of embezzling company assets on a particularly large scale.”

Investigators found that the individuals concerned had deliberately taken out bank loans exceeding the company’s actual operational needs. The funds were then transferred under the guise of dividend payments to the offshore company Liormand Holdings Limited and Tashir Capital CJSC. Both companies are shareholders in Electric Networks of Armenia (ENA) and belong to the Karapetyan family.

“With the aim of laundering funds obtained through the aforementioned criminal activities, executives of more than ten interconnected organisations, under the leadership and direction of S.K., created the appearance of large-scale financial transactions within the framework of civil-law and corporate relations. They concealed the criminal origin of the embezzled funds, converted them and mixed them with their other income. In doing so, they disguised the true nature and origin of the illegally obtained assets and funds, making them appear legitimate and thereby laundering money and obtaining criminal proceeds,” the Investigative Committee said.

As a result, Electric Networks of Armenia allegedly suffered financial losses on a particularly large scale.

The supervising prosecutor decided to initiate criminal proceedings against 36 individuals, and an investigator ordered their detention. The criminal investigation is ongoing.

Opposition alleges “political pressure”

Strong Armenia parliamentary faction leader Narek Karapetyan linked the morning’s developments to his party’s position on the new Constitution. According to him, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan is trying to pressure the party into a “deal”. He claimed that the prime minister would offer to release Samvel Karapetyan in exchange for the party’s agreement to hold a referendum on the new Constitution.

“They are trying to persuade us to allow the Constitution to be put to a referendum and adopted. Look at what is happening. Whatever they are told in Baku, they come back and start trying to convince us [to agree to it]. We are the obstacle preventing them from pushing through a Constitution that suits Aliyev,” he stressed.

Nikol Pashinyan has said that the draft of Armenia’s new Constitution is ready and that its text will be published in November. For a referendum to be held, two-thirds of parliament’s members must vote in favour of the initiative. However, the ruling party does not have enough seats and expects opposition lawmakers to support the proposal. The prime minister has repeatedly stated that constitutional reform is necessary for Armenia itself. ёThe opposition, however, believes that the government’s initiative is driven by a demand from Azerbaijan. Baku has called for amendments to Armenia’s Constitution as a precondition for signing a peace agreement, arguing that it contains territorial claims. The Constitution itself contains no provisions that could directly give rise to such concerns. However, it refers to the Declaration of Independence, which mentions the unification of Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh. It is already known that this reference will be removed from the new Constitution.

Narek Karapetyan said the Strong Armenia party would not change its position even if hundreds of people were arrested.

He argued that the developments had nothing to do with economic crimes and accused the authorities of attempting to exert political pressure on the opposition.

After law enforcement officers detained his uncle, Narek Karapetyan used stronger language:

“He thinks he can achieve something with his birdbrain. Nothing you have planned has worked, and nothing ever will. You are simply afraid of our enemy,” Karapetyan said, addressing Pashinyan.

World.title: Azerbaijan discusses Budget Package documents for 2027 (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. Draft laws "On the 2027 budget of the State Social Protection Fund," "On the 2027 budget of the Unemployment Insurance Fund," "On the subsistence minimum in the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2027," and "On the need criterion in the Republic of Azerbaijan for 2027" were discussed in the first reading at a joint meeting of the Azerbaijani Parliament Committees on Labor and Social Policy and on Economic Policy, Industries and Enterprising Enterprises on November 5.

This was reported by the Press and Public Relations Department of the Milli Majlis (Azerbaijani Parliament).

According to the report, Musa Guliyev, Chairman of the Committee on Labor and Social Policy, presenting the draft laws regarding the 2027 budgets of the State Social Protection Fund (SSPF) and the Unemployment Insurance Fund (UIF) for discussion noted that social policy has consistently held a priority position within the domestic policy of the Azerbaijani state.

During the meeting, it was emphasized that the priorities established by President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev at the 8th Congress of the New Azerbaijan Party, focused on expanding measures to improve the welfare of the population, have also been incorporated into the 2027 budget. These priorities are also reflected in the budgets of the SSPF and the UIF, establishing a reliable financial foundation for improving the social well-being of martyrs' families, veterans, recipients of pensions and allowances, and other vulnerable groups, as well as for ensuring the sustainability of social protection and insurance coverage. He said that the draft laws have been prepared in accordance with the requirements of national legislation and the principles of the budgetary system.

During the meeting, it was noted that SSPF’s revenues will amount to 9.22 billion manat ($5.42 billion) in 2027, up 897.4 million manat ($527.9 million), or 10.8%, from the current year's forecast. Meanwhile, SSPF’s expenditures are projected at 9.27 billion manat ($5.45 billion), an increase of 790 million manat ($464.7 million), or 9.3%.

Mandatory state social insurance contributions are expected to account for over 7.58 billion manat ($4.46 billion), or 82.3% of the fund's revenues. Of these contributions, 67.5% will come from the non-budget sector and 32.5% from budget-funded organizations.

Payments to the population will account for 96.5% of the fund's projected expenditures. The average monthly pension is forecasted to reach 640 manat ($376) in 2027. As in previous years, the replacement rate, defined as the ratio of the average monthly pension amount to the average monthly wage, will remain at the 50% level for the current and coming years, thereby meeting the requirements of the relevant International Labor Organization convention, which sets a 40% minimum standard for social security.

A total of 281 million manat ($165 million) is earmarked for 2027 to finance benefits for temporary disability, maternity, childbirth, childcare for children under three, and funeral expenses through mandatory state social insurance contributions.

Then, the committee chairperson provided information regarding the draft law "On the 2027 budget of the Unemployment Insurance Fund." He said the UIF’s revenues are projected at 269 million manat ($158 million) in 2027, while 50 million manat ($29.4 million) from the fund's unused balances from previous years is earmarked to finance next year's expenditures. Unemployment insurance contribution collections are forecasted to reach 267 million manat ($157 million) next year, up 31 million manat ($18.2 million), or 13%, from the approved 2026 figure.

The UIF's expenditures are projected at 319 million manat ($188 million) in 2027, an increase of 53 million manat ($31.2 million) year-on-year. Of this amount, 36 million manat ($21.2 million) is earmarked for unemployment insurance payments, up 28.6% from the current year. As many as 113 million manat ($66.5 million), or 35% of the fund's expenditures, is earmarked for self-employment programs. Around 14,500 people are expected to participate in these programs in 2027.

The committee chairperson outlined the planned allocations for vocational training, paid public works and other active employment measures under the UIF's 2027 budget.

Presenting the third and fourth items, Guliyev said the draft law on the 2027 living wage sets the nationwide figure at 314 manat ($185). The minimum will stand at 334 manat ($196) for the working-age population, 258 manat ($152) for pensioners and 274 manat ($161) for children, maintaining the annual growth rate.

The draft law "On the need criterion threshold for 2027 in the Republic of Azerbaijan" sets the threshold at 314 manat ($185).

Then, at the meeting, Minister of Labor and Social Protection of Population Anar Aliyev noted that, in line with the reform program of President Ilham Aliyev, consistent and targeted measures aimed at ensuring social protection and employment for the population will continue in the coming year.

During the meeting, it was emphasized that, in accordance with the directive issued by President Ilham Aliyev at the 8th Congress of the New Azerbaijan Party, the necessary financial provision has been made in the 2027 state and consolidated budgets for the next, the 6th, social reform package, aimed at increasing wages and social payments. The meeting highlighted that over the past 8 years, 5 major social reform packages benefiting 4 million citizens have been implemented, with an additional annual financial burden of 8 billion manat ($4.7 billion).

As a result of measures implemented this year, the average monthly pension increased by 10.4% year-on-year to 596 manat ($350.59), while the average old-age pension rose by 10% to 634 manat ($372.94), the average monthly salary grew by 7.2% to 1,173 manat ($690), payments in the form of benefits, scholarships and targeted state social assistance rose by 8.4% to 1.9 billion manat ($1.12 billion).

The minister stressed that the state and consolidated budgets would retain their social focus in 2027. Social expenditures in the state budget are projected at 13 billion manat ($7.65 billion), up 222.7 million manat ($131 million), or 1.7%, while social-oriented expenditures are expected to reach 18.7 billion manat ($11 billion), an increase of 1.6 billion manat ($941 million), or 9.2%. Their share of total state budget expenditures is expected to rise to 44.2%, while their share of GDP is projected at 13.3%.

In his speech, Anar Aliyev also outlined the volume and structure of state budget allocations for the Ministry of Labor and Social Protection's areas of activity next year. The speech noted that the 2027 state budget draft earmarks 5.5 billion manat ($3.24 billion) to finance public payments under the ministry's programs, medical insurance expenses for vulnerable groups and paid public works.

The minister remarked that mandatory state social insurance contributions are expected to account for 82.3%, or 7.58 billion manat ($4.46 billion) of the SSPF's 2027 revenues. This is an increase of 995.4 million manat ($585.5 million), or 15.1%, compared with the current year's figure. Contributions from budget-funded organizations are projected at 2.5 billion manat ($1.47 billion), while non-budget organizations are expected to contribute 5.1 billion manat ($3 billion). Compared with the approved 2026 figures, revenues from budget-funded organizations are expected to increase by 17%, or 357.9 million manat ($210.5 million), while contributions from the non-budget sector will rise by 14.2%, or 637.5 million manat ($375 million).

State budget transfers to finance government obligations under the insurance and pension system are projected at 1.6 billion manat ($941 million), down 100 million manat ($58.8 million), or 5.9%, from the approved 2026 figure.

Public payments account for 96.5% of the fund's total expenditures for 2027, or 8.95 billion manat ($5.26 billion). This figure is 753.6 million manat ($443.3 million) higher than in 2026. Of this amount, about 8.67 billion manat ($5.1 billion) accounts for labor pension expenditures, while 280.6 million manat ($165 million) accounts for benefits paid through social insurance. At the meeting, it was noted that, according to current forecast, 575.5 million manat ($338.5 million) is earmarked for the indexation of labor pensions by approximately 7.5% in 2027.

Anar Aliyev said the UIF's 2027 revenues are projected to increase by 30.6 million manat ($18 million), or 12.9%, compared with the approved 2026 figure. The non-budget sector will account for 77.7% of insurance contribution collections.

The fund's expenditures are expected to rise by 52.8 million manat ($31.06 million), or 19.8%, year-on-year.

In 2027, approximately 444,000 people are expected to participate in active employment programs financed by the UIF. Additionally, unemployment insurance payments are projected to be assigned to 15,600 people during the year. A total of 61%, or 194.2 million manat ($114 million), of the fund's expenditures, is earmarked for employment measures.

During the meeting, it was noted that the ministry will also continue programs providing housing, vehicles, and rehabilitation equipment to eligible individuals. At the meeting, it was pointed out that 40 million manat ($23.5 million) is earmarked for purchasing 600 apartments in 2027 to improve the living conditions of families of martyrs and people with war-related disabilities.

Then, at the meeting, Azer Amiraslanov, Chairperson of the Parliamentary Committee on Economic Policy, Industries and Enterprising Enterprises, shared his views on the items on the agenda.

He noted that the harmonization and coordination of economic and social policies constitute one of the fundamental principles of state policy in Azerbaijan. The committee chairperson said that ensuring financial stability, maintaining a high level of economic activity, and sustaining economic growth are of vital importance for improving the living standards of citizens. In this context, he emphasized the significance of the view expressed by the President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev who stated that it’s impossible to ensure prosperity merely by increasing social expenditures and other budgetary outlays without economic growth.

Amiraslanov highlighted that significant results have been achieved in reducing unemployment in the country, that ensuring effective employment is a key objective for the new phase, and that a social package has been incorporated into the state budget for 2027 to further enhance the well-being of citizens. He noted that the sustainability of the SSPF and the UIF can be ensured through stable inflows, economic growth, and economic activity. It was stated that the execution of the 2027 state budget will both support economic development and establish the necessary financial foundation for further improving the well-being of citizens and strengthening their social protection.

Speaking at the meeting, Vugar Gulmammadov, Chairperson of the Chamber of Accounts, presented the Chamber’s assessments regarding the 2027 draft budgets for the State Social Protection Fund and the Unemployment Insurance Fund. The Chairman noted that the draft budgets for these funds have been prepared in accordance with the requirements of relevant legislation. He highlighted the Chamber’s analyses and observations concerning the funds' revenue and expenditure components, as well as the sustainability of the pension provision system.

Himalay Mamishov, Deputy Minister of Finance of Azerbaijan, also spoke at the event, discussing the ongoing trend of decreasing reliance on oil within the state budget and the objectives established in this regard. Speaking about budget expenditures, the deputy minister said that the spending has been structured in alignment with socio-economic needs. Highlighting the parameters and indicators across various expenditure categories, he characterized the upcoming year’s state budget as the most investment-oriented budget in the region.

Subsequently, Sahib Alakbarov, Deputy Minister of Economy, addressed the event. He noted that the Azerbaijani economy has experienced dynamic growth in recent years, with sustained development projected for the period ahead. Emphasizing the vital role of investment activity in driving economic growth and expanding employment, the deputy minister pointed out that positive trends, such as the improvement of the investment climate and increased investment in the non-oil and gas sector, have contributed to the diversification of the economy, the development of new production and service sectors, and an upsurge in economic activity within the regions. It was emphasized that the primary tasks for the coming period include the full implementation of established support mechanisms and the ongoing assessment of their economic impact; the long-term financing of industrial and production projects; the expansion of the volume and geographical reach of non-oil and gas exports; the acceleration of strategic investment projects; and the promotion of economic activity along transport corridors.

During the meeting, Vahab Mammadov, First Deputy Chairperson of the State Statistical Committee, stated that the draft laws presented for discussion were prepared based on analyses derived from official statistical data. He noted that the demographic burden and the current state of the labor market were taken into account during the drafting process, and that relevant assessments were conducted.

The Deputy Chairperson of the Committee for Economic Policy, Industries and Enterprising Enterprises, as well as several MPs, took part in the discussion of these issues, offering their views and proposals, and raising various questions. Minister of Labor and Social Protection of Population Anar Aliyev and Chairperson of the Chamber of Accounts Vugar Gulmammadov provided clarifications regarding the issues raised during the discussions.

At the meeting, the draft laws on the agenda were recommended for submission to the plenary session of the parliament for a first reading.

The event was attended by Elshad Musayev, Deputy Chairperson of the Committee on Labor and Social Policy, as well as MPs and other official persons.

World.title: Woodside raises cost-cutting target to $400 million a year from 2028
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. Woodside Energy has raised its target for structural cost reductions to $400 million per year from 2028, compared with a 2025 baseline, according to the company's Capital Markets Day 2026 presentation.

According to the presentation, $100 million of the savings will come from portfolio optimization, including exits from Calypso and Sunrise and from Bonaparte CCS. Another $130 million will come from streamlined processes and $170 million from external spending. The original target was based on $50 million in portfolio savings.

About 65 percent of the recurring savings will come from operating expenditure, about 30 percent from capital (including sustaining capital) and about 5 percent from general and administrative costs. The cost base excludes contractor spending on major capital projects.

"Our priority now is to extract more value from our portfolio. We are targeting $400 million of annual structural cost reductions from 2028, improving operational efficiency and productivity," CEO Liz Westcott said.

Woodside Energy, headquartered in Perth, is Australia's largest independent oil and gas company and is listed on the Australian Securities Exchange and the New York Stock Exchange. Calypso is a deep-water gas project offshore Trinidad and Tobago, Sunrise is a gas field in the Timor Sea, and Bonaparte CCS is a carbon capture and storage project offshore northern Australia. Woodside also divested its Greater Angostura assets in Trinidad and Tobago in July 2025. Woodside held its Capital Markets Day 2026 in Sydney on November 5 and will hold a second event in New York on November 12. At last year's Capital Markets Day, in November 2025, the company set out its growth plans to 2032.

World.title: Woodside targets 12-15% return on capital employed by mid-2030s
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 5. Woodside Energy is targeting a portfolio return on average capital employed (ROACE) of 12-15% by the mid-2030s, according to the company's Capital Markets Day 2026 presentation.

According to the company, the base business together with the delivery of Scarborough, Trion, and Louisiana LNG provides a ROACE of about 10 percent at a Brent price of $70 per barrel. Structural cost cuts are expected to add about 0.5 percentage points, and marketing and trading about 1 percentage point. The new capital and distribution framework is expected to add another 1-3 percentage points.

"We are targeting portfolio return on average capital employed of 12-15% by the mid-2030s. Delivery of our committed projects, the structural cost program, active portfolio management and increased value capture through marketing and trading will support this improvement," CEO Liz Westcott said.

Woodside Energy, headquartered in Perth, is Australia's largest independent oil and gas company and is listed on the Australian Securities Exchange and the New York Stock Exchange. Return on average capital employed (ROACE) is calculated as profit before tax and net finance costs divided by average capital employed. Woodside said the target is based on a long-term Brent price of $70 per barrel, JKM of $10 per MMBtu and TTF of $9 per MMBtu in 2026 real terms. Woodside's three major projects under construction are Scarborough in Western Australia (final investment decision in 2021), Trion in Mexico (FID in 2023) and Louisiana LNG in the US (FID in 2025). Woodside held its Capital Markets Day 2026 in Sydney on November 5 and will hold a second event in New York on November 12. At last year's Capital Markets Day, in November 2025, the company set out its growth plans to 2032.
