World.title: Once-green SA landscape now 'barren' in efforts to stop pest
World.content:
A once-green landscape across Adelaide's north-eastern suburbs is being transformed with almost 5,000 pine trees removed in an effort to stop the spread of an invasive pest.

Giant pine scale is an insect that sucks sap to slowly drain trees of moisture and nutrients, eventually killing them.

Authorities say removing infected trees, along with surrounding susceptible trees, is currently "the only scientifically agreed" way to manage the outbreak.

But local residents are critical of the large-scale removal, saying the loss of mature trees had stripped their neighbourhoods of shade, changed the landscape and destroyed important wildlife habitat.

For Highbury resident Simon Roocke, the pine trees behind his home were a major part of the area's charm.

"The trees came down just before winter this year," he said.

"Part of the appeal of this place was the trees up the back, they were beautiful, they gave us some amazing shade in the summertime.

" Now it's gone and the hill looks the worse for it. "

Before: Boundy Road at Highbury in April 2023. . . After: The same road in September 2025 after the removal of pine trees. (Google Street View) . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE Boundy Road at Highbury in April 2023. / The same road in September 2025 after the removal of pine trees. (Google Street View)

Mr Roocke's home now backs onto a largely cleared hillside, with the once-established canopy gone.

"We raised a lot of issues regarding the stability of the hill now that the trees are gone, because it is a significant hill there but at this point it has happened and we'll have to deal with it," he said.

Mr Roocke said he also worried about the practical impact of the lack of trees, particularly the loss of shade.

"Our daughter has just moved out but her bedroom was out the back and within the first few weeks she noticed her bedroom was a lot hotter," he said.

"Naturally we're going to have to be using more air-conditioning."

Greg Atkins shows the view of tree stumps from his back fence at Highbury. (ABC News)

Further along the affected area, resident Greg Atkins said the scale of the clearing left parts of his neighbourhood appearing barren.

Mr Atkins said residents were told the revegetation project would include thousands of replacement plants, but felt the effort had fallen short behind his property.

"We were told there were three and a half thousand plants to be put in. They must've run out when they got to our place," he said.

He hoped the government would continue its replanting efforts to fill the space near his back fence.

"Otherwise, it's going to be barren hillside with weeds," he said.

Loss of wildlife habitat

Community advocate Sonia Blackwell said the loss of mature pine trees raised questions about the impact on local wildlife.

She said the trees provided important habitat and protection for a range of species.

"We have lost a lot of habitat for our red-tailed black cockatoos, for our koalas, for all of our wildlife that use those trees as habitat and weather protection," she said.

Sonia Blackwell says the removed trees provide an important habitat for wildlife. (ABC News)

Ms Blackwell said she was "purely outraged" about the management of giant pine scale, describing the impact on local residents as significant.

"Residents are selling their homes," she said.

"Houses are filling up from displaced wildlife. One lady had to remove three snakes in one week from her yard."

Infected trees 'will die'

The sap-sucking insects continue to be detected in the area, with ForestrySA chief executive Nathan Paine confirming another 19 trees had been found to have giant pine scale at Highbury and Hope Valley.

Elliston Reserve, on the corner of Lower North East Road and Awoonga Road, had its pine trees felled to control giant pine scale. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

He said those trees were being felled, along with others within a 50-metre buffer zone.

"Those trees are being removed around the reservoir, the aqueduct and along Lyons Road," Mr Paine said.

" The reality is that this is a sap-sucker, once the tree is infected it will die. "

Mr Paine said future detections of the pest were also anticipated.

Pine trees have been cleared at the Hope Valley Reservoir. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

A state government spokesperson said it had contributed $5.4 million towards the response to giant pine scale since 2023 and another $5.5 million for revegetation and restoration works.

"Presently, the removal of impacted trees and surrounding susceptible trees is the only scientifically agreed response available to manage giant pine scale," they said.

"While we recognise the significant impact that removing mature trees has on local communities, these measures are critical to reduce the risk of further spread."

The spokesperson said the removed trees would be replaced with native species that are not susceptible to the pest.

World.title: Wallaroos wunderkind eager to tackle 'world's leading' club comp in England
World.content:
Do not let Caitlyn Halse's nickname deceive you.

The Wallaroos fullback, who turned 20 in September, might be known as "The Kid" but she is wise beyond her years.

This was clear when Halse recently explained to ABC Sport how she was approaching an upcoming stint with Leicester Tigers in England's Premiership Women's Rugby (PWR) competition.

"I've still got a lot to learn around my game, in attack and defence," said Halse, who has played 18 Tests.

"I'm willing and eager to learn.

"I just want to go over there and soak up all the information I can and bring it back to Australia and use that to my advantage for the Wallaroos."

Caitlyn Halse (right) has played 18 Tests for the Wallaroos. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Halse has already achieved a great deal in her promising rugby career.

She became the youngest player in Wallaroos/Wallabies history to make a Test debut, managing the feat as a 17-year-old in 2024.

Her first Rugby World Cup appearance came the following year but as Halse points out, she is not the finished product.

She believes her game can reach another level in PWR, which is described by its organisers, with justification, as the "world's leading domestic women's rugby competition".

Nine clubs contest PWR across an 18-round season before two weeks of finals decide the champion.

Australia's domestic equivalent, Super Rugby Women's, has five teams (Waratahs, Reds, Brumbies, Force and Fijian Drua) playing four round-robin matches each ahead of a two-week finals series.

PWR attracts players from Australasia, Europe and North America, and features the entire world champion England squad, who are full-time.

England's governing body, the Rugby Football Union (RFU), recognises PWR's importance.

RFU announced in June it was committing 24 million pounds ($46.1 million) to PWR across 10 years, which is a further illustration of the wise investment it has made in women's rugby since first offering full-time contracts to players in 2019.

Wallaroos back-rower Tabua Tuinakauvadra will also play for Leicester. (Getty Images: Paul Harding)

Rugby Australia (RA) is mindful of PWR's status as the world's best domestic competition, which is why it encourages Wallaroos players to seek opportunities with the English clubs.

Halse will be joined by Wallaroos teammates Tabua Tuinakauvadra and Ash Fernandez at Leicester, while uncapped Australian Grace Freeman is also on the Tigers' books.

Another Wallaroo, prop Bridie O'Gorman, will play for PWR's Gloucester Hartpury.

"Gaining experience in a competition like the PWR will be invaluable for the players' development as we build a Wallaroos program with the goal of competing on the final weekend at the Rugby World Cup in 2029," RA director of high performance Peter Horne said in June.

'A different type of rugby'

One of the Wallaroos' most consistent players in 2026, Kaitlan Leaney, knows firsthand the benefit of playing in PWR.

She spent time with the famous Harlequins club earlier in her career.

"I learned so much," Leaney told ABC Sport last month.

"I definitely think I wouldn't be the player I am or the person I am today without that experience.

"I went over there at the age of 22 and played three years over there.

Kaitlan Leaney had a stint playing for Harlequins in PWR. (Getty Images: Henry Browne)

"The way my game grew in terms of playing consistent games and so many games … you've got internationals all across the park in all the clubs.

"I think the standard and level you're playing at each week is really special."

Halse similarly wants to make the most of her PWR opportunity when the 2026/27 season kicks off in a fortnight's time.

"I'm just super excited to experience a different type of rugby," Halse said.

"They've got girls from Canada, USA and all over Europe.

"I'm just keen to go over there and learn something new and experience something different."

World.title: British artist's immersive works on display as Parramatta Powerhouse opens
World.content:
Es Devlin believes the way to change the world is to spend 15 minutes looking into a stranger's eyes.

In the world-renowned artist's first exhibition in Australia, her audience will be asked to do just that.

"I'll invite you to sit opposite a stranger, not talk, but leave a trace in a drawing of your encounter," Devlin says.

Es Devlin's Memory Palace installation. (ABC News: Rhiannon Soliman-Marron)

This is the "heart" of Devlin's exhibit The Turning, which opens at Powerhouse Parramatta this weekend.

"It's unusual to sustain a gaze with a stranger for 15 minutes, and it shifts you," she says.

" It's quite a humble act, in the context of some more technically complex pieces, but it's where the real work of the exhibition happens. "

The Turning is made up of five large-scale immersive installations by the British set designer, who began her decades-long career in theatre before branching out to concerts, fashion shows, and art installations.

Devlin has been a creative force behind two Olympic ceremonies, a Super Bowl half-time show, and the world tours of artists including Adele, Beyonce, The Weeknd and U2.

Audiences are invited to contribute to each work through drawing and reflection. (ABC News: Rhiannon Soliman-Marron)

"Everything that you see in this exhibition is only possible because I've stood in audiences for 30 years, and the audience has taught me," she says.

"What you'll be experiencing here is the audience as the protagonist. You are a performer in these works — the works aren't complete until you arrive."

After flying into Sydney this week, Devlin and her team have spent the last few days making tweaks to meticulously-planned projections, lights, and sound.

The Turning is on show for Powerhouse Parramatta's opening weekend. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

Three years ago Devlin saw the space and the suburb that her work would eventually inhabit.

"The river delta was my first introduction to this place," she says.

"We went round the park and started to really work with the First Nations team and the other curatorial teams here, to make something that was very specific for this place."

All of The Turning's installations were made in Australia, using local workers and materials.

Many of the concepts have already been exhibited in other galleries around the world, but here, they all have a local touch.

Labyrinth of mirrors

In Forest of Us, a multi-level labyrinth of mirrors thatmimics the structure of the human lungs normally sits still.

But in the Powerhouse, the reflective surfaces ripple slightly, just like the Parramatta River just outside.

"It's something about the aircon, which I hadn't planned," Devlin says.

"All around this building, there's movement."

The 3D models of historically significant place which make up Memory Palace have also been reworked for an Australian audience.

Another installation titled Forest of Us. (ABC News: Rhiannon Soliman-Marron)

Alongside the tree under which the Buddha reached enlightenment and the steps of the Swedish parliament where Greta Thunberg began her first climate strike sits The Block in Redfern, where several Aboriginal-led organisations were founded in the 1970s.

Madjebebe, a sandstone rock shelter in Arnhem Land which holds the earliest evidence of humans in Australia, also features on Memory Palace's topographical landscape.

"It's a map of places where humans have significantly changed people's perspective about something throughout history," Devlin says.

"If people come away with a little bit more sense of their own capacity to shift not only their own perspective, but the perspective of another, then the work has done its job."

All of The Turning's installations were made in Australia. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

Choreography and drawing

Toward the end of the exhibit is Screen Share, which involves a piece of choreography projected onto hundreds of sketchbooks filled with Devlin's drawings.

At the projection's end, the audience is invited to tear off a page for themselves.

Some of the sketches are familiar — larger versions feature in Redraw the Edges of Yourself, which sits outside the museum.

Some of Es Devlin's sketches. (ABC News: Rhiannon Soliman-Marron)

The Australian iteration of that piece a large, egg-shaped sound stage, containing 244 hand-drawn studies of endangered local flora and fauna species — "Sydney citizens who aren't human".

"The invitation is to remember their names … make a habitat for species that aren't human within the human imagination," Devlin says.

es Devlin has been a creative force behind the world tours of artists including Adele and Beyonce. (ABC News: Rhiannon Soliman-Marron)

Devlin hopes her work will encourage visitors to take a moment to engage with the world around them.

"There's a lot to take in in this building, and in order to remember it, you need to feel it," she says.

The Turning, along with the rest of Powerhouse Parramatta, opens to the public on Saturday.

World.title: What campers need to know about Tasmania's new booking system
World.content:
A new online booking system for campsites across Tasmania was rolled out this week, intending to introduce a more consistent approach to camping fees.

It has been described by the Tasmanian Parks and Wildlife Service (PWS) as the first stage of a broader rollout, as part of an effort to stop "ghost camping" — where campers reserve sites with an unoccupied tent or van until they are ready to use the site.

This first stage will allow campers to find, book and manage their bookings for selected campgrounds that already require a booking fee.

It covers 10 Tasmanian national parks and conservation areas:

Narawntapu National Park

Maria Island National Park

Freycinet National Park

Mount Field National Park

South Bruny National Park

Fortescue Bay

Peggs Beach Conservation Area

Arthur Pieman Conservation Area

Mount William National Park

Lime Bay State Reserve

A campsite at Narawntapu National Park, in the state's north. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

How does it work?

The booking platform provides information for each site, including amenities, nearby activities, and relevant alerts for the region.

Loading...

The new system has introduced a flat rate per site for groups of up to six people, rather than being charged per person for a campsite.

For campsites at Freycinet National Park and Fortescue Bay, users will be able to view which numbered campsites are available, along with a map that displays the location of each site.

Those numbered sites can then be booked, and campers must use the site number which corresponds to their booking.

Campsites at Mount Field National Park, in the state's south, will need to be booked through the online system. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

The remaining eight locations all use unnumbered sites.

PWS director of tourism Tory Ross told 936 ABC Hobart those sites will function as a "turn up and camp, first-in, best-dressed" system once they have been booked through the online portal.

"What we have done to allow for some walk-ins and people that don't know about the system over summer is just withhold some of the inventory," Ms Ross said.

" So, there will be some spaces available if people just turn up. "

Ms Ross said over the summer there will be more PWS staff at these sites to help campers who have arrived without booking online.

"We're really hoping that as awareness grows, people will comply with the camping booking system and that will help us manage that issue over time," she said.

How much will it cost to camp?

Campers will be able to book at a flat rate per site for groups of up to six people.

Groups of more than six people will need to book extra campsites.

Tasmania looks to halt 'ghost camping' "Ghost camping" is again a hot topic as frustrated holiday-makers find empty tents or caravans reserving sites at campgrounds.

Standard campsites can be booked for $18 per night, premium unpowered sites will be $24 per night, and premium powered sites will be $35 per night.

Existing rates for bookings made before the new booking system will be honoured.

The Tasmanian government said revenue generated through camp bookings will be reinvested into the management of Tasmania's national parks and reserves.

PWS said many campgrounds across the state will remain free and won't require bookings.

What other changes are planned?

Parks Minister Nick Duigan announced the new booking system at Narawntapu National Park. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

In an announcement of the new service at the beginning of the week, Tasmanian Minister for Parks Nick Duigan said the system will expand over time to include other "products and experiences" managed by PWS.

These include walks, cave tours, accommodation, and park passes, all managed through a single online portal.

World.title: Treaty, tribunal and Māori rights all on the ballot in NZ election
World.content:
As the people of Aotearoa/New Zealand head to the polls, many Māori voters will be wondering what the result will mean for the nation's founding document, the Treaty of Waitangi, and the future of Māori rights.

In recent years, the coalition government has rolled back a range of policies that enshrined the special status of Māori in public life.

Māori make up about 18 per cent of the population, or close to 1 million people.

So how have Māori rights featured in this year's campaign?

And with mounting cost-of-living pressures and struggles to find stable jobs and housing, how significantly will they shape people's voting decisions?

Who are the parties and what are they proposing?

NZ First leader Winston Peters (left), NZ Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and ACT Leader David Seymour (right). (AAP: Mark Coote)

New Zealand's government is a coalition of three parties: New Zealand National Party, ACT New Zealand (ACT NZ) and New Zealand First (NZ First).

Led by David Seymour, ACT believes there should be "one law for all, one future together" and calls for the elimination of "race-based" policies.

Most controversially, it wants the Waitangi Tribunal abolished once all historical claims are completed.

The tribunal is an independent commission of inquiry that was set up to investigate breaches of the nation's founding document: the Te Tiriti O Waitangi.

"The tribunal has expanded beyond its original purpose over time, now acting like an alternative law-making body, passing judgement on decisions that properly belong to elected governments and parliament," a spokesperson for ACT told the ABC.

Maori seats in New Zealand's parliament could be under threat this election. (ABC News: Emily Clark )

The party also wants to end targeted roles for Māori people and compel government departments to deliver services by "need, not race".

On Monday, NZ Prime Minister Christopher Luxon also said the tribunal "could be" abolished if the coalition was re-elected, calling for a debate about its future.

"[It] could be no role, could be evolved role, adjusted role," he told NewstalkZB.

How New Zealand reneged on its treaty with Māori Aotearoa New Zealand has had a treaty in place for almost two centuries but it wasn't until the 1970s that it was truly honoured. So what happened?

The Waitangi Tribunal has been instrumental in protecting Te Reo Māori — the Māori language — after concerns that fluent speakers were rapidly declining.

In 1987, it was made an official language and is now embraced across New Zealand, with Māori broadcasters speaking fluently on-air and 200,000 people speaking the language in casual conversation.

NZ First also backs scrapping the tribunal and has promised to hold a referendum on the future of Māori seats in parliament.

These were created during a period when most Māori people could not vote, despite paying hefty amounts of land tax.

In response, the Māori Representation Act 1867 created four dedicated Māori electorates, which gave Māori men the right to vote, and women two decades later.

Members of the Te Pati Maori party in parliament. (AP Photo: Charlotte Graham-McLay)

Today, there are seven Māori electorates.

ACT also backs the abolition of Māori seats, telling the ABC political rights should "not depend on ancestry".

On the other hand, Indigenous party Te Pāti Māori says Māori seats are "a democratic mechanism that enables Māori representation in parliament, representation that Māori voters continue to choose in growing numbers."

Te Pāti Māori would not only retain the Waitangi Tribunal but make its recommendations binding — saying at present governments "can simply ignore them", its leader Rawiri Waititi has said.

What do Kiwis think about Māori rights?

Lara Greaves has been studying voter trends, particularly with Māori voters, for years. (Supplied: Lara Greaves)

Māori rights have been raised by the minor parties — on the left and right — but have not been a major feature of the campaign, says Lara Greaves, an associate professor of politics at the Victoria University of Wellington

An Ipsos survey revealed the top three issues for voters were inflation and cost of living (64 per cent), access to healthcare and hospitals (45 per cent), and petrol prices (31 per cent).

Only three per cent of participants ranked Māori issues as the most significant issue.

New Zealand's founding document, the Treaty of Waitangi, on display in Wellington. (ABC News: Emily Clark)

The Whakaata Māori–Curia poll of more than 600 registered Māori voters found 84 per cent agreed that upholding the Te Tiriti O Waitangi was important.

But when asked about the election, nearly half nominated the cost of living as the most important issue.

Outside of the election, pride in Māori culture and protecting Indigenous rights is still important for many New Zealanders.

Seventy per cent think the treaty should be protected by legislation and the constitution, according to a 2026 report by the Te Kāhui Tika Tangata Human Rights Commission.

Many New Zealander's take pride in the country's Indigenous culture. (Flickr/Tony)

Nearly 80 per cent agree that protecting and celebrating Māori culture, language and identity is important.

It is not that voters do not see treaty rights as important, Ms Greaves said, but it might not be "front of mind" during an election.

How should Māori flags be represented in national life?

The Māori flag is a show of pride for Māori and non-Māori people. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

This year there is also a live debate happening about the role of the Māori flag.

A petition asking the government to permanently fly the Māori flag alongside the NZ flag on Auckland's harbour bridge has almost 30,000 signatures.

Awerangi Tamihere, who launched the petition, said she took inspiration from Australia.

"We have to acknowledge our Indigenous brothers and sisters in Australia for having the Indigenous flag fly on the Sydney Harbour Bridge," she said.

"That really is an icon and a symbol of the maturity of the nation in some respects."

The Aboriginal flag has been flying permanently on the Harbour Bridge since 2022. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi )

The goal is to reach 80,000 signatures by Waitangi Day in February 2027.

"It's an interesting time in our nation about Indigenous peoples and their rights," Ms Tamihere said.

"It is not about taking down the New Zealand flag, but it's saying there's actually a place for both to be able to fly in New Zealand."

She said the debate about Māori representation should not be seen as "divisive".

"It's just saying instead of … a choice between one or the other, we have to take the word 'or' and say there's a place for both and swap it with 'and'," she said.

"We call them 'Tangata Tiriti', our people who are non-Māori; they use that flag a lot now too, so it's just seen as a wonderful affirmation and pride in identity of the Indigenous peoples of this country."

World.title: How looking inside a cancer's DNA can add years to someone's life
World.content:
Diagnosed with an aggressive and incurable brain cancer at just 31, Emily Capper was given as little as nine months to live.

That was almost five years ago.

After her grade 4 glioblastoma stopped responding to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, the DNA of Ms Capper's tumour was tested in a process known as genomic profiling, providing her team with clues to match her to a more targeted treatment.

"It's meant everything. Without this, I don't know where I would be … this was my last option," she said.

Following a new federal government funding commitment, 25,000 additional Australians will now be able to access comprehensive genomic profiling, which opens the door to more personalised treatments for people with advanced or incurable cancers.

"It's like giving us a topographic map and a compass," said Rob Zielenski, who is a senior medical oncologist at Orange Hospital and leading the clinical trial Ms Capper is enrolled in.

Dr Rob Zielenski is a senior medical oncologist at Orange Hospital and leading the clinical trial Emily Capper is enrolled in. (ABC News: Xanthe Gregory)

"[It] helps me direct the patient to the right treatment and really importantly, avoid the wrong treatment because that comes with toxicity … and wasted time on futile therapy."

Cancer treatment has traditionally focused on where in the body it started and it was difficult for doctors to explain why two patients with the same cancer responded differently to the same treatment.

But "looking under the bonnet", as Dr Zielenski describes it, takes guesswork out of the equation and homes in on about 500 to 600 genes that can be altered in any cancer.

"The evidence is clear that putting patients on matched treatments doubles their survival. And that is profound," he said.

In Ms Capper's case, her cancer had what is known as the BRAF mutation, a change in the gene that helps drive the growth of some cancers.

In the 10 months she has been taking a targeted drug through Dr Zielenski's clinical trial, her cancer has stopped growing and is expected to slowly shrink over time.

"I'm still able to work and live my best life and really enjoy those around me while I can," she said.

One in four with incurable cancers missing out on precision care

Ms Capper was matched to Dr Zielenski's trial by not-for-profit organisation Omico, which is leading the charge on precision oncology in Australia.

Genomic profiling can cost thousands of dollars but Omico provides it for free and, when possible, links patients to the best available clinical trial or treatment for their cancer's "fingerprint".

Ms Capper was matched to Dr Zielenski's trial by not-for-profit organisation Omico. (ABC News: Xanthe Gregory)

The organisation has so far supported more than 30,000 Australians but an injection of $71 million in the latest federal budget has allowed the company to continue working with four laboratories across the country to deliver the program for another three years.

As a result, it's expected more than 1,130 Australians accessing this type of targeted treatment will reach their five-year cancer survivorship.

Omico receives one patient referral every 15 minutes, but chief of science and strategy for Omico, David Thomas, said limited resourcing meant only one in four people with an incurable solid tumour could be helped in this way.

Genomic profiling takes guess work out of the equation and homes in on around 500 to 600 genes that can be altered in any cancer. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"That's about 34,000 Australians [per year] that we unfortunately can't reach at the moment who might potentially benefit," Professor Thomas said.

"There's definitely a need for more clinical trials of these promising treatments but there's also a need to think about how we make those drugs available at the end of the process."

If a patient cannot be linked to a clinical trial by Omico they may have to pay thousands of dollars a month to access the drug on a private prescription, as many emerging cancer therapies aren't subsidised by the government through the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS).

Professor David Thomas said limited resourcing meant only one in four people with an incurable tumour could be helped. (ABC News: Chris Taylor)

Only 25 per cent of medicines launched globally over the past decades are on the PBS, according to a recent report by Medicines Australia.

"Those drugs are coming on thick and fast, they're proving highly effective, but how we can ultimately afford them with an aging population and a diminishing taxpayer base is a problem for the government to think about," Professor Thomas.

Making genomics part of routine cancer care

Queensland University cancer genomics specialist Amy McCart Reed said precision oncology also made the health system more efficient.

"At the moment, a lot of our therapies could be seen to be more like a broad spectrum antibiotic where we just give them and hope that it's killing the cancer cells," she said.

"So any movement we can make in this space where we're being quite targeted about who gets which therapy has an advantage to the patients, but also there are huge flow-on effects for the economy because a lot of these drugs are expensive."

Ms Capper said she wants others with cancer to know about alternative treatment options. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

However, she said the public system was a long way from being equipped to test everyone, and there was no point burdening someone with information about their cancer unless it could inform their treatment.

Health Minister Mark Butler said the federal government was mobilising to scale up health infrastructure, so genomic profiling could be offered more widely across Australia.

"Ultimately of course we want to see this become a standard of care and to become a sort of feature of the health system more broadly, rather than something situated into research programs," he said.

He also pointed to the government's efforts to expedite the listing of medications on the PBS at a time of "turbocharged discovery", which meant a huge number of new cancer therapies were hitting the market and needed to be carefully assessed.

Emily Capper was given just nine months to live. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

As Ms Capper prepares the next generation for the years ahead in her role as a teacher, her own future remains uncertain.

The drug she is taking is not a cure but it will continue to buy her time, hopefully until the next scientific advancement comes along.

When she first received her diagnosis, she hoped she would stay alive long enough to see one of her favourite performers, Taylor Swift, in Australia. Against the odds she made it and has since ticked many other things off her bucket list.

"It's hard to imagine what my life would have been like, and I think that's really hard. But knowing that I've got a chance to live longer is really incredible."

World.title: Nearly $2m compo paid to company over scrapped Macquarie Point power plan
World.content:
The Tasmanian government has paid about $2 million not to build a thermal power plant at Macquarie Point, the site of the planned Hobart stadium.

The government is in final negotiations with BESIX Watpac to build the 23,000-seat stadium at the 9.3-hectare site on Hobart's waterfront.

Waste and energy company Veolia had signed an agreement with the Macquarie Point Development Corporation (MPDC) to develop a District Energy Infrastructure Scheme (DEIS), including a thermal energy plant.

However, it will not go ahead, as the government looks for other options to power the site.

The government is considering connecting the stadium to the existing electricity network, but the cost of the connection is yet to be finalised. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

The minister in charge of the precinct, Eric Abetz, has now written to Tasmanian Greens Deputy Leader Vica Bayley to reveal the cost of exiting that agreement.

"The final invoice received was $1,788,236.50 plus GST and was paid on June 24, 2026," Mr Abetz wrote.

Minister Abetz said connecting to the current network was "lower risk and cost" than continuing with the thermal energy plant concept.

He said the cost was not included in the stadium project budget of $1.13 billion.

Eric Abetz revealed the government paid almost $2 million to exit the agreement with Veolia. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

"The DEIS predated any discussion on the development of a stadium on site and is not required for, or part of, that project," he wrote.

The cost is on top of $667,407 paid to a Melbourne-based firm, Renewable Intelligence, for earlier project work.

Mr Bayley said it was another example of "the slow-moving train wreck that is the Macquarie Point stadium".

"The fact that the government's so willing to just throw away millions of dollars of money, not to proceed with projects that they thought were important once upon a time — it just shows an absolute wilful disregard for our money, the taxpayers' money," Mr Bayley said.

Vica Bayley has criticised the government's spending on abandoned Macquarie Point projects. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Power connection yet to be costed

In his letter, Mr Abetz said Veolia's work would "inform the final power supply and mechanical design solution".

"To deliver power to the stadium, an electrical supply connection will be made from the North Hobart substation, using capacity in the existing network which I understand is more cost effective than proceeding with the DEIS thermal power plant," Mr Abetz wrote.

He said the cost of connecting the stadium was still being finalised, and was not included in the current cost estimates.

Hobart stadium power options uncosted, not finalised Major upgrades to Hobart's power grid to supply the Macquarie Point stadium are yet to be finalised or costed, with the final estimate for the precinct's energy demand increasing by almost 50 per cent in a year.

Mr Abetz told a budget estimates committee earlier this year the stadium would require 9.7 megavolt-amperes (MVA) of power.

However, documents obtained by the ABC show TasNetworks has told MPDC the precinct would require 15.7 MVA — more than the existing capacity within the Hobart network.

At the time, the network operator put forward three potential locations for a new substation, either at Macquarie Point or the nearby suburb of Glebe.

Millions paid to cast aside plans

Property developer Milieu was paid $1.257 million to abandon its plans for the Escarpment housing project, slated for Macquarie Point.

The Hobart Brewing Company was also paid $1.84 million to terminate its 10-year lease of The Goods Shed.

The proposed Macquarie Point stadium is expected to cost $1.13 billion, with the final price still uncertain. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Meanwhile, the ABC revealed last week that an unsuccessful bidder for the stadium construction tender would be reimbursed $2 million for its costs.

Failed stadium bidder to get millions reimbursed A failed bidder in the tender to build Hobart's stadium is set to have $2 million of its costs reimbursed by the Tasmanian government.

The figure was revised up from the original cap of $250,000.

While the stadium was priced most recently at $1.13 billion, it is widely expected to cost more due to worldwide inflation caused by the Middle East war.

When announcing BESIX Watpac as the preferred construction bidder last month, Premier Jeremy Rockliff refused to repeat his commitment to cap the state's contribution at $875 million.

He has committed to releasing the cost before a final contract is signed.

World.title: Michael Parkinson wasn’t as confident as he looked, documentary reveals
World.content:
When the late, great chat show host Michael Parkinson's beloved father died, his grief led him to Australia.

Fast facts about Parky What: A documentary about the Michael Parkinson we didn't see. Directed by: Luke Mazzaferro, Luke Cornish. Starring: Michael Parkinson. When: Now, at the British Film Festival. Likely to make you feel: Like the icon was human, just like us.

He was embraced by local audiences and Parkinson in Australia aired on the ABC from 1979 to 1982.

Mike, the second of Michael's three sons, said his dad "felt safe in Australia".

"They loved him and took him very much to their hearts," he says.

"In a sense, it was a place where he could be himself. He felt comfortable there."

Michael's father, John, was a miner who worked in the South Yorkshire pits. He wanted more for his only son and cast his eye far and wide.

"My grandfather was obsessed with Australians," Mike says.

"He actually described them as a lost tribe of sun-bronzed Yorkshiremen."

Bob Hawke on Michael Parkinson's show. (Supplied)

John passed that love on to Michael.

"My dad's biggest hero was Keith Miller, the Australian cricketer, so there was always that fascination," Mike says.

He insists you can see the shift on camera when his dad landed.

"He really did feel so much solace and happiness there, and I think that's why, in many of his Australian interviews, he was far more relaxed and open than he was over here," Mike says.

Beyond the chair

Michael's work is honoured honoured in Parky, co-directed by Australian filmmakers Luke Mazzaferro (A Fire Inside) and Luke Cornish (Dance Life).

The film, which is being screened at the British Film Festival, features many famous faces, including Helen Mirren, Richard Burton, Judi Dench, Kylie Minogue, Mick Jagger, George Michael and Bob Hawke.

Billy Connolly (middle) and Tom Cruise (right) on Michael Parkinson's chat show, Parky, in 2004. (Supplied)

"He gave to the world these incredible long-form interviews that really are a time capsule, over the decades," Mazzaferro says.

"But it was the insights brought by Mike, his mother Mary, and brothers Andrew and Nick, that revealed the man behind the questions."

Parky goes beyond the black leather chair, giving us a clearer sense of a working-class man who was surprisingly shy and insecure.

"He was born in a pit village," Mike, one of the film's producers, says.

"Now, he was lucky. He had a far-sighted mother who refused to have any more children, because children cost money. His father was a magnificent man who worked six days down the pit, never complained, didn't drink, wasn't violent and loved him.

"But their upbringings were tough, and I think it bred a particular generation that weren't necessarily in touch with their feelings, that didn't lend themselves too much to introspection."

Mazzaferro was struck by an interview with Some Like It Hot star Tony Curtis, who asked a pointed question about what Michael thought of himself.

"It's fascinating, seeing the change in physicality," Mazzaferro says.

"He shifts uncomfortably in his seat and looks quite nervous, almost as if he's catching himself thinking, 'Will I? Won't I?'

"It helped the film click into place.

" It was a proper eureka moment. "

All in the timing

Michael leant on alcohol after his father's death and could get cranky with his sons, but his confidence grew in Australia.

Michael Parkinson with fans in the '70s. (Supplied)

"England is still so class-ridden and the fact is that my father never felt part of it," Mike says.

"He always felt that at any time someone at the BBC or wherever he worked would come up to him, tap him on the shoulder and go, 'You don't belong here.'"

It helped that Australia was becoming surer of itself during the 1970s and '80s.

"It was a vibrant, self-aware, cocky nation and dad wanted to celebrate it and celebrate its talent," Mike says.

"You had George Miller and Mad Max and Men at Work. My father's timing was impeccable."

But opportunity also arose for his mother, Mary, who was also from a mining family and met Michael when she was teaching.

"She met a TV executive who said she should screen-test, and she skyrocketed because, like my dad, she was authentic," Mike says.

"The camera loved her and she was very stylish."

This was after their return to the UK from Australia in 1983. The launch of TV-am failed and Michael was floundering just as Mary's star was rising.

"She couldn't walk around Marks & Spencer's doing her food shopping without someone coming up and thanking her," Mike says.

Swimmer Ian Thorpe revealed he was gay in an interview with Michael Parkinson in 2014. (Channel Ten)

It was a source of friction in their marriage.

"Unfortunately, she was a product of her time," Mike says.

" Shirley MacLaine told my dad he was a male chauvinist, and he was. Mum made the decision that she couldn't be arsed with the hassle, so she stayed at home. "

Mazzaferro knew that they were onto something by exploring these curlier aspects of their otherwise loving family dynamic.

"Karen and I were led by this incredible insight from Mike," he says.

"We started looking at the show through the lens of his questions being an insight into Parky, figuring out things going on in his own life.

"Patterns emerge — the constant questioning about fathers, about marital relationships or addiction, or contending with fame. And so Parky became a treasure hunt, mining all of the interviews to find those rare golden nuggets where he opened up."

Dream big

Mike, who also produced the 2021 documentary Parkinson at 50, knows a time will come when he must step back from his father's archives.

"I don't ever get bored of it, because it's an absolute treat spending time thinking about my father in a way that probably sons don't get a chance to, but there has to come a time where I move on," he says.

He hopes Parky can inspire a new generation to follow his working-class father's journey from an English mining town to Australia and back.

"If you allow kids who don't necessarily have the background, upbringing or the education a chance, it's amazing what they can do," Mike says.

"Hopefully, that's what my father's life story shows."

Parky is screening at the British Film Festival.

World.title: ‘Tech bro concierge service’: State pressured to crack down on data centre clusters
World.content:
PoliticsNSWData centres ‘Tech bro concierge service’: State pressured to crack down on data centre clusters Jessica McSweeney Updated November 6, 2026 — 6:20am ,first published 4:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Smarter planning controls encouraging artificial intelligence companies to develop in special precincts would avoid unwanted US-style data centre clusters in Sydney’s densely populated suburbs, a parliamentary inquiry has found. The committee found that in Sydney, such clusters are being built in areas such as Lane Cove and Ryde simply because AI companies driven by market forces have found the capacity happens to exist there, not because of effective planning. A NSW parliamentary inquiry has called on the government to consider the cumulative impacts of data centres. James Brickwood The state should instead plan for large-scale data centre development in precincts, supported by shared energy and water infrastructure, rather than as isolated developments, the inquiry found. Lane Cove has become a suburban battleground between AI companies and angry locals after a cluster of data centres began opening in industrial-zoned parts of the suburb. Community backlash led to data centre proponent Goodman to abandon their $1.2 billion proposal. Now locals in other parts of the state are looking to launch similar campaigns.



Related Article Updated

Data centres Project Mars set off a war of words. Now the AI data centre is wiped off the face of earth Among the 23 recommendations was a request that the government change planning requirements to place a greater emphasis on assessing the cumulative impacts of data centres, and to require AI companies to properly listen and respond to community concerns. The inquiry also found the state government took an “entirely backwards” approach to data centre planning by opening up fast-track processes, including through the Investment Delivery Authority, but didn’t release data centre guidelines until a year later. That authority has endorsed at least 15 data centre projects in NSW valued at $51.89 billion, and the state has more than 60 data centres already operating or under construction. Committee chair and Greens MP Abigail Boyd said fast-track processes such as the Investment Delivery Authority, which she dubs the “tech bro concierge service”, are leading to growing anguish in communities concerned about data centres popping up in their backyards.



She pointed to this week’s midterm election results in the US, where anti-data centre Democrats swept gubernatorial races. “Unless we want to be where America is now, if we want to have actual sensible investment in data centres, we need to slow down, pause those approvals and give the community time to breathe,” she said. Data centre projects in Sydney. “If we don’t actually do what we’ve recommended in our report, we will end up with people just getting angrier and angrier.” The state government recently removed council powers to automatically trigger a referral to the independent planning commission when they objected to a state significant data centre, and increased the number of public objections needed to trigger a referral from 50 to 100.



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has said new data centre projects must pay for their own energy and must put at least as much energy back into the grid as they take out of it. The NSW inquiry found the rapid growth in electricity demand from data centres has the potential to hinder progress towards emission reduction targets if that growth isn’t matched by a similar growth in energy storage. Related Article Good Weekend AI data centres are springing up in communities across the country. Now, residents are fighting back Data centre proponents will have access to a 75-day express assessment process only if they comply with the state’s new data centre guidelines, which include funding additional water and energy supply. The report stopped short of calling for a pause on new data centre approvals after Labor and Liberal committee members voted together to remove the recommendation from the report. Lane Cove and Penrith councils used their evidence to call for a moratorium on new data centre approvals, citing concerns over community consultations and water and energy consumption. A NSW government spokesperson said many of the committee’s findings reflected what the government already heard while designing the state’s guidelines.



“This growing industry can also help support new investment in the renewable energy projects the state needs, so a moratorium is not the answer.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The ‘aggressive’ cancer battle behind son of a Bronco’s mission to be Wallabies’ future
World.content:
SportRugby UnionReds The ‘aggressive’ cancer battle behind son of a Bronco’s mission to be Wallabies’ future Nick Wright November 6, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. When Nick Conway should have been embracing his final year of school and preparing to stride into adulthood, he was fighting for his health in hospital with Les Kiss by his side. Overcoming adversity had been nothing new to the Conway clan. His father, Bob, represented the Brisbane Broncos on 12 occasions in an injury-riddled career, with his son even revealing a brain bleed played a role in a premature retirement. But what happened to Conway as he readied to leave a lasting legacy on Nudgee College shook the family of the Queensland Reds rookie to the core. Queensland Reds fullback Nick Conway trains. QRU Media “In grade 12, I was diagnosed with testicular cancer,” Conway reveals to this masthead.



“It was an absolute shock, I was as fit as a fiddle and in really good nick – I had no idea this could happen to a healthy person. It was probably a bigger shock for mum and dad; I’ve always sort of had the mindset of ‘fix it and move on’. Related Article Olympics How much will it cost getting to Brisbane 2032? A legend’s daughter and Olympic hopeful reveals “It was really innocuous; I had a hit to the area in a Reds’ under-18s game in 2024, and then I had the pain for a while. One day, it was just immense … my year 12 was a crazy year. “There was a three-week period where I got the scan back, and it was looking pretty dodgy, they sort of didn’t know and didn’t give my mum a straight answer, and then following that they did the surgery and said it was rare and aggressive.” Fortunately, Conway is now cancer-free, and he made a comeback to the field just eight weeks after his surgery. But the battles did not stop there.



An MRI found he had been playing with cracked ribs – suffered scoring a try in round two of Nudgee’s season before travelling to New Zealand for Australia’s under-18s clash. Even last season, as he plotted a Super Rugby debut, a mysterious back issue kept him sidelined. “It was a really tough year because they sort of didn’t know what was wrong for a while. Nothing was really working, we went to two different specialists, and nothing was really coming up on the scan, but I was still getting a lot of pain,” Conway says, having previously contended with stress fractures. Queensland Reds fullback Nick Conway during a beach training session. QRU Media “They actually diagnosed me with chronic back pain for a bit, and then I slowly worked my way through that. It was very mentally challenging, there was nothing on the scan, but I still had the pain – I reckon the frustration would’ve contributed to the pain, to be honest.” Those issues are now behind Conway, as the lightning fullback-winger ventured with the Reds on Wednesday to Japan and Italy for their off-season tour to face Saitama Wild Knights, Italy XV and Benetton in the inaugural Lynagh Cup.



Related Article Australian rugby ‘I just kept believing’: Why Kurtley Beale never gave up on a return to the Wallabies Given his dad’s history, rugby league loomed as an option for the now 19-year-old to pursue, before he arrived at Nudgee College. Despite having never played union before that, he was identified by Queensland rugby as a prospect worth watching. Upon his cancer diagnosis, the Reds’ cohort – led by Kiss and general manager of rugby Sam Cordingley – did not waiver in their commitment to the Junior Wallabies star. “I was tempted by some of the league things, but the Reds provided me with so much care through some tough times. I wouldn’t want to be anywhere else,” Conway says. “Dad sort of pushed me even more towards union because I think he was so grateful for how they supported me and [now for me to be] repaying that favour. They probably wouldn’t even know they were huge, but they were in that aspect.



“I was in a room with Kissy heaps as a 16-year-old and in awe of him, and they backed me and mum and dad all the way through and helped me with the surgery. That was probably one of my darkest times, but it really stuck with me through all that stuff – they’ve backed me in every sense.” On the field, Kiss’ coaching before he departed Ballymore to take the reins of the Wallabies – replaced by Auckland Blues premiership-winning mentor Vern Cotter – had encouraged Conway to trust his instincts. “If I did a chip-and-chase or a massive cutout, whatever I did, and it went wrong, he wouldn’t hammer me. He always backed me with skill,” he says. Now, Conway is viewing the Reds’ tour as a chance to prove he has a long future in Queensland and Australian colours.



He will be vying with close friend Treyvon Pritchard – who has toured with the squad hopeful of returning from a broken leg in its later stages – for the No.15 jumper vacated by departing Test custodian Jock Campbell (Shizuoka Blue Revs). “The leg’s coming along well, we’ve progressed to running over the last two weeks, and with the tour, we’re hoping to progress a bit faster and maybe catch a game towards the back end,” Pritchard confirms. Loading While an attempted poaching raid by the NRL’s Papua New Guinea Chiefs and his footwork to bamboozle All Blacks star Damian McKenzie put Pritchard’s name in lights, Conway believes the obstacles he overcame would ensure he remained locked in a fight for the jumper. “All those dark times and tough situations I feel like have happened for a reason and made me stronger. It just opened my eyes to that there are more important things than rugby, and just to be grateful for every opportunity you get,” he says.



“You don’t know what’s around the corner. To have that mental strength to push through those hard things, when you know you’ve been through something harder, you can always push through.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: How closely police officers stuck to the script at a random traffic stop
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Police How closely police officers stuck to the script at a random traffic stop Felicity Caldwell November 6, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Queensland police officers were given a script to improve relationships with drivers and riders, but found some of the emotional and two-way conversation points too challenging to put into practice. The Griffith University study analysed transcripts from footage taken on body-worn cameras at a random breath-test stop north-west of Brisbane, to observe how police officers applied a script provided by the researchers. The script was informed by elements of procedural justice – a philosophy including neutrality in decision-making, treating people with respect, giving citizens a voice, and demonstrating trustworthy motives through genuine concern. The research project took place at an RBT at Mount Glorious. It was part of a larger road policing project, Operation Whiskey Rider, looking at interactions with drivers and motorbike riders at a high-crash mountain road location, Mount Glorious, in Moreton Bay over a six-month period from April to October 2024.



Officers who were part of the experiment were asked to do an online module in procedural justice, which included a script they had to memorise and adapt into their own words. Griffith University criminology lecturer and former police detective Dr Margo van Felius. Co-author Associate Professor Lyndel Bates said many officers reliably introduced themselves, conveyed road toll information, explained the survey, and offered a courteous farewell. But other parts of the script were far less consistently applied. Lead author and former police detective Dr Margo van Felius said police officers generally followed the respectful and straightforward parts of the script, but elements requiring emotional engagement and two-way conversation were much harder to put into practice.



The researchers suggested it may have been difficult for officers to talk about notifying families about deaths because of the emotional impact on themselves, or they might have thought it was inappropriate in a brief roadside stop. The script - and the delivery rate Hello, my name is... (91%)

You have not been singled out today. We are pulling over as many drivers and riders as we can today. (6%)

Did you know there were 277 deaths on our roads in 2023. The largest group of fatalities was drivers. (70%)

One of the hardest jobs is to tell a person that their loved one has died in a traffic crash. (24%)

Mountain roads are particularly dangerous. (30%)

Can you please help us to reduce crashes by riding carefully and responsibly. (51%)

Thanks for chatting today. Here is a flyer that provides some safety tips. (54%)

The flyer explains that drivers can increase their safety by driving at or below the speed limit and according to the conditions. (11%)

Researchers at the university are running a survey about our interaction today. There is a survey link on the flyer. They would really appreciate your feedback. (89%)

Do you have any other questions for me about this traffic-stop or anything else? (14%)

Thank you for your time and attention today. Enjoy your drive. (92%) The script included mentioning that one of the hardest parts of their job was telling a person their loved one had died in a traffic crash. Point-to-point cameras tracked behaviour after the interaction, revealing a noticeable reduction in speeding. Co-author Chief Inspector Corey Allen said police had worked with Griffith University researchers since 2024 to develop a model officers could use to improve interactions with the public.



“From my own experiences as a police officer, I know that people often remember how an officer made them feel long after the interaction has ended,” he said. “Taking time to listen, explain our actions and treat people with dignity can make a significant difference to their confidence in police and their willingness to do the right thing.” Queensland Police Chief Inspector Corey Allen. The research, by the Griffith Criminology Institute, was published in Police Practice and Research. A police spokeswoman said officers used several tactics to make roads safer, including high visibility operations, to deter dangerous driving and intercept people breaking the law.



“While conducting a traffic intercept, police always aim to engage with the public courteously, informatively and professionally, with the intent of providing education, conducted enforcement and ultimately reduce the risk of serious and fatal traffic crashes.” Related Article Roads Crash victim’s daughter fights for compulsory eye checks So far this year, 250 people have died on Queensland’s roads, nearing the 254 deaths on the road at this time last year. Overall, 2025’s road toll was Queensland’s worst in 16 years. The National Road Safety Strategy aims to reduce road deaths by 50 per cent and serious injuries by 30 per cent by 2030, with a target of zero by 2050.



It is not on track to be met in any state or territory. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

My partner is a learning support assistant at a primary school. On any given day, about 20 per cent of rostered assistants are on sick or personal leave. Although teachers on leave are replaced with relief teachers daily, assistants are not. My partner and other attending colleagues have to continuously cover the duties of absent colleagues. It’s not part of the school’s strategy to run on reduced staff – the day runs smoothly only if everyone is present. My partner is feeling fatigued with the constant extra duties, which they have been undertaking for a long while. Since sick leave and personal leave are taboo subjects, and my partner would never raise or discuss it with colleagues, what are their avenues for discussing the issue with the school management without coming across as unwilling to do the extra work? What could the school even do about it? It’s common for there to be a tension between feeling a personal responsibility to confront a person on such an issue and being anxious about potential repercussions. John Shakespeare Dr Meghan Stacey, an Associate Professor and ARC DECRA Fellow at the University of New South Wales, told me it’s no secret that schools, to a great extent, run on the goodwill of staff.



“Learning support staff, like teachers, are attracted to their work because they see it as inherently worthwhile and valuable, which quite frankly makes it an easy target for exploitation,” she says. “This is a huge problem, and one that education systems have only recently started to show a serious interest in tackling. But while teacher workload has been getting some well-deserved attention in media and policy recently, the plight of learning support staff does not tend to get as much airtime.” As is so often the case with topics raised in Work Therapy, this is clearly a system problem. Stacey says this is concerning for exactly the reason you mention: while teachers are usually replaced if they can’t attend work on a given day, learning support staff may not be. This is true even though they play an essential role at schools across Australia. “The first thing I would say is that this situation does not seem to me to be the fault of the partner’s colleagues. As the writer says, sick leave and personal leave are ‘taboo’ – they are a fundamental right and entitlement,” she says.



“But perhaps more importantly, if around 20 per cent of support staff are away on any given day, then this indicates a problem that is bigger than any one individual. And, given problems of attrition and retention in the education workforce, the problem is likely to be happening in other schools, too.” Editor's pick Opinion

Work therapy Our OH&S officer is on a power trip. How do we make them stop? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor Such high proportions of learning support staff using sick and personal leave points to a lack of proper funding. Such circumstances lead to fatigue among learning support assistants, as you say, as well as stress and the possibility of burnout. Because allocation of money is at the heart of the problem, Stacey says that writing to your local member and agitating for fairer funding arrangements may be a good starting point. The obvious downside, of course, is that such change can happen slowly. Regarding what, if anything, the school can do, Stacey says it depends: “Some funding for support staff is tied to particular students and should be used primarily for that purpose. Other funding is more generalised.



“If they have a good relationship with their principal, the writer’s partner could speak to them about any possibilities within the budget for hiring more support staff to share the load. This might have the bonus effect of making work more manageable, reducing leave-taking before it can become a problem for other staff.” But Stacey acknowledges the budgets of many schools are stretched pretty thin as it is. With that in mind, another option is joining a union. The right union will depend on where you live and in which educational sector your partner works. If your partner were a school learning support officer in a NSW public school, for example, the Public Service Association might be the best option. I commend you for taking an interest in this subject and seeking a way to make a difference in your area or at your partner’s school. But as is so often the case with topics raised in Work Therapy, this is clearly a system problem. Editor's pick Opinion

Political leadership Albanese and Chalmers are mired in the swamp. One could be gone before the next election Niki Savva Award-winning political commentator and author



As Stacey says, for a broader change to happen, those responsible for that system need to seriously consider the structural issue at the heart of the question you’ve raised. “There’s clearly a need to better understand and appreciate the complex work being done in schools and how these institutional ecosystems function. Material supports must catch up soon, to enable staff such as the writer’s partner to do their crucial work,” she says. World.content:

Another wipeout for stocks tied to the buildout of AI data centres is overwhelming Wall Street and more than erasing all its gains from the day before, which was its best in three months. The S&P 500 fell 3.5 per cent after opening with a loss that accelerated through the morning. It’s on track for its worst drop since President Donald Trump shook markets worldwide in April 2025 after announcing his “Liberation Day” tariffs. Stock markets worldwide felt pressure from continued drops for companies that benefited from the boom in the artificial-intelligence technology industry. AP The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1,433 points, or 2.7 per cent, in midday trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 4.7 per cent lower. The losses are set to be more muted on the Australian sharemarket, with futures at 4.51am AEDT pointing to a loss of 36 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX jumped by 2.6 per cent on Thursday as markets rallied following the midterms, with the Democrats’ sweeping win fuelling optimism the Iran war could end soon, sending oil prices plunging. The Australian dollar is weaker at US69.52¢.



Stock markets worldwide felt pressure from continued drops for companies that benefited from the boom in the artificial-intelligence technology industry, and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbled 5.3 per cent. Such stocks have been swinging for months on worries that the construction of further AI data centres may slow because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money. Related Article Data centres Aftermarket raid: Embattled data centre company NextDC’s shares soar Tuesday’s US midterm elections added another challenge. The nationwide victories by Democrats raised the possibility that governments could force pauses in construction of more data centres. That would mean fewer purchases of AI chips, not to mention electricity and other products and services that are getting vacuumed up in the AI frenzy and driving much of the US economy’s growth. Nvidia fell 7.5 per cent and was by far the heaviest weight on the S&P 500, a day after dropping 3.2 per cent. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 14.6 per cent. CoreWeave, a company that rents access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 12.1 per cent. GE Vernova, which has been helping to power data centres, sank 6.1 per cent.



AI chip stocks are some of Wall Street’s most influential because they’ve become some of the largest. A 1 per cent move for Nvidia, for example, has more effect on the S&P 500 than a 1 per cent move for nearly any other US stock. The losses were broad, with every sector in the S&P 500 losing ground. The overwhelming losses drowned out a few big gains, including a 28 per cent jump for AppLovin after the marketing platform reported both revenue and profit that topped analysts’ expectations. The company also approved a program to send up to $US3.2 billion ($4.6 billion) to its investors by buying back its own stock, bringing the program’s total potential value to $US3.6 billion. Tapestry rallied 6.6 per cent after the company behind the Coach and Kate Spade brands likewise delivered a stronger profit than expected. It also raised its forecasts for revenue and earnings this fiscal year. Stock prices tend to follow where corporate profits and interest rates go over the long term, depending on them much more than on who controls what in Washington. In other financial markets, the initial knee-jerk reaction to the US midterm election results faded a bit. The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.6 per cent to $US97.11 and recovered a chunk of its nearly 9 per cent drop from the day before. Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal.



In the bond market, Treasury yields continued to ease. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.83 per cent from 4.90 per cent late Wednesday. It had been at 4.95 per cent on election night and above 5.30 per cent last month. Related Article Opinion

US midterms Down $60b, and counting: The midterms’ biggest loser isn’t Trump. It’s Elon Musk Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist That could be a signal that investors are herding into US Treasury bonds in search of something that’s safer to own than stocks. The drop also came despite some encouraging reports on the US economy. Fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week. A separate report, meanwhile, suggested overall productivity for US workers improved by more during the summer than economists expected. That could help the economy grow without adding pressure to the nation’s high inflation. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. Besides South Korea, Japan’s Nikkei 225 also felt the sting of drops for tech and AI-related stocks and sank 1.8 per cent.



London’s FTSE 100 dipped 0.4 per cent after the Bank of England increased its main interest rate for the first time in three years to help limit high inflation. The bank said its next moves on interest rates largely hinge on what happens with the Iran war, which sent oil prices and inflation higher worldwide. “We’ve seen encouraging news in the past 48 hours,” Bank Governor Andrew Bailey said at a press briefing. “The best thing that can happen is to resolve the conflict in the Middle East; there’s no question about it.” AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading.
