World.title: Sleepless nights, family tension and bullets in his arm: Bondi hero one year on
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For Ahmed Al Ahmed, the scene is still vivid. On a beautiful Sydney summer evening, he is crouching between two cars in a parking area at Bondi Beach. The warm air is full of the sound of gunfire. And screaming. Terrified people are streaming past his hiding spot, running and stumbling. He tries to make sense of what he is seeing and hearing, but his brain seems to have frozen. Even his body is acting strangely. He looks down and registers that the knee he injured in a work accident, the one that hurts like hell to bend, is flexed beneath him. No pain at all. “My god,” he says to his cousin, who is sheltering beside him, “what is happening?” It is just after 6.40pm on Sunday, December 14, 2025. In a couple of minutes, Al Ahmed will do something remarkable – something that will save many lives and irrevocably change his own. His action will be captured in a grainy video, which will be watched by millions of people around the world. He will be hailed as a hero by everyone from US President Donald Trump to King Charles III. He will be presented with a GoFundMe cheque for more than $2.5 million. After the fanfare dies down, he will struggle to regain the use of his bullet-riddled left arm. His two brothers will deny charges of trying to extort money from him. His father will accuse him of assault, then retract the allegation. He will write a memoir. Al Ahmed has quite a year ahead of him. But he doesn’t know any of that yet. For the moment, he is keeping his head down and listening to the shooting, which is getting closer. Heart thudding, he tries to remember the declaration of faith that Muslims are supposed to make to prepare for death. The words won’t come to him. Then a man steps into his line of vision. A man with a gun. Related Article Bondi shooting The world knows how they died. Their families share how they lived I meet Al Ahmed at Bondi on a day of swirling wind and rain. It is spring, but so cold that no one is swimming. The few walkers on the beachfront are wearing puffer jackets. Al Ahmed, 45, is smartly turned out in a blue sports coat, jeans and black loafers. His manner is reserved and courteous. Though he has lived in Australia for two decades, his English is heavily accented. “No one is going to forget that day,” he says. At North Bondi RSL Club, he orders a chai latte. This surprises me a little because I know from his book, Light Will Win, that Al Ahmed is a coffee guy. In fact, it was a craving for caffeine that put him into the middle of the worst act of terrorism on Australian soil. The way he tells it, he had driven to Bondi from his home in the Sutherland Shire, in southern Sydney, picking up his cousin, Hothefa Al Kanj, on the way. By the time they arrived, it was after 6pm. At one cafe after another, they were told the coffee machine had been turned off for the day. Al Kanj was all for giving up and getting a Coke. Al Ahmed, though, was a man on a mission.



Music was coming from a lit-up park at the northern end of the beach. Some kind of market or fair, Al Ahmed presumed. He and Al Kanj walked to the entrance, where security guards said it was a Jewish community festival, Chanukah by the Sea. No coffee cart, unfortunately. “They said, ‘If you want to come in, you’re welcome’,” Al Ahmed remembers. “I said, ‘No, thank you. I want to keep going. For the coffee.’ ” He and Al Kanj turned away from the festival. They had gone about 10 metres when they heard a sharp cracking sound. Then another. And another. “I asked my cousin, ‘What is this? It’s fireworks?’ ” Al Kanj said, “No. Run!” In a parking area overlooked by a pedestrian bridge that gave access to the beach from busy Campbell Parade, they ducked for cover between two vehicles. That’s where Al Ahmed was when the shooter appeared. Ahmed Al Ahmed tackles Sajid Akram during the Bondi Beach shooting. Fear was a familiar sensation to Al Ahmed. In news reports of what became known as the Bondi massacre, he was portrayed as an ordinary man who showed extraordinary courage. “I’m a normal guy,” he assures me more than once during our time together. “I’m the same as anyone.” But Al Ahmed had been tested in the course of his life. “For long stretches of my childhood,” he writes in his memoir, “fear was my only friend.” He grew up in north-western Syria, near the border with Turkey. Wolves prowled in the mountains and, from his village of Al-Nayrab, could sometimes be heard howling in the distance. Most of the men in his family were shepherds, and as a boy he would trek with them into the hills, where they camped under the stars while their sheep grazed in the high pastures. Up there, the wolves sounded very close. He remembers huddling by the campfire, wishing dawn would come. But the threat that felt biggest to Al Ahmed wasn’t out in the wild. It was inside his home. He claims in his book that his father, a policeman, was a hard and controlling figure who hit him at the slightest provocation. To me, he points out that this wasn’t unusual in the culture of the time. His father may have believed he was doing the right thing: his goal was to make his son tough. “Obviously he wanted me to be a strong man. But, you know, I was a child.” His beloved mother – “She’s the one who was caring” – would sometimes try to defend him, he says. As the oldest of seven children, Al Ahmed was expected to contribute to the household income. From the age of nine, he fitted his schoolwork around a string of jobs: labouring, delivering groceries, picking olives. At 18, he embarked on two years’ compulsory military service, at his father’s suggestion opting to do his time in the police wing of the army. He writes that the police training academy was run by officers seemingly selected for their sadism: they subjected conscripts to bizarre acts of cruelty, such as forcing them to lie in the icy exercise yard in their underwear on mid-winter nights, then blasting them with near-freezing water from fire hoses. It seemed to Al Ahmed that the brutality of the regime of then-president, Bashar al-Assad, had poisoned Syrian society as a whole, and he decided he would leave his home country. His other resolution: to be a completely different man from his father. He would be gentle, not domineering. He would live and let live.



There were two shooters, Al Ahmed realised. One was on the pedestrian bridge. The other – 50-year-old Sajid Akram – was standing in front of Al Ahmed, but looking the other way, so hadn’t noticed him. Al Ahmed could see Akram’s likely next victims: people who were lying defenceless on the grass, some of them injured. Thinking back on it, he says he didn’t make a conscious decision to charge at Akram. Rather, he saw the opportunity and took it. Related Article Bondi shooting Four heroes tried to stop the Bondi terrorists. Three paid with their lives “He was a big guy,” he says. “Very muscly. Higher than me.” As Al Ahmed grabbed Akram from behind, he heard himself swearing in what he describes as “the Aussie way”. Something along the lines of, “You motherf---er. You piece of shit.” His right arm was wrapped around Akram’s neck. Al Ahmed’s other arm theoretically wasn’t capable of much: the rotator cuff on his left shoulder had been damaged in a car accident, and recent surgery hadn’t yet restored it to full strength. But as the two men tussled, that arm did everything Al Ahmed asked of it, including seizing Akram’s rifle. Suddenly Akram was lying on the ground and Al Ahmed was aiming the gun at him. For Al Ahmed, getting out of Syria had felt like a release. He moved first to Dubai, where he and an uncle established a business importing and selling used luxury cars, then came to Australia. He arrived in 2006, aged 25, and says he felt at home from day one. He found employment on construction sites in Canberra and eventually qualified as a carpenter. He married Alsu, an Australian of Russian heritage, and in 2014 set himself up as a subcontractor, supplying teams of carpenters to building projects while continuing to ply his trade himself. He was busy and happy. But one day on a worksite he ruptured his anterior cruciate ligament, or ACL. He had reconstruction surgery on his knee in 2020, starting the long process of regaining his mobility just as the COVID-19 pandemic hit the construction industry. He reluctantly closed his company and moved with Alsu to Sydney, where he opened a shop selling tobacco and assorted paraphernalia. (After he became famous, it was reported that he had pleaded guilty to a number of minor tobacco offences in 2022, the same year he was granted citizenship.) He says the shop was only ever a stopgap. He sold it late last year, before Bondi, with the intention of returning to carpentry. When Al Ahmed came to Australia, he was keen to adopt local ways. He tried to learn to ride a surfboard but couldn’t get the hang of it: he kept falling into the water, and he wasn’t a strong swimmer. The waves scared him. He loved beaches, though, Bondi Beach in particular.



During his military service, Al Ahmed learnt how to clean a gun but not how to use it. He didn’t fire a single shot. At Bondi, he didn’t fire, either, which meant that Akram was able to get to his feet and retreat to the bridge. There he picked up another gun and resumed shooting before he was felled by a police bullet. In the days afterwards, amid the outpouring of admiration for Al Ahmed, some wondered why he didn’t shoot Akram when he had the chance. Among them was Gefen Bitton, an Israeli man who had arrived at his side as he tackled Akram and seized the rifle. In a recent book, Bondi Terror, by Sharri Markson and Alex Ryvchin, Bitton says he yelled at Al Ahmed: “What the f--- are you doing? F---ing shoot him or give me the gun.” Al Ahmed aims a rifle at Bondi terrorist Sajid Akram (lying on the ground, behind the bin) moments after wresting it from the gunman. Coming to his side, dressed in maroon, is Israeli man Gefen Bitton. Nine News I ask Al Ahmed if he has ever regretted not pulling the trigger. “Never, never, never,” he says. “My target, when I attacked him, was just to disarm him and stop him from killing people. Attempt to shoot him, no. I’m not the one who can do this. Taking the life of someone – it’s not my job.” The other gunman, Akram’s son, Naveed, kept firing from the bridge, and both Bitton and Al Ahmed were seriously injured. Five bullets entered Al Ahmed’s left arm and shoulder. He says the medics who treated him improvised a way to get him to an ambulance. “They said, ‘Forgive us, but we need to put you on a surfboard.’ ” Lying on his back, looking at the sky as he was carried to the carpark, he reflected that his wife would be amused if she could see him: “Ahmed Al Ahmed, finally on a surfboard.” The Akrams were supporters of Islamic State. Sajid was shot dead by police. Naveed would be charged with 78 offences, including 15 counts of murder and 43 of attempted murder. Al Ahmed says Alsu wasn’t entirely pleased when she learnt what he had done. “She asked me, ‘You didn’t think about your kids?’ I told her, ‘I did think about my kids but forgive me, I couldn’t handle it. People crying. Women. And no one there. It was a hard situation.’ ” He says he emphasised to his wife that he hadn’t intended to put himself in danger. “I ran to protect myself, to hide from the firing, like everyone. But when the evil came in front of me, forgive me, I’m not the person who can sit and wait and look.”



Alsu and Al Ahmed have two daughters, Sofia, now aged 6, and Claudia, 3. Al Ahmed says Sofia had a question for him when she visited him in hospital. “She told me, ‘Dad, why didn’t you go to take the gun from the other guy, on the bridge?’ ” Anthony Albanese visits Al Ahmed at St George Hospital two days after the massacre. Prime Minister’s Office via AP The governor-general, Sam Mostyn, came to his bedside, too, as did Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and the people who started the online appeal that raised more than $2.5 million for him from donors around the world. “He’d become a global story,” says Ian Robertson, a media law specialist and chair of legal firm Holding Redlich, who offered to help Al Ahmed navigate the unfamiliar territory in which he found himself. “He was not only getting inquiries from the Australian media, he was getting them from overseas as well. He was in pain, he wasn’t sleeping at all well, and he had this avalanche of people basically hounding him. So the job was to try to get that under control.” Al Ahmed was part of a small group of Bondi survivors and first responders honoured at the Sydney Cricket Ground before the final Test of the summer’s Ashes series in January. As the applause of the huge crowd washed over him, he bowed his head and put his right hand over his heart. Soon afterwards, he accepted an invitation to the US, where he visited a holy site of the Jewish movement known as Chabad. He was photographed praying alongside Rabbi Yehoram Ulman, founder of Chabad of Bondi and father-in-law of Rabbi Eli Schlanger, one of the 15 people killed by the terrorists. That Al Ahmed wore a yarmulke, the traditional Jewish skullcap, drew criticism in some quarters. In his book, he explains that he believes in respecting others’ religious beliefs and customs. “If they were to visit my mosque, they would remove their shoes,” he writes. “It’s a matter of basic humanity.” In New York, he met Democratic mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and was stopped in Times Square by a couple of cops on the beat, who asked if they could have a photo with him. Then it was on to Washington DC, where he was feted by members of the US Congress. They’d all seen the viral video. Most of them gave him medals. “They gave me their business cards as well,” he says. “Nice people. I love America.” Back in Australia, Ian Robertson watched Al Ahmed get a standing ovation as he was presented with the key to the City of Canterbury-Bankstown, a local government area in south-western Sydney. “He was kind of mobbed by people wanting to shake his hand and pat his back,” Robertson says. “Everywhere I went with him, same reaction. People walked up to him in the street to say, ‘Good on you’.” In March, he was given the key to the City of Waverley, which incorporates Bondi. With the key came a lifetime beach parking permit – a welcome gift for a man who’d collected a few tickets there in his time.

World.title: Stressed? These 10 blissfully serene places offer the perfect escape
World.content:
On a “stillcation” travel becomes less about collecting experiences and more about noticing where we are: the Pyrenees.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Emails. Phone calls. Appointments. Passwords. Protein. Water. Eight hours of sleep. Our lives have become a relentless pursuit of doing – and doing everything better. Even travelling can become a to-do list of bucket-list experiences, country counts and Instagrammable moments. The antidote? The “stillcation”. Although laughably named, this new way of holidaying pushes back against our culture of constant productivity and self-improvement. It’s not necessarily yoga at sunrise or a silent meditation retreat, although it can be. More simply, it’s about the absence of agenda. Of stripping life back to its essentials: good food, beautiful views, fresh air and anchoring yourself in the present moment. Instead of seeking destinations that offer the most to do, it asks where offers the best conditions for doing less. THE LOST ART OF DOING NOTHING “Man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone” was, according to French philosopher Blaise Pascal, the source of all humanity’s problems. Four centuries later, his observation feels oddly prescient. We rarely sit still – even when on holiday. The constant pressure to optimise our lives can put a strain on the nervous system, says Jamie Clements, a wellness retreat facilitator and author of The Next Breath. “Stress has become the baseline, and calm feels like the exception.” Tour operators sense there is a growing market for more profound ways to unplug. In a recent study, British tour company Inghams ranked almost 100 European destinations according to their stillness, with criteria including walking trails per square kilometre, air quality, birdsong richness, stargazing quality, human density and forest cover (Scotland’s Wester Ross took the top spot). 



Slowing down switches our nervous system from a fight-or-flight sympathetic state to a rest-and-digest parasympathetic system that lowers our blood pressure and heart rate. A recent study ranked European destinations according to their stillness. Scotland’s Wester Ross took the top spot. iStock But don’t assume a stillcation will immediately evoke a state of Zen. Like any other holiday – where it can take a week to unwind – the first day or two can feel uncomfortable. The point of a stillcation isn’t simply that sitting around feels nice. Removing the constant demand for attention – and replacing the thrum of traffic, screens and notifications with wind, water, birdsong and walking – may create the conditions in which both mind and body can begin to really recover. And the benefits extend beyond our own wellbeing. The qualities that make a destination “still” – low population density, dark skies, forests, clean air, biodiversity and quiet trails – depend on healthy, protected environments. Perhaps that is the real appeal of the stillcation. It doesn’t ask us to abandon movement, curiosity or adventure. It simply changes the objective. Travel becomes less about collecting experiences and more about noticing where we are; less about escaping life and more about inhabiting it. In a culture that has turned even rest into something to optimise, doing nothing might be the most radical itinerary of all. KANGAROO ISLAND, SOUTH AUSTRALIA



Kangaroo Island, with its salty Southern Ocean air, wineries and long lunches, is a great place to slow down. It’s just 45 minutes on the ferry from Cape Jervis in mainland South Australia to Penneshaw on Kangaroo Island, and yet the world changes completely in that short space of time. Suddenly, it’s all lungfuls of salty Southern Ocean air, visits to wineries, long lunches, strolls along secluded beaches and encounters with kangaroos, koalas and sea lions. This island wilderness is an ideal place to slow down, to do nothing, or at least very little. Kangaroo Island has famously had to recover from some deep wounds, in particular the bushfires of January 2020, which wiped out almost half the island, including its most famous resort, Southern Ocean Lodge. The slow recovery of the land and the wildlife, as well as the resort, has been heartening, and KI is once again an ideal destination for those seeking escape. Make no plans for your stay here. Have no lofty goals. Simply trust that you will explore and discover and enjoy at a pace that suits. How to do it Southern Ocean Lodge overlooks the wild coastline of Kangaroo Island, and costs $3400 a night; two-night minimum stay. Rates include all dining and drinks, signature experiences and island airport transfers. See southernoceanlodge.com.au FLINDERS ISLAND, TASMANIA There are more than 120 beaches to explore on Flinders Island.



Australia has more than its share of remote wilderness areas – the Red Centre, the Kimberley, Far North Queensland – but Flinders Island is a standout for its remarkable isolation. It is a rugged outcrop of land in the Bass Strait, about a 35-minute flight from Launceston or a seven-hour ferry trip from Bridport, an unspoilt landscape of granite mountains, windswept beaches and coastal heath land. Fewer than 1000 people live there. Plenty of wombats, however, call the island home, as do wallabies and abundant birdlife while minimal light pollution creates star-rich skies. There are more than 120 beaches to explore, flawless stretches of sand on which to lose yourself in thought, wrapped up tight against the wind, for hours on end. Hiking tracks here are like meditation paths. There’s a whisky distillery, a vineyard and a couple of nice places to eat. Or simply curl up by a fire and read a book. How to do it Australian Walking Holidays’ four-day Flinders Island Experience in Comfort features guided coastal walks and accommodation at a beachside eco-camp. It costs from $3275 a person, twin share. See australianwalkingholidays.com.au ABISKO, SWEDEN Viewing and photographing the northern lights by the Abisko Sky Station, Lapland, Sweden. Getty Images Most visitors come to this Swedish Lapland village to glimpse magic: the aurora borealis, or northern lights. This is one of the best places on Earth to see the phenomenon, from September to April, due to Abisko’s high latitude and its cloud-free “blue hole” microclimate, which keeps it as dry as the Gobi Desert. The lights aren’t the only reason to visit this gathering of only 85 permanent residents, however. Abisko, 250 kilometres north of the Arctic Circle near the Norwegian border, is also home to an eponymous national park, one that was established more than 100 years ago to protect subarctic flora and native wildlife. Tornetrask, the sixth-largest lake in Sweden, is also nearby and it freezes in winter.



Whatever the seasonal phenomenon you’re visiting to experience – midnight sun or northern lights – the common thread is the area’s natural attractions, the chance to be completely immersed in a world of deep quiet and flawless blue skies. Hike rugged trails, go dog-sledding, snow-shoeing, fishing, bird-watching or stargazing. Lean into the isolation. How to do it Nordic Travel offers a Winter in Swedish Lapland tour, including Abisko, northern lights viewing and accommodation. It costs from $4296 a person. See nordictravel.com.au THE PYRENEES, FRANCE AND SPAIN Mountainside accommodation in the Pyrenees, Andorra. iStock It’s difficult to believe that any sort of natural feature that separates France and Spain, two of the most popular tourist destinations on the planet, could be considered quiet, but the Pyrenees really is. This mountain range creates a wrinkled border between the two countries and offers wide-open spaces with myriad opportunities for mindful hiking, yoga, winter sports and thermal spas. On the French side, take time to wander through Parc National des Pyrenees, a stunningly beautiful reserve known for its karst valleys and caves. Several more national parks can be found along the border, with soaring limestone cliffs and flower-strewn meadows. The Spanish side, too, is dotted with smaller though no less spectacular national parks, many of them secluded and peaceful, where visitors can walk for an entire day without seeing another soul. And then, of course, there’s tiny Andorra, an entirely separate country and home to ski resorts and alpine national parks, with small villages in which to stay and relax and pretend the rest of the world doesn’t exist.

World.title: ‘Tech bro concierge service’: State pressured to crack down on data centre clusters
World.content:
PoliticsNSWData centres ‘Tech bro concierge service’: State pressured to crack down on data centre clusters Jessica McSweeney Updated November 6, 2026 — 6:20am ,first published 4:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Smarter planning controls encouraging artificial intelligence companies to develop in special precincts would avoid unwanted US-style data centre clusters in Sydney’s densely populated suburbs, a parliamentary inquiry has found. The committee found that in Sydney, such clusters are being built in areas such as Lane Cove and Ryde simply because AI companies driven by market forces have found the capacity happens to exist there, not because of effective planning. A NSW parliamentary inquiry has called on the government to consider the cumulative impacts of data centres. James Brickwood The state should instead plan for large-scale data centre development in precincts, supported by shared energy and water infrastructure, rather than as isolated developments, the inquiry found. Lane Cove has become a suburban battleground between AI companies and angry locals after a cluster of data centres began opening in industrial-zoned parts of the suburb. Community backlash led to data centre proponent Goodman to abandon their $1.2 billion proposal. Now locals in other parts of the state are looking to launch similar campaigns.



Related Article Updated

Data centres Project Mars set off a war of words. Now the AI data centre is wiped off the face of earth Among the 23 recommendations was a request that the government change planning requirements to place a greater emphasis on assessing the cumulative impacts of data centres, and to require AI companies to properly listen and respond to community concerns. The inquiry also found the state government took an “entirely backwards” approach to data centre planning by opening up fast-track processes, including through the Investment Delivery Authority, but didn’t release data centre guidelines until a year later. That authority has endorsed at least 15 data centre projects in NSW valued at $51.89 billion, and the state has more than 60 data centres already operating or under construction. Committee chair and Greens MP Abigail Boyd said fast-track processes such as the Investment Delivery Authority, which she dubs the “tech bro concierge service”, are leading to growing anguish in communities concerned about data centres popping up in their backyards.



She pointed to this week’s midterm election results in the US, where anti-data centre Democrats swept gubernatorial races. “Unless we want to be where America is now, if we want to have actual sensible investment in data centres, we need to slow down, pause those approvals and give the community time to breathe,” she said. Data centre projects in Sydney. “If we don’t actually do what we’ve recommended in our report, we will end up with people just getting angrier and angrier.” The state government recently removed council powers to automatically trigger a referral to the independent planning commission when they objected to a state significant data centre, and increased the number of public objections needed to trigger a referral from 50 to 100.



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has said new data centre projects must pay for their own energy and must put at least as much energy back into the grid as they take out of it. The NSW inquiry found the rapid growth in electricity demand from data centres has the potential to hinder progress towards emission reduction targets if that growth isn’t matched by a similar growth in energy storage. Related Article Good Weekend AI data centres are springing up in communities across the country. Now, residents are fighting back Data centre proponents will have access to a 75-day express assessment process only if they comply with the state’s new data centre guidelines, which include funding additional water and energy supply. The report stopped short of calling for a pause on new data centre approvals after Labor and Liberal committee members voted together to remove the recommendation from the report. Lane Cove and Penrith councils used their evidence to call for a moratorium on new data centre approvals, citing concerns over community consultations and water and energy consumption. A NSW government spokesperson said many of the committee’s findings reflected what the government already heard while designing the state’s guidelines.



“This growing industry can also help support new investment in the renewable energy projects the state needs, so a moratorium is not the answer.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The ‘aggressive’ cancer battle behind son of a Bronco’s mission to be Wallabies’ future
World.content:
SportRugby UnionReds The ‘aggressive’ cancer battle behind son of a Bronco’s mission to be Wallabies’ future Nick Wright November 6, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. When Nick Conway should have been embracing his final year of school and preparing to stride into adulthood, he was fighting for his health in hospital with Les Kiss by his side. Overcoming adversity had been nothing new to the Conway clan. His father, Bob, represented the Brisbane Broncos on 12 occasions in an injury-riddled career, with his son even revealing a brain bleed played a role in a premature retirement. But what happened to Conway as he readied to leave a lasting legacy on Nudgee College shook the family of the Queensland Reds rookie to the core. Queensland Reds fullback Nick Conway trains. QRU Media “In grade 12, I was diagnosed with testicular cancer,” Conway reveals to this masthead.



“It was an absolute shock, I was as fit as a fiddle and in really good nick – I had no idea this could happen to a healthy person. It was probably a bigger shock for mum and dad; I’ve always sort of had the mindset of ‘fix it and move on’. Related Article Olympics How much will it cost getting to Brisbane 2032? A legend’s daughter and Olympic hopeful reveals “It was really innocuous; I had a hit to the area in a Reds’ under-18s game in 2024, and then I had the pain for a while. One day, it was just immense … my year 12 was a crazy year. “There was a three-week period where I got the scan back, and it was looking pretty dodgy, they sort of didn’t know and didn’t give my mum a straight answer, and then following that they did the surgery and said it was rare and aggressive.” Fortunately, Conway is now cancer-free, and he made a comeback to the field just eight weeks after his surgery. But the battles did not stop there.



An MRI found he had been playing with cracked ribs – suffered scoring a try in round two of Nudgee’s season before travelling to New Zealand for Australia’s under-18s clash. Even last season, as he plotted a Super Rugby debut, a mysterious back issue kept him sidelined. “It was a really tough year because they sort of didn’t know what was wrong for a while. Nothing was really working, we went to two different specialists, and nothing was really coming up on the scan, but I was still getting a lot of pain,” Conway says, having previously contended with stress fractures. Queensland Reds fullback Nick Conway during a beach training session. QRU Media “They actually diagnosed me with chronic back pain for a bit, and then I slowly worked my way through that. It was very mentally challenging, there was nothing on the scan, but I still had the pain – I reckon the frustration would’ve contributed to the pain, to be honest.” Those issues are now behind Conway, as the lightning fullback-winger ventured with the Reds on Wednesday to Japan and Italy for their off-season tour to face Saitama Wild Knights, Italy XV and Benetton in the inaugural Lynagh Cup.



Related Article Australian rugby ‘I just kept believing’: Why Kurtley Beale never gave up on a return to the Wallabies Given his dad’s history, rugby league loomed as an option for the now 19-year-old to pursue, before he arrived at Nudgee College. Despite having never played union before that, he was identified by Queensland rugby as a prospect worth watching. Upon his cancer diagnosis, the Reds’ cohort – led by Kiss and general manager of rugby Sam Cordingley – did not waiver in their commitment to the Junior Wallabies star. “I was tempted by some of the league things, but the Reds provided me with so much care through some tough times. I wouldn’t want to be anywhere else,” Conway says. “Dad sort of pushed me even more towards union because I think he was so grateful for how they supported me and [now for me to be] repaying that favour. They probably wouldn’t even know they were huge, but they were in that aspect.



“I was in a room with Kissy heaps as a 16-year-old and in awe of him, and they backed me and mum and dad all the way through and helped me with the surgery. That was probably one of my darkest times, but it really stuck with me through all that stuff – they’ve backed me in every sense.” On the field, Kiss’ coaching before he departed Ballymore to take the reins of the Wallabies – replaced by Auckland Blues premiership-winning mentor Vern Cotter – had encouraged Conway to trust his instincts. “If I did a chip-and-chase or a massive cutout, whatever I did, and it went wrong, he wouldn’t hammer me. He always backed me with skill,” he says. Now, Conway is viewing the Reds’ tour as a chance to prove he has a long future in Queensland and Australian colours.



He will be vying with close friend Treyvon Pritchard – who has toured with the squad hopeful of returning from a broken leg in its later stages – for the No.15 jumper vacated by departing Test custodian Jock Campbell (Shizuoka Blue Revs). “The leg’s coming along well, we’ve progressed to running over the last two weeks, and with the tour, we’re hoping to progress a bit faster and maybe catch a game towards the back end,” Pritchard confirms. Loading While an attempted poaching raid by the NRL’s Papua New Guinea Chiefs and his footwork to bamboozle All Blacks star Damian McKenzie put Pritchard’s name in lights, Conway believes the obstacles he overcame would ensure he remained locked in a fight for the jumper. “All those dark times and tough situations I feel like have happened for a reason and made me stronger. It just opened my eyes to that there are more important things than rugby, and just to be grateful for every opportunity you get,” he says.



“You don’t know what’s around the corner. To have that mental strength to push through those hard things, when you know you’ve been through something harder, you can always push through.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: How closely police officers stuck to the script at a random traffic stop
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Police How closely police officers stuck to the script at a random traffic stop Felicity Caldwell November 6, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Queensland police officers were given a script to improve relationships with drivers and riders, but found some of the emotional and two-way conversation points too challenging to put into practice. The Griffith University study analysed transcripts from footage taken on body-worn cameras at a random breath-test stop north-west of Brisbane, to observe how police officers applied a script provided by the researchers. The script was informed by elements of procedural justice – a philosophy including neutrality in decision-making, treating people with respect, giving citizens a voice, and demonstrating trustworthy motives through genuine concern. The research project took place at an RBT at Mount Glorious. It was part of a larger road policing project, Operation Whiskey Rider, looking at interactions with drivers and motorbike riders at a high-crash mountain road location, Mount Glorious, in Moreton Bay over a six-month period from April to October 2024.



Officers who were part of the experiment were asked to do an online module in procedural justice, which included a script they had to memorise and adapt into their own words. Griffith University criminology lecturer and former police detective Dr Margo van Felius. Co-author Associate Professor Lyndel Bates said many officers reliably introduced themselves, conveyed road toll information, explained the survey, and offered a courteous farewell. But other parts of the script were far less consistently applied. Lead author and former police detective Dr Margo van Felius said police officers generally followed the respectful and straightforward parts of the script, but elements requiring emotional engagement and two-way conversation were much harder to put into practice.



The researchers suggested it may have been difficult for officers to talk about notifying families about deaths because of the emotional impact on themselves, or they might have thought it was inappropriate in a brief roadside stop. The script - and the delivery rate Hello, my name is... (91%)

You have not been singled out today. We are pulling over as many drivers and riders as we can today. (6%)

Did you know there were 277 deaths on our roads in 2023. The largest group of fatalities was drivers. (70%)

One of the hardest jobs is to tell a person that their loved one has died in a traffic crash. (24%)

Mountain roads are particularly dangerous. (30%)

Can you please help us to reduce crashes by riding carefully and responsibly. (51%)

Thanks for chatting today. Here is a flyer that provides some safety tips. (54%)

The flyer explains that drivers can increase their safety by driving at or below the speed limit and according to the conditions. (11%)

Researchers at the university are running a survey about our interaction today. There is a survey link on the flyer. They would really appreciate your feedback. (89%)

Do you have any other questions for me about this traffic-stop or anything else? (14%)

Thank you for your time and attention today. Enjoy your drive. (92%) The script included mentioning that one of the hardest parts of their job was telling a person their loved one had died in a traffic crash. Point-to-point cameras tracked behaviour after the interaction, revealing a noticeable reduction in speeding. Co-author Chief Inspector Corey Allen said police had worked with Griffith University researchers since 2024 to develop a model officers could use to improve interactions with the public.



“From my own experiences as a police officer, I know that people often remember how an officer made them feel long after the interaction has ended,” he said. “Taking time to listen, explain our actions and treat people with dignity can make a significant difference to their confidence in police and their willingness to do the right thing.” Queensland Police Chief Inspector Corey Allen. The research, by the Griffith Criminology Institute, was published in Police Practice and Research. A police spokeswoman said officers used several tactics to make roads safer, including high visibility operations, to deter dangerous driving and intercept people breaking the law.



“While conducting a traffic intercept, police always aim to engage with the public courteously, informatively and professionally, with the intent of providing education, conducted enforcement and ultimately reduce the risk of serious and fatal traffic crashes.” Related Article Roads Crash victim’s daughter fights for compulsory eye checks So far this year, 250 people have died on Queensland’s roads, nearing the 254 deaths on the road at this time last year. Overall, 2025’s road toll was Queensland’s worst in 16 years. The National Road Safety Strategy aims to reduce road deaths by 50 per cent and serious injuries by 30 per cent by 2030, with a target of zero by 2050.



It is not on track to be met in any state or territory. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: My partner’s colleagues are always off sick. Is it wrong to speak up?
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceWork therapy Opinion My partner’s colleagues are always off sick. Is it wrong to speak up? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor November 6, 2026 — 5:12am

November 6, 2026 — 5:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

My partner is a learning support assistant at a primary school. On any given day, about 20 per cent of rostered assistants are on sick or personal leave. Although teachers on leave are replaced with relief teachers daily, assistants are not. My partner and other attending colleagues have to continuously cover the duties of absent colleagues. It’s not part of the school’s strategy to run on reduced staff – the day runs smoothly only if everyone is present. My partner is feeling fatigued with the constant extra duties, which they have been undertaking for a long while. Since sick leave and personal leave are taboo subjects, and my partner would never raise or discuss it with colleagues, what are their avenues for discussing the issue with the school management without coming across as unwilling to do the extra work? What could the school even do about it? It’s common for there to be a tension between feeling a personal responsibility to confront a person on such an issue and being anxious about potential repercussions. John Shakespeare Dr Meghan Stacey, an Associate Professor and ARC DECRA Fellow at the University of New South Wales, told me it’s no secret that schools, to a great extent, run on the goodwill of staff.



“Learning support staff, like teachers, are attracted to their work because they see it as inherently worthwhile and valuable, which quite frankly makes it an easy target for exploitation,” she says. “This is a huge problem, and one that education systems have only recently started to show a serious interest in tackling. But while teacher workload has been getting some well-deserved attention in media and policy recently, the plight of learning support staff does not tend to get as much airtime.” As is so often the case with topics raised in Work Therapy, this is clearly a system problem. Stacey says this is concerning for exactly the reason you mention: while teachers are usually replaced if they can’t attend work on a given day, learning support staff may not be. This is true even though they play an essential role at schools across Australia. “The first thing I would say is that this situation does not seem to me to be the fault of the partner’s colleagues. As the writer says, sick leave and personal leave are ‘taboo’ – they are a fundamental right and entitlement,” she says.



“But perhaps more importantly, if around 20 per cent of support staff are away on any given day, then this indicates a problem that is bigger than any one individual. And, given problems of attrition and retention in the education workforce, the problem is likely to be happening in other schools, too.” Editor's pick Opinion

Work therapy Our OH&S officer is on a power trip. How do we make them stop? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor Such high proportions of learning support staff using sick and personal leave points to a lack of proper funding. Such circumstances lead to fatigue among learning support assistants, as you say, as well as stress and the possibility of burnout. Because allocation of money is at the heart of the problem, Stacey says that writing to your local member and agitating for fairer funding arrangements may be a good starting point. The obvious downside, of course, is that such change can happen slowly. Regarding what, if anything, the school can do, Stacey says it depends: “Some funding for support staff is tied to particular students and should be used primarily for that purpose. Other funding is more generalised.



“If they have a good relationship with their principal, the writer’s partner could speak to them about any possibilities within the budget for hiring more support staff to share the load. This might have the bonus effect of making work more manageable, reducing leave-taking before it can become a problem for other staff.” But Stacey acknowledges the budgets of many schools are stretched pretty thin as it is. With that in mind, another option is joining a union. The right union will depend on where you live and in which educational sector your partner works. If your partner were a school learning support officer in a NSW public school, for example, the Public Service Association might be the best option. I commend you for taking an interest in this subject and seeking a way to make a difference in your area or at your partner’s school. But as is so often the case with topics raised in Work Therapy, this is clearly a system problem. Editor's pick Opinion

Political leadership Albanese and Chalmers are mired in the swamp. One could be gone before the next election Niki Savva Award-winning political commentator and author



As Stacey says, for a broader change to happen, those responsible for that system need to seriously consider the structural issue at the heart of the question you’ve raised. “There’s clearly a need to better understand and appreciate the complex work being done in schools and how these institutional ecosystems function. Material supports must catch up soon, to enable staff such as the writer’s partner to do their crucial work,” she says. Send your questions through to Work Therapy by emailing jonathan@theinkbureau.com.au The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Wall Street plunges as AI stocks tumble, ASX set to slide lower
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets Wall Street plunges as AI stocks tumble, ASX set to slide lower Stan Choe November 6, 2026 — 5:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Another wipeout for stocks tied to the buildout of AI data centres is overwhelming Wall Street and more than erasing all its gains from the day before, which was its best in three months. The S&P 500 fell 3.5 per cent after opening with a loss that accelerated through the morning. It’s on track for its worst drop since President Donald Trump shook markets worldwide in April 2025 after announcing his “Liberation Day” tariffs. Stock markets worldwide felt pressure from continued drops for companies that benefited from the boom in the artificial-intelligence technology industry. AP The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1,433 points, or 2.7 per cent, in midday trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 4.7 per cent lower. The losses are set to be more muted on the Australian sharemarket, with futures at 4.51am AEDT pointing to a loss of 36 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX jumped by 2.6 per cent on Thursday as markets rallied following the midterms, with the Democrats’ sweeping win fuelling optimism the Iran war could end soon, sending oil prices plunging. The Australian dollar is weaker at US69.52¢.



Stock markets worldwide felt pressure from continued drops for companies that benefited from the boom in the artificial-intelligence technology industry, and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbled 5.3 per cent. Such stocks have been swinging for months on worries that the construction of further AI data centres may slow because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money. Related Article Data centres Aftermarket raid: Embattled data centre company NextDC’s shares soar Tuesday’s US midterm elections added another challenge. The nationwide victories by Democrats raised the possibility that governments could force pauses in construction of more data centres. That would mean fewer purchases of AI chips, not to mention electricity and other products and services that are getting vacuumed up in the AI frenzy and driving much of the US economy’s growth. Nvidia fell 7.5 per cent and was by far the heaviest weight on the S&P 500, a day after dropping 3.2 per cent. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 14.6 per cent. CoreWeave, a company that rents access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 12.1 per cent. GE Vernova, which has been helping to power data centres, sank 6.1 per cent.



AI chip stocks are some of Wall Street’s most influential because they’ve become some of the largest. A 1 per cent move for Nvidia, for example, has more effect on the S&P 500 than a 1 per cent move for nearly any other US stock. The losses were broad, with every sector in the S&P 500 losing ground. The overwhelming losses drowned out a few big gains, including a 28 per cent jump for AppLovin after the marketing platform reported both revenue and profit that topped analysts’ expectations. The company also approved a program to send up to $US3.2 billion ($4.6 billion) to its investors by buying back its own stock, bringing the program’s total potential value to $US3.6 billion. Tapestry rallied 6.6 per cent after the company behind the Coach and Kate Spade brands likewise delivered a stronger profit than expected. It also raised its forecasts for revenue and earnings this fiscal year. Stock prices tend to follow where corporate profits and interest rates go over the long term, depending on them much more than on who controls what in Washington. In other financial markets, the initial knee-jerk reaction to the US midterm election results faded a bit. The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.6 per cent to $US97.11 and recovered a chunk of its nearly 9 per cent drop from the day before. Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal.



In the bond market, Treasury yields continued to ease. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.83 per cent from 4.90 per cent late Wednesday. It had been at 4.95 per cent on election night and above 5.30 per cent last month. Related Article Opinion

US midterms Down $60b, and counting: The midterms’ biggest loser isn’t Trump. It’s Elon Musk Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist That could be a signal that investors are herding into US Treasury bonds in search of something that’s safer to own than stocks. The drop also came despite some encouraging reports on the US economy. Fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week. A separate report, meanwhile, suggested overall productivity for US workers improved by more during the summer than economists expected. That could help the economy grow without adding pressure to the nation’s high inflation. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. Besides South Korea, Japan’s Nikkei 225 also felt the sting of drops for tech and AI-related stocks and sank 1.8 per cent.



London’s FTSE 100 dipped 0.4 per cent after the Bank of England increased its main interest rate for the first time in three years to help limit high inflation. The bank said its next moves on interest rates largely hinge on what happens with the Iran war, which sent oil prices and inflation higher worldwide. “We’ve seen encouraging news in the past 48 hours,” Bank Governor Andrew Bailey said at a press briefing. “The best thing that can happen is to resolve the conflict in the Middle East; there’s no question about it.” AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Sleepless nights, family tension and bullets in his arm: Bondi hero one year on
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For Ahmed Al Ahmed, the scene is still vivid. On a beautiful Sydney summer evening, he is crouching between two cars in a parking area at Bondi Beach. The warm air is full of the sound of gunfire. And screaming. Terrified people are streaming past his hiding spot, running and stumbling. He tries to make sense of what he is seeing and hearing, but his brain seems to have frozen. Even his body is acting strangely. He looks down and registers that the knee he injured in a work accident, the one that hurts like hell to bend, is flexed beneath him. No pain at all. “My god,” he says to his cousin, who is sheltering beside him, “what is happening?” It is just after 6.40pm on Sunday, December 14, 2025. In a couple of minutes, Al Ahmed will do something remarkable – something that will save many lives and irrevocably change his own. His action will be captured in a grainy video, which will be watched by millions of people around the world. He will be hailed as a hero by everyone from US President Donald Trump to King Charles III. He will be presented with a GoFundMe cheque for more than $2.5 million. After the fanfare dies down, he will struggle to regain the use of his bullet-riddled left arm. His two brothers will deny charges of trying to extort money from him. His father will accuse him of assault, then retract the allegation. He will write a memoir. Al Ahmed has quite a year ahead of him. But he doesn’t know any of that yet. For the moment, he is keeping his head down and listening to the shooting, which is getting closer. Heart thudding, he tries to remember the declaration of faith that Muslims are supposed to make to prepare for death. The words won’t come to him. Then a man steps into his line of vision. A man with a gun. Related Article Bondi shooting The world knows how they died. Their families share how they lived I meet Al Ahmed at Bondi on a day of swirling wind and rain. It is spring, but so cold that no one is swimming. The few walkers on the beachfront are wearing puffer jackets. Al Ahmed, 45, is smartly turned out in a blue sports coat, jeans and black loafers. His manner is reserved and courteous. Though he has lived in Australia for two decades, his English is heavily accented. “No one is going to forget that day,” he says. At North Bondi RSL Club, he orders a chai latte. This surprises me a little because I know from his book, Light Will Win, that Al Ahmed is a coffee guy. In fact, it was a craving for caffeine that put him into the middle of the worst act of terrorism on Australian soil. The way he tells it, he had driven to Bondi from his home in the Sutherland Shire, in southern Sydney, picking up his cousin, Hothefa Al Kanj, on the way. By the time they arrived, it was after 6pm. At one cafe after another, they were told the coffee machine had been turned off for the day. Al Kanj was all for giving up and getting a Coke. Al Ahmed, though, was a man on a mission.



Music was coming from a lit-up park at the northern end of the beach. Some kind of market or fair, Al Ahmed presumed. He and Al Kanj walked to the entrance, where security guards said it was a Jewish community festival, Chanukah by the Sea. No coffee cart, unfortunately. “They said, ‘If you want to come in, you’re welcome’,” Al Ahmed remembers. “I said, ‘No, thank you. I want to keep going. For the coffee.’ ” He and Al Kanj turned away from the festival. They had gone about 10 metres when they heard a sharp cracking sound. Then another. And another. “I asked my cousin, ‘What is this? It’s fireworks?’ ” Al Kanj said, “No. Run!” In a parking area overlooked by a pedestrian bridge that gave access to the beach from busy Campbell Parade, they ducked for cover between two vehicles. That’s where Al Ahmed was when the shooter appeared. Ahmed Al Ahmed tackles Sajid Akram during the Bondi Beach shooting. Fear was a familiar sensation to Al Ahmed. In news reports of what became known as the Bondi massacre, he was portrayed as an ordinary man who showed extraordinary courage. “I’m a normal guy,” he assures me more than once during our time together. “I’m the same as anyone.” But Al Ahmed had been tested in the course of his life. “For long stretches of my childhood,” he writes in his memoir, “fear was my only friend.” He grew up in north-western Syria, near the border with Turkey. Wolves prowled in the mountains and, from his village of Al-Nayrab, could sometimes be heard howling in the distance. Most of the men in his family were shepherds, and as a boy he would trek with them into the hills, where they camped under the stars while their sheep grazed in the high pastures. Up there, the wolves sounded very close. He remembers huddling by the campfire, wishing dawn would come. But the threat that felt biggest to Al Ahmed wasn’t out in the wild. It was inside his home. He claims in his book that his father, a policeman, was a hard and controlling figure who hit him at the slightest provocation. To me, he points out that this wasn’t unusual in the culture of the time. His father may have believed he was doing the right thing: his goal was to make his son tough. “Obviously he wanted me to be a strong man. But, you know, I was a child.” His beloved mother – “She’s the one who was caring” – would sometimes try to defend him, he says. As the oldest of seven children, Al Ahmed was expected to contribute to the household income. From the age of nine, he fitted his schoolwork around a string of jobs: labouring, delivering groceries, picking olives. At 18, he embarked on two years’ compulsory military service, at his father’s suggestion opting to do his time in the police wing of the army. He writes that the police training academy was run by officers seemingly selected for their sadism: they subjected conscripts to bizarre acts of cruelty, such as forcing them to lie in the icy exercise yard in their underwear on mid-winter nights, then blasting them with near-freezing water from fire hoses. It seemed to Al Ahmed that the brutality of the regime of then-president, Bashar al-Assad, had poisoned Syrian society as a whole, and he decided he would leave his home country. His other resolution: to be a completely different man from his father. He would be gentle, not domineering. He would live and let live.



There were two shooters, Al Ahmed realised. One was on the pedestrian bridge. The other – 50-year-old Sajid Akram – was standing in front of Al Ahmed, but looking the other way, so hadn’t noticed him. Al Ahmed could see Akram’s likely next victims: people who were lying defenceless on the grass, some of them injured. Thinking back on it, he says he didn’t make a conscious decision to charge at Akram. Rather, he saw the opportunity and took it. Related Article Bondi shooting Four heroes tried to stop the Bondi terrorists. Three paid with their lives “He was a big guy,” he says. “Very muscly. Higher than me.” As Al Ahmed grabbed Akram from behind, he heard himself swearing in what he describes as “the Aussie way”. Something along the lines of, “You motherf---er. You piece of shit.” His right arm was wrapped around Akram’s neck. Al Ahmed’s other arm theoretically wasn’t capable of much: the rotator cuff on his left shoulder had been damaged in a car accident, and recent surgery hadn’t yet restored it to full strength. But as the two men tussled, that arm did everything Al Ahmed asked of it, including seizing Akram’s rifle. Suddenly Akram was lying on the ground and Al Ahmed was aiming the gun at him. For Al Ahmed, getting out of Syria had felt like a release. He moved first to Dubai, where he and an uncle established a business importing and selling used luxury cars, then came to Australia. He arrived in 2006, aged 25, and says he felt at home from day one. He found employment on construction sites in Canberra and eventually qualified as a carpenter. He married Alsu, an Australian of Russian heritage, and in 2014 set himself up as a subcontractor, supplying teams of carpenters to building projects while continuing to ply his trade himself. He was busy and happy. But one day on a worksite he ruptured his anterior cruciate ligament, or ACL. He had reconstruction surgery on his knee in 2020, starting the long process of regaining his mobility just as the COVID-19 pandemic hit the construction industry. He reluctantly closed his company and moved with Alsu to Sydney, where he opened a shop selling tobacco and assorted paraphernalia. (After he became famous, it was reported that he had pleaded guilty to a number of minor tobacco offences in 2022, the same year he was granted citizenship.) He says the shop was only ever a stopgap. He sold it late last year, before Bondi, with the intention of returning to carpentry. When Al Ahmed came to Australia, he was keen to adopt local ways. He tried to learn to ride a surfboard but couldn’t get the hang of it: he kept falling into the water, and he wasn’t a strong swimmer. The waves scared him. He loved beaches, though, Bondi Beach in particular.



During his military service, Al Ahmed learnt how to clean a gun but not how to use it. He didn’t fire a single shot. At Bondi, he didn’t fire, either, which meant that Akram was able to get to his feet and retreat to the bridge. There he picked up another gun and resumed shooting before he was felled by a police bullet. In the days afterwards, amid the outpouring of admiration for Al Ahmed, some wondered why he didn’t shoot Akram when he had the chance. Among them was Gefen Bitton, an Israeli man who had arrived at his side as he tackled Akram and seized the rifle. In a recent book, Bondi Terror, by Sharri Markson and Alex Ryvchin, Bitton says he yelled at Al Ahmed: “What the f--- are you doing? F---ing shoot him or give me the gun.” Al Ahmed aims a rifle at Bondi terrorist Sajid Akram (lying on the ground, behind the bin) moments after wresting it from the gunman. Coming to his side, dressed in maroon, is Israeli man Gefen Bitton. Nine News I ask Al Ahmed if he has ever regretted not pulling the trigger. “Never, never, never,” he says. “My target, when I attacked him, was just to disarm him and stop him from killing people. Attempt to shoot him, no. I’m not the one who can do this. Taking the life of someone – it’s not my job.” The other gunman, Akram’s son, Naveed, kept firing from the bridge, and both Bitton and Al Ahmed were seriously injured. Five bullets entered Al Ahmed’s left arm and shoulder. He says the medics who treated him improvised a way to get him to an ambulance. “They said, ‘Forgive us, but we need to put you on a surfboard.’ ” Lying on his back, looking at the sky as he was carried to the carpark, he reflected that his wife would be amused if she could see him: “Ahmed Al Ahmed, finally on a surfboard.” The Akrams were supporters of Islamic State. Sajid was shot dead by police. Naveed would be charged with 78 offences, including 15 counts of murder and 43 of attempted murder. Al Ahmed says Alsu wasn’t entirely pleased when she learnt what he had done. “She asked me, ‘You didn’t think about your kids?’ I told her, ‘I did think about my kids but forgive me, I couldn’t handle it. People crying. Women. And no one there. It was a hard situation.’ ” He says he emphasised to his wife that he hadn’t intended to put himself in danger. “I ran to protect myself, to hide from the firing, like everyone. But when the evil came in front of me, forgive me, I’m not the person who can sit and wait and look.”



Alsu and Al Ahmed have two daughters, Sofia, now aged 6, and Claudia, 3. Al Ahmed says Sofia had a question for him when she visited him in hospital. “She told me, ‘Dad, why didn’t you go to take the gun from the other guy, on the bridge?’ ” Anthony Albanese visits Al Ahmed at St George Hospital two days after the massacre. Prime Minister’s Office via AP The governor-general, Sam Mostyn, came to his bedside, too, as did Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and the people who started the online appeal that raised more than $2.5 million for him from donors around the world. “He’d become a global story,” says Ian Robertson, a media law specialist and chair of legal firm Holding Redlich, who offered to help Al Ahmed navigate the unfamiliar territory in which he found himself. “He was not only getting inquiries from the Australian media, he was getting them from overseas as well. He was in pain, he wasn’t sleeping at all well, and he had this avalanche of people basically hounding him. So the job was to try to get that under control.” Al Ahmed was part of a small group of Bondi survivors and first responders honoured at the Sydney Cricket Ground before the final Test of the summer’s Ashes series in January. As the applause of the huge crowd washed over him, he bowed his head and put his right hand over his heart. Soon afterwards, he accepted an invitation to the US, where he visited a holy site of the Jewish movement known as Chabad. He was photographed praying alongside Rabbi Yehoram Ulman, founder of Chabad of Bondi and father-in-law of Rabbi Eli Schlanger, one of the 15 people killed by the terrorists. That Al Ahmed wore a yarmulke, the traditional Jewish skullcap, drew criticism in some quarters. In his book, he explains that he believes in respecting others’ religious beliefs and customs. “If they were to visit my mosque, they would remove their shoes,” he writes. “It’s a matter of basic humanity.” In New York, he met Democratic mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and was stopped in Times Square by a couple of cops on the beat, who asked if they could have a photo with him. Then it was on to Washington DC, where he was feted by members of the US Congress. They’d all seen the viral video. Most of them gave him medals. “They gave me their business cards as well,” he says. “Nice people. I love America.” Back in Australia, Ian Robertson watched Al Ahmed get a standing ovation as he was presented with the key to the City of Canterbury-Bankstown, a local government area in south-western Sydney. “He was kind of mobbed by people wanting to shake his hand and pat his back,” Robertson says. “Everywhere I went with him, same reaction. People walked up to him in the street to say, ‘Good on you’.” In March, he was given the key to the City of Waverley, which incorporates Bondi. With the key came a lifetime beach parking permit – a welcome gift for a man who’d collected a few tickets there in his time.

Soak in the harbour views in a Couples Suite at the new L’Occitane Spa, Sofitel Sydney Darling Harbour. Anna Kucera IF YOU CAN’T GET TO PROVENCE ... If you’re yearning for the south of France, Sofitel Sydney Darling Harbour has opened the country’s very first L’Occitane en Provence Spa. Consider it a useful alternative to booking a flight to Marseille when what you really need is generous slathers of almond oil, lavender-scented steam and a few hours in which nobody can find you. See sofitelspadarlingharbour.com ABBA-fuelled fun at Mamma Mia! The Party at Nikos’ taverna.



… OR GREECE 



DOUBLE DOWN ON ABU DHABI Etihad will double its Sydney-Abu Dhabi service from December 15, adding four weekly flights to bring the route to two departures daily, meaning easier connections to European cities including London, Paris and Rome. The extra frequency also makes a stopover more tempting: Etihad’s program offers a complimentary one- or two-night hotel stay, with the oasis city of Al Ain now in the mix. See etihad.com The Dior Spa at Rio’s Copacabana Palace is the first for Latin America. The wellness club offers Brazilian jiu-jitsu studios and a post-sun facial conceived with renowned dermatologist Dr Maria Bussade. Dior’s Rio connection goes back to 1961, when Marc Bohan presented a couture collection in the hotel’s gardens. See belmond.com
