World.title: Stressed? These 10 blissfully serene places offer the perfect escape
World.content:
On a “stillcation” travel becomes less about collecting experiences and more about noticing where we are: the Pyrenees.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Emails. Phone calls. Appointments. Passwords. Protein. Water. Eight hours of sleep. Our lives have become a relentless pursuit of doing – and doing everything better. Even travelling can become a to-do list of bucket-list experiences, country counts and Instagrammable moments. The antidote? The “stillcation”. Although laughably named, this new way of holidaying pushes back against our culture of constant productivity and self-improvement. It’s not necessarily yoga at sunrise or a silent meditation retreat, although it can be. More simply, it’s about the absence of agenda. Of stripping life back to its essentials: good food, beautiful views, fresh air and anchoring yourself in the present moment. Instead of seeking destinations that offer the most to do, it asks where offers the best conditions for doing less. THE LOST ART OF DOING NOTHING “Man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone” was, according to French philosopher Blaise Pascal, the source of all humanity’s problems. Four centuries later, his observation feels oddly prescient. We rarely sit still – even when on holiday. The constant pressure to optimise our lives can put a strain on the nervous system, says Jamie Clements, a wellness retreat facilitator and author of The Next Breath. “Stress has become the baseline, and calm feels like the exception.” Tour operators sense there is a growing market for more profound ways to unplug. In a recent study, British tour company Inghams ranked almost 100 European destinations according to their stillness, with criteria including walking trails per square kilometre, air quality, birdsong richness, stargazing quality, human density and forest cover (Scotland’s Wester Ross took the top spot). 



Slowing down switches our nervous system from a fight-or-flight sympathetic state to a rest-and-digest parasympathetic system that lowers our blood pressure and heart rate. A recent study ranked European destinations according to their stillness. Scotland’s Wester Ross took the top spot. iStock But don’t assume a stillcation will immediately evoke a state of Zen. Like any other holiday – where it can take a week to unwind – the first day or two can feel uncomfortable. The point of a stillcation isn’t simply that sitting around feels nice. Removing the constant demand for attention – and replacing the thrum of traffic, screens and notifications with wind, water, birdsong and walking – may create the conditions in which both mind and body can begin to really recover. And the benefits extend beyond our own wellbeing. The qualities that make a destination “still” – low population density, dark skies, forests, clean air, biodiversity and quiet trails – depend on healthy, protected environments. Perhaps that is the real appeal of the stillcation. It doesn’t ask us to abandon movement, curiosity or adventure. It simply changes the objective. Travel becomes less about collecting experiences and more about noticing where we are; less about escaping life and more about inhabiting it. In a culture that has turned even rest into something to optimise, doing nothing might be the most radical itinerary of all. KANGAROO ISLAND, SOUTH AUSTRALIA



Kangaroo Island, with its salty Southern Ocean air, wineries and long lunches, is a great place to slow down. It’s just 45 minutes on the ferry from Cape Jervis in mainland South Australia to Penneshaw on Kangaroo Island, and yet the world changes completely in that short space of time. Suddenly, it’s all lungfuls of salty Southern Ocean air, visits to wineries, long lunches, strolls along secluded beaches and encounters with kangaroos, koalas and sea lions. This island wilderness is an ideal place to slow down, to do nothing, or at least very little. Kangaroo Island has famously had to recover from some deep wounds, in particular the bushfires of January 2020, which wiped out almost half the island, including its most famous resort, Southern Ocean Lodge. The slow recovery of the land and the wildlife, as well as the resort, has been heartening, and KI is once again an ideal destination for those seeking escape. Make no plans for your stay here. Have no lofty goals. Simply trust that you will explore and discover and enjoy at a pace that suits. How to do it Southern Ocean Lodge overlooks the wild coastline of Kangaroo Island, and costs $3400 a night; two-night minimum stay. Rates include all dining and drinks, signature experiences and island airport transfers. See southernoceanlodge.com.au FLINDERS ISLAND, TASMANIA There are more than 120 beaches to explore on Flinders Island.



Australia has more than its share of remote wilderness areas – the Red Centre, the Kimberley, Far North Queensland – but Flinders Island is a standout for its remarkable isolation. It is a rugged outcrop of land in the Bass Strait, about a 35-minute flight from Launceston or a seven-hour ferry trip from Bridport, an unspoilt landscape of granite mountains, windswept beaches and coastal heath land. Fewer than 1000 people live there. Plenty of wombats, however, call the island home, as do wallabies and abundant birdlife while minimal light pollution creates star-rich skies. There are more than 120 beaches to explore, flawless stretches of sand on which to lose yourself in thought, wrapped up tight against the wind, for hours on end. Hiking tracks here are like meditation paths. There’s a whisky distillery, a vineyard and a couple of nice places to eat. Or simply curl up by a fire and read a book. How to do it Australian Walking Holidays’ four-day Flinders Island Experience in Comfort features guided coastal walks and accommodation at a beachside eco-camp. It costs from $3275 a person, twin share. See australianwalkingholidays.com.au ABISKO, SWEDEN Viewing and photographing the northern lights by the Abisko Sky Station, Lapland, Sweden. Getty Images Most visitors come to this Swedish Lapland village to glimpse magic: the aurora borealis, or northern lights. This is one of the best places on Earth to see the phenomenon, from September to April, due to Abisko’s high latitude and its cloud-free “blue hole” microclimate, which keeps it as dry as the Gobi Desert. The lights aren’t the only reason to visit this gathering of only 85 permanent residents, however. Abisko, 250 kilometres north of the Arctic Circle near the Norwegian border, is also home to an eponymous national park, one that was established more than 100 years ago to protect subarctic flora and native wildlife. Tornetrask, the sixth-largest lake in Sweden, is also nearby and it freezes in winter.



Whatever the seasonal phenomenon you’re visiting to experience – midnight sun or northern lights – the common thread is the area’s natural attractions, the chance to be completely immersed in a world of deep quiet and flawless blue skies. Hike rugged trails, go dog-sledding, snow-shoeing, fishing, bird-watching or stargazing. Lean into the isolation. How to do it Nordic Travel offers a Winter in Swedish Lapland tour, including Abisko, northern lights viewing and accommodation. It costs from $4296 a person. See nordictravel.com.au THE PYRENEES, FRANCE AND SPAIN Mountainside accommodation in the Pyrenees, Andorra. iStock It’s difficult to believe that any sort of natural feature that separates France and Spain, two of the most popular tourist destinations on the planet, could be considered quiet, but the Pyrenees really is. This mountain range creates a wrinkled border between the two countries and offers wide-open spaces with myriad opportunities for mindful hiking, yoga, winter sports and thermal spas. On the French side, take time to wander through Parc National des Pyrenees, a stunningly beautiful reserve known for its karst valleys and caves. Several more national parks can be found along the border, with soaring limestone cliffs and flower-strewn meadows. The Spanish side, too, is dotted with smaller though no less spectacular national parks, many of them secluded and peaceful, where visitors can walk for an entire day without seeing another soul. And then, of course, there’s tiny Andorra, an entirely separate country and home to ski resorts and alpine national parks, with small villages in which to stay and relax and pretend the rest of the world doesn’t exist.

World.title: Wellington Region's second Pacific-led medical centre opens in Hutt Valley
World.content:
A 27-year vision for a Pacific-led health centre in the Hutt Valley has become a reality.

The Epuni Medical Centre, owned by Pacific Health Service Hutt Valley (PHSHV), is only the second Pacific-owned and led general-practice in the Wellington Region.

It opened its doors on Monday, marking an important moment for Pacific primary healthcare in Aotearoa's capital.

The only other Pacific-led health centre is in Porirua.

The centre represents a long-term commitment to strengthening Pacific ownership and leadership within primary healthcare.

The PHSHV's aim is to provide high-quality care that is welcoming and accessible to everyone.

Ribbon cutting ceremony for the Epuni Medical Centre on 30 October, 2026. (L-R) Dr Tua Lealaiauloto Taueetia-Su'a and Reverend Au Liko. Pacific Health Service - Hutt Valley

Before its doors opened to the public a blessing ceremony led was held by Revered Au Liko, who is also the chairperson of the PHSHV's Board.

Rev Liko paid tribute to those who envisioned the centre.

"Today is the combination and fruition of a 27-year dream of Pacific health services which started by three Pasifika nurses and our CEO, Mr Nanai Muaau, and various boards over the years.

"I am currently the chairperson of the board, and I've been chairperson for the last 12 years, and this has always been a dream carried by successive boards," Liko said.

He said that Pacific communities want to have a stronger role in shaping and delivering their own healthcare.

"Access has been one of the huge barriers to our people getting quality healthcare, and for a lot of our unenrolled people, who either can't afford to be with a GP of who find it difficult to communicate GPs, we are trying to meet the gaps that a lot our people are falling through," he said.

Audio player for " New Pacific health clinic opens its doors in Wellington " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/pacific/2311138%2Fwellington-region-s-second-pacific-led-medical-centre-opens-in-hutt-valley

New Pacific health clinic opens its doors in Wellington Pacific Waves Download MP3 5m

Dr Tua Lealaiauloto Taueetia-Su'a, who was involved from the start, told RNZ Pacific why she felt it was important to have a Pacific-led health centre.

"In the time that I had been working at Hutt Hospital for a while. I noticed there was a need for our own people to service our own people, like Pacific people for Pacific people," she said.

One of the nurses who helped start the journey 27 years ago sadly passed away.

Members of the Hutt Valley's Pacific community joined funders at the blessing ceremony.

(L-R) CEO Tu Ora Compass, Justine Thorpe, Reverend Au Liko, Candice Apelu Mariner and Executive Director of Kupega o Moana, Joy Sipeli RNZ Pacific

Health NZ national chief of Pacific health Pauline Fuimaono-Sanders said the significance of the new centre's opening is the increased capacity of Pacific-led health services for the area and the wider Hutt Valley.

"Because for the central region, this will only be the second Pacific GP clinic that the central region has right now, so very significant for providing services for Pacific peoples," she said.

PHSHV general manager Candice Apelu Mariner admits the journey to building the new centre had its fair share of early challenges.

But she said over the past three decades relationships have been built and lessons learned.

"I think every part of the system has worked to enable this to happen, meaning our funders, like Te Whatu have seen the vision of investing in more Pacific providers to establish GP services because we are still dealing with our Pacific having negative outcomes.

"So, when I say partners, you need allies, you need people who also believe in your vision both Pacific and non-Pacific, so establishing this hasn't really been a challenge this time around."

She said what has certainly been a challenge is securing a workforce as the Pacific clinical workforce is small.

"We know that 2.8 percent of the total clinical workforce is Pacific, so there are very few and most of them are in Auckland.

"One of the challenges for any new services is its workforce. But to by-pass that, we worked really hard in the last four years to build the workforce, because we always knew that at a certain time we will set up a GP practice. But we needed to grow our own workforce so that's something that we really thought hard about and put a plan in place," Mariner said.

The medical centre will form part of PHSHV's wider two-site model in the Hutt Valley, extending the organisation's ability to provide more connected care across clinical and community settings.

Mariner said Pacific care takes a holistic approach, considering not just a patient's medical condition but also other factors in their life.

World.title: National and Labour stuck in the middle
World.content:
Audio player for " Jo Moir and Craig McCulloch wrap up the campaign " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2367000%2Fnational-and-labour-stuck-in-the-middle

Jo Moir and Craig McCulloch wrap up the campaign Morning Report Download MP3 10m

Analysis - The consistent theme of this year's election campaign has been the decline of the major parties and the growing fascination with their traditionally smaller rivals.

Thursday night's Q+A People's Debate put that on full display with all seven parties in real contention for seats in the next Parliament side-by-side with no hierarchy and no special treatment for National or Labour.

There is a reason Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins are adamant a place remains for leader head-to-head debates.

It's because the alternative would require bringing a lot more personality while having to fight to get a word in alongside leaders who are talking directly to a smaller voter base that is easier to impress.

New Zealand First's Shane Jones. TVNZ/Supplied

Opportunity's Qiulae Wong went into the debate with fire in her belly after two days of national coverage about sexist and offensive comments made about her and her fellow candidate by New Zealand First's Michael Laws.

She went in armed with the knowledge that every other leader she was debating was unified in their disgust and disapproval of Laws, including New Zealand First's Shane Jones who described the diatribe as "reckless and foolish".

Greens' co-leader Chloe Swarbrick was riding high on multiple polls putting her party in record-winning territory.

Te Pāti Māori MP Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke was a late sub for her colleague Oriini Kaipara, and despite the lack of warning or prep time she held her own and constantly brought every question back to an issue she was more comfortable speaking to.

Te Pāti Māori MP Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke. TVNZ/Supplied

For the coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First it was about pointing out where together the coalition had made good change while simultaneously distinguishing themselves.

Jones played his usual agitator role roaring about fast-track and mining, but also made a considered and impassioned case for greater access to respite care for whanau affected by methamphetamine addiction, and amnesty for families wanting to report it.

ACT leader David Seymour looked equal parts alarmed and hopeful when he realised he and Swarbrick were singing from the same songsheet on how best to handle a teenage social media ban, proving even the most opposite ends of the political spectrum can live in harmony.

ACT leader David Seymour (C) and Greens' co-leader Chloe Swarbrick (R). TVNZ/Supplied

While Labour's Kieran McAnulty brought the fun to the debate with his ramblings about Homer Simpson and his journey from smoking to vaping to nicotene gum, he found it almost impossible to insert himself into the debate when he wanted to.

Instead he was left answering questions he wasn't so schooled up on that moderator Jack Tame directed at him, and failed to muscle in on the ones he had talking points for.

Likewise National's Nicola Willis struggled to fire.

Despite being the most senior politician on show, Willis seemed to have her back up from the get-go.

National's Nicola Willis and Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong (L). TVNZ/Supplied

The first question out of the blocks was how "political leaders can lead by example and show respect for differing views and work together to unite New Zealand".

Willis used it to take another whack at Swarbrick, a tactic the National Party has deployed relentlessly in recent weeks.

Despite being a skillful debater with political nous, it is completely plausible Willis' misfire was simply her realisation the sun might well set on her time as a minister and MP in two days' time.

McAnulty and Willis had the toughest jobs on Thursday night trying to sell a vision to a much broader church than any of the other parties.

They're also not able to make the same sweeping promises and declarations that smaller parties often get away with.

Labour's Kieran McAnulty. TVNZ/Supplied

But even in a format where there aren't seven people on the stage competing for less than 90 minutes of airtime, the two major parties haven't been convincing in their vision or plan to lift out of crisis those doing it the toughest.

Luxon and Hipkins have had three opportunities to do that in the leader debates in recent weeks but based on polling neither party has been rewarded for their efforts.

On the eve of the election the polls remain close as ever, and any one of many variables could tip the balance of which parties could negotiate the next government.

The defining moment of this election could end up being Laws' inability to keep his thoughts to himself.

World.title: Last poll before election puts Labour slightly ahead of National, with Opportunity just making it to Parliament
World.content:
Audio player for " Jo Moir and Craig McCulloch wrap up the campaign " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2368732%2Flast-poll-before-election-puts-labour-slightly-ahead-of-national-with-opportunity-just-making-it-to-parliament

Jo Moir and Craig McCulloch wrap up the campaign Morning Report Download MP3 10m

Labour is up two points in the latest The Post/Freshwater Strategy poll.

The poll, with Infrastructure NZ, puts Labour slightly ahead at 30.7 per cent, against National's 26.4 per cent.

The party had climbed two points since the last The Post poll in October, while National dropped 1.2 points.

The poll shows Opportunity edging across the five per cent threshold, at 5.1 per cent - down 0.3 points since the last poll.

The Green Party is down 1.2 points to 13 per cent, while NZ First is up 0.2 per cent to 12 per cent.

Act is up by 0.8 to 9.8 per cent, and Te Pati Māori up 0.1 to 2 per cent.

According to The Post, Opportunity Party would hold the balance of power if its 5.1 per cent holds through special votes.

If there was a 120-seat parliament, National, Act and NZ First would win a combined 59 seats, two short of the 61 needed to govern.

Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori would hold 55 seats.

Under the poll, Labour leader Chris Hipkins is more popular with female voters - 37.9 per cent to Nationl's 26.2 per cent, while the left block is leading amongst younger voters. Labour is at 40.7 per cent with the under 35s, the Greens are on 22.8 per cent, and National is on 17.9 per cent with that group.

World.title: Skin cancer patients pushed towards less effective treatment by insurance shortfalls
World.content:
Dermatologists are worried insurance changes are pushing patients with skin cancer towards less effective treatment because they can't get cover for the full cost.

Southern Cross has narrowed the criteria for Mohs surgery, which has a 99 percent cure rate.

Mohs is a treatment for skin cancer that removes the tumour, layer by layer, while saving as much healthy tissue as possible.

Changes to insurance coverage have seen people paying more, or choosing cheaper, less effective options.

President-elect of the NZ Dermatological Society Dr AJ Seine said the 20 Mohs surgeons around the country mostly carried out the surgery in the private system as it was largely unavailable in public hospitals.

"It's the gold standard internationally recognised treatment for certain skin cancers, particularly for heads and necks."

Southern Cross, the country's biggest health insurer, announced a year ago it was tightening the criteria for funding Mohs surgery.

The criteria changes in December stated that, to get coverage, the lesion needs to be a basal cell carcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma.

Additionally: "At least one (a or b) of the following apply to the skin lesion.

"a) The lesion has either recurred, has aggressive histopathology, or is clinically justified as high risk AND the lesion is on the head and neck OR site of previous radiation or burn scarring.

"b) The lesion is on eyelids, periorbital skin, ears, pre and post auricular, lips, nose, chin, mandible, temple, fingers, toes, or genitals ONLY, AND tissue preservation is critical for maintaining function (as evidenced by clinical photography which must be retained for audit purposes)."

However, it has since broadened the access criteria after being approached by the society, Dr Seine said.

"The bigger issue now comes with the funding of people's skin cancer treatments and most policies have limits with regard to their skin lesion benefit."

Mohs surgery used to sit outside that area, so it wasn't limited on price, however, since April patients were having to choose between Mohs surgery and having less effective treatments, based on the amount of money that had left under their policy.

Specialists were having to inform patients of the funding shortfall every day and for some that amounted to thousands of dollars.

For patients who were older needing three or four surgeries a year usually only the first one would be covered and after that "they're out of pocket", he said.

Many patients had paid their premiums for years and then found when they got skin cancers in their 70s their premiums were even more expensive but they weren't covered for the treatment they needed, Dr Seine said.

The less effective option was to cut out the lesion and hope it was all removed. The Mohs surgery looked at 100 percent of the surgical margin while the lesser option left surgeons and patients in the position of "you don't know what you don't know".

The standard incisions had a high failure rate, Dr Seine said, meaning a re-incision might be needed.

"When you start cutting skin cancer out for the second time it becomes less effective, no matter which modality you're looking at, be that Mohs or a standard incision."

Dr Seine agreed all health treatments were becoming more expensive, however, specialists were upset Southern Cross had introduced the limits without consultation.

He was pleased that recently the insurer had become more willing to meet with consultants to discuss the problems.

"It is a real issue when you start compromising your decisions on health care based on money. You do start seeing increasing rates of complications. You see poorer health decisions simply due to finances."

Southern Cross Health Insurance spokesperson Regan Savage told RNZ in October the eligibility criteria focus Mohs cover on circumstances where there is a clinical need for the procedure, and are intended to ensure members for whom the surgery is most clinically important continue to have access to the specialised treatment.

"Where the Mohs eligibility criteria are not met, standard surgical excision remains available as an established treatment for skin cancer, subject to the member's policy."

World.title: Former All Blacks in Pacific rugby teams for Nations Cup
World.content:
Two former All Blacks have joined the Manu Samoa camp ahead of this weekend's Nations Cup clash against Zimbabwe in Wakefield, England.

Looseman Akira Ioane and fullback Shaun Steveson get the chance to play for their country of origin at the competition.

Another former All Black, Ngani Laumape, has joined Tonga's 'Ikale Tahi, who are also preparing for the second round of the Nations Cup series.

All three players have become eligible for their countries of origin following the fullfillment of the World Rugby eligibility rules, where they had not played for any national teams for three years after their last matches for the All Blacks.

Ioane played for the All Blacks from 2017 to 2022, playing against Scotland on 19 November 2022 in his last international.

Stevenson played just one game for the All Blacks, on 5 August 2023 against Australia, while Laumape last played for the All Blacks on 7 November 2020, also against Australia, in Brisbane.

Former Chiefs player Stevenson said he is proud to be with Manu Samoa.

"Such a great feeling to be named in my first Manu Samoan camp to represent my Manu side of my family," he said as the team prepared in Wakefield during the week.

"They are very proud Samoans and to come out here is very special.

"It's going to be an exciting next few weeks and as we lead up to the World Cup it's going to be a hell of a journey."

Ioane and Stevenson join fellow former All Black Josh Ioane and former Wallaby Scott Sio in the squad.

Manu Samoa's tour squad is the strongest assembled since the 2023 Rugby World Cup, with key forwards Michael Ala'alatoa, Theodore McFarland, Miracle Failangi, Alamanda Motuga and Samuel Slade all available.

Stevenson joins a backline that will feature Otago halfback Joel Lam, tough centre Lalomilo Lalomilo, Peter Umaga-Jensen and AJ Lam.

Samoa is currently tied with Tonga on seven points in the Americas and Pacific pool of the Nations Cup, which has the United States of America, with 10 points, at the top of the pool.

Mixed fortunes

Meanwhile, Tonga head coach Tevita Tuifua said from Bucharest this week that veterans Ben Tameifuna and former Wallaby Adam Coleman will join the team next week.

He said the duo will miss the clash against Romania this weekend.

Tuifua and fellow former 'Ikale Tahi player Nili Latu have assembled a mixed squad - made up of players who had been part of the campaign in the past two years and some returning from club commitments that tied them down in 2025.

The inclusion of Laumape, who played for Moana Pasifika this year and featured for Manawatu in New Zealand's National Provincial Championship this season, is a big win for the Tongans.

"Ngani is an experienced player and his inclusion has been a positive for the team," Tuifua said.

"We will miss Ben and Adam but we have replacements who will get the chance to play.

"Our focus is on building our team and combinations for the World Cup."

Tuifua said there might be some injury replacements for the side, especially with two more matches over the next two weeks.

World.title: NZ Navy supports Cooks' illegal fishing fight
World.content:
The Royal New Zealand Navy has recently assisted efforts by the Cook Islands Police Service Maritime Unit to combat illegal fishing in the western Pacific.

Four NZ Navy personnel joined the crew aboard the Te Kukupa II last month as it covered more than 30 million square kilometres of ocean as part of Operation Kurukura.

The operation is run by the Pacific Islands Forum Fisheries Agency (FFA) and involves 17 member nations, with operational support from Australia, France, NZ and the United States.

Te Kukupa II undertook a number of compliance inspections of fishing vessels as part of wider efforts to crack down on illegal fishing activities in the region.

Overall, the operation recorded a total of 149 vessel sightings, 82 at-sea and dockside boardings and inspections, while the FFA also recorded more than 27,000 satellite detections.

From left, Able Seamanship Combat Specialist Theo Fyfe, Able Electronics Technician Liam Gleeson, Able Weapons Technician Kyle Dymock-Smith and Able Seamanship Combat Specialist Reece Speechly, aboard Te Kukupa II SUPPLIED / NZDF

The navy personnel who spent two weeks aboard the Te Kukupa II were Able Weapons Technician Kyle Dymock-Smith, Able Seamanship Combat Specialist (ASCS) Theo Fyfe, Able Electronics Technician Liam Gleeson and Able Seamanship Combat Specialist Reece Speechly.

Fyfe said the camaraderie on board the vessel remained high throughout the voyage.

"It's very close-knit, very family-oriented and very professional. They are very good at what they do, very efficient. On a big vessel you might not run into other people the whole voyage but in Te Kukupa I felt like I was one of the family."

Speechly, meanwhile, highlighted that it wasn't a trip for those not used to choppy seas.

World.title: Superstar Cristiano Ronaldo retires from international football
World.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo announced his retirement from international soccer following a fallout with Portugal coach Jorge Jesus.

Ronaldo, 41, has scored the most goals (146) and made the most appearances (234 matches) in Portugal's men's international soccer history.

"To the Portuguese people, the day has come to hand back the No. 7 shirt of the national team that belongs to us all. I never felt it was exclusively mine," Ronaldo said in a video posted on Instagram.

Loading Instagram content

"But for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it and taking it with me to stadiums all over the world. Today the time has come to hand it over to the future.

"It was not an easy decision, because there are decisions that are not made solely with the head; they are also made with the heart."

Ronaldo's announcement comes one day before Jesus names the roster for the Nations League matches against Denmark and Wales.

It also comes on the heels of the superstar forward serving a 30-day suspension for walking out on the national team.

In his explanation, Ronaldo admitted his decision to leave camp was not the best way to handle the situation. But he added that Jesus "broke his word" more than once.

Jesus told Portugal's Channel 11 that he asked Ronaldo to stay on with the team.

"We already had the chance to talk about this before the first squad announcement. I asked him to stay on with me," the coach said. "He will always be in the hearts of the Portuguese people, and in the national team.

"He will always be a point of reference for our national team, for our people, and for our history."

World.title: Raiders 'couldn't have offered any more' to want-away Hudson Young
World.content:
Ricky Stuart says the Canberra Raiders "bent over backwards" to keep Hudson Young at the club, as the star back-rower touched down in Port Moresby ahead of a potential move the the PNG Chiefs.

Canberra stunningly pulled their $4.4 million, four-year offer to the Blues star on Monday.

Young travelled to Papua New Guinea this week, with the 2028 expansion club having already offered the six-time Kangaroo international $900,000 per year.

That tax-free package would have meant he would take home far more in his pay packet than the Raiders' offer, but the NRL established Young's market value at $1.1 million, which has since been revised to $1 million.

ARLC chairman Peter V'landys told Nine Newspapers that players can seek to challenge their "official" market value and make their own submissions to the salary cap auditor.

"Let's say a player wanted to be with his family or there are other specific reasons," V'landys said.

"We just don't want the salary cap rorted. However, we know that at times there are exceptional circumstances, so we take those exceptional circumstances into account.

"We won't have a situation where people manipulate the salary cap.

"The unfortunate thing is with the tax-free status of PNG, we have to be extra cautious with the market value of the players there."

Hudson Young has played nine State of Origin matches for the Blues. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The Raiders' $1.1 million per season offer was understood to be the biggest in the club's history, with Stuart saying the club could go no higher.

"We couldn't have offered Hudson any more," Stuart told 666 ABC Radio Canberra.

"I mean, we bent over backwards to try and keep Hudson and it would have been unfair on the club if we had went any further.

"We were at a stage where it was probably too much, yet we look after our players and we do everything we possibly can for them.

"But it gets to a stage where you've got to make a decision [and] my position and [Raiders CEO] Don Furner's position is we have to look after the club."

The 28-year-old made his NRL debut with the Raiders in 2019 and has played 155 NRL games for the Green Machine.

Stuart acknowledged that Young was well within his rights to seek out new opportunities, and that all the clubs agreed with the expansion to PNG and the challenges that would hold for the rest of the competition.

However, the veteran coach was under no illusions why Young was looking for pastures new.

Ricky Stuart says money was the driving factor moving forward. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

"Money," Stuart said.

"Absolutely it is [all about money].

"That doesn't bother me one bit. If Hudson wants to make that decision and take those tax-free dollars, you've got to understand he's got to live in Papua New Guinea."

It was put to Stuart that Young, who is currently recovering from an Achilles rupture that he suffered against South Sydney in July, may well look for a release from his contract for the 2027 season, with the Chiefs not coming in until 2028.

Stuart said any decision on that would be up to the player's management, but bemoaned the "messy" process that allowed players to sign a year in advance for a new club.

"Unfortunately … with our rules and the regulations, the guidelines we have with our ability for players to go off and sign at another club 12 months in advance, it makes it very messy," he said.

"I don't agree with that interpretation or the guidelines we've got in the competition. I think it makes it very messy and I feel very, very sorry for the fans, because you got some of your favourite players, players you want to watch, players you want to keep with your club in 12 months' time playing elsewhere.

"I think it's very unfair on the fans, but it is what it is."

Hudson Young has played for the Raiders since 2019. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

Stuart, despite acknowledging that players moving on was just business, said he did take it "personally" when players move on.

"I do take it personally, and I take it very personally about coaching this team, this club," Stuart said.

"I do find it difficult at times, but you got to lose the emotion and see the business side of it.

"I'm not disgruntled with the fact that Hudson's looking elsewhere, that's his choice and decision.

"But what my club's done is give him probably the highest offer that's ever been offered to a player at this club in its time. It was a very, very generous offer, probably too big of an offer. But we did it [and] now he's knocked it back.

"We've got to move forward. We've got to move on."

ABC/AAP

World.title: NAS weighs in more than 33kg heavier than Paul Gallen
World.content:
Nelson Asofa-Solomona has landed another low blow on Paul Gallen, claiming that even his premiership-winning former Cronulla teammates want the Sharks legend laid out on Friday night.

A day after the Big Nasty riled his rival by dragging Gallen's wife into the verbal sledging, Asofa-Solomona got even nastier as he lobbed explosive accusations about the Sharks' only grand final-winning captain.

"There's been so many people jumping in my DMs," Asofa-Solomona said on Thursday.

"People that have played with him, people that have played against him, people who have worked with them in the past. They were telling me all these stories about him and saying 'Yeah, bro, please do a job on him.'

"That was my plan all along anyway."

Nelson Asofa-Solomona says his plan is to knock Paul Gallen out. (Supplied: No Limit Boxing)

The Cronulla-Melbourne rivalry is one of the fiercest in the NRL, with the two sides featuring in a series of spiteful encounters either side the Sharks' stirring 2016 grand final triumph over the Storm.

Having already copped a drugs spray from Asofa-Solomona (3-0, 3KOs) in light of the Cronulla peptides saga, Gallen (16-2-1, 8KOs) will be livid after the ex-Storm star's latest verbal jabs.

Asofa-Solomona would not be drawn on specifics but said Gallen's former State of Origin teammates and "work colleagues" were among those who he claimed had reached out to him in the hope of doing over the 2014 series-winning Blues skipper.

"I can't say too much, but probably just stuff to do with money and bits and pieces," Asofa-Solomona said.

"But, look, he's grown up in a different era. He's a bit of a different cat, but the new era is here."

Asofa-Solomona's inflammatory allegations came after the two heavyweights featured in a spicy weigh-in at Sydney's TikTok Entertainment Centre.

The ex-New Zealand Test enforcer promised Gallen he would proudly take the mantle of NRL-boxing crossover king on Friday night.

"And if it's not a knockout, I don't want it," the 200cm, 137.56-kilogram behemoth said.

"That's the only result I'm here to get. I'm here for a highlight-reel finish."

Nelson Asofa-Solomona is much heavier than Paul Gallen. (Supplied: No Limit Boxing)

But the retiring Gallen, 45, is having none of it, despite weighing in at 104.18kg.

"I'm really proud I'm fighting a bloke now, 30-odd kilos heavier than me, 15 years younger than me and I'm still willing to compete — and I'll win this fight, at my age," he said.

"That's what I'm proud of, and this is a no-lose situation for me. I'm going to get paid a ton of money and go home happy and healthy and live the rest of my life with my family.

"That's my goal in life and that's what I'm here to do."

What time is the fight?

Paul Gallen and Nelson Asofa-Solomona meet on Friday, November 6, with the main card getting underway from 7:00pm AEDT.

How can I watch the fight?

The fight is exclusive to Fox Sports and Kayo's pay per view channel, Main Event and will cost $69.95.

ABC Sport will live-blog the fight card.

Who else is fighting?

Here's the card.

Ahmad Reda vs Jake Wyllie — 10 rounds, lightweight

Paulo Aokuso vs Mobin Khahrazeh — 10 rounds, light heavyweight

Blair Geraghty vs Peter Lee — 6 rounds, super lightweight

Prelims, from 5:30pm AEDT

Kya Sparks vs Zidane Tavares — 5 rounds, super welterweight

Alex Naman vs Zain Adams — 6 rounds, 54kg catchweight

Jayden Fadel vs Rajesh Kumar — 5 rounds, lightweight

World.title: Netball blindsided by leak of likely inclusion at Brisbane Olympics
World.content:
Netball has been blindsided by a leak of its likely inclusion at the Brisbane 2032 Olympic Games.

Media reports by NewsCorp suggest it is "near the top of the list" in priority for the 2032 organising committee, which is permitted to put forward up to six local sports to feature as one-offs at the Games.

Cricket, surf lifesaving, rugby league and lawn bowls are also in the frame.

This would set netball up for a historic Games debut. Despite being part of the Commonwealth Games since 1998, it has tried and failed at least four times to join the Olympic programme previously.

Loading Instagram content

The endorsement is a positive sign, the significance of which is not lost on Netball Australia, who have garnered more than 115,000 signatures on their petition since officially launching a bid to join the Brisbane Games in 2021.

In January, a survey conducted by independent market and social research agency Insightfully, found 66 per cent of Australians support netball's inclusion at the Olympics. It polled 10 points higher than any other sport.

However, key figures at Netball Australia were tight-lipped on Thursday, for fear of speaking out of turn and jeopardising their chances.

Earlier this week, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) revised its timeline for determining which sports and disciplines would make it onto the programme for the Brisbane Games.

In December, the IOC will make recommendations in three different categories: existing disciplines to have automatic inclusion; existing or proposed disciplines that require further assessment; and candidate disciplines eliminated from consideration.

A formal verdict will be handed down in April next year after votes are taken at the IOC session in the Dominican Republic.

Former Australian defender turned-commentator Bianca Chatfield shared her initial reaction with ABC Sport.

"Everyone is really shocked that it's come out and there has been this leak," Chatfield said.

"I was so excited when I saw the news, but then I dug deeper and realised it's not official.

"We're all just holding on with hope that the news is real and that it'll come to fruition next year."

Bianca Chatfield (left) faces New Zealand in the 2013 Constellation Cup. (Getty: Michael Dodge)

Chatfield said the Olympics always felt out of reach as an option for netball, but the sport deserved its chance to shine at the Games.

"It would mean everything to the sport, there's been a lot of work done behind the scenes," she said.

"For the athletes especially it would be a once in a lifetime opportunity to have a crack at an Olympic gold medal.

"The Olympics was just something that we never thought would happen so the fact it's a tangible thing now, we'd all be absolutely stoked to see it happen."

Bianca Chatfield now works as a commentator and presenter in the game. (Getty: Graham Denholm)

The Australian team's recent form sees it on the brink of losing the world number one ranking for the first time since 2013, but that lapse in dominance could perhaps help a greater cause.

The Diamonds missed the Commonwealth Games final for the first time in Glasgow, falling to Jamaica in the semifinals before rallying to claim bronze. They also conceded the Constellation Cup to New Zealand for just the fourth time in 16 series.

"I do think a competitive environment really helps [our Olympic case]," Chatfield said.

"As we're seeing internationally, with the rise of teams like Jamaica and New Zealand, it's not a forgone conclusion that Australia would get the gold."

Federal Minister for Communications and Sport Anika Wells, who is also vice chair on the board of the Brisbane 2032 committee, pledged her support at the Queensland Media Club on Thursday.

She also told ABC Sport that it was feasible that multiple team sports like cricket and netball could be selected, despite there being pressure to remain inside the overall 10,500 athlete quota.

Sports Minister Anika Wells fronts the media. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

"Today I am publicly committing my support to netball as part of Brisbane 2032," Wells said.

"Netball is quintessentially Australian and the leading team sport for women and girls here and across our region.

"It connects communities, it creates leaders, it builds confidence and inspires dreams.

"It would be a massive moment for the million little girls and women, and increasingly men and boys, who pull on their netball bibs and get out to play."

Former Diamond Kathryn Harby-Williams is the CEO at ANPA. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

Chief executive of the Australian Netball Players' Association Kathryn Harby-Williams said the athletes welcomed the news.

"It would be an incredible opportunity for the athletes if it is true, to compete at one of the biggest sports events in the world," Harby-Williams told ABC Sport.

Meanwhile, a Netball Australia spokesperson said it would follow due process.

"We are focused on putting our best foot forward with the Brisbane 2032 Organising Committee and the IOC and we respect their processes," a statement read.

"We will continue to advocate for netball and our incredible community across the globe.

"There are countless Australian netball players who dream of one day becoming an Olympian and we believe Brisbane 2032 would be the perfect stage for those dreams."

World.title: Swans 'need to be better' as club launches investigation in culture
World.content:
The Sydney Swans say they have commissioned a "comprehensive examination of the club's AFL program" as they grapple with another off-field incident.

On Monday, Papley, a high-profile forward and one of the team's most experienced players, allegedly returned a positive roadside test for methylamphetamine, and will appear in court this month for driving with a suspended licence.

The club has penned a letter to members from chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich saying the club commissioned the review in September and will feature "a board endorsed independent process".

"What is already clear from our work to date is that the actions and attitudes of some within our club has damaged and diminished the many great things we do, and the great people who do them," the statement read.

"This is unacceptable and must change.

"We have a long and proud history but clearly, we have work to do to get back to the standards we have long set. We will make the necessary changes that are required and will work to be better.

"The standards we expect of every player and employee, on and off the field, are central to who we are. They reflect the behaviour rightly expected of professional athletes and public role models.

"The incident involving Tom Papley this week and the separate incident in Melbourne in August, fall a long way short of those expectations."

If Papley's second sample is positive, the 216-gamer is likely to face an AFL penalty separate from any legal sanction.

Pavlich admitted the embattled AFL club had a "long way to go" when he spoke briefly to reporters outside the club headquarters in Moore Park on Thursday, conceding the Swans had again let down the football community.

"We're bitterly disappointed that we're here talking about this today," Pavlich said.

"We're really disappointed in Tom himself. We voiced that pretty directly to him yesterday.

"We apologise unreservedly to our members, fans and corporate partners.

"We've let them down again. We must be better.

"It's a really disappointing time for the footy club, but given this is a police matter, we cannot make any further comment."

Tom Papley (centre) allegedly returned a positive roadside test for methylamphetamine on Monday. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Papley's looming court appearance comes after the Swans suspended five players for breaching club behavioural standards last August.

Vice-captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice were stood down for the remainder of the AFL season and missed the finals.

"We're looking at that right now," Pavlich said, when asked if the Swans had a culture problem.

"We've been identifying that over the last eight weeks.

"We've started some deep work on that with our AFL men's department, independent advisers helping us through that.

"These are the questions we are asking ourselves right now and asking our players."

Pavlich added "we need to be better".

"This is not something that anyone is stopping short of, knowing that we've got a long way to go," he said.

"We've got some deep work to do to understand how we can get better."

Second test results to take weeks

Papley was pulled over by police in Sydney's Centennial Park on Monday for random testing.

He was subjected to a roadside drug test, with checks revealing his licence was suspended due to non-payment of a parking fine.

A secondary sample of oral fluid was taken for further analysis, with the results from the second test expected to take at least four weeks.

Papley was issued a 24-hour driving prohibition and will appear before Waverley Local Court on November 26.

The 30-year-old's test result has overshadowed a landmark week for the Swans, who on Sunday will host their first AFLW home final at Henson Park.

No update on hotel incident

Meanwhile, Victoria Police are yet to provide an update on an investigation into sexual assault allegations at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel following a round 23 AFL game.

Detectives in early September travelled to NSW to interview a 30-year-old Maroubra man, a 25-year-old Paddington man and two Randwick men aged 25 and 26.

It is understood the men interviewed were Heeney, Warner, Jordon and Blakey.

No charges have been laid. AAP is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the suspended players.

Bice is no longer a person of interest for police, while Blakey departed the Swans during last month's trade period to join North Melbourne.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Australian racing icon and F1 world champion Alan Jones dies
World.content:
Alan Jones, the 1980 Formula 1 world champion, has died aged 80.

He won 12 grands prix during his F1 career and joined Sir Jack Brabham as the only Australian to be crowned world champion.

Jones turned 80 on Monday.

A statement released on behalf of Jones's wife, Amanda Butler-Davis, said the legendary racer died following a short illness.

"We are extremely saddened to announce the passing of our beloved Alan, who passed away on 5 November following a short illness," Butler-Davis said.

"He will be dearly missed and fondly remembered by those closest to him, as well as the many fans whose support he was always grateful for.

"Alan dedicated his life to motorsport, building a legacy that will live on through the countless people he touched along the way.

"Through his achievements, passion and unmistakable character, both on and off the track, Alan left an enduring mark on the sport both nationally and across the globe.

"As a family, we would like to take this opportunity to thank everyone who was part of Alan's journey for the many years of friendship, love and support. He was incredibly fortunate to have so many wonderful people around him."

Alan Jones won five races in the 1980 Formula 1 world championship race. (Getty Images: Rainer Schlegelmilch)

Jones was born in Melbourne on November 2, 1946.

His father, Stan, was a racing driver who won the 1959 Australian Grand Prix.

Jones wanted to follow in his father's footsteps and left for Europe in the late 60s, but could not afford to kick-start his racing career overseas.

He returned to Australia, but determined not to give up his dream, Jones moved to London in 1970.

He got his break in 1973 when he got a sponsored Formula 3 gig with GRD. He took his first win at Silverstone that year and went on to finish second in the British F3 championship.

He made his F1 debut in 1975 for Hesketh at the Spanish Grand Prix, a race remembered in infamy for a crash that caused the death of five spectators.

The team went out of business before the season finished, but Jones moved to Graham Hill's team, where a fifth-place finish at the Nürburgring was the highlight.

An ill-fated season with Surtees in 1976 left his F1 career in limbo, before the tragic death of driver Tom Pryce at the 1977 South African Grand Prix led to Jones being signed by the Shadow team.

Jones claimed his maiden win in Austria, which led to Ferrari offering and then reneging on a deal for the Australian.

Ferrari instead signed Gilles Villeneuve, while Jones ultimately signed for Williams.

Alan Jones drove his Williams to victory in the 1980 British Grand Prix. (Getty Images: LAT Images)

Jones won five grands prix in 1980 — Argentina, France, Britain, Canada and the USA — to claim the world title and become just the second Australian to achieve that honour.

He first retired from F1 at the end of the 1981 season, after winning the season finale at Caesars Palace.

He made a few brief returns before his final grand prix in 1986.

Jones continued racing internationally for many years, while also entering media. He was a commentator with Channel Nine as part of the F1 coverage in Australia from 1987 to 2002, and was also on Network 10 when it had the F1 races in the early 2010s.

He is survived by his wife and his six children, Christian, Amber, Zara, Jack, Camilla and Emma.

World.title: Brazil soccer match sets world record for most red cards after mass brawl
World.content:
An under-20s soccer match in Brazil is making headlines for all the wrong reasons, with more than 50 red cards handed out after a mass brawl.

The match happened on Sunday between Uberlândia and Mamoré in the first leg of their Minas Gerais Under-20 Championship semifinal.

As reported by the BBC, a brawl broke out when one of the Mamoré players taunted the opposition bench after his side took a 3-1 lead.

The mass brawl resulted in 40 players and eight staff members being dismissed.

Three players had earlier been shown red cards, as well as two Uberlândia board members afterwards, according to ESPN, taking the total to 53.

The damage to the Estádio Parque do Sabiá led to the military police being called, according to Brazilian news outlet O Tempo.

Uberlândia released a statement announcing it was withdrawing from the competition in a "gesture of fair play", allowing Mamoré to advance to the final.

The previous record for most red cards in a match was 36. That happened in an Argentinian fifth-division game between Atlético Claypole and Victoriano Arenas in 2011.

World.title: Rugby league great Paul Langmack dies aged 61
World.content:
Canterbury-Bankstown triple premiership winner Paul Langmack has died aged 61 after suffering a heart attack.

The club confirmed the death of the former Bulldogs, Western Suburbs and Sydney player, who represented New South Wales in four State of Origin matches.

After his playing career, at the end of the 1999 season, Langmack became an assistant coach at Wests Tigers, then head coach of South Sydney in 2003 and 2004.

"I am devastated to learn of Paul's sudden passing this morning," rugby league great Phil Gould said.

"He was a larger-than-life character. Paul was energetic, bubbly and enthusiastic.

"He loved his rugby league. He was so loyal to his many teammates and ex-coaches over the years. He loved them all.

"Paul also started many mental health support programs to help young kids, plus both current and former players.

"He was always thinking of other people. This is a significant loss to so many."

Phil Gould (left) and Paul Langmack (right) celebrate Canterbury-Bankstown's 1988 NSWRL grand final win over Balmain. (NRL.com)

Langmack's 174-game stint at the Bulldogs during the 80s was headlined by premiership wins in 1984, 1985 and 1988.

In total, he played 314 first grade matches in Australia, as well as 19 for Halifax in England.

Langmack was part of Australia's 1986 tour of Great Britain and France, playing 10 tour matches, but no Tests.

Benny Elias played alongside Langmack for NSW and on the 1986 Kangaroos's tour, as well as against him in the 1988 grand final.

Speaking to ABC Sport, Elias said the rugby league community will be saddened by the loss of a man who gave so much on and off the field.

"His name in rugby league will be forever remembered and always respected and regarded" Elias said.

"He was a champion of a player, champion of a man, and to see someone die so young is very sad."

Langmack had previously had cancer, and was an active member of the community.

He was passionate about mental health, working on programs with the NSW Rugby League.

"The greatest thing is philanthropy, and when you give your time back to people, and you help other people in society, in the community, it's certainly a real big tick," Elias said.

"That's what Paul did."

Tech.title: Claude AI can plug directly into your bank account
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Anthropic has a new pitch for managing your personal finances: let Claude do it instead, with a new Personal Finance feature that connects it to your bank and card accounts via the Plaid bank bridging platform. You can ask the chatbot “where did my money go this month,” for example, and it’ll create an overview with a breakdown of spending by category, including rent and utilities, shopping, and food. Claude can also answer broader questions around what bills are left before your next payday, if you can afford big purchases like holiday trips, and how much money you could be saving each month.

Its access is read-only, and with Plaid facilitating the connection, Claude doesn’t see your banking passwords and your bank doesn’t have to deal with unvetted AI bots crawling around your accounts.

Claude can’t move, manage, or invest your money, according to Anthropic, and it “isn’t designed to give investment advice.”, but it can see the bank’s name, account names, account type, the last four digits of the number associated with it, your balances and credit limits, and up to two years’ worth of your transaction history.

If you choose to give it access to all that, Claude can explain financial terms you don’t understand and answer questions about your balances and transactions.

Personal Finance in Claude is rolling out in beta this week to Claude Pro, Max, and Ultra plan subscribers in the US. Anthropic’s announcement follows OpenAI introducing a similar feature for ChatGPT in May, which also plugs into your bank accounts through Plaid. Allowing AI to have oversight into your finances might ring some alarm bells, but according to the sign-off in Anthropic’s press release, it’s just the beginning:

“Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust. We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it.”

Tech.title: ‘Total repudiation’: The blue wave is about to hit AI
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

On Tuesday night, Democrats made history as they took control of the House and the Senate, and a blue wave swept through traditionally red and swing states — with the nation’s first Black woman governor elected in Georgia, the country’s first Native American woman governor elected in New Mexico, and a Maine Senator ceding to a Democrat after 30 years in office. In these and other campaigns, one theme kept coming up: holding AI companies accountable to the American people. Now, the AI industry is left considering the prospect of regulation, data center construction slowdowns, and more.

Publicly, most major AI company CEOs have remained silent. OpenAI and Anthropic did not provide comments to The Verge; Elon Musk’s call on X to vote “red” for the midterms — the SpaceX CEO had spent close to $450 million backing Republican campaigns for the election — vanished after results poured in.

Tuesday’s results were a “total repudiation” of the AI field, says Wes McEnany, the former Deputy Labor Policy Director of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, & Pensions, who now works with the nonprofit Future of Life Institute. He said that AI touches “every aspect of people’s lives,” whether they’re applying for jobs, using social media, or even paying electricity bills while living near a data center, and that they’re tired of not having “any agency in that conversation.”

The bipartisan backlash against data center construction is the most tangible manifestation of that backlash. It’s going to be unquestionably more difficult to build them across the country, after 43 out of 44 local data center moratoria on Tuesday’s ballots passed, sending a clear message to AI companies. In Texas, the fastest-growing data center buildout area and a key battleground state, governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she plans to “issue a moratorium — a ban — on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans.” Similar promises have been made in a handful of other key states.

“Data centers were clearly on the ballot,” said Guru Sethupathy, GM of AI governance at Optro.

In recent months, there’s been an increasing number of protests and collective bipartisan action to battle data centers being built in a wide range of states. Residents are concerned about noise pollution, electricity bill rate hikes, and more. When NBC News polled voters on Tuesday, 76 percent opposed data centers in their communities.

“The data center backlash is one of the most bipartisan political issues I’ve ever seen,” Shaunna Thomas, co-founder and director of the Guardrails Alliance, a Super PAC pushing for AI regulation.

“Data centers are an entry point to looking at this broader corporate accountability lens of, ‘My bill is going up, why?’” said Kyle Jacobs-Morse, deputy executive director at The Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit tech industry watchdog. “People found that it was big tech companies that were the culprit.” He added that particularly in the gubernatorial races in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio, Democratic campaigns prioritized potential local issues stemming from data centers, including “spillover costs” for local residents, communities, and state governments.

“I do think we’ll hear more questions about who benefits from and who pays for AI, especially as it pertains to infrastructure, but what I’m more curious about is what changes we can expect around regulation,” said François Ajenstat, CEO and founder of Golden Analytics.

Experts say the midterm results have likely ended Trump and congressional Republicans’ repeated attempts to bar state-level AI restrictions. Thomas considers the idea “completely dead,” while McEnany said “any member who votes to wipe out state AI laws is going to be looking for a job in the next [election].” Jacobs-Morse expects to generally see more “tech accountability bills.”

OpenAI recently began calling its data centers “compute campuses,” and President Trump in September attempted to change the name of AI as a technology to “super intelligence.” But midterm results suggest that a significant portion of American voters aren’t buying the rebranding efforts.

“I don’t think it was working, and I think the prospect of it working is extremely low after the election,” Thomas said.

“The Trump idiosyncrasies around some of this stuff… they did not play well at the ballot box,” Jacobs-Morse said.

But some in and around the tech industry are taking the news more positively than others. One X user wrote that “we’re *maybe* back to being a rational, steady hand as a country and can really lead,” while others wrote that the recent results could be good for preventing an AI bubble burst. Katie Barr, CEO of Glen Echo Group and a partner at Orchestra, said she wouldn’t “over-read” the results as an overwhelming tech rejection but rather a reckoning on “affordability, jobs, safety, and whether people have a say in what’s happening in their communities and their lives.”

Analysts at Yorkville Ives & Co. wrote in a note that though tech investors should prepare for “major hurdles for AI and tech legislation” and a slowdown of the planned construction of up to 1,000 data centers across the country, there could be a “slight positive” in that it could help avoid a bubble and slow capital fundraising flooding the market.

There will also likely be a reckoning on AI safety. Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) was reelected after campaigning for AI safety policy, and in a victory speech Tuesday by Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Ossoff said, “The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.” Some AI safety legislation is already being considered, like the bill to “ban superintelligence” introduced in September by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas).

President Trump has dismissed the idea of a safety crisis in AI as a “hoax,” writing on social media that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.” After the midterms, however, Republican lawmakers will need to decide whether to fall in line or negotiate with Democrats on safety-focused policy measures. Either way, Adam Kovacevich, founder and CEO of Chamber of Progress, a pro-tech industry advocacy group, said he expects AI safety legislation to continue to happen in blue states.

“There’s a lot of open questions about where democrats go next on tech policy. Do we revert to the Biden era war on tech, the Obama era tech honeymoon, or something in between?” Kovacevich said.

Tech.title: Ember’s smallest self-heating mug is on sale for just $33
Tech.content:
We’ve been fans of Ember’s temperature-controlled mugs for years, though given the price tag, we admit that they’re somewhat of a luxury purchase. Thankfully, if you’ve been looking for a more affordable option, Woot is selling the Ember Cup in black for $32.99 ($67 off) with a 90-day warranty through November 7th. You can potentially save even more as part of Woot’s larger Home and Kitchen Sale, which lets you save an additional $20 off orders of $100 or more when you use code COOK at checkout.

Granted, six ounces isn’t much, but the smaller, handle-free cup is well-suited for cappuccinos, cortados, flat whites, and other espresso-based drinks. It’s also a perfectly fine option if you don’t mind refilling your cup of coffee, cocoa, or tea throughout the day. I’m actually tempted to pick one up myself at this price, especially since I’ve been trying (with varying degrees of success) to cut back on coffee.

Like Ember’s larger mugs, the smart cup lets you choose and set your drinking temperature between 120 and 145 degrees Fahrenheit using a companion app, then remembers your setting for future drinks. It can then maintain that temperature for up to 95 minutes on a charge, up to four hours with a lid, or even all day if you leave it on the included charging dock. The cup also automatically enters sleep mode after two hours of inactivity to conserve power. Just keep in mind that, despite its IPX7 water-resistance rating, the cup is hand-wash only.

Tech.title: The FAA is finally ditching floppy disks
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

It’s the year 2026 and the Federal Aviation Administration is still running critical pieces of American airspace on 3.5-inch magnetic floppy disks.

But those technology artifacts could be headed for the dustbin after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced an effort to ditch floppy disks in favor of a new digital system.

Duffy announced Thursday that the FAA is rolling out the Enterprise – Information Display System (E-IDS) to replace four legacy setups across more than 400 air traffic control facilities. E-IDS aggregates real-time weather alerts, equipment outages, restricted airspace changes, and pilot reports onto a modern digital dashboard, replacing manual workflows and archaic physical storage media.

Upgrades have already kicked off at five sites — including control hubs in Atlantic City, Nashville, Rochester, Atlanta, and Salt Lake City — with a targeted rollout across 435 facilities by the end of 2028.

“Good news America: floppy disks are out, 21st century tech is in,” Duffy said in a release.

Duffy, a former reality TV star and Fox Business host, has been using floppy disks as a scapegoat for the air travel disruptions that have plagued the country for years now. He waves them around during speeches or TV interviews, while highlighting that the FAA still uses “copper wires and floppy disks” as a symbol of government obsolescence.

Indeed, our air traffic control system is deeply out of date, especially when held up alongside the more modern approaches of other nations. A Government Accountability Office report from September 2024 found that 90 percent of the nation’s critical air traffic control infrastructure was due or past due for a “technology refresh.” Nearly half of the 138 systems surveyed were “considered unsustainable” or “potentially unsustainable” due to shortfalls in funding, insufficient maintenance expertise, or even a lack of spare parts.

But E-IDS is not an overnight breakthrough cooked up in a single executive sprint; it’s an existing FAA contract that has spent years working through procurement, safety validation, testing, and vendor timelines. The initial contract for E-IDS was awarded to Leidos, a defense contractor headquartered in Reston, Virginia, by the FAA back in August 2020, during the first Trump administration.

The scope of the problem was understood, even back then. But since then, it has gotten much worse. The FAA has faced backlash in recent years over ground stops, close calls on runways (including one involving President Donald Trump), chronic burnout among air traffic controllers, and high-profile software meltdowns, like the 2023 NOTAM outage. Duffy is clearly trying the frame the system’s problems around relics like the floppy disk, as if obsolete tech is the only reason for the disruptions.

But as we’ve noted before, it’s a much bigger problem than just the systems themselves. Replacing an information system with digital panels is relatively low-hanging fruit compared to the systemic crises plaguing American aviation, such as a crippling deficit of thousands of certified professional controllers. Duffy has been lobbying Congress for an additional $30 billion, on top of the $12.5 billion “down payment” he got in 2025, for his ATC modernization plan.

Under Duffy, the USDOT has made a big deal about recruiting gamers, specifically, to take on these roles. And the administration is also relying on its tech oligarch allies, including Elon Musk and Peter Thiel, to help them clean up the mess — even if they happen to make it worse in the process.

Tech.title: Grimes is going to star in an AI movie that’s coming to theaters
Tech.content:
The AI-generated sci-fi film Gods Don’t Give Gifts has added a bit of star power: Pop star Grimes is going to appear in the movie. Billed as “the first AI film to come to theatres,” Gods Don’t Give Gifts is a notable test case for the commercial potential of AI films, and it releases on December 4th. Grimes — who will be lending both her likeness and vocal performance to the movie, which you can see in the clip above — potentially gives the project some legitimacy.

AI studio Fable, which is producing the film, claimed in a press release that “casting the likeness of an actor with their spoken vocal performance will become more common with animated films using AI: audiences will see actors, athletes, musicians giving vocal performances with their likeness in films.” Gods Don’t Give Gifts is being directed by Jack London, better known under the online handle Gossip Goblin.

Gods Don’t Give Gifts is an anthology that’s set in a future “where bodies are disposable and consciousness has been commoditized” and depicts what happens when “four interconnected stories collide with the horrifying consequences of humanity’s attempt to transcend the flesh.” Those themes seem to fit pretty snugly with Grimes’ interests, as she has explored themes of transhumanism and artificial intelligence in the past. It’s also not the only AI project she’s working on, with an AI-themed album called Psy Opera in the works.
